Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Put $p=\min(m,n)$ and $M=\max(m,n)$. If $m\ge n$, set $C=A$; if $m<n$, set $C=A^*$. Thus $C\in\mathbb F^{M\times p}$.

Save the input as $C_0=C$ and initialize $U=I_M$, $V=I_p$, and empty ordered lists of stored local left and right transformations. For $k=1,\ldots,p$, in this order:

1. Let $x=C_{k:M,k}$. If $x=0$, use the identity left transformation. Otherwise choose $\phi=x_1/|x_1|$ when $x_1\ne0$ and $\phi=1$ when $x_1=0$, set $\alpha=-\phi\|x\|_2$, $v=x-\alpha e_1$, and $h=v/\|v\|_2$. Use the Householder reflector $H=I-2hh^*$ on rows $k:M$. Update $C\leftarrow H^*C$ on those rows and append this local transformation to the left list. In exact arithmetic update $U\leftarrow U\operatorname{diag}(I_{k-1},H)$. In finite precision update columns $k:M$ of the dense accumulator $U$ by right application of the same stored local reflector data, using the separate-block branch of [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] and making no target-zero write to $U$.
2. If $k<p$, let $y=C_{k,k+1:p}^*$. If $y=0$, use the identity right transformation. Otherwise apply the same phase and normalization rule to $y$ to form the Householder reflector $G$, then apply $C\leftarrow C\operatorname{diag}(I_k,G)$ and append this local transformation to the right list. In exact arithmetic update $V\leftarrow V\operatorname{diag}(I_k,G)$. In finite precision update columns $k+1:p$ of the dense accumulator $V$ by right application of the same stored local reflector data, using the separate-block branch of [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] and making no target-zero write to $V$.

Set $B$ to the leading $p\times p$ block of the final work matrix $C$, and return $B,U,V$ together with the ordered local transformation lists.

In finite precision, each left/right reflector uses [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], including its real/complex scaled formation, range checks and exact target-column/row zero writes. This is the arithmetic realization of the exact steps above. A zero active vector takes the identity branch. Any helper `range-failure`, invalid operation, nonfinite value, or nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range returns `range-failure` with the partial factors and stored local transformations; otherwise return `success`, $B,U,V$, the ordered stored local transformations, the reconstruction residual $\|C_0-U\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}V^*\|_F$, and the two orthogonality residuals $\|U^*U-I\|_F$ and $\|V^*V-I\|_F$. The reconstruction uses the saved input $C_0$, not the overwritten work matrix. The exact products of the stored unitary representatives are the theoretical factors; the dense finite-precision accumulators are rounded and their residuals are computed quantities, not certified bounds by themselves. Matrix residuals use the Frobenius norm defined in [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]].

Input the original $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, the successful output record of [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] for $C=A$ if $m\ge n$ and $C=A^*$ otherwise, a deflation tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a finite nonnegative integer sweep budget $N$. The reduction record supplies the upper bidiagonal work matrix $B_0$, dense accumulators $U_B,V_B$, and ordered stored local transformation data. Initialize $B=B_0$, the sweep accumulators $U_\Sigma,V_\Sigma$ to identities of order $p=\min(m,n)$, empty ordered left/right transformation lists, an empty deflation record, a pass counter $t=0$, and a sweep counter $s=0$. Write the diagonal as $d_i$ and superdiagonal as $e_i$, and set $e_0=0$.

At the start of each pass, set $t\leftarrow t+1$, set $e_i$ to zero and append $(t,i,e_i^{old})$ to the deflation record whenever $|e_i|\le\tau(|d_i|+|d_{i+1}|)$. The corresponding additive matrix change has entry $-e_i^{old}$ at $(i,i+1)$ and zero elsewhere. Record any later non-target sparsity cleanup the same way with its row, column, and old value. The zero entries split the active blocks. If every active block has size one, stop with `converged`. Otherwise process the active blocks in increasing order of $\ell$, skipping singleton blocks. Before each block sweep, if $s=N$, stop with `budget-exhausted`; otherwise form only the tridiagonal entries of $T=B^*B$ on that block: $T_{ii}=|d_i|^2+|e_{i-1}|^2$ and $T_{i,i+1}=\overline{d_i}e_i$. Choose $\mu$ to be the eigenvalue of the trailing Hermitian block $\begin{bmatrix}T_{r-1,r-1}&T_{r-1,r}\\T_{r,r-1}&T_{rr}\end{bmatrix}$ closest to $T_{rr}$, resolving a tie by the smaller eigenvalue. If the leading pivot $d_\ell$ is zero or has magnitude at most $\tau\max(|e_{\ell-1}|,|e_\ell|)$, use the zero-shift branch $\mu=0$ and choose the initial right Givens factor $G_\ell$ so that $(d_\ell,e_\ell)G_\ell=(\rho,0)$, avoiding division by the small or zero diagonal.

In the ordinary branch choose the first right Givens factor $G_\ell$ so that $G_\ell^*(T_{\ell\ell}-\mu,T_{\ell+1,\ell})^T=(\rho,0)^T$, where $T_{\ell+1,\ell}=\overline{e_\ell}d_\ell$. In either branch, apply $B\leftarrow BG_\ell$, update columns $\ell,\ell+1$ of $V_\Sigma$ by right multiplication by this same stored rotation, and append its exact unitary representative to the right list. For $j=\ell,\ldots,r-1$, choose a left Givens factor $H_j$ so that $H_j^*(B_{j,j},B_{j+1,j})^T=(\rho,0)^T$; apply it to rows $j,j+1$, update columns $j,j+1$ of $U_\Sigma$ by right multiplication by this same stored rotation, and append its exact unitary representative to the left list. If $j<r-1$, choose a right Givens factor $G_{j+1}$ so that $(B_{j,j+1},B_{j,j+2})G_{j+1}=(\rho,0)$; apply it to columns $j+1,j+2$, update the corresponding columns of $V_\Sigma$ by right multiplication by this same stored rotation, and append its exact unitary representative to the right list. Continue until the bulge reaches the active block endpoint. A zero annihilation vector uses the identity rotation. In finite precision each Givens formation/update uses [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], conjugate-transposed as needed for the stated left/right orientation; accumulator multiplications use the same stored local data but omit all target-zero writes. The dense accumulator multiplications follow the operationwise arithmetic model, while the ordered lists retain the exact unitary representatives used in analysis. Target zero writes to $B$ are included in their local error bounds. The initial shift-vector rotation does not zero an unrelated entry of $B$. Each Givens factor is chosen using [[def-real-and-complex-givens-transformations]] and its annihilation guarantee in [[thm-householder-reflectors-and-givens-transformations-are-unitary-and-annihilate-targeted-entries]].

After each processed block, increment $s$ by one. Once all current active blocks have been processed, start a new pass. If any operation, norm or pivot is invalid or nonfinite, or a nonzero exact intermediate is outside the normal range, return `range-failure` with the partial $B$, accumulators, transformation lists, deflation record, and available residual reports. On `budget-exhausted`, return the current $B$, accumulators, transformation lists, deflation record, triplet residuals, and orthogonality residuals. On `converged`, set $B_{\mathrm{final}}=B$ and return it with both dense accumulators, both transformation lists, the deflation record, triplet/orthogonality residuals, and its tall embedding $\overline B_{\mathrm{final}}=\begin{bmatrix}B_{\mathrm{final}}\\0_{M-p,p}\end{bmatrix}$.

For every exit other than `range-failure`, let $B_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the current work matrix, and let $d_i=(B_{\mathrm{out}})_{ii}$. Obtain each candidate value as $\widehat\sigma_i=|d_i|$ by the scaled two-component modulus evaluation (real absolute value is exact). On `converged`, the active-block condition makes $B_{\mathrm{out}}=B_{\mathrm{final}}$ diagonal; after `budget-exhausted`, the diagonal values are estimates only and carry no accuracy claim.

Let $W_B=\operatorname{diag}(U_\Sigma,I_{M-p})$. In exact arithmetic the tall-orientation accumulated factors are $U_C=U_BW_B$ and $V_C=V_BV_\Sigma$. In finite precision form each dense product by row-by-column multiplication, with six-real-operation complex products and sequential componentwise rounded additions under the operationwise model; return `range-failure` if any required intermediate is invalid, nonfinite, or outside the normal range. Their exact theoretical factors are the products represented by the ordered local transformation lists together with the bidiagonal-reduction lists. If $m\ge n$, set $\widehat U=U_C$ and $\widehat V=V_C$; for each nonzero $d_i$, multiply column $i$ of $\widehat U$ by $d_i/|d_i|$ in exact arithmetic, using componentwise division by the successful scaled modulus readout in finite precision. If $m<n$, set $\widehat U=V_C$ and $\widehat V=U_C$; in this wide orientation multiply column $i$ of $\widehat V$ by $d_i/|d_i|$ instead. Sort the candidate values in nonincreasing order, breaking ties by their original diagonal index, and permute the corresponding columns of the returned triplet vectors in the same way; leave $B_{\mathrm{out}}$ and the transformation lists in their algorithmic order. For every candidate triplet $(\widehat\sigma_i,\widehat u_i,\widehat v_i)$, report $\|A\widehat v_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat u_i\|_2$ and $\|A^*\widehat u_i-\widehat\sigma_i\widehat v_i\|_2$. Also report $\|\widehat U^*\widehat U-I\|_F$ and $\|\widehat V^*\widehat V-I\|_F$. The reports expose finite-budget and rounding behavior; they do not certify convergence by themselves. Matrix residuals use the Frobenius norm defined in [[def-frobenius-matrix-norm]]. Any additional sparsity cleanup is recorded separately in the deflation record with its discarded-entry perturbation.

For $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, the exact-arithmetic algorithm [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]] returns unitary $U,V$ and an upper bidiagonal $B\in\mathbb F^{p\times p}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, such that if $m\ge n$ then $U^*AV=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$, and if $m<n$ then $U^*A^*V=\begin{bmatrix}B\\0\end{bmatrix}$.

Consider one exact-arithmetic sweep of [[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]] on an unreduced upper bidiagonal block, with no nonzero deflation. If its right rotations have product $V_s$ and its left rotations have product $U_s$, the restored bidiagonal block is $B_+=U_s^*BV_s$. Consequently $B_+$ and $B$ have the same singular values. If a set $D$ of superdiagonal entries is deflated, then the transformed output instead equals the corresponding unitary transform of $B+E_D$, where $E_D$ has those entries negated and all other entries zero.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. The **Frobenius norm** of $A$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_F\;:=\;\Bigl(\,\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|^{2}\Bigr)^{1/2},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value on $\mathbb R$
([[def-abs-value]]) for $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ and the modulus on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]) for
$\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, and the outer power is the nonnegative real square root.

**The displayed quantity is a norm.** Regard $A$ as the element of the
coordinate space $\mathbb F^{mn}$ whose $j+in$-th entry is $a_{ij}$. The
standard coordinate inner product of [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]]
satisfies $\langle A,A\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}\overline{a_{ij}}$, which equals
$\sum_{i,j}|a_{ij}|^{2}$ because $z\overline z=|z|^{2}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]). Thus $\lVert A\rVert_F$ is
exactly the inner-product norm of [[def-inner-product-norm]] evaluated at $A$,
and the three norm axioms hold for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_F$ because they hold for
every inner-product norm. For real matrices the same sum is
$\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}^{2}$, since $|x|^{2}=x^{2}$ for real $x$ by the two cases of
[[def-abs-value]].

The Frobenius norm is the Euclidean norm of the full entry list, not the
largest factor by which the matrix stretches a single vector. It can coincide
with an induced $2$-norm in one-row or one-column cases, but in general it is a
different matrix norm from the induced operator norms used on this page. Its
relation to the spectral norm, its unitary invariance and its singular-value
formula are
[[thm-spectral-and-frobenius-norms-are-unitarily-invariant-with-singular-value-formulas-and-rank-comparison]].

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Use [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]] successfully, with $0<u<1$ and $(r-1)u<1$ for every Householder dimension $r$. For a nonzero Householder column define
$$e=(1+u)^{r+3}-1,\quad a_\phi=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^4}-1,\quad a_\alpha=(1+a_\phi)(1+e)(1+u)-1,\quad d_v=a_\alpha+u(2+a_\alpha),$$
$$a_\tau=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^{2r}}-1,\quad g=\frac{1+6u}{1-(r-1)u}-1,\quad c_U=2\bigl((1+a_\tau)(1+u)(1+6u)(1+g)-1\bigr),$$
$$\eta_H(r)=\max\{a_\alpha+8d_v,(1+u)c_U+3u\}.$$
For a Givens step define
$$a_2=\frac{1+u}{(1-u)^2}-1,\quad q=\max\left\{\left(\frac{1+u}{1-u}\right)^3-1,\frac{(1+a_2)(1+6u)(1+u)}{(1-u)^3}-1\right\},$$
$$\epsilon=\sqrt2(7u+6u^2)(1+q),\quad v=q+\epsilon,\quad \eta_G=2v+u+2q.$$
Each complete left update, including its target zero write, has an exact unitary representative $W$ and perturbation $E$ with
$$W(C+E)=C_+,\qquad \|E\|_F\le\eta\|C\|_F,$$
where $\eta=\eta_H(r)$ or $\eta_G$. Identity branches have $E=0$. The corresponding right relation follows by conjugate transposition. For a Givens application without an annihilation overwrite use the smaller coefficient $v$; for a Householder separate-block application use $(1+u)c_U+3u$. Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let $b\in\mathbb F^m$. Then $A^+b$ is
a least-squares solution of $Ax=b$, and among all least-squares solutions it
is the unique one of minimum Euclidean norm.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, let

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

be a singular value decomposition with $s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0$, and fix an
integer $k$ with $0\le k<\dim V$. Define

$$T_kv:=\sum_{j=1}^{\min(k,r)} s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j.$$

Then $\operatorname{rank}T_k\le k$, one has

$$\lVert T-T_k\rVert=s_{k+1}$$

with the convention $s_{k+1}=0$ when $k\ge r$, and every linear map
$A:V\to W$ with $\operatorname{rank}A\le k$ satisfies

$$\lVert T-A\rVert\ge s_{k+1}.$$

Let $m,n\ge1$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, and $\tau\ge0$. For the spectral norm, the numerical rank defined by [[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]] satisfies
$$\operatorname{rank}_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$. A matrix $B\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is a
**Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse** of $A$ when

$$ABA=A,\qquad BAB=B,$$

and the two square products are self-adjoint:

$$ (AB)^*=AB,\qquad (BA)^*=BA. $$

When such a matrix exists and is unique, it is denoted by $A^+$.

The four displayed relations are the **Penrose equations**. They are written in
the matrix product and adjoint conventions of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] and
[[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]].

For every matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or
$\mathbb C$, there exists a unique matrix $A^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$
satisfying the four Penrose equations of
[[def-moore-penrose-pseudoinverse]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let
$\lVert\cdot\rVert$ be a declared norm on the matrix space
$M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and let
$\tau\ge 0$ be a declared tolerance. The **numerical rank of $A$ at
tolerance $\tau$** is

$$\operatorname{rank}_{\tau}(A)\;:=\;\min\Bigl\{\,\operatorname{rank}B\;:\;B\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F),\ \lVert A-B\rVert\le\tau\,\Bigr\}.$$

The minimum exists: it is a minimum of a nonempty subset of the finite set
$\{0,1,\dots,\min(m,n)\}$, the value $\operatorname{rank}A$ being attained at
$B=A$.

**Scale.** The tolerance may be declared absolutely, as a real number
$\tau\ge 0$, or relative to a scale, as $\tau=\tau_0\lVert A\rVert$ for a
declared factor $\tau_0\ge 0$. Both enter the definition through the single
threshold $\tau$; the scale only fixes which threshold is meant, and every
statement about $\operatorname{rank}_{\tau}$ is a statement about that one
threshold.

**Why the exact-rank discontinuity forces the parameter.** Exact rank is
locally constant at the full-rank matrices but discontinuous at every
nonmaximal-rank matrix
([[thm-exact-rank-is-locally-constant-at-full-rank-and-discontinuous-at-nonmaximal-rank-matrices]]);
an exact rank read from noisy data is therefore unstable. Numerical rank
replaces exact rank by the smallest exact rank attainable within the declared
norm tolerance $\tau$: it is, by construction, constant on every open ball of
radius below the relevant gaps, and it counts as rank exactly those directions
that perturbation of size at most $\tau$ cannot erase.

Orthonormality gives $A_\tau A_\tau^+=\sum_{i\in I}u_i u_i^*$ and $A_\tau^+A_\tau=\sum_{i\in I}v_i v_i^*$, which are self-adjoint. Using $u_i^*u_j=v_i^*v_j=\delta_{ij}$ in those sums verifies the two Penrose product equations. Together with self-adjointness, these are the four equations; by [F6], $A_\tau^+$ is the unique Moore--Penrose pseudoinverse of $A_\tau$. Let $C_0\in\mathbb F^{M\times p}$, $M\ge p$, be the tall orientation used by [[alg-householder-bidiagonalization]], and let $B_J\in\mathbb F^{p\times p}$ be the final bidiagonal-QR work matrix returned by [[alg-implicit-shifted-bidiagonal-qr-with-deflation]]. Set $C_J=\begin{bmatrix}B_J\\0_{M-p,p}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb F^{M\times p}$. Suppose the computed bidiagonal reduction and QR sweeps perform $J$ stages, each either an elementary left/right unitary update or an identity update for a deflation/cleanup write. At stage $j$, assume the actual active matrix obeys
$$C_j=L_j^*(C_{j-1}+E_j)R_j+D_j,$$
where $L_j,R_j$ are unitary and $\eta_j\ge0$, $\|E_j\|_F\le\eta_j\|C_{j-1}\|_F$, and $D_j$ is the additive representation of entries discarded by deflation or cleanup at that stage, with $\delta_j=\|D_j\|_F$. A deflation/cleanup write is represented by $L_j=R_j=I$, $E_j=0$, and the recorded additive change $D_j$. The deflation record returned by the algorithm identifies each such entry and its old value, so it determines $D_j$. Then the returned tall transformed matrix $C_J$ satisfies
$$C_0+E=L C_J R^*$$
for unitary accumulated factors $L,R$ and some $E$ with
$$\|E\|_F\le\left(\prod_{j=1}^J(1+\eta_j)-1\right)\|C_0\|_F+\sum_{j=1}^J\delta_j\prod_{\ell=j+1}^J(1+\eta_\ell).$$
If no deflation or other cleanup is performed, every $\delta_j=0$. For the successful scaled arithmetic realization [[alg-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-updates]], [[lem-scaled-complex-householder-and-givens-local-backward-error]] establishes these hypotheses: choose $\eta_j=\eta_H(r_j)$ for Householder updates, $\eta_j=\eta_G$ for Givens updates with an actual target zero write, and its smaller separate-block coefficient when no matrix entry is overwritten. Let $A,E\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and put $p=\min(m,n)$. Then for every $1\le i\le p$,
$$|\sigma_i(A+E)-\sigma_i(A)|\le\|E\|_2.$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,

Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. Let $m,n\ge1$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $p=\min(m,n)$, and $\tau\ge0$. For the spectral norm, the numerical rank defined by [[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]] satisfies
$$\operatorname{rank}_\tau(A)=\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,p\}:\sigma_i(A)>\tau\}.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

derivations.claim: The determinant of $A_\epsilon$ is $\epsilon\ne0$, so its exact rank is two. Its first column has norm one, hence [F4] gives $\sigma_1=\|A_\epsilon\|_2\ge1$; by [F3], $\sigma_1\le\|A_\epsilon\|_F=\sqrt{2+\epsilon^2}<2$. Therefore $\epsilon/2<\sigma_2\le\epsilon$.

Applying [F1] to the two counts in step 2.1 gives numerical ranks one and two, respectively, although the exact rank remains two.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

Input a real or complex matrix $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ with $m\ge n$, a target $k$ with $0\le k<n$, a factor $f\ge1$, and a finite swap cap $S\in\mathbb N\cup\{0\}$. The exact-arithmetic version is specified below. A finite-precision implementation uses the same branches, tests finiteness after each operation, and returns `range-failure` if a required quantity is nonfinite.

1. If $A$ is not full column rank, return `rank-deficient-input`. Otherwise initialize a column permutation $\Pi$ and the full column-pivoted QR factorization $A\Pi=QR$, where $Q\in\mathbb F^{m\times m}$ is unitary and $R\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ is upper trapezoidal. At each pivot choose a remaining column of maximal residual $2$-norm, resolving ties by the smallest original column index. Partition $R=\begin{bmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&R_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ after the first $k$ rows and columns. Do not return the reduced QR form. The selected first $k$ columns then have a nonsingular leading block. For $k=0$, return this full factorization with `success`.
2. For $k>0$, refactor the current fixed column order in the full QR form, without further pivoting whenever needed, using unitary Householder or Givens transformations. If the selected leading block is singular, return `singular-selected-block`.
3. Form $X=R_{11}^{-1}R_{12}$. For $1\le i\le k$ let $\omega_i=\|e_i^*R_{11}^{-1}\|_2$; for $1\le j\le n-k$ let $\gamma_j=\|R_{22}(:,j)\|_2$. Define the swap score $s_{ij}=\bigl(|X_{ij}|^2+(\omega_i\gamma_j)^2\bigr)^{1/2}$.
4. If $\max_{i,j}|X_{ij}|>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest $|X_{ij}|$. Otherwise, if $\max_{i,j}s_{ij}>f$, choose the lexicographically first pair attaining the largest score. If neither inequality holds, return `success` and the factors, permutation, $X$, and maximum score. The first branch retains the usual coefficient-triggered swap; the second controls the trailing residual needed for the strong spectral comparison.
5. When a violating pair was chosen, if the swap count is already $S$, return `swap-budget-exhausted` with the current partial factors. Otherwise interchange the chosen selected and trailing columns, restore triangular form with Givens rotations, increment the swap count, and return to step 2.

The statuses are `success`, `rank-deficient-input`, `singular-selected-block`, `swap-budget-exhausted`, and `range-failure`. In particular, ordinary column-pivoted QR is only the initialization: the procedure does not assert that its output alone satisfies the strong bounds. Both exact and finite-precision outputs use the full factor shape. A finite-precision `success` is a candidate until the following certificate is verified. Retain the ordered local transformation data representing an exact unitary product $W$ separately from the rounded dense $Q$. Let $\widehat R$ denote the returned upper trapezoidal matrix. A certificate consists of a nonsingular $\widehat R_{11}$, rigorous upper bounds $b_{ij}$ on the exact real numbers $\bigl(|(\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\widehat R_{12})_{ij}|^2+\|e_i^*\widehat R_{11}^{-1}\|_2^2\|\widehat R_{22}(:,j)\|_2^2\bigr)^{1/2}$, and $\varepsilon\ge0$ with $\|A\Pi-W\widehat R\|_2\le\varepsilon$. All $b_{ij}\le f$ are required. For $k=0$ there are no score or inverse conditions. The bounds must account for arithmetic and input representation; ordinary rounded score and residual evaluations do not constitute this certificate. Exact arithmetic on represented data or validated outward enclosures may establish it. If certification is unavailable or a bound exceeds its threshold, report `uncertified` for the certificate, retaining the algorithm status and all candidate outputs.

Let $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$
have rank $r$, and let

$$A\Pi=QR$$
be an exact column-pivoted QR factorisation in which, at each step, the next
column is chosen with maximal residual $2$-norm among the remaining columns.
Then
$$R=\begin{pmatrix}R_{11}&R_{12}\\0&0\end{pmatrix},$$

where $R_{11}\in M_r(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal and
hence is invertible.

derivations.claim: Column $j$ of $A$ has entries $-cs^{i-1}$ for $i<j$, $s^{j-1}$ for $i=j$, and zero below. Its squared norm is $c^2\sum_{r=0}^{j-2}s^{2r}+s^{2(j-1)}=1$, using $c^2=1-s^2$. After the first $r$ columns have been selected, they span the first $r$ coordinate vectors because their leading triangular block has nonzero diagonal. The residual of each remaining column $j>r$ has squared norm $s^{2r}\left(c^2\sum_{t=0}^{j-r-2}s^{2t}+s^{2(j-r-1)}\right)=s^{2r}$ (the sum is empty when $j=r+1$). Thus all remaining residuals tie at every step, and the declared tie rule makes CPQR select columns in their original order.

By [F1] and step 1.1, the resulting permutation is the identity. The matrix $A$ is upper triangular with positive diagonal, so the QR factors can be taken as $Q=I$ and $R=A$. For $k=3$, solving $R_{11}x=R_{12}$ gives $x_3=-c$, $x_2=-c(1+c)$, and $x_1=-c(1+c)^2=-9/8$. Hence $\max_i|x_i|\ge9/8>1$, violating the coefficient condition in [F2].

This CPQR output therefore fails the strong coefficient test with $f=1$. It does not contradict the strong RRQR procedure: that procedure performs additional swaps when its coefficient or combined residual score exceeds the threshold.

Let $A,E\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, and put $p=\min(m,n)$. Then for every $1\le i\le p$,
$$|\sigma_i(A+E)-\sigma_i(A)|\le\|E\|_2.$$

Let $n\ge1$, and let $B,\widetilde B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$ be upper bidiagonal, $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with $0\le\epsilon<1$. Suppose each corresponding nonzero diagonal or superdiagonal entry is multiplied by a scalar whose modulus lies in $[1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon]$, and every zero entry remains zero. Put $q=(1+\epsilon)/(1-\epsilon)$. Then $B$ and $\widetilde B$ have the same number of zero singular values, and for each positive singular value in descending order,
$$q^{-2n}\sigma_i(B)\le\sigma_i(\widetilde B)\le q^{2n}\sigma_i(B).$$

This is a relative perturbation theorem. A computed bidiagonal SVD inherits it only when a separate backward-error analysis verifies this componentwise relative assumption; an absolute normwise perturbation estimate by itself is not that verification.

derivations.claim: The singular values of $B$ are $1$ and $\epsilon$. Set $E_0=\operatorname{diag}(0,-\epsilon)$. Then $B+E_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $\|E_0\|_2=\epsilon$, and the small singular value changes by absolute error $\epsilon$ and relative error $\epsilon/\epsilon=1$. This attains the absolute bound in [F1].

Set $E_1=\eta B$. Each nonzero diagonal entry is multiplied by $1+\eta$ and the zero superdiagonal remains zero, so [F2] applies. Directly, $B+E_1=(1+\eta)B$, whose small singular value is $(1+\eta)\epsilon$ and whose relative error is exactly $\eta$.

Since $\eta$ can be fixed while $\epsilon$ tends to zero, step 1.2 gives a relative guarantee independent of the small singular value; step 1.1 shows that the absolute error scale alone permits complete loss of that value.

**Scalar execution order.** These conventions expand every arithmetic
expression below into a fixed finite scalar schedule; they do not execute the
exact theoretical representatives. Visit vector indices increasingly and matrix
columns increasingly, with row indices increasing within each column. Visit the
real component before the imaginary component. For a complex vector $z$, its
real-component list is $(\Re z_1,\Im z_1,\ldots,\Re z_r,\Im z_r)$.
Evaluate displayed assignments in their written order and nested operations
from the inside out, left operand before right operand. For inputs $a+ib$ and
$c+id$ with real components $a,b,c,d$, a complex product uses
rounded real products $ac,bd,ad,bc$, in that order, followed by the rounded real
subtraction $ac-bd$ and rounded imaginary addition $ad+bc$. Do not fuse
operations. Return immediately at the first failing primitive; indices refer
to this expanded order. Copies, sign changes and conjugations are exact.

For a scaled norm, first form every rounded component divided by the common
scale in list order. Then, in that same order, round each component square and
accumulate it: copy the first square to the accumulator, and round each
subsequent accumulator-plus-square addition. Use this same square-and-sum
schedule for the stored-vector squared norm $w$, without scaling. An empty
sum is exact zero and requests no primitive. Apply square root and rescaling
only at their prescribed subsequent stages. The two-component and
four-component norm calls use their displayed component lists in this order.

For the Householder dot row $d$, visit columns $j$ increasingly. For each
column visit $i=1,\ldots,r$, form the declared complex product
$\overline v_iB_{ij}$, copy the first product as the partial dot, then add each
later product by rounded real-component addition followed by rounded
imaginary-component addition. Finish all of $d$ before forming $p$ in
increasing row order, then all of $Z$ in the matrix order above, then all
entries of $B-Z$ in that order. Evaluate both components of the formation of
$v$ and every scalar scaling or division in real-then-imaginary order. A
separate block call uses already stored $v,\widehat\tau$ and the same
$d,p,Z,B-Z$ stages, omitting formation and target overwrite.

For a Givens application, visit columns increasingly and copy the two old
entries before changing either. Compute the upper output first, then the
lower output, each by its two products in written order followed by its
componentwise addition. Each of the prescribed two complex products uses
the six-operation schedule above, including a real coefficient viewed as a
complex number with zero imaginary component. Both outputs use the copied
old entries.
Perform an instructed target zero write only after these outputs. Right
applications execute the stated conjugate-transpose reduction with these
same conventions. No intermediate is reused across different expressions
unless explicitly stored by the procedure.

Use the operationwise real/complex arithmetic model, with six-real-operation complex products and componentwise division by positive real scalars. A scaled norm of a nonzero complex vector first chooses the largest absolute real or imaginary component $s>0$, rounds every real component divided by $s$, sums their rounded squares sequentially, rounds the positive square root, and rounds multiplication by $s$. A norm of already scaled components omits the last multiplication. Zero input has exact norm zero. Reject every nonzero exact intermediate outside the normal range, nonfinite/invalid operation, and nonpositive required norm; return the first range-failure. All sign changes and conjugations are exact.

For a Householder active block $C=[x\;B]$, $x\in\mathbb C^r$, a zero $x$ copies the block with identity action. Otherwise compute $\widehat N$ by the scaled norm. If $x_1=0$ put $\widehat\phi=1$; otherwise compute its modulus $\widehat a$ by its own two-component scaled norm and divide its real and imaginary parts by $\widehat a$. Set $\widehat\alpha=-\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\widehat N)$ using real-scalar component multiplication, and $v=\operatorname{fl}(x-\widehat\alpha e_1)$. Compute $w$ by sequential summation of all $2r$ rounded real component squares of $v$, and $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. Compute $d=\operatorname{fl}(v^*B)$, $p=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v)$, $Z=\operatorname{fl}(pd)$, and $\widehat B=\operatorname{fl}(B-Z)$. Return $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, writing exact zeros below the target diagonal, and store $v,\widehat\tau$. Its theoretical representative is $H(v)=I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. For a separate block application omit the column overwrite. For a right step apply these instructions to the conjugate-transposed block and transpose back.

For a Givens target pair $(a,b)$, use the identity when $b=0$, including $(0,0)$. Otherwise choose $\lambda$ as the largest absolute real/imaginary component of $(a,b)$, round $z=a/\lambda$ and $w=b/\lambda$ componentwise, and compute $h$ as the norm of their four already scaled components. If $z\ne0$, compute $n_z$ as the norm of its two components, $\widehat\phi=\operatorname{fl}(z/n_z)$, $c=\operatorname{fl}(n_z/h)$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\phi\overline w)/h)$. If $z=0$, set $c=0$ and $s=\operatorname{fl}(\overline w/h)$. Store $T=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix}$ and apply it to the chosen two rows using two complex products and one rounded componentwise addition for each output entry. For an actual target column, set its intended annihilated entry to exact zero after the update. The initial shift-vector rotation is formed from the shift vector but applied to the matrix without zeroing an unrelated matrix entry. Right applications use the conjugate-transposed form. Its exact unitary representative is $Q=T/\sqrt{c^2+|s|^2}$; this normalization defines a mathematical representative and is not an additional rounded operation.

These are arithmetic realizations of the canonical Householder and Givens methods. Returned dense transformation accumulators may be rounded; the exact unitary products used in backward-error statements are represented by the stored local data. Additional discarded matrix entries must be recorded separately, including their magnitudes. Their omission is never implicit in a sparsity convention.

Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $n\ge 1$, let $u\ge 0$, let
$\delta_0,\dots,\delta_{n-1}\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|\delta_i|\le u$ for every
$i<n$, and suppose $n u<1$. Then

$$\prod_{i<n}(1+\delta_i)=1+\theta_n\qquad\text{with}\qquad|\theta_n|\le\gamma_n:=\frac{n u}{1-n u}.$$

derivations.claim: A complex product's real/imaginary error is at most $2(2u+u^2)|z||w|\le6u|z||w|$: bound each of its four real products and then its two component additions. A sequential complex dot of length $r$ therefore has error at most $[6u+\gamma_{r-1}(1+6u)]\sum_i|z_i||w_i|=g\sum_i|z_i||w_i|$. These expansions include exact zeros.

A scaled norm with $2r$ real components has its positive squared sum multiplied termwise by between $(1-u)^{2r+2}$ and $(1+u)^{2r+2}$, including two scaling factors. Square root and rescaling give relative norm error at most $e$. The independently scaled modulus of $x_1$ has lower/upper factors $(1-u)^4,(1+u)^4$, so the phase division error relative to $x_1/|x_1|$ is at most $a_\phi$; when $x_1=0$ it is zero. Thus for $N=\|x\|$, $\alpha_0=-\operatorname{phase}(x_1)N$ and $v_0=x-\alpha_0e_1$, one has $|\widehat\alpha-\alpha_0|\le a_\alpha N$ and $\|v-v_0\|\le d_vN$. For exponents at least one the lower deviation is bounded by the upper by convexity, justifying these two-sided estimates.

The identity $H(v)^*H(v)=I$ follows by multiplying $I-2vv^*/(v^*v)$. The exact phase choice gives $H(v_0)x=\alpha_0e_1$ and $\|v_0\|\ge N$ by direct inner-product expansion. Normalization gives $\|a/\|a\|-b/\|b\|\|\le2\|a-b\|/\|b\|$; expanding the difference of unit-vector projectors therefore gives $\|H(v)-H(v_0)\|\le8d_v$. The target-column error is at most $(a_\alpha+8d_v)N$.

For Givens formation at stored $z,w$, the norm $h$ has relative factors between $(1-u)^3$ and $(1+u)^3$, since its unscaled four-component squared sum has at most four rounding factors per term. Let $F$ be either $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $n\ge1$, fix the coordinate
order $1,\ldots,n$, and let $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(F)$. Define $D,L,U\in M_n(F)$
by

$$D_{ij}=\begin{cases}a_{ii}&i=j,\\0&i\ne j,\end{cases}\qquad L_{ij}=\begin{cases}-a_{ij}&i>j,\\0&i\le j,\end{cases}\qquad U_{ij}=\begin{cases}-a_{ij}&i<j,\\0&i\ge j.\end{cases}$$

Thus $D$ is diagonal, $L$ is strictly lower triangular, $U$ is strictly upper
triangular (in the sense of
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]), and
$A=D-L-U$. If $A=A^*$, then $U=L^*$, where $*$ denotes conjugate transpose.
The decomposition uses the fixed coordinate order and is an exact-arithmetic
identity.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Check dimensions; on a mismatch return
`invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D$ and $N=L+U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, compute the diagonal solve

$$D x^{(k+1)}=(L+U)x^{(k)}+b,$$

equivalently, simultaneously for every $i$,

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i-\sum_{j\ne i}a_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}}.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The solve is the unique diagonal instance of
[[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] when the pivot
check succeeds; [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]]
gives its well-definedness. A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure
reports no convergence or accuracy certificate.

Input $n\ge1$, $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $b,x^{(0)}\in\mathbb C^n$, and an
iteration budget $m\in\mathbb N_0$. Use the fixed order $1,\ldots,n$. Check
dimensions; on a mismatch return `invalid-input`. Form $D,L,U$ by
[[def-diagonal-lower-upper-splitting-convention]]. If some diagonal entry of
$A$ is zero, return `pivot-failure(i)` for the least such index $i$.

Otherwise set $M=D-L$ and $N=U$, so $A=M-N$. For each
$k=0,\ldots,m-1$, solve the lower-triangular system

$$ (D-L)x^{(k+1)}=Ux^{(k)}+b $$

by forward substitution in increasing index order. Equivalently, the component
updates are

$$x_i^{(k+1)}=\frac{b_i+\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}x_j^{(k+1)}+\sum_{j>i}U_{ij}x_j^{(k)}}{a_{ii}},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.$$

Return `completed` with $x^{(m)}$. The lower-triangular solve is unique after
the pivot check by [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]]
and [[thm-forward-and-back-substitution-are-correct-unique-and-quadratic-cost]].
A zero budget returns $x^{(0)}$. The procedure reports no convergence or
accuracy certificate.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

1. If $L\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with nonzero diagonal, the forward
   substitution recursion of
   [[def-forward-and-back-substitution-for-triangular-systems]] produces the
   unique solution of $Lx=b$.
2. If $U\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with nonzero diagonal, the backward
   substitution recursion produces the unique solution of $Ux=b$.

Each solve uses exactly $n$ divisions,
$\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ multiplications, and $\frac{n(n-1)}{2}$ additions or
subtractions, hence $O(n^2)$ scalar operations.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ admit a **matrix splitting**

$$A=M-N,$$

where $M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\mathbb F)$ is invertible in the sense of
[[def-invertible-matrix-and-general-linear-group]]. The associated
**stationary iteration** for the system $Ax=b$ is

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b.$$

Its iteration matrix is

$$B:=M^{-1}N.$$

Let $A=M-N$ be a matrix splitting in $M_n(\mathbb C)$ with stationary iteration

$$x_{k+1}=M^{-1}Nx_k+M^{-1}b,$$

and let $B:=M^{-1}N$ be its iteration matrix. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. For every right-hand side $b$ and every initial vector $x_0$, the iterates
   converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$.
2. The spectral radius $\rho(B)$ is strictly less than $1$.

derivations.claim: By [A1], every $a_{ii}\ne0$. Thus $D$ and the lower-triangular matrix $D-L$ have nonzero diagonal, so the solves in [F1] and [F2] are uniquely defined by [L2].
By [F1]–[F2] and [L3], the iteration matrices are $G_J=D^{-1}(L+U)$ and $G_G=(D-L)^{-1}U$.

For each row $i$, set $q_i=\sum_{j\ne i}|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ and $q_J=\max_i q_i<1$. Since $L_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ below the diagonal and $U_{ij}=-a_{ij}$ above it, $\sum_j|(G_J)_{ij}|=q_i$. Hence for any eigenpair $G_Jz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|$; the row equation gives $|\lambda||z_i|\le q_i|z_i|\le q_J|z_i|$, so $|\lambda|<1$ and $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Let $G_Gz=\lambda z$ with $z\ne0$, and choose $i$ with $|z_i|=\max_j|z_j|=:R$. The equation $Uz=\lambda(D-L)z$ in row $i$ is $\sum_{j>i}U_{ij}z_j=\lambda(a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j)$, so $|\lambda|\,|a_{ii}z_i-\sum_{j<i}L_{ij}z_j| \le\sum_{j>i}|U_{ij}||z_j|$. By the reverse triangle inequality and [A1], the left factor is at least $|\lambda|(|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|)R$, while the right side is at most $\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|R$. Therefore $|\lambda|\le\max_i\frac{\sum_{j>i}|a_{ij}|}{|a_{ii}|-\sum_{j<i}|a_{ij}|}<1$; the denominators are positive and each strict inequality follows from [A1]. Thus $\rho(G_G)<1$.
The bounds in steps 3.1 and 3.2 and [L4] imply that both methods converge to the unique solution of $Ax=b$ for every $b$ and every initial vector.

Define $C_{ii}=0$ and $C_{ij}=|a_{ij}|/|a_{ii}|$ for $i\ne j$. Its row sums are at most $1$, one is strictly below $1$, and its positive-entry graph is the graph in [A1]. By [L2], choose $v>0$ with $Cv<v$, and set $q_J=\max_i (Cv)_i/v_i<1$.

By [F1], $|G_J|=C$ entrywise. For $\|z\|_v:=\max_i |z_i|/v_i$, nonnegativity gives $|G_Jz|\le C|z|\le\|z\|_v Cv\le q_J\|z\|_v v$. Thus every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $G_J$ satisfies $|\lambda|\le q_J<1$, so $\rho(G_J)<1$.

Set $B_L=|D|^{-1}|L|$ and $B_U=|D|^{-1}|U|$. Then $C=B_L+B_U$, $B_L$ is strictly lower triangular, and $(I-B_L)^{-1}=\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}B_L^r\ge I$. derivations.claim: By [A1] and [F1], $M_\omega$ is lower triangular with diagonal $a_{ii}/\omega\ne0$, hence invertible by [L5]. Also $A=M_\omega-N_\omega$ by [L1], so [L2] applies with iteration matrix $G_\omega$. The matrix $N_\omega$ is upper triangular with diagonal entries $(\omega^{-1}-1)a_{ii}$. Thus [L6]–[L7] give $\det(M_\omega)=\omega^{-n}\prod_i a_{ii}$ and $\det(N_\omega)=(\omega^{-1}-1)^n\prod_i a_{ii}$. From $M_\omega G_\omega=N_\omega$ and multiplicativity, $\det(G_\omega)=\det(N_\omega)/\det(M_\omega)=(1-\omega)^n$.

For sufficiency, suppose $A$ is positive definite and $0<\omega<2$. Then $Q:=M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A=(2/\omega-1)D$ is positive definite. For an eigenpair $G_\omega v=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, one has $\lambda\ne1$ since $Av=(1-\lambda)M_\omega v$ and $A$ is invertible. Put $a=v^*Av>0$. Then $v^*M_\omega v=a/(1-\lambda)$, so $v^*Qv=a\left(2\operatorname{Re}\frac{1}{1-\lambda}-1\right) =a\frac{1-|\lambda|^2}{|1-\lambda|^2}>0$. Therefore $|\lambda|<1$ for every eigenvalue and $\rho(G_\omega)<1$.

If SOR converges for every right-hand side and start, [L3] gives $\rho(G_\omega)<1$. By [L8]–[L9], $|\det(G_\omega)|=\prod_{j=1}^n|\lambda_j|\le\rho(G_\omega)^n<1$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $|1-\omega|<1$, which for real $\omega$ is equivalent to $0<\omega<2$.

Assume now that SOR converges for every right-hand side and start. Then $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ by [L3], so $1$ is not an eigenvalue of $G_\omega$ and $I-G_\omega$ is invertible. By [L2], $A=M_\omega(I-G_\omega)$ is invertible. For $b=0$, its unique solution is $x_*=0$. For arbitrary $e^{(0)}:=x^{(0)}$, set $e^{(k)}:=x^{(k)}-x_*=x^{(k)}$ and $\delta_k=e^{(k+1)}-e^{(k)}$. The homogeneous SOR recurrence gives $M_\omega e^{(k+1)}=N_\omega e^{(k)}$, hence $Ae^{(k)}+M_\omega\delta_k=0$. Expanding the Hermitian quadratic form gives $(e^{(k)})^*Ae^{(k)}-(e^{(k+1)})^*Ae^{(k+1)} =\delta_k^*(M_\omega+M_\omega^*-A)\delta_k =(2/\omega-1)\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. The last equality follows from [L1] and [F1].

By step 2.1, $c:=2/\omega-1>0$. Summing the identity in step 2.2 from $k=0$ to $N-1$ and taking $N\to\infty$ (the error tends to $0$ by the assumed convergence) gives $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}=c\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\delta_k^*D\delta_k$. Moreover $\delta_0\ne0$: otherwise step 2.2 implies $Ae^{(0)}=0$, contrary to invertibility of $A$. Since $D$ has positive diagonal, the first summand is strictly positive and all others are nonnegative. Thus $(e^{(0)})^*Ae^{(0)}>0$ for every nonzero $e^{(0)}$, so [L4] gives that $A$ is positive definite.
By [L3], $\rho(G_\omega)<1$ implies convergence to the unique solution for every right-hand side and every initial vector. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 prove the reverse implication.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]). If $f$ is differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) then $f$ is continuous at $c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]).

Consequently, if $f$ is differentiable on a set $S \subseteq A$ then $f$ is
continuous at every point of $S$.

**No converse is asserted, and none holds.** Continuity at $c$ does not give
differentiability at $c$, and the standard witness is worked out on the
companion page.

derivations.claim: Define $h(u)=\sin u-u\cos u$. By [F1], [F2], and [F5], $h$ is differentiable and hence continuous, with $h'(u)=u\sin u\geq0$ on $(0,\pi/2)$ by [F4]. For $u>0$, the mean value theorem on $[0,u]$ gives $h(u)\geq h(0)=0$; at $u=0$ equality is immediate.

For $0<u<\pi/2$, define $r(u)=\sin u/u$. By the quotient rule, the identity derivative in [F5], and step 1.1, $r'(u)=(u\cos u-\sin u)/u^2=-h(u)/u^2\leq0$. The function $r$ is continuous on $[u,\pi/2]$ by [F5], so the mean value theorem gives $r(u)\geq r(\pi/2)=2/\pi$ by [F3] and [F4]; at $u=\pi/2$ equality holds. Multiplying by $u$ and checking $u=0$ proves the first inequality.

If $u\ne v$, sine is continuous on the closed interval between them and differentiable inside by [F1] and [F5]. The mean value theorem gives $|\sin u-\sin v|=|\cos c|\,|u-v|\leq|u-v|$ for some interior $c$, by [F3] and [F4]. If $u=v$, both sides are zero.

Let $C[-1,1]$ be the real continuous functions on $[-1,1]$, with
$\|f\|_\infty:=\sup_{x\in[-1,1]}|f(x)|$. Let $\mathcal P_n$ be the
restrictions to $[-1,1]$ of real polynomials of degree at most $n$, including
the zero polynomial. Interval notation is that of [[def-interval]]. Continuity and polynomial degree have the conventions of
[[def-continuity-real]] and
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]].

For each $n\in\mathbb N$ (with naturals in real expressions interpreted by
their canonical real images), the first-kind Chebyshev root angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{R,n}=\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2n+2},\qquad x_j^{R,n}=\cos\theta_j^{R,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They are the roots of $T_{n+1}$ by
[[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]]. For $n\geq1$, the
Chebyshev–Lobatto angles and nodes are
$$\theta_j^{L,n}=\frac{j\pi}{n},\qquad x_j^{L,n}=\cos\theta_j^{L,n},\qquad 0\leq j\leq n.$$
They include both endpoints and are the extrema of $T_n$ by the same
identity. At $n=0$, define the Lobatto node to be $x_0^{L,0}=0$. The
cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$, so each listed family has
distinct nodes; the root family at $n=0$ also consists of $0$.

For either family $\sigma\in\{R,L\}$, write its nodes as
$x_0,\ldots,x_n$ and define
$$\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)= \prod_{\substack{0\leq k\leq n\\k\ne j}} \frac{x-x_k}{x_j-x_k},\qquad I_n^\sigma f=\sum_{j=0}^n f(x_j)\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}.$$
These are the cardinal formula and interpolation sum of
[[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] specialized to this node family.
The displayed cosine arrays decrease, whereas that supplier orders nodes
increasingly: use $z_i=x_{n-i}$ and data $y_i=f(z_i)$. Its cardinal
function with index $n-j$ is exactly the displayed $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma$,
by reindexing the finite product, and its interpolation sum is $I_n^\sigma$.
The empty product at $n=0$ is $1$, so the same identification holds for the
single node. Distinctness makes every denominator nonzero;
[[lem-cardinal-basis-degree-and-values]] supplies the degree and cardinal
values. The finite sum is linear in the data and maps $C[-1,1]$ into
$\mathcal P_n$. Its operator norm is
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma:= \sup\{\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty:g\in C[-1,1],\ \|g\|_\infty\leq1\}.$$
If $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, then
$|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|\leq\sum_{k=0}^n|a_{jk}|$ for $|x|\leq1$; hence
$\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty\leq\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|<\infty$ whenever
$\|g\|_\infty\leq1$. Define the best degree-$n$ uniform
approximation error by
$$E_n(f):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\|f-p\|_\infty .$$

These quantities are real and well-defined. Polynomial functions are
continuous, and sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions remain
continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. The interval
$[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded, so
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] implies
that for every such continuous function $h$ there are finite minimum and
maximum values $m_h,M_h$. Since $m_h\leq h(x)\leq M_h$, one has
$|h(x)|\leq\max(|m_h|,|M_h|)$, so each supremum norm above is finite. The set defining $\Lambda_n^\sigma$ contains
the zero function and is bounded above by the displayed finite coefficient
sum. The set defining $E_n(f)$ contains the zero polynomial and is bounded
below by zero. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])
therefore gives the stated finite supremum and infimum. Also, $n+1$ has
positive real image by [[def-canonical-natural]] and
[[lem-of-naturals-positive]], and $n$ has positive real image when $n\geq1$;
thus the root-angle denominator and the Lobatto denominator in its stated
range are nonzero.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Each cardinal function $\ell_j$ of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree $n$. The node function $\omega_n$ is the evaluation of a monic formal polynomial of degree $n+1$, and $\omega_n(x)\ne0$ whenever $x$ differs from every node. The function $I_n y$ is the evaluation of a formal polynomial of degree at most $n$. At every pair $i,j\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, $\ell_j(x_i)=1$ if $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise.

derivations.claim: Put $z_i=x_{n-i}$, so $z_0<\cdots<z_n$ by [F1]. Under this reverse indexing, the supplier cardinal function at index $n-j$ is $\ell_j$ by the specialization in [F1]. Applying [F3] gives its degree and cardinal values, including the one-node empty-product case $n=0$.
Put $L(x)=\sum_j|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|$. For every $g$ with $\|g\|_\infty\leq1$, the defining sum gives $|I_n^\sigma g(x)|\leq L(x)$, hence $\Lambda_n^\sigma\leq\sup_xL(x)$.

Prescribe data $y_i=1$ at $i=n-j$ and $0$ otherwise on the increasingly ordered nodes $z_i$ from step 1.1. The polynomial $\ell_j$ has these data by step 1.1. The supplier uniqueness theorem [F2] makes it the unique degree-at-most-$n$ polynomial with the required cardinal values.

Prescribe $y_i=p(z_i)$ on the ordered nodes in step 1.1. By [F1] and [F3], their cardinal sum is $I_n^\sigma p$ and has degree at most $n$. The polynomial $p$ itself interpolates those data, so the supplier uniqueness theorem [F2] gives $I_n^\sigma p=p$.

Fix $x$. Define $\operatorname{sgn}(t)=1$ for $t>0$, $-1$ for $t<0$, and $0$ for $t=0$, and prescribe $\operatorname{sgn}(\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x))$ at each node. These values lie in $[-1,1]$ and satisfy $\operatorname{sgn}(t)t=|t|$ by cases. Sort nodes increasingly, interpolate these values linearly, and extend constantly to the interval endpoints; each interpolated value is a convex combination of endpoint values, so the resulting continuous $g_x$ has norm at most $1$. The cardinal sum gives $I_n^\sigma g_x(x)=L(x)$, so $\Lambda_n^\sigma\geq\|I_n^\sigma g_x\|_\infty\geq L(x)$. Taking the supremum in $x$ and using step 1.2 proves equality. For $n=0$ the same construction is constant on the interval.

and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

values. The finite sum is linear in the data and maps $C[-1,1]$ into
$\mathcal P_n$. Its operator norm is
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma:= \sup\{\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty:g\in C[-1,1],\ \|g\|_\infty\leq1\}.$$
If $\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)=\sum_{k=0}^n a_{jk}x^k$, then
$|\ell_{j,n}^\sigma(x)|\leq\sum_{k=0}^n|a_{jk}|$ for $|x|\leq1$; hence
$\|I_n^\sigma g\|_\infty\leq\sum_{j,k}|a_{jk}|<\infty$ whenever
$\|g\|_\infty\leq1$. Define the best degree-$n$ uniform
approximation error by
$$E_n(f):=\inf_{p\in\mathcal P_n}\|f-p\|_\infty .$$

These quantities are real and well-defined. Polynomial functions are
continuous, and sums and scalar multiples of continuous functions remain
continuous by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]]. The interval
$[-1,1]\subset\mathbb R$ is nonempty, closed, and bounded, so
[[thm-euclidean-heine-borel-pseudocompactness-and-extreme-values]] implies
that for every such continuous function $h$ there are finite minimum and
maximum values $m_h,M_h$. Since $m_h\leq h(x)\leq M_h$, one has
$|h(x)|\leq\max(|m_h|,|M_h|)$, so each supremum norm above is finite. The set defining $\Lambda_n^\sigma$ contains
the zero function and is bounded above by the displayed finite coefficient
sum. The set defining $E_n(f)$ contains the zero polynomial and is bounded
below by zero. Completeness of $\mathbb R$ ([[def-complete-ordered-field]])
therefore gives the stated finite supremum and infimum. Also, $n+1$ has
positive real image by [[def-canonical-natural]] and
[[lem-of-naturals-positive]], and $n$ has positive real image when $n\geq1$;
thus the root-angle denominator and the Lobatto denominator in its stated
range are nonzero.

For either Chebyshev node family and every $n\geq0$, the cardinal
polynomials in [[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]]
satisfy $\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x_k^{\sigma,n})=1$ when $j=k$ and $0$
otherwise. They are the unique degree-at-most-$n$ polynomials with those
cardinal values. Consequently $I_n^\sigma p=p$ for every $p\in\mathcal P_n$.
Moreover,
$$\Lambda_n^\sigma= \sup_{x\in[-1,1]}\sum_{j=0}^n|\ell_{j,n}^{\sigma}(x)|.$$

Let $n\geq1$, $0\leq\theta\leq\pi$, and choose $j$ so
$\theta\ne\theta_j^{R,n}$. Then
$$|\ell_{j,n}^{R}(\cos\theta)| =\frac{|\cos((n+1)\theta)|\sin\theta_j^{R,n}} {(n+1)|\cos\theta-\cos\theta_j^{R,n}|}.$$
For the Lobatto family, put $c_j=1/2$ for $j=0,n$ and $c_j=1$
otherwise. If $\theta\ne\theta_j^{L,n}$, then
$$|\ell_{j,n}^{L}(\cos\theta)| =\frac{c_j|\sin\theta\,\sin(n\theta)|} {n|\cos\theta-\cos\theta_j^{L,n}|}.$$

For all real $u,v$,

For all real $x,y$,

$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $F$ be a field ([[def-field]]) with additive identity $0_F$ and
multiplicative identity $1_F$. Define
$\iota : \mathbb{N} \to F$ by recursion on $\mathbb{N}$
([[def-natural-numbers]], [[thm-recursion]]):

$$\iota(0) \;:=\; 0_F, \qquad \iota(n+1) \;:=\; \iota(n) + 1_F .$$

$\iota(n)$ is the **canonical natural** of $n$ in $F$. It is also written
$n \cdot 1_F$, and for $n \ge 1$ it is $1_F$ added to itself $n$ times.

**Why the notation is needed at all.** A natural number in this library is a von
Neumann natural, that is a set ([[def-natural-numbers]]), and a set is not an
element of $F$. So $1/n$, $n^{\alpha}$ and $x/n$ are not expressions of $F$ when
$n$ is a natural: what they mean is $1/\iota(n)$, $\iota(n)^{\alpha}$ and
$x/\iota(n)$. The map $\iota$ is what carries a counting number into the field,
and writing it is the whole reason a reader meets $1/\iota(k+1)$ where an
informal text would write $1/(k+1)$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

In particular,

derivations.claim: In either angular grid the spacing is $h=\pi/(n+1)$ for roots and $h=\pi/n$ for Lobatto nodes. Choose a nearest grid angle $\theta_k$ and put $d_j=|\theta-\theta_j|$. Then $d_k\leq h/2$; if $|j-k|=r\geq1$, the triangle inequality gives $d_j\geq rh-d_k\geq(r-\tfrac12)h$. At most two indices occur for each $r$.

For $\theta\ne\theta_j$, put $s=(\theta+\theta_j)/2$ and $d=\theta-\theta_j$. Since the two angles lie in $[0,\pi]$, $|d|/2\leq\min(s,\pi-s)$. The addition/subtraction formulas in [F5] give $\sin\theta_j,\sin\theta\leq\sin s+|\sin(d/2)|$; the monotonicity and supplementary identity in [F5] then give $|\sin(d/2)|\leq\sin s$, so each numerator is at most $2\sin s$. Those same formulas give $|\cos\theta-\cos\theta_j|=2\sin s\sin(|d|/2)$, and [F4] gives $\sin(|d|/2)\geq|d|/\pi$. Thus both ratios $\sin\theta_j/|\cos\theta-\cos\theta_j|$ and $\sin\theta/|\cos\theta-\cos\theta_j|$ are at most $\pi/d_j$.

For roots, [F3] and step 2.1 give $|\ell_{j,n}^R(\cos\theta)|\leq\pi|\cos((n+1)\theta)|/((n+1)d_j)$. At the nearest node $k$, $\cos((n+1)\theta_k)=0$, and the cosine addition formula plus [F4] gives $|\cos((n+1)\theta)|\leq(n+1)d_k$, so its term is at most $\pi$. For other nodes use $|\cos((n+1)\theta)|\leq1$ and step 1.1; summing over at most two nodes per distance rank yields $\sum_j|\ell_{j,n}^R(\cos\theta)|\leq\pi+2\sum_{r=1}^n1/(r-\tfrac12)$. At a node the cardinal sum is $1$.

For Lobatto nodes, [F3] and step 2.1 give $|\ell_{j,n}^L(\cos\theta)|\leq\pi c_j|\sin(n\theta)|/(nd_j)$. At the nearest node $k$, $\sin(n\theta_k)=0$, so [F4] gives $|\sin(n\theta)|\leq nd_k$ and its term is at most $\pi$ because $c_k\leq1$. For other nodes use $|\sin(n\theta)|\leq1$ and step 1.1; summing over at most two nodes per distance rank yields $\sum_j|\ell_{j,n}^L(\cos\theta)|\leq\pi+2\sum_{r=1}^n1/(r-\tfrac12)$. At a node the cardinal sum is $1$.

Since $1/(r-\tfrac12)\leq2/r$, the shifted sum is at most $2H_n$, where $H_n=\sum_{r=1}^n1/r$. For $r\geq2$, $1/r\leq\int_{r-1}^r dt/t$, so [F6] gives $H_n\leq1+\log n$. Positivity of the real image of $n$ is [F7], so these logarithms are defined. The integral formula also gives $0=\log1\leq\log n\leq\log(n+1)$ and $\log2\leq\log(n+1)$ by integrating $1/t>0$ over $[1,n]$, $[n,n+1]$, and $[2,n+1]$. Since $\log2=\int_1^2dt/t>0$ and $\pi>0$, we have $C>0$ and $1<C\log2$. Thus both sums are at most $\pi+4+4\log n\leq(4+(\pi+4)/\log2)\log(n+1)$. By [F8], the angular supremum is over exactly $[-1,1]$; taking it and using [F2] proves both bounds. At $n=0$, each one-node operator has norm $1$ directly.
