Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

Assume Countable Choice and the conforming Galerkin setting of
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]]. Let
$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with inner product linear in the first slot, and
let $J:V\to H$ be a continuous linear inclusion with
$\|Jv\|_H\le C_E\|v\|_V$. Put $e:=J(u-u_h)$. The adjoint solution $z_e$ is
the unique element of $V$ satisfying
$$a(v,z_e)=(Jv,e)_H\qquad(v\in V);$$
it exists by [[thm-adjoint-problem-for-bounded-coercive-variational-forms]].
Let $s\in(0,1]$, and let $R_s\subseteq V$ be a specified normed space of
adjoint-regular functions. Assume constants $C_R,C_I$ independent of $h$ and
the error satisfy
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_H,\qquad \inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_V\le C_Ih^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le M C_I C_R h^s\|u-u_h\|_V.$$
The symbol $R_s$ means exactly the chosen regularity norm space in the two
displayed assumptions; no fractional Sobolev interpolation estimate is
asserted unless it verifies the second inequality. The integer endpoint may
be instantiated with $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap V$, using the
$H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$ norm. If $H^2(\Omega)\subseteq V$,
this is simply $R_1=H^2(\Omega)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. On $H^1(\Omega)=W^{1,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]) define $$(u,v)_{H^1}:=(u,v)_{L^2}+\sum_{i=1}^n(D_iu,D_iv)_{L^2},$$ with the $L^2$ inner product of [[lem-l-two-with-the-integral-pairing-is-a-hilbert-space]]. Then $(\cdot,\cdot)_{H^1}$ is an inner product on the Sobolev classes whose induced norm is the $W^{1,2}$ norm of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], and $H^1(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space for it. The zero-boundary space $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a closed subspace of $H^1(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]) and hence a Hilbert space for the restricted inner product. The pairing is linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, in the convention of [[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]].

derivations.claim: Since $I_hu\in V_h$ by the finite-element approximation hypotheses, $\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_{H^1}\le\|u-I_hu\|_{H^1}\le C_{\rm FE}h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}}$ by [F1].

By [F4], $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a Hilbert space in its stated $H^1$ norm. Apply the Aubin–Nitsche estimate [F3] with $V=H^1_0(\Omega)$ in its $H^1$ norm, $C_I=C_D$, and the two dual bounds [A1]. This gives $\|u-u_h\|_{L^2}\le M C_DC_Rh^s\|u-u_h\|_{H^1}$.
Apply [F2] on the Hilbert space supplied by [F4] to the best-approximation bound in step 1.1. This gives $\|u-u_h\|_{H^1}\le \frac M\alpha C_{\rm FE}h^r|u|_{W^{r+1,2}}.$

Substitute the $H^1$ bound from step 2.1 into step 1.2. This gives $\|u-u_h\|_{L^2}\le(M^2/\alpha)C_{\rm FE}C_DC_Rh^{r+s}|u|_{W^{r+1,2}}$, including zero error without division. Setting $s=1$ gives $h^{r+1}$ under the stated full adjoint hypotheses.

derivations.claim: For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $Ax=(x_1-x_2,x_1+x_2)$, so $\|Ax\|_2^2=2\|x\|_2^2$ and $|a(x,y)|\le\sqrt2\|x\|_2\|y\|_2$. Also $a(x,x)=x_1^2+x_2^2$, so the coercivity constant is $\alpha=1$. Finally, $a(e_1,e_2)=1$ and $a(e_2,e_1)=-1$, so the form is not symmetric.

Since $u=e_2$ and $F(v)=a(e_2,v)$, the continuous variational equation holds for every $v\in\mathbb R^2$. Write $u_h=ce_1$. Testing the discrete equation with $e_1$ gives $c\,a(e_1,e_1)=a(e_2,e_1)$, hence $c=-1$ because $a(e_1,e_1)=1$ and $a(e_2,e_1)=-1$. Thus $u_h=-e_1$.

For $v_h=te_1$, $\|u-v_h\|_2^2=\|e_2-te_1\|_2^2=1+t^2$, whose infimum is $1$ at $t=0$. Meanwhile $u-u_h=e_1+e_2$, so $\|u-u_h\|_2=\sqrt2$. Therefore the ratio is $\sqrt2=M/\alpha$, and the constant in [F1] cannot be decreased in general.

Assume the hypotheses and notation of
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]], and
suppose additionally that $a$ is Hermitian:
$a(v,w)=\overline{a(w,v)}$. Then
$$\|v\|_a:=\sqrt{a(v,v)}$$
is the energy norm and the Galerkin solution is its best approximation:
$$\|u-u_h\|_a=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_a.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $I=(0,1)$ and define
$$\phi(x)=\begin{cases}2x,&0\le x\le\frac12,\\2(1-x),&\frac12\le x\le1,\end{cases} \qquad p(x)=\frac12x(1-x).$$
Then $\phi|_I,p|_I\in H^1_0(I)=W^{1,2}_0(I)$, the closure of
$C_c^\infty(I)$ in $W^{1,2}(I)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion is vacuous: there is only the zero
class and every displayed test identity is zero.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

For each finite $m\ge0$, the same conclusions hold on tuples $F=(f_j)_{j<m}$, with pairing $B(F,G)=\sum_{j<m}\langle f_j,g_j\rangle$ and $\|F\|^2=\sum_{j<m}\|f_j\|_2^2$. For $G\ne0$, equality means $f_j=cg_j$ a.e. for every $j$, with one common scalar $c$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, with $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ the zero-boundary Sobolev space $W^{1,2}_0$ over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]). Define
$$H^{-1}(\Omega):=\{\,F:H^1_0(\Omega)\to\mathbb K : F\text{ is bounded and conjugate-linear}\,\},$$
with
$$\|F\|_{H^{-1}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_{H^1_0}\le1}|F(v)| .$$
**Pairing convention.** The pairing $\langle F,v\rangle:=F(v)$ is linear in $F$ and conjugate-linear in $v$; it is the dual pairing of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ with $H^1_0(\Omega)$, not the $L^2$ inner product. The map $F\mapsto\overline{F(\cdot)}$ is an isometric conjugate-linear bijection of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ onto the Banach dual $(H^1_0(\Omega))^*$ of [[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]] ([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); the design's notation $(H^1_0)^*$ is read through this identification, which is the one compatible with the page's sesquilinear convention (linear in the first argument, conjugate-linear in the second) fixed in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]. The space $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ is a normed space, complete because $(H^1_0(\Omega))^*$ is complete and $\overline{F(\cdot)}$ is an isometry in both directions ([[thm-bounded-operator-space-is-banach]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the map $v\mapsto(f,v)_{L^2}$ is the corresponding element of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ under the conventions of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], where complex integrability is in the sense of the latter; identifying a general element of $H^{-1}$ with an $L^2$ function is an embedding statement, never a definition. Elements of $H^{-1}$ are defined here by their action on Sobolev classes; this does not exclude their identification with distributions through smooth test functions.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]]
implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$**
by
$$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$
where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

Let $f:X\to\mathbb R$ be measurable. Its positive and negative parts are
$$f^+:=\max\{f,0\},\qquad f^-:=\max\{-f,0\};$$
they are measurable by
[[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] and
satisfy $f=f^+-f^-$ and $|f|=f^++f^-$.

The **Lebesgue integral of a real measurable function** is defined whenever at
most one of $\int f^+\,d\mu$ and $\int f^-\,d\mu$ is $+\infty$, in which case
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\int f^+\,d\mu-\int f^-\,d\mu.$$
The function is **integrable** when both integrals are finite, equivalently
when $\int|f|\,d\mu<+\infty$.

For a complex measurable function $h=u+iv$ with
$u=\operatorname{Re}h,\ v=\operatorname{Im}h$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]), define $h$ to be
**integrable** when $|h|$ is integrable, and then define
$$\int h\,d\mu:=\int u\,d\mu+i\int v\,d\mu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Direct integration gives $a(\phi,\phi)=\int_0^{1/2}4\,dx+\int_{1/2}^1 4\,dx=4,\qquad \int_0^1\phi(x)\,dx=\frac12.$ For $u_h=c\phi$, the Galerkin equation tested with $\phi$ is $4c=\int_0^1\phi=\frac12$, hence $c=\frac18$ and $u_h=\frac18\phi$.

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under

[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

Because $\beta$ is smooth and positive on $(0,\infty)$, the denominator is positive on $(0,1)$, while $\sigma(t)=0$ for $t\le 0$ and $\sigma(t)=1$ for $t\ge 1$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

On every measure space the pairing $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f\overline g$ on complex $L^2$ is representative-independent, linear in the first variable, conjugate-linear in the second, conjugate symmetric and positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$. Moreover,
$$|\langle f,g\rangle|\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$
If $g\ne0$ as a class, equality holds iff $f=cg$ a.e. for some $c\in\mathbb C$. If $g=0$, equality holds for every $f$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $L$ and its form $a$ be as in [[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] on an open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$. **Homogeneous problem.** Given $F\in H^{-1}(\Omega)$ ([[def-h-minus-one-as-the-dual-of-h-one-zero]]), a **weak solution** of $Lu=F$ with zero boundary values is a class $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H^1_0(\Omega).$$ **Inhomogeneous problem.** Additionally assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) for the trace supplier, and let $n\ge2$ and $\Omega$ be a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]]), let $g\in H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega):=W^{1/2,2}(\partial\Omega)$ in the boundary scale of [[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]] and let $T$ be the trace operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. A weak solution with boundary data $g$ is a class $u\in H^1(\Omega)$ with $Tu=g$ and $a(u,v)=F(v)$ for every $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$. The defining identities are identities between functionals on the $H^1_0$ classes, so they are independent of the chosen almost-everywhere representatives of $u$, of the coefficients and of the data ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]); the boundary condition is imposed through the trace of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]], never by pointwise evaluation. The Dirichlet condition is imposed by $u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ in the homogeneous problem and by $Tu=g$ in the inhomogeneous problem; testing against $v\in H^1_0$ expresses the weak equation and does not by itself impose boundary data; the integrals are the ones proved absolutely convergent in [[lem-elliptic-form-is-well-defined-and-bounded]].

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, with $H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ the zero-boundary Sobolev space $W^{1,2}_0$ over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]], [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[def-hk-and-hk-zero-notation]]). Define
$$H^{-1}(\Omega):=\{\,F:H^1_0(\Omega)\to\mathbb K : F\text{ is bounded and conjugate-linear}\,\},$$
with
$$\|F\|_{H^{-1}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_{H^1_0}\le1}|F(v)| .$$
**Pairing convention.** The pairing $\langle F,v\rangle:=F(v)$ is linear in $F$ and conjugate-linear in $v$; it is the dual pairing of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ with $H^1_0(\Omega)$, not the $L^2$ inner product. The map $F\mapsto\overline{F(\cdot)}$ is an isometric conjugate-linear bijection of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ onto the Banach dual $(H^1_0(\Omega))^*$ of [[def-dual-space-of-a-normed-space]] ([[def-operator-norm]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]); the design's notation $(H^1_0)^*$ is read through this identification, which is the one compatible with the page's sesquilinear convention (linear in the first argument, conjugate-linear in the second) fixed in [[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]. The space $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ is a normed space, complete because $(H^1_0(\Omega))^*$ is complete and $\overline{F(\cdot)}$ is an isometry in both directions ([[thm-bounded-operator-space-is-banach]], [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). For $f\in L^2(\Omega)$ the map $v\mapsto(f,v)_{L^2}$ is the corresponding element of $H^{-1}(\Omega)$ under the conventions of [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]], where complex integrability is in the sense of the latter; identifying a general element of $H^{-1}$ with an $L^2$ function is an embedding statement, never a definition. Elements of $H^{-1}$ are defined here by their action on Sobolev classes; this does not exclude their identification with distributions through smooth test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open,
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $u:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ have real
and imaginary parts of class $C^k$. For each multi-index
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ with $|\alpha|\le k$, the componentwise classical
derivative $\partial^\alpha u$ is locally integrable and is the weak
derivative $D^\alpha u$. By the uniqueness lemma, it represents the unique
locally integrable weak-derivative class. For $\alpha=0$, this says
$D^0u=u$.

Assume Countable Choice and the conforming Galerkin setting of
[[thm-cea-quasi-optimality-for-conforming-galerkin-approximations]]. Let
$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with inner product linear in the first slot, and
let $J:V\to H$ be a continuous linear inclusion with
$\|Jv\|_H\le C_E\|v\|_V$. Put $e:=J(u-u_h)$. The adjoint solution $z_e$ is
the unique element of $V$ satisfying
$$a(v,z_e)=(Jv,e)_H\qquad(v\in V);$$
it exists by [[thm-adjoint-problem-for-bounded-coercive-variational-forms]].
Let $s\in(0,1]$, and let $R_s\subseteq V$ be a specified normed space of
adjoint-regular functions. Assume constants $C_R,C_I$ independent of $h$ and
the error satisfy
$$\|z_e\|_{R_s}\le C_R\|e\|_H,\qquad \inf_{w_h\in V_h}\|z_e-w_h\|_V\le C_Ih^s\|z_e\|_{R_s}.$$
Then
$$\|u-u_h\|_{L^2(\Omega)} \le M C_I C_R h^s\|u-u_h\|_V.$$
The symbol $R_s$ means exactly the chosen regularity norm space in the two
displayed assumptions; no fractional Sobolev interpolation estimate is
asserted unless it verifies the second inequality. The integer endpoint may
be instantiated with $R_1=H^2(\Omega)\cap V$, using the
$H^2(\Omega)=W^{2,2}(\Omega)$ norm. If $H^2(\Omega)\subseteq V$,
this is simply $R_1=H^2(\Omega)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point. Hessians and their quadratic forms have the conventions of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. For $n\ge1$, these are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

For $n=0$, use the zero-space case directly, without invoking that supplier's positive-codomain standing hypothesis. The space $\mathbb R^0$ has only its zero vector and carries the zero Euclidean norm and its induced metric ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5, [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Whenever the line map is defined near $0$, every difference quotient for real $t\ne0$ is this zero vector; define $D_vf(a)=0$. This is the unique possible derivative value, and its normwise difference-quotient error is exactly zero for all such $t$, so the real parameter still approaches an actual limit point. Every existing coordinate direction therefore has $\partial_jf(a)=0$; these zero-valued partial maps are continuous in the induced norm metrics. If the source dimension is zero, there are no partial indices and the sole direction is $v=0$; its constant line map is defined near $0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

derivations.claim: For any $x,y\in U$, convexity keeps the segment from $x$ to $y$ in $U$. Applying [F1] with Taylor order one gives $f(y)=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac12(y-x)^TH_f(x+\theta(y-x))(y-x)$ for some $\theta\in(0,1)$. The Hessian hypothesis makes the last term at least $\mu\|y-x\|_2^2/2$, proving the first inequality. Since $H_f\succeq\mu I\succeq0$, [F2] also makes $f$ convex on $U$.

Let $x^*$ be an interior minimizer. For each standard basis vector $e_j$, openness gives an interval around $0$ on which $x^*+te_j\in U$. The one-variable function $t\mapsto f(x^*+te_j)$ has a minimum at $0$, so its derivative there is $0$; [F4] identifies this derivative with $\partial_j f(x^*)$. Thus every coordinate of $\nabla f(x^*)$ is zero.
Apply the first inequality from step 1.1 once to $(x,y)$ and once to $(y,x)$, and add. The function-value terms cancel, leaving $\langle\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\ge\mu\|y-x\|_2^2$.
Apply step 1.1 with $x=x^*$ and $y=x$. Using $\nabla f(x^*)=0$ gives $f(x)-f^*\ge\mu\|x-x^*\|_2^2/2$. This also proves uniqueness, because equality of the minimum values forces $x=x^*$.

Apply step 1.1 with the ordered pair $(x,x^*)$ and write $d:=x-x^*$. Rearrangement gives $f(x)-f^*\le\langle
abla f(x),dangle-\mu\|d\|_2^2/2$. By [F5] and completing the square, the right-hand side is at most $\|
abla f(x)\|_2^2/(2\mu)$, since $0\le(\|
abla f(x)\|_2-\mu\|d\|_2)^2$. This is the gradient-gap inequality.

boundaries.evidence: If $U$ were empty, the pointwise conclusions are vacuous and the minimizer clause has no instance; the stated conditional remains consistent. The quantified domain is explicit in the Statement.
At $x=y$, the displacement and both sides of the strong-monotonicity inequality vanish; step 1.1 applies Taylor on this coincident segment.
The proof includes dimension $d=1$: the standard-basis stationarity argument in step 1.2 has one coordinate and all norm inequalities remain scalar.
The hypothesis requires $\mu>0$; the distance and gradient-gap conclusions are not claimed at zero curvature, which is necessary for uniqueness and division by $\mu$ in step 3.1.
Both endpoints are required to lie in the open convex set, so the segment used in step 1.1 stays in the domain; the argument makes no claim for boundary points outside $U$.
The minimizer is supplied as $x^*$ and the standard basis is finite; steps 1.2–3.1 construct no choice from an infinite family.

risk_review.notes: Read all five proof steps and six local suppliers. Taylor k=1 gives the lower quadratic estimate on the segment; adding both orientations gives strong monotonicity. Openness gives stationarity at an attained minimizer, hence uniqueness and the distance bound. Cauchy–Schwarz and square completion give the gradient-gap bound. Empty U is vacuous; coincident points and d=0 give zero identities; mu>0 is essential. No AC or converse assertion is used. Reader/refuter report no finding here; no defect identified.

This is an ideal one-step line-search oracle that uses the negative-gradient direction of [[alg-gradient-descent]] and replaces only its step-selection rule. It is not a second definition of the gradient-descent iteration.

**Inputs:** an open convex set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, a $C^2$ objective $f:U\to\mathbb R$, an initial point $x_0\in U$ whose sublevel set $K:=\{y\in U:f(y)\le f(x_0)\}$ is compact, and a current point $x\in K$. **Admissible conditions:** for some $0<m\le M$, there is a convex open set $V\subseteq U$ containing $K$ on which the Hessian satisfies $mI\preceq H_f(y)\preceq MI$. **Output:** if $\nabla f(x)=0$, return $(x,\texttt{stationary})$. Otherwise set $g:=\nabla f(x)$ and return $(x-t_*g,\texttt{exact-step})$, where $t_*$ is the unique minimizer of $t\mapsto f(x-tg)$ over all $t\ge0$ with $x-tg\in U$. The set $K$ is nonempty because $x_0\in K$, and the continuous restriction $f|_K$ attains a minimum at some $x^*\in K$ by [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]. Every $y\in U\setminus K$ satisfies $f(y)>f(x_0)\ge f(x^*)$, so $x^*$ is an attained global minimizer of $f$ on $U$. Thus the algorithm inputs supply the minimizer premise of [[thm-exact-line-search-gradient-descent-global-contraction]], whose remaining hypotheses are stated above.

The minimization is an exact real-valued oracle; this definition gives no finite evaluation procedure or floating-point accuracy claim. A finite implementation must report its own search status and error bounds.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point. Hessians and their quadratic forms have the conventions of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$, and fix $\mu>0$. Suppose $v^TH_f(z)v\ge\mu\|v\|_2^2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^d$. Then for every $x,y\in U$,

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac\mu2\|y-x\|_2^2,$$

and

$$\langle\nabla f(y)-\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\ge\mu\|y-x\|_2^2.$$

If $x^*\in U$ is a global minimizer and $f^*:=f(x^*)$, it is unique and every $x\in U$ satisfies

$$f(x)-f^*\ge\frac\mu2\|x-x^*\|_2^2,\qquad \|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\ge2\mu(f(x)-f^*).$$

Here $H_f$ is the matrix of second partial derivatives and $\nabla f$ is the vector of first partial derivatives, as in [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]] and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $K \subseteq X$ be a
compact subset ([[def-metric-compactness]]). Then $K$ is closed in $X$
([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).

No choice principle is used: both covers below are given by a rule, and the
indexed form of [[lem-compactness-is-intrinsic]] returns indices rather than
sets.

**The converse is false in general.** A closed and bounded subset of an arbitrary
metric space need not be compact
([[fs-closed-and-bounded-implies-compact-in-every-metric-space]]); it is exactly
in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that the converse holds ([[thm-heine-borel-rn]]).

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: If $g=0$, [F6] gives $0\ge2m(f(x)-f^*)$; since $f(x)\ge f^*$ and $m>0$, $f(x)=f^*$, and uniqueness gives $x=x^*$. Now assume $g\ne0$ and put $r(t):=x-tg$ for $t\ge0$. [F3] gives $\phi'(0)=-\|g\|_2^2<0$ for $\phi(t):=f(r(t))$. Openness of $U$ and this strict derivative provide a sufficiently small $t>0$ with $r(t)\in U$ and $f(r(t))<f(x)\le f(x_0)$, so $S:=\{t\ge0:r(t)\in K\}$ is nonempty.

By [F4], $f$ is convex on $V$, so its sublevel set $K$ is convex because $K\subset V$. By [F7], $K$ is closed and bounded. The affine map $r$ is continuous since $\|r(s)-r(t)\|_2=|s-t|\|g\|_2$, so [F8] makes $S=r^{-1}(K)\cap[0,\infty)$ closed. Boundedness gives $c\in\mathbb R^d$ and $R_0>0$ with $K\subset B(c,R_0)$; hence $\|y\|_2\le\|c\|_2+R_0=:R$ on $K$. For $t\in S$, the triangle inequality [F11] yields $t\|g\|_2=\|x-r(t)\|_2\le\|x\|_2+R$. Thus $S$ is bounded and compact by [F9].

The continuous restriction of $\phi$ to the nonempty compact set $S$ attains a minimum $t_*\in S$ by [F10]. Since $0\in S$, we have $f(r(t_*))\le f(x)$. Every feasible ray parameter $t$ with $r(t)\in U$ but $t\notin S$ has $f(r(t))>f(x_0)\ge f(x)\ge f(r(t_*))$, so $t_*$ is a global feasible-ray minimizer. If two distinct parameters minimized, their endpoints $y_1,y_2$ would be distinct because $g\ne0$; their midpoint $z$ lies in $K$ by step 2.1. Apply the strong-convexity inequality [F6] from $z$ to each endpoint and add: $f(z)\le(f(y_1)+f(y_2))/2-m\|y_1-y_2\|_2^2/8$, strictly below their common minimum. Thus the minimizer is unique and the output specified by [F1] is well-defined.

The small step in step 1.1 strictly decreases $f$, so the minimizer from step 3.1 has $t_*>0$. Since $r(t_*)\in K\subset U$ and $U$ is open, $t_*$ is interior to the feasible ray and $\phi'(t_*)=0$. Convexity of $V$ and step 2.1 put the segment $[x,r(t_*)]$ in $V$. By [F2], [F3], and the Hessian bounds, $m\|g\|_2^2\le\phi''(s)=g^TH_f(r(s))g\le M\|g\|_2^2$ on this segment, so $\phi'$ is strictly increasing. The mean-value theorem [F12] applied to $\phi'$ on $[0,t_*]$ gives $\|g\|_2^2=\phi'(t_*)-\phi'(0)=t_*\phi''(s_0)\le t_*M\|g\|_2^2$ for some $s_0\in(0,t_*)$. Since $g\ne0$, division yields $t_*\ge1/M$.

The candidate $t_0:=1/M$ lies in $[0,t_*]$ by step 4.1, so $r(t_0)$ lies on the segment from $x$ to $r(t_*)$ and belongs to $V$. The lower Hessian bound makes $\phi''(s)>0$ there; since $\phi'(t_*)=0$, $\phi'(s)<0$ for $0\le s<t_*$. Hence $f(r(t_0))\le f(x)\le f(x_0)$ and $r(t_0)\in K$. Taylor's formula [F5] with the upper Hessian bound gives $f(r(t_0))\le f(x)-M^{-1}\|g\|_2^2+(M/(2M^2))\|g\|_2^2=f(x)-\|g\|_2^2/(2M)$. By the minimization proved in step 3.1, $f(x_+)\le f(r(t_0))$.

Subtract $f^*$ in step 5.1 and use [F6] to get $f(x_+)-f^*\le f(x)-f^*-\|g\|_2^2/(2M)\le(1-m/M)(f(x)-f^*)$. The factor is nonnegative because $m\le M$. Exact steps never increase the objective, so every later iterate remains in $K$; applying the one-step bound successively proves the stated rate for all generated iterates.

boundaries.evidence: The initial point $x_0$ belongs to its own sublevel set $K$, and step 1.1 constructs a nonempty feasible ray portion when the gradient is nonzero.
The zero-gradient branch is handled separately in step 1.1: the gradient-gap inequality forces zero objective gap and uniqueness gives $x=x^*$.
The statement allows every finite dimension $d\ge1$; the proof uses Euclidean facts valid also for $d=1$.
The permitted endpoint $m=M$ gives contraction factor zero for every generated $k\ge1$; the Statement explicitly avoids a $0^0$ convention.
For nonzero gradient, step 4.1 proves the minimizer is interior to the feasible ray because $r(t_*)\in K\subset U$ and $U$ is open.
Step 1.1 makes $S$ nonempty, step 2.1 proves it compact, and the nonempty EVT hypothesis supplies a minimizer in step 3.1 without a choice principle.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all six steps and fifteen directly cited items. Stationary branch uses the curvature gap bound on V containing x and x*. For g!=0, strict descent gives a positive ray parameter in K; convexity on V makes K convex, while compactness gives closedness/boundedness of its ray preimage S. Heine–Borel is used on the real parameter line, even if the ambient objective dimension is zero (then g!=0 never occurs). EVT gives a ray minimizer; every feasible point outside K has strictly larger value. Strong convexity rules out two distinct minimizers. Openness gives interior ray stationarity; MVT on phi-prime yields t*>=1/M, putting the comparison trial inside V before Taylor is applied. The contraction and induction preserve K; m=M has zero factor only at k>=1, with no 0^0. Closed-preimage direction is choice-free; no AC or circular use of the oracle property found. Reader/refuter have no finding here.

citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]].

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with

For any trial $0<t\le T_N$, [F4] and $H_f\preceq MI$ on its segment give $f(x+tp)\le f(x)-t\lambda^2+(M/2)t^2\|p\|_2^2\le f(x)-at\lambda^2$, where the last inequality uses $\lambda^2\ge m\|p\|_2^2$. Starting the canonical local theorem [F2] at the first generated iterate in $B(x^*,\rho)$ shows that every later generated iterate remains in that ball. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained global minimum $f^*=f(x^*)$ at $x^*\in U$, and fix $x_0\in U$. Suppose the initial sublevel set $K:=\{y\in U:f(y)\le f(x_0)\}$ is compact and is contained in a convex open set $V\subseteq U$ on which

$$mI\preceq H_f(y)\preceq MI\qquad(y\in V)$$

for constants $0<m\le M$. For every current iterate $x\in K$, the oracle [[alg-exact-gradient-line-search-step]] is well-defined. If $g:=\nabla f(x)\ne0$ and $x_+$ is its returned point, then

$$f(x_+)-f^*\le\left(1-\frac mM\right)(f(x)-f^*).$$

If $g=0$, the oracle returns the unique minimizer $x=x^*$. Repeated exact steps from $x_0$ therefore satisfy

$$f(x_k)-f^*\le\left(1-\frac mM\right)^k(f(x_0)-f^*)$$

for every generated $k\ge1$. When $m=M$, the factor is zero for $k\ge1$; no $0^0$ convention is used. This is an objective-gap statement and does not identify an iterate-error bound without an additional curvature estimate.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained global minimum $f^*=f(x^*)$ at $x^*\in U$. Fix $x_0\in U$ and suppose $K:=\{y\in U:f(y)\le f(x_0)\}$ is compact. Let $V\subseteq U$ be convex and open, contain $K$ and every backtracking trial segment under consideration, and satisfy

$$mI\preceq H_f(y)\preceq MI\qquad(y\in V)$$

for $0<m\le M$. Run [[alg-gradient-descent]] in backtracking mode with Armijo parameter $a\in(0,1/2)$ and shrink factor $b\in(0,1)$. For every accepted update at a nonstationary iterate $x_k$, the accepted step satisfies

$$t_k\ge\tau:=\min\left\{1,\frac{2b(1-a)}{M}\right\},$$

and

$$f(x_{k+1})-f^*\le(1-2am\tau)(f(x_k)-f^*).$$

Consequently, for every generated $k\ge1$,

$$f(x_k)-f^*\le(1-2am\tau)^k(f(x_0)-f^*).$$

The factor lies in $(0,1)$. If the algorithm's caller-stop predicate fires, no later iterate is asserted. These are objective-gap bounds, not iterate-error bounds.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be continuously
Fréchet differentiable. The gradient $\nabla f(x)$ is the vector of partial
derivatives in the Euclidean coordinates, with the convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]; differentiability is the Fréchet
condition of [[def-real-frechet-derivative-on-real-and-complex-matrix-spaces]].

**Inputs:** an initial point $x_0\in U$; either a positive fixed-step
sequence $(t_k)_{k\ge0}$ or backtracking parameters $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and
$\beta\in(0,1)$; and an optional caller stopping predicate
$S(k,x,g)\in\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$, with
$S:\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\times U\times\mathbb R^d\to\{\mathrm{false},\mathrm{true}\}$.
If no predicate is supplied, use $S\equiv\mathrm{false}$. **Output:** when the
procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and the status
`stationary`, `caller-stop`, or `domain-failure`.
If no stopping status occurs, the sequence continues and there is no finite
return.
For example, an outer procedure's at-most-$M$-updates limit, for finite real
$M\ge0$, is implemented by $S(k,x,g):=(k+1>M)$.

At iteration $k$, where $k$ is the number of accepted updates so far and the
current iterate is $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$ and set $p_k:=-g_k$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $S(k,x_k,g_k)$ is true, return $(x_k,\texttt{caller-stop})$. Check this
   predicate at the current iterate after its gradient is computed and before
   any step is selected.
3. In fixed-step mode, set $t=t_k$. If $x_k+tp_k\notin U$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{domain-failure})$ without accepting that candidate.
4. In backtracking mode, start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by
   $\beta t$ until $x_k+tp_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+tp_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The fixed-step update map is $x\mapsto x-t_k\nabla f(x)$; at a stationary
point its value is $x$, which is the returned iterate. A backtracking search
that is reached at a nonstationary iterate is well-defined by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. The
procedure asserts no convergence or global-minimization property for an
arbitrary objective.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

derivations.claim: The Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(1,4)$, so $m=1$ and $M=4$; $x^*=(0,0)$ is the unique minimizer and $f(x_0)=5/2$. The sublevel set is closed by continuity and bounded because $\tfrac12u^2\le5/2$ and $2v^2\le5/2$ on it; it is compact by [F4]. The gradient at $x_0$ is $(1,4)$.

Along the negative-gradient ray, $\phi(t)=\tfrac12(1-t)^2+2(1-4t)^2$ and $\phi'(t)=65t-17$, so the unique minimizer is $t_*=17/65$. It gives $x_+=(48/65,-3/65)$ and $f(x_+)=234/845$. The theorem [F1] bounds the gap by $(1-1/4)(5/2)=15/8$, and $234/845<15/8$.

For Armijo, the first trial $t=1$ has candidate $(0,-3)$ with value $18$ and threshold $5/2-17/4=-7/4$, so it fails. The second trial $t=1/2$ has candidate $(1/2,-1)$ with value $17/8$ and threshold $3/8$, so it fails. At $t=1/4$, the candidate is $(3/4,0)$ with value $9/32<23/16$, the Armijo threshold; hence [F3] accepts $t=1/4$.

Here $\tau=\min\{1,2b(1-a)/M\}=3/16$, so [F2] gives the gap factor $1-2am\tau=29/32$. The actual new gap $9/32$ is below $(29/32)(5/2)=145/64$. The exact and Armijo calculations concern objective gaps; neither calculation supplies an iterate-error bound.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained global minimum $f^*=f(x^*)$ at $x^*\in U$, and fix $x_0\in U$. Suppose $K:=\{y\in U:f(y)\le f(x_0)\}$ is compact and is contained in a convex open $V\subseteq U$ that contains every Newton backtracking trial segment under consideration. For constants $0<m\le M$, assume

$$m\|v\|_2^2\le v^TH_f(y)v\le M\|v\|_2^2\qquad(y\in V,\ v\in\mathbb R^d).$$

Assume also that there are $R>0$ and $L_H\ge0$ with $B(x^*,R)\subseteq V$ and $\|H_f(y)-H_f(z)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le L_H\|y-z\|_2$ for $y,z\in B(x^*,R)$, where $\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}:=\sup_{\|v\|_2=1}\|Av\|_2$. Run [[alg-damped-newton]] with $a\in(0,1/2)$, $b\in(0,1)$, and positive decrement tolerance $\varepsilon$. Let $\rho>0$ and $C<\infty$ be constants furnished by [[thm-newton-local-quadratic-convergence-under-lipschitz-hessian]] for these data, and set

$$\tau_N:=\min\left\{1,\frac{2b(1-a)m}{M}\right\},\qquad q_N:=1-\frac{2am\tau_N}{M}.$$

For every accepted update before entry into $B(x^*,\rho)$,

$$f(x_{k+1})-f^*\le q_N(f(x_k)-f^*),\qquad 0<q_N<1.$$

Thus, after finitely many such updates the method either has stopped at its positive decrement test or has entered $B(x^*,\rho)$. More explicitly, if $\varepsilon<m^2\rho^2/(2M)$, the decrement test cannot stop outside that ball, so the method reaches it after finitely many accepted updates. Once in this ball, every later attempted update has step $t_k=1$ and satisfies

$$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|_2\le C\|x_k-x^*\|_2^2.$$

The last assertion is conditional on the decrement test not stopping first. No post-stop iterate or update is asserted. This is a strongly convex objective result; it does not apply to arbitrary vector roots or indefinite Hessians.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be twice
continuously Fréchet differentiable. Write $g(x)=\nabla f(x)$ and
$H(x)=\nabla^2 f(x)$ using [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The Hessian is symmetric by
[[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

**Inputs:** $x_0\in U$, a Newton-decrement tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and
line-search parameters $\alpha\in(0,1/2)$ and $\beta\in(0,1)$. **Output:**
when the procedure stops, return the last valid iterate $x_k$ and one of the
statuses `stationary`, `decrement`, or
`positive-definite solve unavailable`.
If none of these stopping conditions occurs, the sequence continues and there
is no finite return.

At iteration $k$ with current iterate $x_k$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
2. If $H_k:=H(x_k)$ is not positive definite, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{positive-definite solve unavailable})$ without a Newton
   update. Otherwise compute its Cholesky factorization $H_k=L_kL_k^T$, solve
   $L_kw=-g_k$ and $L_k^Tp_k=w$, and set
   $$\lambda_k^2:=-\langle g_k,p_k\rangle=g_k^TH_k^{-1}g_k>0.$$
3. Before line search, if $\lambda_k^2/2\le\varepsilon$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{decrement})$. This is the Newton-decrement stopping test.
4. Start with $t=1$ and repeatedly replace $t$ by $\beta t$ until
   $x_k+t p_k\in U$ and
   $f(x_k+t p_k)\le f(x_k)+\alpha t\,\langle g_k,p_k\rangle$.
5. Set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t p_k$ and continue at iteration $k+1$.

The Cholesky factor exists and is unique when the symmetric Hessian is positive
definite by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Its positive diagonal makes both triangular solves unique. The backtracking
branch terminates whenever it is reached, since $g_k\ne0$ and $H_k$ is
positive definite, by
[[lem-armijo-backtracking-terminates-for-strict-descent-directions]]. This
procedure makes no global-optimality claim.

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let
$f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$.
Use the Hessian convention of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]].
Suppose $x^*\in U$ is an interior critical point,
$H(x^*):=\nabla^2f(x^*)$
is positive definite, and for some $R>0$, $K\ge0$ the ball $B(x^*,R)$ lies
in $U$ and
$$\|H(x)-H(y)\|_{\rm op}\le K\|x-y\| \qquad(x,y\in B(x^*,R)).$$
Fix any Newton-decrement tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ and the Armijo parameters
$0<\alpha<1/2$ and $0<\beta<1$ in [[alg-damped-newton]]. There are
$\rho>0$ and $C<\infty$ such that every generated iterate from a start
$x_0\in B(x^*,\rho)$ remains in this ball. At each generated nonstationary
iterate $x_k$ for which the algorithm's decrement test satisfies
$\lambda_k^2/2>\varepsilon$ and a Newton update is therefore attempted, the
line search accepts the full step $t_k=1$ and
$$\|x_{k+1}-x^*\|\le C\|x_k-x^*\|^2.$$
If the decrement test stops the procedure, no next iterate or update bound is
asserted at that point.
Here $\lambda_k^2=\nabla f(x_k)^TH(x_k)^{-1}\nabla f(x_k)$ is the decrement
computed by [[alg-damped-newton]].
This is a local statement; it supplies no global optimum or convergence
claim for a nonconvex objective.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ have second partial derivatives. Its **Hessian** at $a\in U$ is the matrix $H_f(a)=(\partial_i\partial_j f(a))_{i,j<m}$ in the matrix space of [[def-matrix-space]], using the multi-index notation of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. A point $a$ is **critical** when its gradient $\nabla f(a)$ is zero, with the gradient convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

derivations.claim: Differentiation gives $g(x)=x+10x/\sqrt{1+x^2}$, $H(x)=1+10/(1+x^2)^{3/2}$, and $H'(x)=-30x/(1+x^2)^{5/2}$. Thus $1\le H(x)\le11$, $g(x)$ has the sign of $x$, and $x^*=0$ is the unique minimizer. Also $|H'(x)|\le30$, since $|x|\le1+x^2\le(1+x^2)^{5/2}$; [F4] makes $H$ globally $30$-Lipschitz. The initial sublevel set is closed by continuity and bounded because $f(x)\ge x^2/2$, hence compact by [F5].

At $x_0=2$, $g=2+4\sqrt5$, $H=1+2/\sqrt5$, and the Newton direction is $p=-g/H=30-16\sqrt5$. Its decrement is $\lambda^2=g^2/H=260-88\sqrt5>62$, since $5<81/16$ gives $\sqrt5<9/4$; hence the positive tolerance test does not stop before the first line search.

Step 1.1 gives $g(0)=0$, $H(0)=11>0$, and a $30$-Lipschitz Hessian on $B(0,1)$, so [F3] applies there; we directly verify the local radius $\rho=10^{-6}$ and constant $C=10$. For $0<|x|\le\rho$, $H(x)\ge1$ and $|g(x)|\le11|x|$, so the Newton direction $p=-g(x)/H(x)$ satisfies $|p|\le11|x|$. Every point $\xi$ between $x$ and $x+p$ therefore satisfies $|H(\xi)-H(x)|\le30|p|\le330\rho$. Since $330\rho=33/100000<49/50=1-2a$ and $H(x)\ge1$, we have $H(\xi)\le H(x)+330\rho\le2(1-a)H(x)$. Taylor's formula [F7] and $g(x)p=-H(x)p^2$ now give $f(x+p)-f(x)-ag(x)p=-(1-a)H(x)p^2+H(\xi)p^2/2\le0$, so the full step passes Armijo. Also $x+p=(xH(x)-g(x))/H(x)=-10x^3/((1+x^2)^{3/2}H(x))$, hence $|x+p|\le10|x|^3\le10|x|^2$ because $|x|\le\rho<1$, and $|x+p|\le10\rho^2|x|<\rho$ since $10\rho^2=10^{-11}<1$. Thus $C=10$ and this $\rho$ give a directly verified invariant local ball and quadratic bound whenever the decrement test permits an update.

The full-step point is $x_1=32-16\sqrt5$, whose absolute value exceeds $2$ because $289/64<5$ gives $\sqrt5>17/8$. The objective is even and strictly increasing as a function of $|x|>0$, so $f(x_1)>f(2)$; its Armijo threshold $f(2)+agp=f(2)-a\lambda^2$ is smaller than $f(2)$, and the unit step fails.

The half-step point is $x_{1/2}=17-8\sqrt5=-r$, where $0<r=8\sqrt5-17<1$: indeed $289/64<5<324/64$ implies $17/8<\sqrt5<9/4$. Thus $f(x_{1/2})=r^2/2+10\sqrt{1+r^2}<1/2+10\sqrt2<31/2$, using $2<9/4$ and so $\sqrt2<3/2$, while $f(2)=2+10\sqrt5>22$ because $\sqrt5>2$. The objective drop exceeds $13/2$. The half-step Armijo decrease required is $q/200$, where $q=\lambda^2<84$ because $\sqrt5>2$, so $q/200<21/50<13/2$. Hence $t=1/2$ passes, and it is accepted after the failed unit trial.

Choose $V=\mathbb R$, which contains every trial segment and $B(0,1)$. By step 1.1 the global Hessian bounds are $m=1$, $M=11$, and the decrement threshold in [F1] is $m^2\rho^2/(2M)=10^{-12}/22$. The chosen $\varepsilon=10^{-16}$ is smaller, since $22<10^4$ gives $10^{-16}<10^{-12}/22$, so the decrement test cannot stop outside $B(0,\rho)$. The first accepted step was the damped half-step in step 2.3; [F1] now gives finite entry into the local ball, followed by unit quadratic updates whenever the decrement test does not stop.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained interior global minimizer $x^*$, and suppose $H_f(x)\succeq\mu I$ on $U$ for some $\mu>0$. For a candidate $\widetilde x\in U$, let $\widehat g\in\mathbb R^d$ be a computed gradient vector. If independently verified bounds

$$\|\widehat g\|_2\le\eta,\qquad \|\widehat g-\nabla f(\widetilde x)\|_2\le\delta$$

hold for $\eta,\delta\ge0$, then

$$\|\widetilde x-x^*\|_2\le\frac{\eta+\delta}{\mu}.$$

The residual $\eta$ and discrepancy $\delta$ are mathematical hypotheses. A software stopping flag alone establishes neither bound.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

derivations.claim: The Hessian is $\operatorname{diag}(10^{-8},1)$, so the unique minimizer is $x^*=(0,0)$ and the strong-convexity constant is $\mu=10^{-8}$. At $\widetilde x=(1,0)$, $\nabla f(\widetilde x)=(10^{-8},0)$, so $\eta=\|\nabla f(\widetilde x)\|_2=10^{-8}$ and the true distance is $\|\widetilde x-x^*\|_2=1$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $f\in C^2(U,\mathbb R)$ have an attained interior global minimizer $x^*$, and suppose $H_f(x)\succeq\mu I$ on $U$ for some $\mu>0$. For a candidate $\widetilde x\in U$, let $\widehat g\in\mathbb R^d$ be a computed gradient vector. If independently verified bounds

$$\|\widehat g\|_2\le\eta,\qquad \|\widehat g-\nabla f(\widetilde x)\|_2\le\delta$$

hold for $\eta,\delta\ge0$, then

$$\|\widetilde x-x^*\|_2\le\frac{\eta+\delta}{\mu}.$$

The residual $\eta$ and discrepancy $\delta$ are mathematical hypotheses. A software stopping flag alone establishes neither bound.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

derivations.claim: On $U=\mathbb R$, $f$ is $C^2$ and $f''(x)=1$, so $\mu=1$. Thus $\nabla f(\widetilde x)=1/10$, and the computed residual is $\eta=|\widehat g|=1/50$. The independently verified discrepancy is $\delta=|1/50-1/10|=2/25$. The actual distance is $|\widetilde x-x^*|=1/10$.
The certificate [F1] gives $(\eta+\delta)/\mu=(1/50+2/25)=1/10$, exactly the actual distance. If the discrepancy were omitted, the proposed bound $1/50$ would be false.

boundaries.evidence: The real line and candidate are explicit, and the quadratic has the stated attained minimizer; the example is nonempty by construction.
Both the computed vector $1/50$ and true gradient $1/10$ are nonzero in step 1.1; the example also retains a nonzero discrepancy.
The example is one-dimensional and uses absolute value as its Euclidean norm in steps 1.1–2.1.
Step 1.1 proves that the quadratic has $\mu=1>0$; the computed residual and discrepancy are positive and finite, with no singular-curvature case.
Step 2.1 shows the complete certificate equals the true endpoint distance $1/10$, whereas omitting the discrepancy gives the false smaller value $1/50$.
Every object and discrepancy is evaluated explicitly in step 1.1; no minimizer or error bound is chosen nonconstructively.

derivations.claim: Integrating gives $f(x)=(x^5-(x-1)^5)/5$, hence $f'(x)=x^4-(x-1)^4$ and $f''(x)=12(x-1/2)^2+1\ge1$. Thus $\mu=1$ is valid and the minimizer is $x^*=1/2$.

At $\widetilde x=3/5$, the true gradient is $f'(3/5)=13/125=104/1000$. The two midpoint nodes are $1/4$ and $3/4$, so the composite midpoint estimate is $\widehat g=\tfrac12\bigl(4(7/20)^3+4(-3/20)^3\bigr)=79/1000$. Therefore the computed residual is $\eta=79/1000$ and the exact discrepancy is $\delta=|104/1000-79/1000|=1/40=25/1000$.

The actual distance is $|3/5-1/2|=1/10=100/1000$. By [F1] the certificate is $(\eta+\delta)/\mu=104/1000$, which is valid and close to the actual distance. The objective's inner integral was evaluated approximately, so its gradient discrepancy was not inferred from the residual.
