citations.quote:
For $y'=f(t,y)$, take the shared explicit stages
$$K_1=f(t_n,y_n),\qquad K_2=f(t_n+h,y_n+hK_1).$$
The Euler member is $Y_E=y_n+hK_1$ and the Heun explicit trapezoidal member is $Y_H=y_n+\frac h2(K_1+K_2)$. Their embedded difference is $Y_H-Y_E=\frac h2(K_2-K_1)$. The local orders are proved separately. In [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]] notation, the common tableau has $c=(0,1)$, $A_{21}=1$, high weights $(1/2,1/2)$ and low weights $(1,0)$.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Fix one initial value problem and initial state. Let $D_p(h):=\widehat Y(h)-y(t+h)$ be the low member's one-step defect and $D_{p+1}(h):=Y(h)-y(t+h)$ the high member's defect, using the same exact initial state and step start. Suppose, as $h\downarrow0$,
$$D_p(h)=a h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2}),\qquad D_{p+1}(h)=O(h^{p+2})$$
for a fixed vector $a\in\mathbb R^d$. Here $O(h^r)$ for a vector means a remainder whose Euclidean norm is at most $C h^r$ for all sufficiently small positive $h$. Then $\widehat Y(h)-Y(h)=a h^{p+1}+O(h^{p+2})$. If $a\ne0$, the estimator satisfies $E(h)/\|D_p(h)\|_2\to1$. If $a=0$, these hypotheses do not imply that this ratio tends to one or that the estimator is nonzero; the Euler–Heun pair on $y\prime=t^2$, $y(0)=0$, has ratio $3/2$ as computed below.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Define $F(s):=f(s,y(s))$. On the open segment, [F3] gives $F'(s)=\partial_t f(s,y(s))+D_yf(s,y(s))f(s,y(s))$, which extends continuously to $s=t$ with value $g$. For each component and $0<u\le h$, the mean value theorem [F6] on $[t,t+u]$ shows its secant slope equals $F_i'(c_i)$ for some $t<c_i<t+u$; as $u\downarrow0$ this tends to $g_i$. Thus the right derivative of $F$ at $t$ is $g$, so $y''(t)=g$. Since $f$ is $C^2$, differentiating the displayed formula on the open segment shows $F''$ is bounded there and extends continuously to the endpoints; hence $y'''=F''$ is bounded on the segment. For a coordinate $y_i$ and $0<u\le h$, let $R_i(u):=y_i(t+u)-y_i(t)-u y_i'(t)-\frac12u^2y_i''(t)$, set $C_i:=R_i(u)/u^3$, and put $G_i(v):=y_i(t+v)-y_i(t)-v y_i'(t)-\frac12v^2y_i''(t)-C_iv^3$ on $[0,u]$. Then $G_i(0)=G_i(u)=G_i'(0)=G_i''(0)=0$. Three successive applications of Rolle's theorem [F6] give $G_i'''(\xi_i)=0$ for some $0<\xi_i<u$, so $R_i(u)=y_i'''(t+\xi_i)u^3/6$. At $u=0$ the remainder is zero. Applying this to $u=h$ and every $u=\theta h$, and using the common derivative bounds and finite dimension, proves both the endpoint expansion and the uniform-in-$\theta$ expansion in the Statement.

For fixed $h$, the segment from $(t,y_0)$ to the Euler stage $(t+h,y_0+hK_1)$ lies in the compact convex time-state set. Since that set lies in an open neighborhood where $f$ is $C^2$, compactness gives a smaller open convex neighborhood of the segment on which the Taylor theorem [F4] applies. Taylor expansion of each component of $f$ there along the increment $(h,hK_1)$ has linear term $h\partial_t f+hD_yf K_1=hg$ and a second-derivative remainder $O(h^2)$, uniformly by the boundedness assumption. Therefore $K_2=K_1+hg+O(h^2)$. Substitution into [F1] gives $Y_E=y_0+hK_1$ and $Y_H=y_0+hK_1+\frac12h^2g+O(h^3)$.

Subtract the exact expansion in step 1.1 to obtain the two defect formulas and subtract the Euler output from the Heun output to obtain the estimator expansion. These are uniform $O(h^2)$ and $O(h^3)$ defect bounds, so [F2] gives the stated local orders. For $p=1$, the Euler defect coefficient is $-g/2$ and the Heun defect is $O(h^3)$; if $g\ne0$, [F5] gives the ratio-one conclusion. If $g=0$, both leading coefficients vanish and [F5] supplies no such inference.

boundaries.evidence: Statement uses d>=1 and a compact convex starting/stage neighborhood containing the actual initial point; this is not an empty set of starting data.
Proof step 3.1 treats g=0 separately and withholds the ratio-one conclusion; no norm of g is divided out in that branch.
Statement: Proof steps 1.1–2.1 apply Taylor componentwise and include a one-dimensional ODE, with the same time derivative and scalar state derivative in g.
Proof step 3.1 keeps the defect orders when g vanishes but states that the estimator ratio does not follow; bounded common derivatives and a common admissible h0 remain required for uniformity.
Statement gives both endpoint and uniform-in-theta expansions; proof step 1.1 uses one-sided derivatives and Rolle on the closed short segment, so theta=0 and theta=1 are included.

boundaries.reason: The short solution segment and fixed two-stage outputs are supplied; the componentwise Taylor remainder estimates use finite-dimensional bounds rather than a choice function.
The local-order result gives asymptotic expansions under C2 bounds and one sufficient nonvanishing coefficient for ratio one; it is not an order characterization of arbitrary pairs.
Observed ratio one or second-order Heun error is not claimed to recover the common compact-neighborhood or bounded-derivative hypotheses.

risk_review.notes: Reviewed all three steps and six suppliers. Along the exact path C2 f yields bounded continuous y triple derivative, including one-sided endpoints. The explicit Rolle auxiliary function has G(0)=G(u)=Gprime(0)=Gsecond(0)=0; three MVT applications give remainder ytriple(xi)*u^3/6. The Euler-stage increment lies in a compact convex set and has a small open convex neighborhood for scalar component Taylor. Common bounds give uniform theta and compact-start estimates with a common admissible h0. Defect signs and Heun cancellation agree; ratio is asserted only for g!=0. Accepted reader repair including the added uniform within-step expansion. The only direct result consumer is dense output; its new F2 uses exactly the stronger supplier statement, with no outside consumer repair needed.

citations.quote:
Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, rational times $a<T$, a rational initial vector $y_0$, and an ODE field $f$ represented by a finite acyclic expression DAG with rational constants, time/state inputs, and only $+,-,\times,\div$ nodes. Its domain consists of points where every division is defined. Write $D_yf$ for the matrix of partial derivatives with respect to the state coordinates. A **finite rational residual-tube certificate** consists of the following exact rational data:

1. A finite partition $a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$. On each panel $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, a vector polynomial $U_j(t)$ with dyadic (hence rational) coefficients, whose neighboring endpoint values agree exactly. These stored coefficients define the actual reconstruction, including any endpoint correction or rounded stage value used by an implementation.
2. For each panel, a closed rational state box $X_j\subset\mathbb R^d$, rational bounds $L_j\ge0$, $\rho_j\ge0$, a rational $d_j\ge0$, and a polynomial radius $R_j(t)$ with rational coefficients. The radius polynomials agree at neighboring endpoints. For a panel's finite rational subdivision, the intended inequalities are $R_j(t)>0$, $R'_j(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j>0$, and $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$.
3. A finite rational subdivision of every panel, with exact endpoint coverage, no gaps, and pairwise-disjoint interiors. It supplies cells on which each required range test below is performed. Rational cell endpoints and constants are enclosed by directed outward rounding to finite dyadic endpoints before interval evaluation; an unrepresentable or overflowing conversion cannot validate.
4. An initial check target $d_0\ge0$ with $\sum_i(U_0(a)_i-(y_0)_i)^2\le d_0^2$ and $d_0<R_0(a)$.

The certificate is **validated** only if outward-rounded real-interval evaluation on every supplied cell proves all three radius/tube inequalities, the range inclusion in $X_j$, that every division denominator in the field and its state derivatives excludes zero on the time-state box $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d \sup|U'_{j,i}-f_i(t,U_j(t))|^2\le\rho_j^2,\qquad \sum_{i,k=1}^d \sup|\partial_{y_k}f_i(t,y)|^2\le L_j^2$$
there. Here each supremum is replaced in the check by the maximum absolute endpoint of a finite outward interval enclosure; the residual expression is evaluated at the actual polynomial $U_j$, so interpolation, stage, and storage errors already present in that reconstruction are included. Strict inequalities must have a certified positive interval lower endpoint; an inconclusive, nonfinite, unsupported, or failed test is not validation.

This format certifies only rational expression fields and polynomial reconstructions using the stated finite checks. It uses real intervals, not complex rectangles or balls, and does not claim an evaluator for transcendental functions or general library floating-point operations. The page proves the soundness of a validated certificate separately.

The finite DAG and real-interval conventions are those of [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] and [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]].

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open in the metric induced by its Euclidean norm, let $a\in U$, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is **totally differentiable at $a$** when there is a linear map $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^n$ ([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) such that for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ for which

$$\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2\le\varepsilon\|h\|_2\qquad\text{whenever }a+h\in U\text{ and }\|h\|_2<\delta.$$

The map $L$, when it exists, is denoted $Df(a)$ and called the **total derivative**. Equivalently, $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+r(h)$ with the displayed remainder estimate for every $\varepsilon>0$. At $h=0$ the remainder is zero because $L0=0$.

For $m\ge1$, openness of $U$ provides admissible nonzero increments arbitrarily near zero, and dividing the estimate by $\|h\|_2>0$ gives the usual notation

$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\|f(a+h)-f(a)-Lh\|_2}{\|h\|_2}=0,$$

where the quotient is considered for $h\ne0$ with $a+h\in U$. Conversely this punctured normwise limit gives the estimate above (using a smaller positive tolerance if necessary). Thus the positive-dimensional definition is unchanged. This is the multivariate normwise remainder condition; no limit at an isolated point is asserted.

When $m=0$, the Euclidean zero space consists only of $0$, so $a=0$ and $U=\{0\}$; its Euclidean norm and induced metric exist by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]. The unique linear map $L:\mathbb R^0\to\mathbb R^n$ sends $0$ to $0$, and its remainder is identically zero. It is therefore the total derivative by the displayed estimate, with any $\delta>0$. When $n=0$, the unique map $f$ and the unique linear map into $\mathbb R^0$ likewise have zero remainder, in every source dimension.

derivations.claim: Order the finite acyclic graph topologically. A constant node defines a constant smooth function with derivative zero; an input node is a coordinate projection with its coordinate derivative. Assume inductively that the parent nodes define $C^1$ functions with their assigned derivatives.

For an addition or subtraction node, [F2] gives the sum or difference of the parent derivatives. For a product node, apply its bounded-bilinear product rule to real multiplication, which is bounded by $|ab|\le|a||b|$, to obtain $vDu+uDv$. These derivatives are continuous because the parent values and derivatives are continuous.

At a division node write $u_0=u(x)$, $v_0=v(x)
e0$, $A=Du(x)$, $B=Dv(x)$, and $\Delta u=Ah+r_u$, $\Delta v=Bh+r_v$, where $r_u,r_v=o(\|h\|_2)$ by [F6]. Continuity of $v$ keeps $v_0+\Delta v
e0$ near $x$. Put $L(h)=v_0Ah-u_0Bh$ and $R=v_0r_u-u_0r_v$. Direct algebra gives $ rac{u(x+h)}{v(x+h)}- rac{u_0}{v_0}- rac{L(h)}{v_0^2}= rac{v_0^2R-v_0L(h)\Delta v}{v_0^3(v_0+\Delta v)}$. Here $R=o(\|h\|_2)$, $L(h)=O(\|h\|_2)$, and $\Delta v=O(\|h\|_2)$, while the denominator stays bounded away from zero. Thus the right side is $o(\|h\|_2)$, so the quotient derivative is $(v_0Du(x)-u_0Dv(x))/v_0^2$. Its formula is continuous wherever $v
e0$.

Induction through the topological order, using steps 2.1–2.2, proves that every node is $C^1$ with its recursively assigned derivative, so the root derivative is correct. Continuity and nonvanishing of the finitely many denominator functions give a ball around the input on which all denominators stay nonzero. Shrink it so every partial derivative of every root component is bounded in absolute value by a common finite $M$, using continuity at the center and the finite number of entries. For two points $u,v$ in this convex ball, apply [F4] to each scalar component along $v+s(u-v)$: its derivative has magnitude at most $M\sum_j|u_j-v_j|\le M\sqrt{d+1}\|u-v\|_2$ by [F5]. Combining the finitely many component bounds gives a Lipschitz constant for the root map. Thus the field is locally Lipschitz.

For one Heun step from $(t_n,y_n)$ of size $h$ with stages $K_1,K_2$ as in [[def-heun-euler-embedded-runge-kutta-pair]], define its quadratic continuous extension for $0\le\theta\le1$ by
$$P_n(\theta):=y_n+h\left(\theta K_1+\tfrac12\theta^2(K_2-K_1)\right).$$
It has $P_n(0)=y_n$ and $P_n(1)=Y_H$, the accepted Heun endpoint. It is a separate within-step approximation; its order is analyzed independently of the endpoint order.

For $y'=f(t,y)$, take the shared explicit stages
$$K_1=f(t_n,y_n),\qquad K_2=f(t_n+h,y_n+hK_1).$$
The Euler member is $Y_E=y_n+hK_1$ and the Heun explicit trapezoidal member is $Y_H=y_n+\frac h2(K_1+K_2)$. Their embedded difference is $Y_H-Y_E=\frac h2(K_2-K_1)$. The local orders are proved separately. In [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]] notation, the common tableau has $c=(0,1)$, $A_{21}=1$, high weights $(1/2,1/2)$ and low weights $(1,0)$.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f$ be $C^2$ on an open neighborhood of a compact convex time-state set containing the initial point, the short exact solution segment, and the Euler stage points. Assume the first and second derivatives of $f$ are bounded there. For the exact solution $y'=f(t,y)$ starting from $y(t)=y_0$, put
$$g:=\partial_t f(t,y_0)+D_yf(t,y_0)f(t,y_0).$$
Here $\partial_t f$ is the time derivative and $D_yf$ is the Jacobian in the state variables. The notation $O(h^k)$ means a norm bounded by a constant times $h^k$ for sufficiently small positive $h$, uniformly over the compact starting set when stated. For all sufficiently small $h>0$, the Euler and Heun one-step values in [[def-heun-euler-embedded-runge-kutta-pair]] satisfy
$$Y_E-y(t+h)=-\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-y(t+h)=O(h^3),\qquad Y_H-Y_E=\tfrac12h^2g+O(h^3).$$
Moreover, uniformly for $0\le\theta\le1$,
$$y(t+\theta h)=y_0+\theta hK_1+\tfrac12\theta^2h^2g+O(h^3),\qquad K_1=f(t,y_0).$$
For a family of starting points, assume one common $h_0>0$ for which all exact segments and stage points stay in the same neighborhood. Under this condition the estimates are uniform over the compact starting set because the derivative bounds are common. Thus Euler has local order one and Heun has local order at least two on that set. If $g\ne0$, the embedded norm estimates Euler's defect asymptotically with ratio one; when $g=0$, that ratio conclusion does not follow from these orders.

derivations.claim: From [F1] and [F2], $\frac h2(K_2-K_1)=\frac12h^2g+O(h^3)$; since $h>0$, division by $h/2$ gives $K_2-K_1=hg+O(h^2)$. Substituting this into the defining formula for $P_n$ in [F1], and using $0\le\theta^2\le1$, gives $P_n(\theta)=y_n+\theta hK_1+\frac12\theta^2h^2g+O(h^3)$ uniformly in $\theta$.

The uniform exact-path expansion in [F2] has the same first two terms as step 1.1, with an $O(h^3)$ remainder independent of $\theta$. Subtracting it from the expansion of $P_n(\theta)$ proves the asserted uniform estimate.

Proof step 2.1 bounds |theta h|^3 by h^3, so zero theta or vanishing Taylor terms require no separate inverse or nondegeneracy assumption.
Proof steps 1.1 and 2.1 cover theta=0 and theta=1 through uniform bounds and exact endpoint formulas.

Fix a dimension $d\ge1$, rational times $a<T$, a rational initial vector $y_0$, and an ODE field $f$ represented by a finite acyclic expression DAG with rational constants, time/state inputs, and only $+,-,\times,\div$ nodes. Its domain consists of points where every division is defined. Write $D_yf$ for the matrix of partial derivatives with respect to the state coordinates. A **finite rational residual-tube certificate** consists of the following exact rational data:

1. A finite partition $a=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T$. On each panel $[t_j,t_{j+1}]$, a vector polynomial $U_j(t)$ with dyadic (hence rational) coefficients, whose neighboring endpoint values agree exactly. These stored coefficients define the actual reconstruction, including any endpoint correction or rounded stage value used by an implementation.
2. For each panel, a closed rational state box $X_j\subset\mathbb R^d$, rational bounds $L_j\ge0$, $\rho_j\ge0$, a rational $d_j\ge0$, and a polynomial radius $R_j(t)$ with rational coefficients. The radius polynomials agree at neighboring endpoints. For a panel's finite rational subdivision, the intended inequalities are $R_j(t)>0$, $R'_j(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j>0$, and $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$.
3. A finite rational subdivision of every panel, with exact endpoint coverage, no gaps, and pairwise-disjoint interiors. It supplies cells on which each required range test below is performed. Rational cell endpoints and constants are enclosed by directed outward rounding to finite dyadic endpoints before interval evaluation; an unrepresentable or overflowing conversion cannot validate.
4. An initial check target $d_0\ge0$ with $\sum_i(U_0(a)_i-(y_0)_i)^2\le d_0^2$ and $d_0<R_0(a)$.

The certificate is **validated** only if outward-rounded real-interval evaluation on every supplied cell proves all three radius/tube inequalities, the range inclusion in $X_j$, that every division denominator in the field and its state derivatives excludes zero on the time-state box $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, and
$$\sum_{i=1}^d \sup|U'_{j,i}-f_i(t,U_j(t))|^2\le\rho_j^2,\qquad \sum_{i,k=1}^d \sup|\partial_{y_k}f_i(t,y)|^2\le L_j^2$$
there. Here each supremum is replaced in the check by the maximum absolute endpoint of a finite outward interval enclosure; the residual expression is evaluated at the actual polynomial $U_j$, so interpolation, stage, and storage errors already present in that reconstruction are included. Strict inequalities must have a certified positive interval lower endpoint; an inconclusive, nonfinite, unsupported, or failed test is not validation.

This format certifies only rational expression fields and polynomial reconstructions using the stated finite checks. It uses real intervals, not complex rectangles or balls, and does not claim an evaluator for transcendental functions or general library floating-point operations. The page proves the soundness of a validated certificate separately.

The finite DAG and real-interval conventions are those of [[def-intervals-rectangles-and-complex-balls]] and [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]].

For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$; the denominator interval is strictly positive because at
least one coordinate interval excludes zero. Division multiplies by this
reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

Let $d\ge1$ and $a<T$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous, and let $y$ be an exact solution of $y'=f(t,y)$ on $[a,T]$. Let $U:[a,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous and $C^1$ on each member of a finite partition (continuously differentiable on each closed panel, with one-sided endpoint derivatives), with graph in $D$. Let $\ell,\rho:[a,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous on each partition interval, with one-sided endpoint values, and suppose on every open panel
$$\langle U-y,f(t,U)-f(t,y)\rangle\le\ell(t)\|U-y\|_2^2,\qquad \|U'(t)-f(t,U(t))\|_2\le\rho(t).$$
Then for every $t\in[a,T]$,
$$\|U(t)-y(t)\|_2\le e^{\int_a^t\ell(v)\,dv}\|U(a)-y(a)\|_2+\int_a^t e^{\int_s^t\ell(v)\,dv}\rho(s)\,ds.$$
The proof uses only finite-piece ordinary calculus and no choice axiom. The general absolutely continuous case is treated separately.

Let $d\ge1$ and $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable. There is no maximal solution $x:I\to\mathbb R^d$ of $x'=f(t,x)$ whose interval has a finite right endpoint $b$ and for which some $t_0\in I$, $t_0<b$, and compact set $C\subseteq D$ satisfy $(t,x(t))\in C$ for every $t\in[t_0,b)$. The compact tube condition supplies boundedness of $f$ along the graph and a limit point inside the open domain.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

derivations.claim: A certified return means each interval operation was finite and every listed inclusion and strict inequality passed. By [F2], all exact rational-DAG values and their derivative-DAG values lie in the checked intervals. Thus on each panel $f$ is defined on $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$. The residual interval tests bound each component's absolute value by its checked supremum, whose squared sum is at most $\rho_j^2$; [F12] and [F13] give $\|U'_j-f(t,U_j)\|_2\le\rho_j$. Define $\|A\|_F:=(\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^2)^{1/2}$; the Jacobian interval tests bound this sum by $L_j^2$, so [F13] gives $\|D_yf\|_F\le L_j$. The checker also proves $U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$. Its exact initial squared comparison and [F12]–[F13] give $\|U_0(a)-y_0\|_2\le d_0<R_0(a)$. For each coordinate, $|U_0(a)_i-(y_0)_i|^2\le\sum_k|U_0(a)_k-(y_0)_k|^2=\|U_0(a)-y_0\|_2^2$, so [F13] places $y_0$ in $U_0(a)+[-R_0(a),R_0(a)]^d\subseteq X_0$. Hence $(a,y_0)$ lies in the checked open ODE domain.

Fix $w=u-v$ and define $\phi(s)=\langle w,f(t,v+sw)\rangle$ for $0\le s\le1$. The segment stays in $X_j$ by convexity. By [F3] and bilinearity in [F12], $\phi'(s)=\langle w,D_yf(t,v+sw)w\rangle$. The bound in step 1.1 and rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|D_yf\,w\|_2\le\|D_yf\|_F\|w\|_2\le L_j\|w\|_2$, and [F7] then gives $|\phi\prime(s)|\le L_j\|w\|_2^2$. [F6] on $[0,1]$ yields $\phi(1)-\phi(0)=\langle u-v,f(t,u)-f(t,v)\rangle\le L_j\|u-v\|_2^2$. Thus the one-sided Lipschitz hypothesis in [F4] holds with $\ell=L_j$ whenever the exact and reconstructed states lie in the certified box.

Picard–Lindelöf applies locally by [F3], and [F8] gives a unique maximal solution through $(a,y_0)$. On any interval where it exists and lies in the checked panel boxes, apply [F4] panel by panel. Write $\delta_j(t):=R_j'(t)-L_jR_j(t)-\rho_j$, which is strictly positive by the checker. Integrating the scalar identity $R_j'=L_jR_j+\rho_j+\delta_j$ with the same integrating factor shows that the radius dominates the error bound strictly: the initial gap is positive because $d_0<R_0(a)$, and each panel adds the positive integral of $e^{\int_s^t L_j}\delta_j(s)$, using positivity of the exponential [F11] and the fundamental theorem [F10]. For $e=y-U_j$, each coordinate satisfies $|e_i|^2\le\sum_k|e_k|^2=\|e\|_2^2$, so [F13] gives $|e_i|\le\|e\|_2$; hence $\|e\|_2<R_j(t)$ implies $y(t)\in U_j(t)+[-R_j(t),R_j(t)]^d\subseteq X_j$. The comparison therefore applies up to any first exit and gives a strict radius bound there, ruling out that exit. At each panel endpoint the stored reconstructions and radii agree, so the strict inequality continues across the finite partition.

If the maximal solution ended before or at $T$, the no-first-exit conclusion in step 3.1 would keep its graph inside the finite union of the closed bounded boxes $[t_j,t_{j+1}]\times X_j$, which is compact by [F9] and lies in the rational field's open domain. All divisions stay away from zero there by step 1.1. This contradicts [F5], so the maximal solution reaches $T$. Applying the panelwise error estimate on the whole interval gives $\|y(t)-U_j(t)\|_2<R_j(t)$ and hence $y(t)\in X_j$ for every panel time. Uniqueness follows from local Lipschitz continuity in [F3] and the local uniqueness clause of Picard–Lindelöf.

The soundness theorem states certified implies a unique exact solution in the strict tube; it is not an equivalence between solvability and certification.

supplier_excerpts.quote:
Input a finite rational certificate of [[def-validated-residual-tube-certificate]], an outward-rounded real interval format, and the matching operation evaluator of [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. Return either `certified` or `inconclusive` by this finite procedure:

1. Parse and structurally check the rational field DAG, finite mesh, panel polynomials, state boxes, radius polynomials, rational bounds, and subdivisions. Reject malformed syntax, noncanonical/nonfinite numbers, gaps, nontrivial interior overlaps, endpoint mismatches, or a non-acyclic graph as `inconclusive`.
2. In topological order, construct the formal time/state derivative DAG for each field output by [[lem-rational-expression-derivative-recursion-correct]]. If any recursion node is unsupported, return `inconclusive`.
3. Convert each exact rational cell endpoint and constant to a directed outward dyadic interval. On each supplied time cell and panel box, evaluate the field, derivative DAG, reconstruction, its derivative, radius and strict-margin expressions using only outward-rounded real interval addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and rational constants. If any operation returns `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or `inconclusive`, return `inconclusive`.
4. Check exactly that the time cells cover each panel and that neighboring reconstruction/radius endpoints agree; verify the initial squared-error inequality separately. From interval endpoints check: each radius and each strict supersolution margin has strictly positive lower endpoint; the componentwise reconstruction-plus-radius boxes lie inside $X_j$; the residual component intervals satisfy the displayed squared-norm bound by $\rho_j^2$; all field and derivative denominator intervals exclude zero; and the squared Frobenius bound on the state Jacobian is at most $L_j^2$. Check the initial squared error bound and strict comparison $d_0<R_0(a)$ by exact rational arithmetic.
5. Return `certified` only when every check passes. Any failed inclusion or comparison returns `inconclusive` with the first failed check identifier. No automatic subdivision, transcendental evaluation, complex rectangle operation, or ball operation is performed.

The finite interval evaluator and its DAG interpretation are those of [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] and [[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. A separate theorem proves soundness of every `certified` result.

Squared residual/Jacobian/initial tests imply norm bounds by nonnegative square monotonicity. Convex box MVT and rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz give the required one-sided state Lipschitz bound. Strict initial gap and positive supersolution margin persist via the C1 panel integrating-factor identity; ||error||<R gives strict coordinate inequalities, hence an interior point of the radius cube and checked box, excluding first exit. For real intervals $X=[a,b]$ and $Y=[c,d]$, compute the displayed exact
endpoint formulas and round the lower endpoint down and the upper endpoint up
in the format of
[[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. If either exact
endpoint overflows, return `overflow` with the outward extended endpoints;
never substitute a finite endpoint for an overflow sentinel. Addition is
$[a+c,b+d]$, subtraction is $[a-d,b-c]$, and multiplication is
$[\min(ac,ad,bc,bd),\max(ac,ad,bc,bd)]$. Division is defined only when
$0\notin Y$ and is $X[1/d,1/c]$, with reciprocal endpoints computed as exact
rationals before outward rounding. Squaring is
$[0,\max(a^2,b^2)]$ when $0\in X$ and
$[\min(a^2,b^2),\max(a^2,b^2)]$ otherwise. Square root is defined only for
$X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and is enclosed by applying
[[alg-dyadic-square-root-bisection]] to the exact dyadic endpoints with
request $n=p$, where $p$ is the selected format precision, and rounding
outward for storage.

If $0\in Y$ for division, return `split-domain` with the two subdomains
$Y\cap(-\infty,0)$ and $Y\cap(0,\infty)$, or `entire` when the caller does not
request subdivision. No finite quotient interval is returned in this case.
An invalid square-root domain returns `domain-error` or an explicitly
restricted nonnegative subdomain.

Complex-rectangle addition, subtraction and multiplication use
$(x+iy)(u+iv)=(xu-yv)+i(xv+yu)$, applying the real interval operations to
each component. For a rectangle $X+iY$ excluding $0$, define its reciprocal by
$(X-iY)/(X^2+Y^2)$, computing the square hulls, their sum, and the
component quotient endpoint formulas as exact rationals before rounding the
final reciprocal components outward. The exact denominator interval is
strictly positive because at least one coordinate interval excludes zero;
do not round it before division, since underflow could introduce zero.
Propagate any final endpoint overflow. Division multiplies by this reciprocal.

For a ball $B(c,r)$, let $X_B=[\Re c-r,\Re c+r]$ and
$Y_B=[\Im c-r,\Im c+r]$ be its coordinate projection intervals. For a real
interval $J$, let $M(J)=\max(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$ and let $d(J)=0$ if
$0\in J$, otherwise $d(J)=\min(|\inf J|,|\sup J|)$. Put
$M_B=M(X_B)+M(Y_B)$ and $m_B=\max(d(X_B),d(Y_B))$. Then
$|z|\le M_B$ for every $z\in B(c,r)$ and $|z|\ge m_B$ for every such $z$.
Define ball addition and subtraction as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}+M_{B_2}))$, multiplication as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}M_{B_2}))$, and division as
$B(0,\operatorname{ru}(M_{B_1}/m_{B_2}))$ only when $m_{B_2}>0$. These
origin-centered output balls are conservative but inclusion-isotone. If
$m_{B_2}=0$, return `split-domain`, `entire`, or `inconclusive`; if a radius
overlows, return `overflow`.

For $y'=f(t,y)$, take the shared explicit stages
$$K_1=f(t_n,y_n),\qquad K_2=f(t_n+h,y_n+hK_1).$$
The Euler member is $Y_E=y_n+hK_1$ and the Heun explicit trapezoidal member is $Y_H=y_n+\frac h2(K_1+K_2)$. Their embedded difference is $Y_H-Y_E=\frac h2(K_2-K_1)$. The local orders are proved separately. In [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]] notation, the common tableau has $c=(0,1)$, $A_{21}=1$, high weights $(1/2,1/2)$ and low weights $(1,0)$.

Inputs are an IVP in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], $y'=f(t,y)$ on an open domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ with initial data $(t_0,y_0)\in D$ and requested interval $[t_0,T]$, where $t_0\le T$ and $d\ge1$; an initial proposal $0<h_{\rm init}\le h_{\max}$; an embedded pair with low order $p\ge1$ as in [[def-embedded-runge-kutta-pair-and-error-estimator]]; tolerances $\mathrm{atol}>0$ and $\mathrm{rtol}\ge0$; safety $0<\sigma<1$; scale bounds $0<\gamma_{\min}\le1\le\gamma_{\max}$; step bounds $0<h_{\min}\le h_{\max}$; and a positive integer attempt budget $N$.

**Output.** Return a record consisting of one of `success`, `failure`, `minimum-step-rejected`, or `attempt-budget-exhausted`, together with the accepted mesh $\mathcal A=((t_0,y_0),\ldots,(t_m,y_m))$. The mesh always contains the initial pair and every accepted endpoint; on `success`, $t_m=T$ and $y_m$ is the returned endpoint approximation. On any other status, $\mathcal A$ is the accepted prefix and $y_m$ is the last accepted approximation.

Every maximum and minimum below is over a displayed nonempty finite list of real numbers; existence follows from [[lem-finite-set-has-max]].

**Procedure.** Initialize $t:=t_0$, $y:=y_0$, $\mathcal A:=((t_0,y_0))$, and proposal $h_{\rm prop}:=h_{\rm init}$. If $t_0=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. For each attempt index $k=1,\ldots,N$, perform exactly the following steps:

1. Set $h:=\min(h_{\rm prop},h_{\max},T-t)$. The last term permits a final clipped step shorter than $h_{\min}$. If $h\le0$ before reaching $T$, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
2. Evaluate the shared stages in tableau order, checking before each evaluation that its time-state input lies in $D$. If a stage input is outside $D$, its evaluation is undefined, or its value is nonfinite, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Compute both pair outputs; if either output or any arithmetic needed to compute them is undefined, fails, or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$.
3. Define $s_i:=\mathrm{atol}+\mathrm{rtol}\max(|(y)_i|,|(Y)_i|)$ and $Q:=\max_i |(\widehat Y-Y)_i|/s_i$, where $Y$ is the high-order value and $\widehat Y$ the low-order value. If any scale or $Q$ operation fails or is nonfinite in the rounded realization, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. If $Q\le1$, first check $(t+h,Y)\in D$; if not, return `failure` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise accept: set $t:=t+h$, $y:=Y$, and append $(t,y)$ to $\mathcal A$. If $Q>1$, reject and retain $t,y,\mathcal A$.
4. If the attempt was accepted and $t=T$, return `success` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise, if it was rejected and $h\le h_{\min}$, return `minimum-step-rejected` with $\mathcal A$. These terminal checks precede the budget check, so a final accepted step that reaches $T$ succeeds and a rejection at the minimum step reports that safeguard.
5. If $k=N$, return `attempt-budget-exhausted` with $\mathcal A$. Otherwise compute
$$g=\begin{cases}\gamma_{\max},&Q=0,\\ \min(\gamma_{\max},\max(\gamma_{\min},\sigma /\sqrt[p+1]{Q})),&Q>0.\end{cases}$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ be continuously differentiable, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. Write $\nabla U$ for its Euclidean gradient, and let $\epsilon>0$.

For $a,b\in\mathbb R$, define the **force kick** and **drift shear**
$$K_a(q,p)=(q,p-a\nabla U(q)),\qquad D_b(q,p)=(q+bM^{-1}p,p).$$
The one-step leapfrog map is
$$\Phi_\epsilon=K_{\epsilon/2}\circ D_\epsilon\circ K_{\epsilon/2},$$
where composition is read right to left. For a finite integer $L\ge1$, its $L$-step map is $\Phi_\epsilon^L$. Define the momentum flip $R(q,p)=(q,-p)$ and the flipped proposal map $T_{\epsilon,L}=R\circ\Phi_\epsilon^L$.

Each kick and drift is a continuous bijection with inverse $K_{-a}$ or $D_{-b}$, respectively. These finite maps use only $\nabla U$ and do not require a solution of Hamilton's ODE. The classical derivative of a force kick is not part of this definition: for merely $U\in C^1$, $\nabla U$ need not be differentiable.

citations.quote:
Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.

$$F(q,p):=\bigl(\nabla_pH(q,p),-\nabla_qH(q,p)\bigr)=J\nabla H(q,p).$$

Given $z\in U$ and a signed step $h$, supply a candidate radius $\rho\ge0$. If no radius is supplied or $\rho<0$, return `branch-not-certified`. If the closed ball $\overline B(z,\rho)$ is certified not to lie in $U$, return `domain-failure`; if its containment in $U$ cannot be certified, return `branch-not-certified`. For a ball contained in $U$, supply certified bounds $M,L\ge0$ with
$$M\ge\sup_{W\in\overline B(z,\rho)}\|F(W)\|,\qquad L\ge\sup_{W\in\overline B(z,\rho)}\|DF(W)\|.$$
If either bound or its certificate is unavailable, or if either admissibility inequality $|h|M/2\le\rho$ or $|h|L/2<1$ fails, return `branch-not-certified`. Otherwise the **exact local implicit midpoint step** selects the unique $Z\in\overline B(z,\rho)$ satisfying
$$Z=z+\frac h2F(Z)$$
and returns $z^+=2Z-z$. The returned state is in $\mathbb R^{2d}$; a further step is admitted only when that state lies in $U$ and passes a new ball check.

For a finite iteration implementation of an admitted branch, input an output tolerance $\tau>0$ and an update budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$. Use $\theta=|h|L/2$ and proceed as follows.

1. Set $Z_0=z$. If $B=0$, return `inconclusive` with current stage iterate $Z_0$, approximate output $z$, and output-error bound $2\rho$.
2. If $B\ge1$, compute $Z_1=z+(h/2)F(Z_0)$ and set $d_1=\|Z_1-Z_0\|$.
3. For $k=1,\ldots,B$, set $b_k=\theta^k d_1/(1-\theta)$ and the output radius $r_k=2b_k$. If $r_k\le\tau$, return the approximation $2Z_k-z$ with output-error certificate $r_k$. Otherwise, if $k<B$, compute $Z_{k+1}=z+(h/2)F(Z_k)$ and continue. If the check fails at $k=B$, return `inconclusive` with current stage iterate $Z_B$, approximate output $2Z_B-z$, and output-error bound $2b_B$.

When $\theta=0$, use $\theta^k=0$ for $k\ge1$; the procedure never evaluates $0^0$. If a finite implementation cannot certify an input or an exact operation needed for these instructions, return `inconclusive` without a tolerance claim. $$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.

citations.quote:
1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

citations.quote: Let $X$ be a Banach space, $a<b$, and let $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$ in the sense of [[def-frechet-derivative-between-banach-spaces]]. If there is $C\ge0$ with $\|\varphi'(s)\| \le C$ for all $s\in(a,b)$, then $\|\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)\| \le C(b-a)$. In particular, if $\varphi$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ and $\varphi'=0$ there, then $\varphi$ is constant.

derivations.claim: Since $H\in C^2(U)$, the coordinate field $F$ is $C^1$. On the admitted closed ball, $T_z(W)=z+(h/2)F(W)$ maps the ball into itself because $\|T_z(W)-z\|\le |h|M/2\le\rho$. For $W,V$ in the ball, the curve $\gamma(t)=F(V+t(W-V))$ lies in it and [F6] gives $\|\gamma'(t)\|\le L\|W-V\|$; the mean-value inequality [F9] therefore gives $\|T_z(W)-T_z(V)\|\le\theta\|W-V\|$, where $\theta=|h|L/2<1$. The ball is nonempty and complete by [F7], so [F1] gives a unique fixed point $Z$, keeps all iterates in the ball, and gives $\|Z_k-Z\|\le b_k=\theta^k\|Z_1-Z_0\|/(1-\theta)$. Multiplication by two gives $\|(2Z_k-z)-(2Z-z)\|=2\|Z_k-Z\|\le2b_k$, and $Z\in\overline B(z,\rho)$ gives $\|(2Z-z)-z\|\le2\rho$. The convention $\theta^0=1$ makes the bound valid at $k=0$. If $\theta=0$, $T_z$ is constant on the ball, hence $Z_1=T_z(z)=T_z(Z)=Z$ and every later iterate equals $Z$; thus $b_k=0$ for $k\ge1$. These assertions require only the $C^2$ hypotheses.

For the remaining claims, assume the additional $C^3$ and uniform branch hypotheses. Fix an admitted initial value $z$ and let $z_j\to z$ through admitted initial values with selected roots $Z_j$. Since $\|Z_j-z_j\|\le\rho$ and $z_j\to z$, $(Z_j)$ is bounded. If $Z_j$ did not converge to $Z$, some subsequence would stay a positive distance from $Z$; by [F8] it would have a convergent subsequence $Z_{j_\ell}\to Z_*$. The bound $\|Z_{j_\ell}-z\|\le\rho+\|z_{j_\ell}-z\|$ puts $Z_*$ in $\overline B(z,\rho)\subset U$, and continuity in $Z_{j_\ell}=z_{j_\ell}+(h/2)F(Z_{j_\ell})$ gives $Z_*=z+(h/2)F(Z_*)$. The contraction in step 1.1 gives uniqueness of this fixed point in $\overline B(z,\rho)$, so $Z_*=Z$, a contradiction; hence $Z_j\to Z$. Now put $G(z,Z)=Z-z-(h/2)F(Z)$. At the selected root, $D_ZG=I-(h/2)A$ with $A=DF(Z)$. Since $\|(h/2)A\|<1$, this matrix is invertible by the Neumann series, and [F2] supplies a local $C^1$ root branch. The continuity just proved and the IFT's local uniqueness identify the selected roots with this branch at every nearby admitted initial value. Differentiating $G=0$ gives $D_zZ=(I-(h/2)A)^{-1}$ and hence $S:=D\Psi_h=(I-B)^{-1}(I+B),\qquad B=(h/2)A.$

Put $m=2d$ and $\delta=Z-z$. The admitted fixed-point equation gives $\|\delta\|\le |h|\|F(Z)\|/2\le |h|M/2$, hence $\delta=O(|h|)$ uniformly. Since $H\in C^3$, $F\in C^2$. Apply the scalar theorem [F4] to each $F_i$ along $[z,Z]$: $F_i(z+\delta)=F_i(z)+DF_i(z)\delta+R_i$, where $R_i=\tfrac12D^2F_i(z+\vartheta_i\delta)[\delta,\delta]$ for some $\vartheta_i\in(0,1)$. These points may differ with $i$. Bounded second derivatives on the tube give $|R_i|\le C_i\|\delta\|^2$, hence $\|R\|_2\le(\sum_{i=1}^m C_i^2)^{1/2}\|\delta\|^2$. Substitution into $\delta=(h/2)F(z+\delta)$ first gives $\delta=(h/2)F(z)+O(h^2)$ and then $\delta=(h/2)F(z)+(h^2/4)DF(z)F(z)+O(|h|^3)$. Thus $2Z-z=z+hF(z)+(h^2/2)DF(z)F(z)+O(|h|^3)$. For the exact flow, write $g_i(t)=(\varphi_t(z))_i$. By [F3] and [F6], $g_i^{(1)}=F_i(\varphi_t(z))$, $g_i^{(2)}=DF_i(\varphi_t(z))F(\varphi_t(z))$, and $g_i^{(3)}=D^2F_i(\varphi_t(z))[F(\varphi_t(z)),F(\varphi_t(z))]+DF_i(\varphi_t(z))DF(\varphi_t(z))F(\varphi_t(z))$ are defined, with the third derivative uniformly bounded on the controlled trajectories. Scalar Taylor in time gives $g_i(h)=z_i+hF_i(z)+(h^2/2)(DF(z)F(z))_i+(h^3/6)g_i^{(3)}(\eta_i h)$ for $h\ne0$, with possibly distinct $\eta_i\in(0,1)$. Each last term is bounded by $C_i'|h|^3$; summing their squares gives a Euclidean remainder bound $(\sum_{i=1}^m(C_i')^2)^{1/2}|h|^3$. The case $h=0$ is immediate. The exact flow therefore has the same terms through degree two as $2Z-z$, giving the uniform one-step defect $C|h|^3$ for either sign of $h$. No common Lagrange intermediate point for the vector is used.
By [F5], $A=J\nabla^2H(Z)$ and $A^TJ+JA=0$; therefore $B^TJ+JB=0$. Expanding both products gives $(I+B)^TJ(I+B)-(I-B)^TJ(I-B)=2(B^TJ+JB)=0$. Thus $(I-B)^TJ(I-B)=(I+B)^TJ(I+B)$.

From step 2.1, $S-I=h(I-B)^{-1}DF(Z)$, and $\|B\|\le h_0L/2\le1/2$ gives $S=I+hDF(Z)+O(h^2)$ uniformly. Also $\|Z-z\|\le |h|M/2$; Taylor's formula applied to the entries of $DF$ along the stipulated segments, with $D^2F$ uniformly bounded, gives $DF(Z)=DF(z)+O(|h|)$. Thus $D\Psi_h=I+hDF(z)+O(h^2)$ and, after decreasing $h_0$ if needed, $\|D\Psi_h\|\le1+L_1|h|$. For each $n$, split $e_{n+1}$ into the change of $\Psi_h$ between $z_n$ and $\varphi_{nh}(z_0)$ and the one-step defect at $\varphi_{nh}(z_0)$. Applying [F9] on the comparison segment and the local estimate of step 2.2 gives $e_{n+1}\le(1+L_1|h|)e_n+C|h|^3$; the flow law in [F3] identifies $\varphi_h(\varphi_{nh}(z_0))=\varphi_{(n+1)h}(z_0)$. Iteration and $(1+L_1|h|)^n\le e^{L_1T}$ when $n|h|\le T$ give $e_n\le e^{L_1T}e_0+CTe^{L_1T}|h|^2$.

The matrices $I-B$ and $I+B$ commute. Multiplying the equality in step 3.1 on the left by $(I-B)^{-T}$ and on the right by $(I-B)^{-1}$ yields $J=(I-B)^{-T}(I+B)^TJ(I+B)(I-B)^{-1}=S^TJS$. This proves the exact branch is symplectic.

Step 1.1 proves existence, uniqueness, convergence, and the stage and output certificates under the $C^2$ hypotheses. The implementation returns immediately for $B=0$; for $B\ge1$ its finite loop either meets the tolerance earlier or takes at most $B$ updates before its final inconclusive branch, and step 1.1 proves every reported radius valid. Under the additional $C^3$ and tube hypotheses, step 2.1 proves the exact branch's stated regularity, step 4.1 proves symplecticity, and steps 2.2 and 3.2 prove local second order and the finite-time error.

The returned map is the partial composition $D_h\circ K_h$ in the notation of [[def-local-leapfrog-domain-on-an-open-configuration-set]].

Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, let $V\in C^1(Q,\mathbb R)$, and let $M$ be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix. Use the force-kick $K_a$ and drift $D_b$ already defined in [[def-leapfrog-step-map]], with $U$ there replaced by $V$. The local kick is the restriction of $K_a$ to $Q\times\mathbb R^d$. The local drift is the restriction of $D_b$ to
$$\{(q,p):q\in Q,\ q+bM^{-1}p\in Q\}.$$

For a signed step $h$, the local leapfrog map is the restriction of $K_{h/2}\circ D_h\circ K_{h/2}$ to the states for which all three intermediate configurations lie in $Q$. Its output is defined only on that admitted set. This definition changes the configuration domain of the published map; it does not redefine the global leapfrog map or assert that the local map is complete.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open, $V\in C^3(Q)$, and $M$ symmetric positive definite. Set $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$ and $F(q,p)=(M^{-1}p,-\nabla V(q))$. Fix $T>0$ and $h=T/N$ with $N\ge1$. Suppose the exact solution, numerical states, all kick/drift intermediate states, and every line segment used below lie in one compact convex tube $K\Subset Q\times\mathbb R^d$, with the derivatives of $F$ through order two bounded there. For $z_0$ in that tube, write $e_n^E$ for the error of iterated kick-then-drift symplectic Euler and $e_n^V$ for the error of iterated local leapfrog relative to the exact solution at $t_n=nh$. Write $\Psi_h^E$ and $\Psi_h^V$ for their admitted one-step maps and $\varphi_h$ for the exact flow. For sufficiently small $h$, constants $C_E,C_V,L$ independent of $h,N,n$ satisfy
$$\|\Psi_h^E(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Eh^2,\qquad \|\Psi_h^V(z)-\varphi_h(z)\|\le C_Vh^3$$
for admitted $z\in K$, and whenever $nh\le T$,
$$e_n^E\le e^{LT}e_0+C_ETe^{LT}h,\qquad e_n^V\le e^{LT}e_0+C_VTe^{LT}h^2.$$
Thus symplectic Euler has global order one and leapfrog has global order two on the stated controlled tube. No unconditional domain-admissibility claim is made.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ be open, and let $H\in C^2(U)$. Write $z=(q,p)$ in canonical coordinates, set $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$, and use the Euclidean norm and its induced operator norm. Define the finite-regularity coordinate field
$$F(q,p):=\bigl(\nabla_pH(q,p),-\nabla_qH(q,p)\bigr)=J\nabla H(q,p).$$

Given $z\in U$ and a signed step $h$, supply a candidate radius $\rho\ge0$. If no radius is supplied or $\rho<0$, return `branch-not-certified`. If the closed ball $\overline B(z,\rho)$ is certified not to lie in $U$, return `domain-failure`; if its containment in $U$ cannot be certified, return `branch-not-certified`. For a ball contained in $U$, supply certified bounds $M,L\ge0$ with
$$M\ge\sup_{W\in\overline B(z,\rho)}\|F(W)\|,\qquad L\ge\sup_{W\in\overline B(z,\rho)}\|DF(W)\|.$$
If either bound or its certificate is unavailable, or if either admissibility inequality $|h|M/2\le\rho$ or $|h|L/2<1$ fails, return `branch-not-certified`. Otherwise the **exact local implicit midpoint step** selects the unique $Z\in\overline B(z,\rho)$ satisfying
$$Z=z+\frac h2F(Z)$$
and returns $z^+=2Z-z$. The returned state is in $\mathbb R^{2d}$; a further step is admitted only when that state lies in $U$ and passes a new ball check.

For a finite iteration implementation of an admitted branch, input an output tolerance $\tau>0$ and an update budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$. Use $\theta=|h|L/2$ and proceed as follows.

1. Set $Z_0=z$. If $B=0$, return `inconclusive` with current stage iterate $Z_0$, approximate output $z$, and output-error bound $2\rho$.
2. If $B\ge1$, compute $Z_1=z+(h/2)F(Z_0)$ and set $d_1=\|Z_1-Z_0\|$.
3. For $k=1,\ldots,B$, set $b_k=\theta^k d_1/(1-\theta)$ and the output radius $r_k=2b_k$. If $r_k\le\tau$, return the approximation $2Z_k-z$ with output-error certificate $r_k$. Otherwise, if $k<B$, compute $Z_{k+1}=z+(h/2)F(Z_k)$ and continue. If the check fails at $k=B$, return `inconclusive` with current stage iterate $Z_B$, approximate output $2Z_B-z$, and output-error bound $2b_B$.

When $\theta=0$, use $\theta^k=0$ for $k\ge1$; the procedure never evaluates $0^0$. If a finite implementation cannot certify an input or an exact operation needed for these instructions, return `inconclusive` without a tolerance claim. The certificates concern the displayed exact recurrence and exact output operations; inexact evaluations require additional certified error accounting. An approximate result is not asserted to be exactly symplectic. The exact map is the selected branch value $2Z-z$.

citations.quote:
Let $d\ge1$, $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{2d}$ be open, $H\in C^2(U)$, $z=(q,p)$, and $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$. Use the Euclidean norm and its induced operator norm, and define $F(q,p)=(\nabla_pH(q,p),-\nabla_qH(q,p))=J\nabla H(q,p)$. For a signed step $h$, suppose a declared closed ball $\overline B(z,\rho)\subset U$, with $\rho\ge0$, has certified bounds $\|F\|\le M$ and $\|DF\|\le L$ satisfying $|h|M/2\le\rho$ and $\theta:=|h|L/2<1$. The exact implicit midpoint branch [[alg-implicit-midpoint-hamiltonian-step]] then has a unique stage root $Z$ in this ball. The exact iterates $Z_0=z$, $Z_{k+1}=z+(h/2)F(Z_k)$ stay in the ball, converge to $Z$, and for every $k\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
$$\|Z_k-Z\|\le b_k:=\frac{\theta^k\|Z_1-Z_0\|}{1-\theta},\qquad \|(2Z_k-z)-(2Z-z)\|\le2b_k.$$
Here $\theta^0=1$, including when $\theta=0$; if $\theta=0$, the first update equals $Z$ and $b_k=0$ for $k\ge1$. Also $\|(2Z-z)-z\|\le2\rho$, which supplies an output-error bound when no update is computed.

For every finite tolerance $\tau>0$ and budget $B\in\mathbb N_0$, the implementation in [[alg-implicit-midpoint-hamiltonian-step]] terminates after at most $B$ updates and at most $B$ evaluations of $F$; each reported error radius is a valid bound.

Assume additionally $H\in C^3(U)$ and that these ball hypotheses hold uniformly for initial values $z$ in a compact convex tube for all $|h|\le h_0$, with some $h_0>0$ and common $\rho,M,L$, where $h_0L/2\le1/2$. Let U⊂R^n be open and Y:U→R^n be C¹. There is a unique maximal flow Φ on an open domain
D⊂R×U containing {0}×U, and Φ is jointly C¹. Its time slices are local C¹
diffeomorphisms with inverse Φ_{−t}; $\partial_t\Phi=Y(\Phi)$ and $D_p\Phi$ is the
unique solution V of $V′=DY(\Phi)V$, V(0)=I. Each regular point has a C¹ flow box. If Y
is C², Φ and those flow boxes are C²; the second state variation W satisfies
$W′=DY(\Phi)W+D²Y(\Phi)[Ve_i,Ve_j]$, W(0)=0. Individual trajectories of a C¹ field are
C² in time. A trajectory remaining in a compact K⊂⊂U cannot have a finite maximal
endpoint. These Euclidean conclusions use no full AC or DC.

Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and star-shaped about a point $q_*\in Q$, meaning $q_*+t(q-q_*)\in Q$ for every $q\in Q$ and $t\in[0,1]$. Let $M$ be real symmetric positive-definite, $U=Q\times\mathbb R^d$, and equip $U$ with the canonical form $\omega=\sum_{i=1}^d dq_i\wedge dp_i$ and matrix $J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}$. Set $H(q,p)=\tfrac12p^TM^{-1}p+V(q)$ with $V\in C^\infty(Q)$. Let $\Phi_h$ be the kick-then-drift symplectic-Euler map, the local leapfrog map, or an admitted implicit-midpoint branch, on a compact subset where the chosen map is defined. Write $r=1$ for the kick-then-drift symplectic-Euler map and $r=2$ for leapfrog or implicit midpoint, as proved in [[thm-local-symplectic-euler-and-leapfrog-trajectory-errors]] and [[thm-implicit-midpoint-branch-symplectic-order-and-error]]. For a smooth test function $f$, define the pullback $P_hf=f\circ\Phi_h$ by its Taylor coefficients at $h=0$. For fixed finite $N\ge r$, its truncated logarithm is the polynomial
$$\log_N(P_h)=\sum_{k=1}^{N+1}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}(P_h-I)^k,$$
computed modulo terms of order $h^{N+2}$. There are smooth vector fields $X_r,\ldots,X_N$ and globally defined functions $H_r,\ldots,H_N$ on $U$ such that
$$h^{-1}\log_N(P_h)=\mathcal L_{X_H}+\sum_{j=r}^Nh^j\mathcal L_{X_j}\pmod{h^{N+1}},\qquad \iota_{X_j}\omega=dH_j,$$
where $\mathcal L_Xf:=Df[X]$. Thus $H_h^{[N]}=H+\sum_{j=r}^Nh^jH_j$ is a globally defined finite modified Hamiltonian. The logarithm is a finite formal polynomial for each fixed $N$; no convergence of an infinite series is asserted.
