citations.quote:
Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

Suppose proper closed convex $f,g$ have a saddle point $(x_*,z_*,y_*)$ for the
Lagrangian in [[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], with $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$, and every
subproblem in the exact ADMM sequence is attained. Put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and
$$V^k=\frac1\rho\|y^k-y_*\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2.$$
For every $k\ge1$,
$$V^{k+1}\le V^k-\rho\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2-\rho\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2.$$
The index begins at $k=1$: an arbitrary initial $z^0$ need not satisfy a
previous $z$-subproblem optimality condition. Also, with $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$
and $p_*=f(x_*)+g(z_*)$, every exact sweep satisfies
$$p_{k+1}-p_*\le-\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+ \rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},r^{k+1}-L(z^{k+1}-z_*)\rangle,$$
$$p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle.$$

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$. Its **Fenchel conjugate** is the
extended-real function on the same Euclidean space
$$f^*(s):=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}\{\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$
When $f(x)=+\infty$, the corresponding term is $-\infty$ and does not increase
the supremum. Its effective domain is
$\operatorname{dom}f^*=\{s:f^*(s)<+\infty\}$.

If $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper, closed and convex, then its
conjugate $f^*$ from [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]]
is also proper, closed and convex. The affine-minorant result cited below is
used only to prove properness; closedness and convexity follow directly from
the supremum formula.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper and convex. For every
$x,s\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)+f^*(s)\ge\langle s,x\rangle,$$
with extended-real interpretation. Equality holds exactly when
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $f^*(s)<+\infty$, and
$s\in\partial f(x)$; equivalently, for proper convex $f$, equality itself
forces the two finiteness conditions and the subgradient membership.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $\bigl(x^{(j)}\bigr)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$
be a sequence in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ whose range
$\{\, x^{(j)} : j \in \mathbb{N} \,\}$ is a bounded subset of
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]], [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).
Then there are a strictly increasing $i : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$
([[def-sequence]], [[lem-index-map-grows]]) and a point $p \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$
with

$$x^{(i_j)} \longrightarrow p \quad \text{in } (\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$$

([[def-metric-convergence]]). By [[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]] the same
statement holds with $d_2$ replaced by the metric of any norm on
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$, boundedness and convergence both being unchanged by that
replacement ([[def-equivalent-norms]]).

**This is assembled from published theorems and is not proved again by
bisection.** The bisection is in [[thm-heine-borel-rn]], published at order 120;
what is added here is the passage from compactness to sequential compactness and
the reading of the conclusion in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

**Choice cost: none.** [[thm-heine-borel-rn]] is proved by bisection and uses no
choice principle, and "compact implies sequentially compact" is a theorem of ZF
([[thm-compact-implies-the-other-compactness-forms]]). The five-way equivalence
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] is **not** used, precisely because it is
stated under countable choice and dependent choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]) and
would overcharge this corollary; the arrow-by-arrow account is
[[rem-compactness-choice-ledger-metric]].

For any exact two-block ADMM sweep from
[[alg-two-block-admm-scaled]], put
$\Delta z^{k+1}=z^{k+1}-z^k$ and $y^{k+1}=\rho u^{k+1}$. Then
$$-K^*(y^{k+1}-\rho L\Delta z^{k+1})\in\partial f(x^{k+1}),\qquad -L^*y^{k+1}\in\partial g(z^{k+1}).$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: The left saddle inequality forces $Kx_*+Lz_*=c$: otherwise taking $y=y_*+t(Kx_*+Lz_*-c)$ and letting $t\to+\infty$ contradicts its finite upper bound. The right saddle inequality then says every feasible pair has objective at least $p_*$, so $(x_*,z_*)$ is primal optimal. For every $y$, the dual value $d(y)$ is at most $\mathcal L((x_*,z_*),y)=p_*$. At $y_*$, the right saddle inequality gives $d(y_*)\ge p_*$; hence $d(y_*)=p_*$ and $y_*$ is dual optimal.

The subgradient inequalities underlying [F3] imply, for every fixed $x,z$ and every sweep, $$f(x)+g(z)+\langle y^{k+1},Kx+Lz-c\rangle\ge p_{k+1}+\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle+\rho\langle L\Delta z^{k+1},Kx-Kx^{k+1}\rangle.$$ Indeed, apply the $f$- and $g$-subgradient inclusions [F8] at the new iterates, use their defining inequalities, add them, and substitute $Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c=r^{k+1}$.

Fixing $z=z_*$ and then $x=x_*$ in the right saddle inequality gives $-K^*y_*\in\partial f(x_*)$ and $-L^*y_*\in\partial g(z_*)$. By [F6], $f(x_*)+f^*(-K^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Kx_*\rangle,\qquad g(z_*)+g^*(-L^*y_*)=-\langle y_*,Lz_*\rangle.$ Each component infimum is below a finite value because $f,g$ are proper, so neither equals $+\infty$. If both are finite, choosing independent points within any $\epsilon>0$ of them proves that the joint infimum is their sum; if either is $-\infty$, fixing a finite competitor in the other block and sending the first block value down shows the joint infimum is $-\infty$. Thus separating the $x$ and $z$ infima and using [F4] gives the extended-real identity $$d(y)=-f^*(-K^*y)-g^*(-L^*y)-\langle y,c\rangle.$$ The terms are well-defined because [F5] excludes $-\infty$ conjugate values. Substituting the two equalities and feasibility into the formula gives $d(y_*)=p_*$. The dual solution set $Y_*:=\{y:d(y)=p_*\}$ is nonempty. Weak duality gives $d(y)\le p_*$, so $y\in Y_*$ iff $\mathcal L((x,z),y)\ge p_*$ for every $x,z$. Each finite-valued pair $(x,z)$ imposes a closed affine half-space in $y$; an infinite-valued pair imposes no restriction. Thus $Y_*$ is closed and convex as an intersection of closed convex sets.

Sum the descent inequality [F3] from $k=1$ to $N$. Since $V^{N+1}\ge0$, $$\sum_{k=1}^N\bigl(\|r^{k+1}\|_2^2+\|L\Delta z^{k+1}\|_2^2\bigr)\le V^1/\rho.$$ Each nonnegative term of a convergent bounded partial sum tends to zero, so $r^k\to0$ and $L\Delta z^k\to0$. The energy bound also makes $y^k$ and $L(z^k-z_*)$ bounded.

The objective estimates [F3] now force convergence. In the upper estimate, $\langle y^{k+1},r^{k+1}\rangle\to0$ by boundedness and residual convergence; both terms paired with $L\Delta z^{k+1}$ tend to zero because $r^{k+1}\to0$ and $L(z^{k+1}-z_*)$ is bounded. The lower estimate $p_*-p_{k+1}\le\langle y_*,r^{k+1}\rangle$ also tends to zero. Hence $p_{k+1}\to p_*$.

Along any convergent subsequence $y^{k_j+1}\to\bar y$, the quantities $Kx^{k_j+1}=c-Lz^{k_j+1}+r^{k_j+1}$ are bounded by step 2.2. Taking limits in step 1.2, using steps 2.2–2.2, gives $$f(x)+g(z)+\langle\bar y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle\ge p_*\qquad\text{for all }x,z.$$ Since the primal optimizer is feasible, $d(\bar y)\ge p_*$, while weak duality from step 1.1 gives $d(\bar y)\le p_*$. Thus every dual cluster point belongs to $Y_*$. The inequality at the fixed primal optimizer also makes it a saddle point with $\bar y$.

If $p=0$, then $\mathbb R^p=\{0\}$ by [F10], so $y^k=0$ for every $k$; step 2.1 shows this unique dual vector is optimal, and dual convergence follows. Assume henceforth $p\ge1$. Boundedness from step 2.2 and [F7] give at least one dual cluster point. Let $y_1,y_2\in Y_*$ be any two cluster points. Each pairs with the same primal optimizer to form a saddle point, so [F3] makes both energy sequences $$V^k(y_i)=\rho^{-1}\|y^k-y_i\|_2^2+\rho\|L(z^k-z_*)\|_2^2\quad(i=1,2)$$ nonincreasing from $k=1$ and bounded below; each therefore converges. Expanding the two squared norms gives $V^k(y_1)-V^k(y_2)=\frac2\rho\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle+\frac{\|y_1\|_2^2-\|y_2\|_2^2}{\rho},$ so $\langle y^k,y_2-y_1\rangle$ converges. Along subsequences tending to $y_1$ and $y_2$ the limits are equal, so $\langle y_1-y_2,y_2-y_1\rangle=-\|y_1-y_2\|_2^2=0$ and $y_1=y_2$.

In the remaining case $p\ge1$, there is exactly one cluster point. If the bounded sequence $y^k$ did not converge to it, some subsequence would stay a fixed positive distance away; [F7] would give a convergent subsubsequence with a different cluster point, a contradiction. Therefore the whole unscaled dual sequence converges to a point of $Y_*$. No convergence of primal iterates was used.

Given maximal-monotone $A,B$ on $E=\mathbb R^n$, $\rho>0$, and $w_0\in E$,
define for $k\ge0$
$$p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k),\qquad q_k=J_{\rho A}(2p_k-w_k),\qquad w_{k+1}=w_k+q_k-p_k.$$
The **shadow** is $p_k$. Each exact update exists and is unique by
[[thm-maximal-monotone-resolvent-is-firmly-nonexpansive]]. This recurrence
specifies exact real arithmetic; a finite implementation that cannot evaluate
a resolvent must report failure and must not advance the exact recurrence. No
termination or convergence claim is part of this algorithm definition.

For maximal-monotone $A,B$ and $\rho>0$, let
$$T=I-J_{\rho B}+J_{\rho A}(2J_{\rho B}-I).$$
Then $T:E\to E$ is firmly nonexpansive:
$$\|T(w)-T(w')\|_2^2\le\langle T(w)-T(w'),w-w'\rangle.$$

Let $T:E\to E$ be firmly nonexpansive on $E=\mathbb R^n$, suppose
$\operatorname{Fix}(T)=\{p:T(p)=p\}$ is nonempty, and start at any $w_0$.
Then the Picard sequence $w_{k+1}=T(w_k)$ converges to a fixed point of $T$.

Let $A$ be maximal monotone on $E=\mathbb R^n$ and let $\rho>0$. For every
$y\in E$ there is a unique $x\in E$ with $y-x\in\rho A(x)$. Thus the
resolvent from [[def-resolvent-of-a-monotone-relation]] is an everywhere-defined
map and, for all $y,y'\in E$,
$$\|J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y'\|_2^2\le \langle J_{\rho A}y-J_{\rho A}y',y-y'\rangle.$$
This is firm nonexpansiveness; it also implies the map is 1-Lipschitz.

derivations.claim: Choose $b\in B(p)$ and $a\in A(p)$ with $a+b=0$. The resolvent identities give $J_{\rho B}(p+\rho b)=p$ and $J_{\rho A}(p-\rho b)=p$. At $w_*=p+\rho b$, the second input is $2p-w_*=p-\rho b$, so the update has $p_B=q=p$ and $T(w_*)=w_*$. Thus $T$ has a fixed point.
Apply [F3] using firm nonexpansiveness [F2]. It follows that the states $w_k=T^k(w_0)$ converge to some $w_*'$ with $T(w_*')=w_*'$.
Put $p'=J_{\rho B}(w_*')$ and $q'=J_{\rho A}(2p'-w_*')$. Fixedness says $q'=p'$. The resolvent inclusions yield $w_*'-p'\in\rho B(p')$ and $p'-w_*'\in\rho A(p')$; adding them gives $0\in(A+B)(p')$.
The shadow $p_k=J_{\rho B}(w_k)$ converges to $p'$ because the resolvent is 1-Lipschitz by [F4] and $w_k\to w_*'$. Thus the shadow converges to a zero of the sum.

Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

For the exact recurrence of [[alg-pdhg-primal-dual-hybrid-gradient]], put
$\kappa=\sqrt{\tau\sigma}\,\|K\|_2<1$ and
$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y)$. For every
$x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, $y\in\operatorname{dom}g^*$ and integer $N\ge1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})\bigr) \le\frac{\|x-x^0\|_2^2}{2\tau}+\frac{\|y-y^0\|_2^2}{2\sigma}.$$
The formula includes $K=0$ and uses $\bar x^0=x^0$.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

derivations.claim: Every exact proximal output lies in the effective domain of its function. Convexity therefore puts $\bar x_N$ in $\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\bar y_N$ in $\operatorname{dom}g^*$.

By convexity in [F1], $f(\bar x_N)\le N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}f(x^{k+1})$ and $g^*(\bar y_N)\le N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}g^*(y^{k+1})$; linearity gives $K\bar x_N=N^{-1}\sum Kx^{k+1}$. Hence $$\Phi(\bar x_N,y)-\Phi(x,\bar y_N) \le\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\Phi(x^{k+1},y)-\Phi(x,y^{k+1})\bigr).$$ Apply [F2] and divide by $N$ to get the bound.

By the saddle inequalities [F3], $\Phi(\bar x_N,y_*)\ge\Phi(x_*,y_*)$ and $\Phi(x_*,\bar y_N)\le\Phi(x_*,y_*)$, so their difference is nonnegative. Step 2.1 at $(x_*,y_*)$ supplies the same $O(1/N)$ upper bound. The ergodic estimate makes no claim about a single nonaveraged objective difference or pointwise iterate convergence.

For proper closed convex $f_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to(-\infty,+\infty]$, linear
$A_i:\mathbb R^{n_i}\to\mathbb R^p$, data $b\in\mathbb R^p$, penalty
$\rho>0$, and scaled multiplier $u^k$, the **naive sequential three-block
ADMM** sweep is
$$x_1^{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x_1}f_1(x_1)+\frac\rho2\|A_1x_1+A_2x_2^k+A_3x_3^k-b+u^k\|^2,$$
then $x_2^{k+1}$ minimizes the same augmented residual with $x_1^{k+1}$,
$x_2$ variable and $x_3^k$ fixed; then $x_3^{k+1}$ minimizes it with the
first two new blocks; finally
$$u^{k+1}=u^k+A_1x_1^{k+1}+A_2x_2^{k+1}+A_3x_3^{k+1}-b.$$
Only exact attained block minimizers advance the state. A finite solver must
return an explicit failed or cap-exhausted status if it cannot certify a
minimizer. This is a definition of a procedure and asserts no convergence.

Let $p(z)=z^n+a_{n-1}z^{n-1}+\cdots+a_0$ be a real monic polynomial of
degree $n\ge1$ with $|a_0|<1$. Define the reversed polynomial
$p^\#(z)=z^np(1/z)$ and
$$q(z)=\frac{p(z)-a_0p^\#(z)}{z(1-a_0^2)}.$$
If every zero of $p$ lies strictly inside the unit disk, then every zero of
$q$ does too.

Let $f \in \mathbb C[x]$ have degree $n \ge 1$. Then there exist distinct
complex numbers $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_r$ and positive integers
$m_1,\dots,m_r$ such that
$$ f(x)=c\prod_{j=1}^r (x-\alpha_j)^{m_j} $$
for some $c \in \mathbb C^\times$, with
$$ m_1+\cdots+m_r=n. $$
These exponents are uniquely determined by $f$. Equivalently, $f$ has exactly
$n$ roots counted with multiplicity.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

derivations.claim: Write the columns of $A$ as $a_1=(1,1,1)^T$, $a_2=(1,1,2)^T$, $a_3=(1,2,2)^T$. Their squared norms are $3,6,9$, so every scalar block subproblem has a strictly positive quadratic coefficient and a unique attained minimizer. Also $det A=-1$, so $Ax=0$ has only $x=0$. The dual function is $d(y)=inf_x\langle y,Ax\rangle$: it is $0$ when $A^Ty=0$ and $-\infty$ otherwise. Since $A$ is invertible, $A^Ty=0$ only for $y=0$, so the dual optimum is unique.

For state $s^k=(x_2^k,x_3^k,u_1^k,u_2^k,u_3^k)^T$, exact differentiation of the three scalar subproblems gives $x_1^{k+1}=-\frac{a_1^T(u^k+a_2x_2^k+a_3x_3^k)}3$, $x_2^{k+1}=-\frac{a_2^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_3x_3^k)}6$, and $x_3^{k+1}=-\frac{a_3^T(u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1})}9$. Substitute these into $u^{k+1}=u^k+a_1x_1^{k+1}+a_2x_2^{k+1}+a_3x_3^{k+1}$; exact rational simplification gives $s^{k+1}=Ms^k$ with $$M=\frac1{162}\begin{pmatrix}144&-9&9&9&-18\\8&157&5&-13&8\\-64&-122&122&-58&-64\\-56&35&-35&91&-56\\88&26&-26&-62&88\end{pmatrix}.$$ The vector $v=(0,0,1,1,1)^T$ satisfies $Mv=0$. Exact rational matrix multiplication gives $p_1=\operatorname{tr}(M)=\frac{301}{81}$, $p_2=\operatorname{tr}(M^2)=\frac{20860}{6561}$, $p_3=\operatorname{tr}(M^3)=\frac{2588159}{1062882}$, and $p_4=\operatorname{tr}(M^4)=\frac{132553799}{86093442}$. Newton's identities $e_1=p_1$, $e_2=(p_1^2-p_2)/2$, $e_3=(p_3-e_1p_2+e_2p_1)/3$, and $e_4=(-p_4+e_1p_3-e_2p_2+e_3p_1)/4$ give $e_1=301/81$, $e_2=287/54$, $e_3=280/81$, $e_4=70/81$; $Mv=0$ gives $e_5=\det M=0$. Therefore $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda q(\lambda)$, where $q(\lambda)=\lambda^4-\frac{301}{81}\lambda^3+\frac{287}{54}\lambda^2-\frac{280}{81}\lambda+\frac{70}{81}$.

For $z=e^{it}$, direct expansion gives $\operatorname{Im}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=\frac{\sin t(22\cos t-21)}{81}$. If this vanishes because $\sin t=0$, substitution gives $q(1)=1/162$ and $q(-1)=775/54$, both nonzero. Otherwise $\cos t=21/22$, and substitution into the real part gives $\operatorname{Re}(e^{-2it}q(e^{it}))=19/19602\ne0$. Thus $q$ has no unit-circle zero.

Suppose every zero of $q$ lies inside the unit disk. By [F2], its normalized Schur reduction is the stable monic cubic $q_1(z)=z^3-\frac{4781}{1661}z^2+\frac{861}{302}z-\frac{1610}{1661}$. Since $|q_1(0)|=1610/1661<1$, another application gives the stable monic quadratic $q_2(z)=z^2-\frac{317086}{166821}z+\frac{336511}{333642}$. By [F3], $q_2$ factors as $(z-\zeta_1)(z-\zeta_2)$ over $\mathbb C$, with both roots inside the unit disk by the reductions. Its constant term is $\zeta_1\zeta_2$, so $|q_2(0)|=|\zeta_1||\zeta_2|<1$, contradicting $q_2(0)=336511/333642>1$. Therefore not all zeros of $q$ lie inside. The coefficients of $q_1,q_2$ follow by substituting into $(p-p(0)p^\#)/(z(1-p(0)^2))$ and collecting powers.

By [F3], $q$ has four roots counted with multiplicity. Steps 2.1 and 3.1 show that none is on the unit circle and not all are inside, so some root $\lambda$ satisfies $|\lambda|>1$. Since $\det(\lambda I-M)=\lambda q(\lambda)=0$ by step 1.2, [F4] gives a nonzero complex vector $v$ with $Mv=\lambda v$. Suppose each of the five standard basis vectors $e_j\in\mathbb Q^5$ had a bounded orbit under $M$. Then every column of $M^k$ would be uniformly bounded in $k$, and since there are only five columns, every entry would be bounded by one common constant $C$. Choose $i$ with $v_i\ne0$. The finite-sum triangle inequality would give $|(M^kv)_i|\le C\sum_j|v_j|$ for every $k$, but $M^kv=\lambda^kv$ makes $|(M^kv)_i|=|\lambda|^k|v_i|\to\infty$, a contradiction. Hence at least one standard basis vector has an unbounded orbit. Taking $s^0=e_j$ for that index and $x_1^0=0$ gives a rational initial state with unbounded iterates; each subproblem remains uniquely attained as shown in step 1.1.

Let $f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, let
$K:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p$ and $L:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^p$ be linear,
let $c\in\mathbb R^p$, and let $\rho>0$. The primal problem is
$$\min_{x,z}\ f(x)+g(z)\quad\text{subject to }Kx+Lz=c,$$
and its Lagrangian is
$\mathcal L((x,z),y)=f(x)+g(z)+\langle y,Kx+Lz-c\rangle$.
A saddle point means a saddle pair in the sense of
[[def-saddle-point-for-convex-concave-lagrangian]].

For an exact outer sweep with scaled dual $u^k$, compute, in order,
$$x^{k+1}\in\arg\min_x\left(f(x)+\frac\rho2\|Kx+Lz^k-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
$$z^{k+1}\in\arg\min_z\left(g(z)+\frac\rho2\|Kx^{k+1}+Lz-c+u^k\|_2^2\right),$$
then set $r^{k+1}=Kx^{k+1}+Lz^{k+1}-c$ and
$u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}$. Report also the unscaled dual
$y^k=\rho u^k$, objective $p_k=f(x^k)+g(z^k)$, and primal residual $r^k$.
If an exact subproblem has multiple minimizers, choose the unique minimum-norm
member of its nonempty closed convex minimizer set; existence and uniqueness of
that tie-break follow from [[thm-nearest-point-in-a-nonempty-closed-convex-set]].

A finite implementation supplies finite inner iteration caps for both solves.
A solve is accepted only with a certificate of an attained global minimizer
before its cap. Return **invalid-input** for invalid dimensions or $\rho\le0$;
return **x-solve-failed**, **x-cap-exhausted**, **z-solve-failed**, or
**z-cap-exhausted** if the corresponding solve fails, is uncertified, or reaches
its cap. A failed sweep does not change the outer state, even if its first
subproblem was solved. These statuses give no approximate convergence guarantee.

Let $X,Y$ be nonempty subsets of finite-dimensional real Euclidean spaces and
let $\Psi:X\times Y\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be an extended-real function. A
pair $(x_*,y_*)$ is a
**saddle point** of $\Psi$ if $\Psi(x_*,y_*)$ is finite and
$$\Psi(x_*,y)\le \Psi(x_*,y_*)\le \Psi(x,y_*)\qquad(x\in X,\ y\in Y).$$
The inequalities must be defined at the arguments they display. For an
equality-constrained problem the primal set may be a product set of
finite-valued pairs $(x,z)$.

A subset is convex when it contains the segment joining each pair of its
points ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). A function
$F:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ is proper if it never equals
$-\infty$ and is finite at at least one point. Its domain is
$\operatorname{dom}F=\{x:F(x)<+\infty\}$. Its epigraph is
$\operatorname{epi}F=\{(x,t):F(x)\le t\}$. It is closed convex when its
epigraph is a closed convex set. For a nonempty convex set $S$,
$\operatorname{aff}S$ is its smallest containing affine subspace and
$\operatorname{ri}S$ is its interior relative to $\operatorname{aff}S$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $m,p\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed, let
$f_0,g_1,\ldots,g_m$ be proper closed convex functions on $\mathbb R^n$,
let $A\in\mathbb R^{p\times n}$ have full row rank, and let
$b\in\mathbb R^p$. Full row rank means that the rows are linearly
independent, vacuously when $p=0$. The common domain is
$D=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{dom}g_i$. The primal
problem is to minimize $f_0(x)$ over $x\in D$ satisfying $Ax=b$ and
$g_i(x)\le0$. An inequality is removable if, with
$D_{-i}=\operatorname{dom}f_0\cap\bigcap_{j\ne i}\operatorname{dom}g_j$,
$D_{-i}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}g_i$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $x\in D_{-i}$.
Then $D=D_{-i}$, so removing that function and its inequality leaves the
feasible set unchanged. Remove such inequalities one at a time, recomputing
$D_{-i}$ after each deletion. An inequality that is nonpositive only on $D$
but whose function domain restricts $D$ is not removable. Unless stated
otherwise, the inequalities below are the remaining ones after only these
domain-preserving deletions. The primal value is
$$
p^*=\inf\{f_0(x):x\in D,\ Ax=b,\ g_i(x)\le0\text{ for all }i\}.
$$

For $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m_+$ and $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$, the extended
Lagrangian is
$$
L(x,\lambda,\nu)=\begin{cases}f_0(x)+\lambda^Tg(x)+\nu^T(Ax-b),&x\in D,\\+\infty,&x\notin D.\end{cases}
$$
The dual function and dual value are
$$
q(\lambda,\nu)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}L(x,\lambda,\nu),\qquad d^*=\sup_{\lambda\ge0,\ \nu\in\mathbb R^p}q(\lambda,\nu).
$$
The dual supremum is attained when some admissible $(\lambda,\nu)$ has
$q(\lambda,\nu)=d^*$; the optimal duality gap is $p^*-d^*$ when both values
are finite.

Slater's condition means that there is
$x_s\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_0)\cap
\bigcap_i\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g_i)$ with $Ax_s=b$ and
$g_i(x_s)<0$ for every remaining inequality. Relative interior is used in
the affine hull of each domain, so the domain need not have ambient interior.

For the convex program and Lagrangian dual of
[[def-convex-program-duality-and-slater-condition]], every primal feasible
$x$ and every dual feasible $(\lambda,\nu)$ satisfy
$$q(\lambda,\nu)\le f_0(x).$$
Consequently, when the primal feasible set is nonempty, $d^*\le p^*$.

derivations.claim: On the feasible set $z=x$, the objective is $$f(x)+g(x)=\tfrac12(x-1)^2+\tfrac12(x+1)^2=x^2+1,$$ which is uniquely minimized at $x=z=0$ with value $1$. For $y_*=1$, $$\mathcal L((x,z),1)=f(x)+g(z)+x-z=1+\tfrac12x^2+\tfrac12z^2\ge1,$$ with equality at $(0,0)$; feasibility makes $\mathcal L((0,0),y)=1$ for every $y$. These are exactly the saddle inequalities [F2].

Differentiating the first strictly convex quadratic in [F1] gives $2x^{k+1}=1+z^k-u^k$. At $k=0$ this yields $x^1=1/2$. Differentiating the second gives $2z^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+u^k-1$, hence $z^1=-1/4$ and then $u^1=u^0+x^1-z^1=3/4$.

The equality matrix is $A=(1,-1)$, whose single row is linearly independent, so the dual definition [F3] applies. Its dual function is $$d(y)=\inf_x\{\tfrac12(x-1)^2+yx\}+\inf_z\{\tfrac12(z+1)^2-yz\}=(y-\tfrac12y^2)+(y-\tfrac12y^2)=1-(y-1)^2.$$ Thus its maximum is $1$ at $y=1$, consistent with weak duality [F4] and the saddle value.

The same two equations give $x^2=(1-1/4-3/4)/2=0$, $z^2=(0+3/4-1)/2=-1/8$, and $u^2=3/4+0-(-1/8)=7/8$. Each subproblem is a strictly convex quadratic, so both minimizers in each of these sweeps are attained and unique. The recurrence values are exact rationals.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, be symmetric with ordered eigenvalues
$\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_n$. Let $r$ be the multiplicity of $\lambda_1$.
If $r<n$, assume $\lambda_1>\lambda_{r+1}$, and let $P$ be the orthogonal
projection onto the $\lambda_1$-eigenspace. Let $b\in\mathbb R^n$ be a unit
vector and, for $m\ge1$, define

$$K_m:=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\ldots,A^{m-1}b\},\qquad \theta_m:=\max_{0\ne x\in K_m}\frac{x^{\mathsf T}Ax}{x^{\mathsf T}x}.$$

Thus $\theta_m$ is the largest Rayleigh–Ritz value on $K_m$; if Lanczos runs
through step $m$ without breakdown, it is the largest Ritz value of
$Q_m^{\mathsf T}AQ_m$. If $r=n$, then $A=\lambda_1I$ and $\theta_m=\lambda_1$
for every $m\ge1$. Suppose $r<n$.

1. If $Pb=0$, then $\theta_m\le\lambda_{r+1}$ for every $m$; no convergence
   to $\lambda_1$ is asserted.

2. If $Pb\ne0$, put
   $$\tau:=\frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2}{\|Pb\|_2}.$$
   If $\lambda_{r+1}>\lambda_n$, then for every $m\ge1$,
   $$0\le\lambda_1-\theta_m\le \frac{(\lambda_1-\lambda_n)\tau^2} {T_{m-1}\!\left(1+2\frac{\lambda_1-\lambda_{r+1}} {\lambda_{r+1}-\lambda_n}\right)^2}.$$
   For a simple top eigenvalue ($r=1$), $\tau$ is the tangent of the angle
   between $b$ and a unit top eigenvector, so the starting-angle denominator
   is explicit.

3. If $Pb\ne0$ and $\lambda_{r+1}=\lambda_n$, then
   $$\lambda_1-\theta_1=(\lambda_1-\lambda_n) \frac{\|(I-P)b\|_2^2}{\|b\|_2^2},\qquad \theta_m=\lambda_1\quad(m\ge2).$$

When $r<n$, $Pb\ne0$, and exact Lanczos breakdown occurs at dimension $d$, then
$\theta_d=\lambda_1$ and $K_m=K_d$ for all $m\ge d$. These are exact-arithmetic
claims; they give no finite-precision grade-termination guarantee.

Let $X=\mathbb R^n$, $Y=\mathbb R^m$, let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ and
$g:Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper closed convex, and let $K:X\to Y$ be
linear. Its unique adjoint $K^*:Y\to X$ exists by
[[thm-adjoint-exists-and-is-unique-in-finite-dimension]], including zero-dimensional
spaces. Identify $K$ with its matrix in the standard Euclidean bases when using
the induced matrix norm below. The primal problem is $\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)$, with saddle function
$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$
where $g^*$ is defined by [[def-fenchel-conjugate-on-finite-dimensional-euclidean-space]].
The saddle function $\Phi$ is evaluated on
$\operatorname{dom}f\times\operatorname{dom}g^*$, where both function values
are finite; no undefined extended-real subtraction is used outside this domain.
Assume $\tau,\sigma>0$ and
$\tau\sigma\|K\|_2^2<1$, where $\|K\|_2$ is the induced Euclidean operator
norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Starting from $x^0,y^0$ and
$\bar x^0=x^0$, the exact recurrence is
$$y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=2x^{k+1}-x^k.$$
In positive-dimensional spaces the proximal maps are everywhere single-valued
by [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]; in a
zero-dimensional space its sole input and output are the zero vector, so that
proximal call is single-valued directly. The proper closed convexity of $g^*$
follows from [[lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-convex]]. A finite implementation
uses finite call caps and advances an iterate only after both exact proximal
outputs are certified; otherwise it returns **prox-call-failed** or
**prox-cap-exhausted** and makes no convergence claim for that run.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: Since $Kb=e_1=b$, every power $K^j b=b$. For $m=0$, the spanning list is empty and its span is $\{0\}$, with no nonzero vector on which to evaluate a Rayleigh quotient. For every $m\ge1$, the spanning set in [F1] consists of repetitions of the single nonzero vector $e_1$, and the Rayleigh quotient on this one-dimensional subspace is $e_1^TKe_1/(e_1^Te_1)=1$. Exact Lanczos terminates after one vector with Ritz value $1$.

For $x=(x_1,x_2)$, $\|Kx\|_2^2=x_1^2+4x_2^2\le4(x_1^2+x_2^2)$, with equality at $e_2$, so [F4] gives $\|K\|_2=2$. The top eigenspace is $\operatorname{span}\{e_2\}$ and $Pb=0$; [F2] identifies exactly this degenerate branch and supplies no top-eigenvalue convergence bound. Therefore the Ritz value $1$ is not the norm upper bound $2$ required by [F3].

$$\Phi(x,y)=f(x)+\langle Kx,y\rangle-g^*(y),$$

Let $F$ be a field, and let $m,n,s\in\mathbb N$, where $\mathbb N$ includes
$0$. A **compressed sparse row (CSR) record** for an $m$ by $n$ matrix over
$F$ consists of integer arrays $r=(r_0,\ldots,r_m)$ and
$c=(c_0,\ldots,c_{s-1})$, and a value array $v=(v_0,\ldots,v_{s-1})\in F^s$,
satisfying

$$r_0=0,\qquad 0=r_0\le r_1\le\cdots\le r_m=s,\qquad 0\le c_t<n\quad(0\le t<s).$$

For each row $i<m$, its **stored entries** are the indices
$t$ with $r_i\le t<r_{i+1}$. The row is empty exactly when
$r_i=r_{i+1}$. Repeated column indices within one row and stored values
$v_t=0_F$ are permitted; each such entry remains a separate stored entry.

The represented matrix $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ is defined entrywise by

$$A_{ij}:=\sum_{r_i\le t<r_{i+1}}\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}v_t\qquad(0\le i<m,\ 0\le j<n),$$

where $\mathbf 1_{c_t=j}$ is $1_F$ when $c_t=j$ and $0_F$ otherwise, and an
empty sum is $0_F$. Repeated entries in column $j$ are therefore added. The
number $s$ is the **stored-entry count**; it is not in general the number of
nonzero entries of $A$.

A CSR record is **canonical** when no row repeats a column and no stored value
is zero. In that case every nonzero matrix entry is stored exactly once and
$s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$, where $\operatorname{nnz}(A)$ denotes the number of
nonzero entries of $A$. If $m=0$, the endpoint conditions force $s=0$ and the
row-pointer array has its single entry $r_0=0$. If $n=0$, the column-index
condition forces $s=0$ as well.

Fix a field $F$. The **validated CSR matrix-vector product** takes integer
dimension candidates $m,n$, integer arrays $r,c$, a value array $v$ of elements
of $F$, and a vector candidate $x$ of elements of $F$. All input arrays are
finite; write $s=\operatorname{length}(v)$.

1. If $m\notin\mathbb N$, $n\notin\mathbb N$,
   $\operatorname{length}(r)\ne m+1$,
   $\operatorname{length}(c)\ne s$, or
   $\operatorname{length}(x)\ne n$, return the status `invalid-dimension`.
2. For $i=0,\ldots,m$, check that $r_i\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$; return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails. Check $r_0=0$ and $r_m=s$, and for each
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$ check $r_i\le r_{i+1}$; return `invalid-index` if any
   check fails. For each $t=0,\ldots,s-1$, check $0\le c_t<n$ and return
   `invalid-index` if a check fails.
3. Initialize $y_i=0_F$ for $0\le i<m$. For each row
   $i=0,\ldots,m-1$, and then each stored index
   $t=r_i,\ldots,r_{i+1}-1$, update
   $$y_i\gets y_i+v_t x_{c_t}.$$
4. Return the status `ok` together with $y\in F^m$.

For valid CSR data, each update uses exact field arithmetic. This procedure
makes no floating-point rounding, backward-stability, convergence, runtime, or
memory-bandwidth claim.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, let a valid CSR record represent
$A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, and let $x=(x_j)_{j<n}\in F^n$. Let
$X\in M_{n\times1}(F)$ be the column matrix with $X_{j0}=x_j$ for $j<n$, and
define $Ax\in F^m$ by
$$(Ax)_i:=(AX)_{i0}=\sum_{j<n}A_{ij}x_j\qquad(i<m),$$
using [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Then the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] returns `ok` with output
$Ax$ in exact field arithmetic.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n\in\mathbb N$, and let a valid CSR record have
$s$ stored entries. Its input arrays use exactly $s$ field-value slots, $s$
integer column-index slots, and $m+1$ integer row-pointer slots, for a total of
$2s+m+1$ data slots. On valid input, the algorithm
[[alg-csr-matrix-vector-product-with-validation]] performs exactly $s$ field
multiplications, $s$ field additions, and $m$ zero initializations. Its index
validation and loop-control work is $O(m+s+1)$. Counting the CSR arrays and
returned output but excluding the supplied vector $x$ and constant-size
workspace, it uses exactly $2s+2m+1$ data slots, hence $O(m+s+1)$ slots; for
$m\ge1$ this is $O(m+s)$. Here $O(g)$ means bounded by $Cg$ for a constant $C$ independent of
the dimensions and input values.

For a square record of order $m\ge1$ with at least one stored entry in each
row, $s\ge m$, so the work and storage are $O(s)$. For a canonical record as defined in
[[def-csr-matrix-with-stored-entry-semantics]], $s=\operatorname{nnz}(A)$;
without that convention, the cost is in terms of stored entries, not
$\operatorname{nnz}(A)$. These are arithmetic, index, and storage counts, not
runtime, memory-bandwidth, convergence, or factorization-cost bounds.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map

$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
Every self-adjoint endomorphism is normal, because $TT^*=T^2=T^*T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$
finite-dimensional. Then

$$\dim_F V=\operatorname{nullity}T+\operatorname{rank}T.$$

Equivalently,

$$\dim_F V=\dim_F(\ker T)+\dim_F(\operatorname{im}T).$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

derivations.claim: Identify $z=x+iy\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. For any $Z=X+iY\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$, direct multiplication gives $\mathcal R(Z)(x,y)=(\Re(Zz),\Im(Zz))$, so realification respects every compatible product. The displayed inner products make the standard coordinate bases orthonormal, so [F7] gives $Z^*=X^{\mathsf T}-iY^{\mathsf T}$ and $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\begin{pmatrix}X^{\mathsf T}&Y^{\mathsf T}\\-Y^{\mathsf T}&X^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix}=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}.

For $z=x+iy$, $\|z\|_2^2=\sum_j|x_j+iy_j|^2=\sum_j(x_j^2+y_j^2)=\|(x,y)\|_2^2$ by [F5, F6]. Thus for $n>0$ the identification bijects the complex and real unit spheres, so the maxima in [F4] coincide for $E$ and $\mathcal R(E)$. If $n=0$, both operator norms are zero by [F4]. If square $Z$ is invertible, $\mathcal R(Z^{-1})$ is an inverse of $\mathcal R(Z)$ by step 1.1; conversely, if $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible, its kernel is zero, so $Zz=0$ implies $z=0$, and [F3] makes $Z$ invertible.

If $n=0$, the spectral assertion is immediate. Otherwise, [F7] identifies the Hermitian matrix $H=H^*$ with a self-adjoint endomorphism in the standard orthonormal basis; [F2] makes it normal, so [F1] gives $H=U\Lambda U^*$ with $U$ unitary and $\Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)$ real. By step 1.1, $\mathcal R(U)$ is real orthogonal and $\mathcal R(H)=\mathcal R(U)\mathcal R(\Lambda)\mathcal R(U)^{\mathsf T}$, where $\mathcal R(\Lambda)=\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda,\Lambda)$. Hence $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with each eigenvalue of $H$ repeated twice.

be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

For $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$ and $Z=X+iY\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ with real $X,Y$, define its realification
$$
\mathcal R(Z)=\begin{pmatrix}X&-Y\\Y&X\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{2m\times2n}.
$$
Use the standard coordinate inner products $\langle z,w\rangle=\sum_j z_j\overline{w_j}$ on $\mathbb C^k$ and $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_j x_jy_j$ on $\mathbb R^k$, with their induced 2-norms. For compatible $Z\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$ and $W\in\mathbb C^{n\times p}$,
$$
\mathcal R(ZW)=\mathcal R(Z)\mathcal R(W).
$$
For any $Z\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$, $\mathcal R(Z^*)=\mathcal R(Z)^{\mathsf T}$. For square $Z\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $Z$ is invertible exactly when $\mathcal R(Z)$ is invertible. If $H=H^*$ is Hermitian with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$ counted with multiplicity, then $\mathcal R(H)$ is real symmetric with eigenvalue multiset $\{\lambda_j,\lambda_j:1\le j\le n\}$. For every complex matrix $E\in\mathbb C^{m\times n}$, $\|\mathcal R(E)\|_2=\|E\|_2$.

Let $A,B$ be self-adjoint endomorphisms of an $n$-dimensional real inner
product space. Order the eigenvalues of $A$, $B$, and $A+B$ by

$$\alpha_1\ge\cdots\ge\alpha_n,\qquad \beta_1\ge\cdots\ge\beta_n,\qquad \gamma_1\ge\cdots\ge\gamma_n.$$

Then, for integers $1\le i,j\le n$:

1. If $i+j-1\le n$, then $\gamma_{i+j-1}\le \alpha_i+\beta_j$.
2. If $i+j-n\ge1$, then $\gamma_{i+j-n}\ge \alpha_i+\beta_j$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Input $n\ge1$, a nonempty family of Hermitian $n\times n$ matrices enclosed by complex rectangles, a point matrix $V\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a real diagonal matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and proposed nonnegative bounds $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$. Treat point data as exact dyadics and the family as any subset of its enclosure.

1. With outward interval evaluation, enclose $V^*V-I$ and every $AV-V\Theta$ for the full family. Form Frobenius upper bounds $d,r$ for these two matrices. Also form Frobenius upper bounds $m_A$ for every $A$ in the family and $m_\Theta$ for $\Theta$. If any enclosure or square-root operation is non-finite, return `inconclusive`.

2. Verify by outward scalar comparisons that $d\le\delta<1$, $r\le\rho$, $m_A\le M_A$, $m_\Theta\le M_\Theta$, and that $1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau$. If any comparison is undecided or false, return `inconclusive` with the failed check. Otherwise outward-compute a finite upper bound $\bar\eta\ge\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$. For each increasingly sorted diagonal entry $\theta_{(k)}$, outward-compute finite endpoints $\ell_k\le\theta_{(k)}-\bar\eta$ and $u_k\ge\theta_{(k)}+\bar\eta$, and set $I_k=[\ell_k,u_k]$. If the radius bound or any final endpoint cannot be enclosed finitely, return `inconclusive`; otherwise return `certified` with radius bound $\bar\eta$ and intervals $I_1,\ldots,I_n$.

The checks use the Frobenius norm as an upper bound for the operator 2-norm. An inconclusive check makes no statement about the true spectrum.

A **residual and orthogonality certificate** is a tuple of nonnegative numbers $\delta,\rho,M_A,M_\Theta,\tau$ such that, for every $A\in\mathcal A$,
$$\|V^*V-I\|_2\le\delta<1,\quad \|AV-V\Theta\|_2\le\rho,\quad \|A\|_2\le M_A,\quad \|\Theta\|_2\le M_\Theta,\quad 1-\sqrt{1-\delta}\le\tau.$$
The certificate uses exact inequalities or separately verified upper bounds. Its eigenvalue enclosure radius is $\eta=\rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau$. This definition does not assert that computed residuals or Gram matrices satisfy the bounds; that is a separate certification procedure.

Sort the diagonal entries of $\Theta$ increasingly as $\theta_{(1)}\le\cdots\le\theta_{(n)}$. Then every $A\in\mathcal A$ has ordered eigenvalues $\lambda_1(A)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(A)$ satisfying
$$
|\lambda_k(A)-\theta_{(k)}|\le \rho+(M_A+M_\Theta)\tau,\qquad 1\le k\le n.
$$

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper

Input $n\ge1$, stored finite real or complex square data $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb C^n$, a proposed computed inverse $R\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and a proposed computed solution $\widehat x\in\mathbb C^n$. All stored entries are interpreted as exact dyadics. Use the operationwise arithmetic model with unit roundoff $u$; if $(n-1)u\ge1$, return `inconclusive` before applying the rounded-residual bounds. The procedure validates the proposals; it does not assume that the solver which produced them is stable.

1. Set $g_n=(1+6u)/(1-(n-1)u)-1$. Evaluate each column $a_j$ of $A$ through the operationwise model as $\widehat m_j=\operatorname{fl}(Ra_j)$. If any operation returns range-failure, return `range-failure` with its first operation index. Compute an outward upper bound $v_j$ for $g_n\|R\|_F\|a_j\|_2$, which by the rounded-linear-residual lemma bounds $\|\widehat m_j-Ra_j\|_2$. Every dot product used for these allowances must complete successfully under the no-underflow model. Outward-evaluate $I-[\widehat m_1\ \cdots\ \widehat m_n]$ and let $q$ be an outward upper bound for its Frobenius norm plus $\sqrt{\sum_jv_j^2}$.

2. Evaluate $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(A\widehat x)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-b)$. Compute an outward upper bound $W$ for $g_n\|A\|_F\|\widehat x\|_2+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+\|b\|_2)$, which bounds $\|\widehat w-(A\widehat x-b)\|_2$. Evaluate $\widehat c=\operatorname{fl}(R\widehat w)$ and compute an outward upper bound $v_c$ for $g_n\|R\|_F\|\widehat w\|_2$, which bounds $\|\widehat c-R\widehat w\|_2$. Let $r$ be an outward upper bound for
$$
\|\widehat c\|_2+\|R\|_F W+v_c.
$$
The Frobenius norm bounds $\|R\|_2$.

3. All norm bounds, square roots, and final scalar operations are evaluated outward. If a bound cannot be enclosed finitely, return `inconclusive`. If $q\ge1$, return `inconclusive` with the computed bounds. If $q<1$, outward-compute $s\ge r/(1-q)$ and return `certified` with the Euclidean ball $B(\widehat x,s)$.

The output `range-failure` describes failure of a requested floating operation. `inconclusive` means only that this validation did not prove a usable bound; it does not assert that $A$ is singular or that the proposed solution is inaccurate.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

If $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ is usable uniform residual certificate data for nonempty $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, then for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$, the equation $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and
$$
\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le\frac{r}{1-q}.
$$

derivations.claim: On a successful run, the columnwise rounded products enclose every column of $RA$ with Euclidean errors at most $v_j$, by [F1]. The Frobenius error between the rounded product matrix and $RA$ is therefore at most $\sqrt{\sum_jv_j^2}$. Outward soundness [F2] encloses $I-\widehat{RA}$, so the reported $q$ bounds $\|I-RA\|_2$ by the triangle inequality and $\|M\|_2\le\|M\|_F$.

The rounded residual allowance $W$ bounds $\|\widehat w-(A\widehat x-b)\|_2$ and the rounded product allowance $v_c$ bounds $\|\widehat c-R\widehat w\|_2$ by [F1]. Thus $\|R(b-A\widehat x)\|_2\le\|\widehat c\|_2+\|R\|_2W+v_c\le r$, where [F2] makes each reported upper bound outward and $\|R\|_2\le\|R\|_F$.

These are usable point residual certificate data with $q<1$. By [F3] the system has a unique solution and $\|x-\widehat x\|_2\le r/(1-q)\le s$. The latter inequality is exactly the returned ball membership.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Input $n\ge1$, nonempty families $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, each enclosed entrywise by finite complex rectangles, together with stored point proposals $R$ and $\widehat x$. The represented family need only be a subset of the supplied product of rectangles; correlations between entries may be discarded. All stored point data are exact dyadics.

1. Use outward rectangle operations to evaluate the expression DAGs
$$
E(A)=I-RA,\qquad c(A,b)=R(b-A\widehat x)
$$
over the full input rectangles. If an operation has no finite enclosure or returns a domain or range status, return `inconclusive`.

2. For each complex rectangle entry $X+iY$, outward-enclose its modulus by computing $\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ and taking the upper endpoint. Combine those bounds by outward sums of squares and square roots to obtain $q\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}\|E(A)\|_F$ and $r\ge\sup_{A\in\mathcal A,b\in\mathcal b}\|c(A,b)\|_2$. If any modulus, sum, square root or final division has no finite outward result, return `inconclusive`. The Frobenius upper bound also bounds the operator 2-norm. If $q\ge1$, return `inconclusive` with $q,r$. Otherwise return `certified` with the uniform residual data $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ and radius $r/(1-q)$, rounded outward if represented as a ball.

The interval DAG encloses every value for every admitted pair, including dependencies between repeated inputs because natural interval evaluation may enlarge the range. `inconclusive` makes no assertion that a member is singular.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty set of matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and let $\mathcal b$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb C^n$. A **uniform residual certificate** consists of a point matrix $R\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a point vector $\widehat x\in\mathbb C^n$, and numbers $q,r\ge0$ such that
$$
\|I-RA\|_2\le q,\qquad \|R(b-A\widehat x)\|_2\le r
$$
for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$. Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the operator norm induced by the Euclidean vector norm, as in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. The certificate is **usable** when $q<1$; in that case its reported error radius is $r/(1-q)$. The point-data case is $\mathcal A=\{A\}$ and $\mathcal b=\{b\}$.

This definition specifies mathematical upper bounds; it does not specify how a computation establishes them.

If $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ is usable uniform residual certificate data for nonempty $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, then for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$, the equation $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and
$$
\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le\frac{r}{1-q}.
$$

derivations.claim: By [F1], the interval DAGs for $I-RA$ and $R(b-A\widehat x)$ enclose these expressions simultaneously for every admitted $A,b$. The component modulus bounds, sums of squares and square roots therefore bound their Frobenius or Euclidean norms uniformly. By [F2], the first Frobenius bound also bounds $\|I-RA\|_2$. Thus the returned $q,r$ satisfy the inequalities in the uniform residual certificate definition.
The run returns `certified` only with $q<1$. Apply [F4] to the uniform certificate: for every admitted pair there is a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and $\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le r/(1-q)$.

If $n\ge1$, $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $M\ge\|A\|_F$, then every eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ satisfies $|\lambda|\le M$. More generally, if a nonempty Hermitian matrix family $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ satisfies $\|A\|_F\le M$ for all $A\in\mathcal A$, then every eigenvalue of every member lies in $[-M,M]$.

If [[alg-interval-hermitian-ldl-inertia-certifier]] returns `certified-inertia` with $(n_+,n_-,n_0)$, every Hermitian matrix in its input family has exactly that inertia. A `pivot-inconclusive` return does not imply that any family member is singular.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty family of Hermitian $n	imes n$ matrices, and let a closed interval $[L,U]$ initially contain every ordered eigenvalue $\lambda_k(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$, with eigenvalues listed increasingly. For a query shift $	au$, suppose the query either returns inconclusive or returns an integer $
u(	au)$ such that every $A\in\mathcal A$ is nonsingular at $A-	au I$ and exactly $
u(	au)$ of its eigenvalues lie below $	au$. For each $k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$, start with $[L,U]$ and repeat at most $N\in\mathbb N_0$ times: query its midpoint $	au$; if $
u(	au)\ge k$, replace $U$ by $	au$, and otherwise replace $L$ by $	au$; stop when width is at most $\varepsilon>0$. An inconclusive query returns the current interval without changing it. Every returned interval contains $\lambda_k(A)$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$. After $s$ successful queries its width is $(U-L)2^{-s}$.

derivations.claim: If the interval norm calculation succeeds, [F1] makes its returned $M$ an upper bound for every $\|A\|_F$. By [F2], every eigenvalue of every member lies in $[-M,M]$, so all initial brackets are valid.

At a successful shift, [F3] supplies one inertia for every $A-\tau I$ and its zero count is checked to be zero. Its negative count is therefore exactly the number of eigenvalues of each $A$ below $\tau$. The algorithm's update is the successful query of [F4]; on pivot failure or a zero pivot it leaves the interval unchanged, which is the inconclusive branch of [F4].

Apply [F4] to each index, treating later unexecuted queries after a blocked index or budget exhaustion as no-op inconclusive queries. Each bracket therefore continues to contain the corresponding ordered eigenvalue for every family member. Certified updates halve its width, while statuses only describe why the requested tolerance or query count may not have been reached.

citations.quote: Let $n\ge1$ and let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty family of real $n\times n$ matrices. Suppose a real interval $D$ contains $\det A$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$. If $0\notin D$, then every $A\in\mathcal A$ is nonsingular; if $D$ is positive or negative, its sign is the common determinant sign. If $D=\{0\}$, every member is singular. When neither condition holds, the certificate makes no singularity or sign assertion.

If $(R,\widehat x,q,r)$ is usable uniform residual certificate data for nonempty $\mathcal A\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ and $\mathcal b\subseteq\mathbb C^n$, then for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$, the equation $Ax=b$ has a unique solution $x_A(b)$ and
$$
\|x_A(b)-\widehat x\|_2\le\frac{r}{1-q}.
$$

derivations.claim: For each $t\in[-1,1]$, $\det A(t)=1-t^2\in[0,1]$. The direct interval product $[-1,1]\cdot[-1,1]=[-1,1]$ encloses $t^2$, so the Leibniz interval expression $1-[-1,1]=[0,2]$ contains every determinant. At $t=1$, $A(1)(1,-1)^{\mathsf T}=0$ with a nonzero vector, so $A(1)$ is singular. The interval $[0,2]$ includes zero and is not $\{0\}$; [F1] therefore makes no uniform nonsingularity claim from this enclosure.

If uniform residual data with $q<1$ existed for this whole family and any nonempty right-hand-side set, [F2] would make $A(1)$ invertible. This contradicts the nonzero null vector just exhibited. Hence such a usable uniform residual certificate cannot hold for the family.

More precisely, there is a unique $q\in R[x]$ such that $f=q(x-a)+f(a)$.

If $R$ is an integral domain and $f,g\in R[x]$ are nonzero, then $fg\ne0$ and

$$ \deg(fg)=\deg f+\deg g,\qquad \operatorname{lc}(fg)=\operatorname{lc}(f)\operatorname{lc}(g). $$

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

Let $F$ be a field and let $f,g\in F[x]$ be not both zero. Since $F[x]$ is a principal ideal domain ([[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-field-is-a-pid]]), the ideal $(f,g)$ generated by $f$ and $g$ ([[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]]) has a nonzero generator $d$. The resulting polynomial is the **monic greatest common divisor** $\gcd(f,g)$.

Equivalently, $d=\gcd(f,g)$ is the unique monic polynomial such that $d$ divides both $f$ and $g$, and every common divisor of $f$ and $g$ divides $d$. The equivalence and the Bézout identity are proved in [[thm-bezout-identity-for-polynomials]]. The expression $\gcd(0,0)$ is left undefined.

$$ Af+Bg=d. $$

The same argument defines $p_k$; if $\deg p_{k-1}>0$, then $p_{k-1}'\ne0$ and has smaller degree by [F3] and characteristic zero, so $\deg p_k<\deg p_{k-1}$. Thus $p_d=1$, and each $s_k=p_{k-1}/p_k$ is a polynomial.

By [F4], repeated application of [F5] factors $f$ over $\mathbb C$: $f(x)=\prod_{\alpha}(x-\alpha)^{m_\alpha}$, where the finite list contains each distinct root once and $m_\alpha\ge1$. The induction is finite because each division by $x-\alpha$ lowers degree by one by [F6].

The product rule [F3] gives $p'=(x-\alpha)^{m-1}\bigl(mu+(x-\alpha)u'\bigr)$, whose parenthesized factor is nonzero at $\alpha$ because the field has characteristic zero. Hence the gcd of $p$ and $p'$ has multiplicity exactly $m-1$ at $\alpha$; a root absent from $p$ is absent from their gcd. By [F9] for the field extension $\mathbb Q\subseteq\mathbb C$, the monic gcd computed over $\mathbb Q$ is exactly the monic gcd over $\mathbb C$. Thus this root-multiplicity computation applies to each $p_k$.

Induction on $k$ now shows that the multiplicity of $\alpha$ in $p_k$ is $\max(m_\alpha-k,0)$. Therefore $\alpha$ occurs once in $s_k=p_{k-1}/p_k$ exactly when $k\le m_\alpha$, and it occurs in $s_k/s_{k+1}$ exactly when $k=m_\alpha$. This root factorization proves $s_{k+1}$ divides $s_k$ over $\mathbb C[x]$; division over $\mathbb Q[x]$ has the same zero remainder, so $q_k=s_k/s_{k+1}$ lies in $\mathbb Q[x]$.

Each complex root of $f$ occurs in exactly one $q_k$, with exponent one there and exponent $k$ in $q_k^k$. The factorization in step 1.2 therefore gives $f=\prod_{k=1}^d q_k^k$; it also proves that each $q_k$ is squarefree and that distinct $q_k$ have no common root, hence are pairwise coprime. The degree-zero case has $f=1$ and an empty root list.

Let $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d$ be the distinct roots from [F1] and set $D=a_d^{2d-2}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2$. Form the coefficient map $\Phi(u,v)=uP+vP'$ from pairs with $\deg u\le d-2$, $\deg v\le d-1$ to polynomials of degree at most $2d-2$. Its square coefficient matrix $S$ has integer entries, so $\det S$ is an integer-coefficient polynomial in $a_d,\ldots,a_0$.

Divide each output polynomial by $P$ and record its quotient and remainder. In coefficient order from highest degree down, the map $(q,r)\mapsto qP+r$ has triangular diagonal consisting of $d-1$ copies of $a_d$ and $d$ copies of $1$, so the inverse coordinate change has determinant $\pm a_d^{-(d-1)}$. Under this change, $\Phi$ has block form $\begin{pmatrix}I&*\\0&M\end{pmatrix}$, where $M$ is multiplication by $P'$ on $\mathbb C[x]/(P)$. Hence $\det S=\pm a_d^{d-1}\det M$.

For each $i$ define $L_i(x)=\prod_{j\ne i}(x-\alpha_j)/(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$. These degree-$(d-1)$ polynomials satisfy $L_i(\alpha_j)=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. For every degree-$<d$ representative $q$, the difference $q-\sum_iq(\alpha_i)L_i$ has degree $<d$ and vanishes at all $d$ distinct roots; [F7] and [F9] force this difference to be zero. Thus evaluation is an isomorphism $\mathbb C[x]/(P)\to\mathbb C^d$. It conjugates $M$ to the diagonal matrix with entries $P'(\alpha_i)$, so [F4] gives $\det M=\prod_iP'(\alpha_i)$. By [F2], $P'(\alpha_i)=a_d\prod_{j\ne i}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)$; pairing the two factors for each $i<j$ yields $\det S=\pm a_d^{2d-1}\prod_{i<j}(\alpha_i-\alpha_j)^2=\pm a_dD$.

Set the variable $a_d$ to zero in the integer-coefficient polynomial $\det S$. Then $\deg P\le d-1$ and $\deg P'\le d-2$, so every $uP+vP'$ has degree at most $2d-3$; the coefficient map misses the $x^{2d-2}$ coordinate and its determinant is zero. Therefore the constant term in $a_d$ of $\det S$ is zero, so $a_d$ divides $\det S$ as an integer-coefficient polynomial. At the given integer coefficients, $\det S/a_d$ is an integer, and [step 3.1] shows that $D$ is an integer up to sign.
Squarefreeness makes every root distinct, so every factor in $D$ is nonzero and $|D|\ge1$.

Let $\delta=\min_{i<j}|\alpha_i-\alpha_j|$ and choose a pair attaining it. Every other pairwise distance is at most $2R$ by [step 1.1] and the triangle inequality [F5]. Thus $1\le |D|\le H^{2d-2}\delta^2(2R)^{d(d-1)-2}$. Rearranging gives $\delta\ge H^{-(d-1)}(2R)^{-(d(d-1)-2)/2}=\sigma(P)$.
