Let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be the residual map of an implicit equation, where $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is the admissible set for the unknown vector. An exact solution is a point $z^*\in U$ with $G(z^*)=0$.

The **update residual** at an approximate solution $\widetilde z\in U$ is the vector $G(\widetilde z)$, measured in the same units as $z$. If the original equation was divided by a positive step scale $\sigma$, then the **derivative residual** is $G(\widetilde z)/\sigma$, and the corresponding update residual is $\sigma$ times that derivative residual. A residual norm is not a forward-error bound unless a separate inverse or stability estimate converts it to $\|\widetilde z-z^*\|$.

For a first-order vector field $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ ([[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]), take a time $t$, input $y\in\mathbb R^d$, and step $h>0$ with $(t,y)\in D$. For backward Euler, an endpoint $z$ is admissible only when $(t+h,z)\in D$, and its update residual is

$$G_{\rm BE}(z)=z-y-hf(t+h,z),$$

so the derivative residual is $G_{\rm BE}(z)/h$.

For an $s$-stage implicit Runge–Kutta tableau $(A,b,c)$, a stage vector $Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_s)$ is admissible only when $(t+c_jh,Y_j)\in D$ for every $j$. On that admissible set, its stage update residual has blocks

$$G_i(Y)=Y_i-y-h\sum_{j=1}^s a_{ij}f(t+c_jh,Y_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,s.$$

The stage derivative residual is $G(Y)/h$. These conventions distinguish an equation residual from the distance to its exact root.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $G:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$, $z_0\in U$, residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, correction budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$, and refresh period $q\in\mathbb N$, $q\ge1$. Use the coordinate Jacobian convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Since $G$ is $C^1$, [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]] identifies this Jacobian with the matrix of $DG(z)$; write it as $J(z)$. Residual and Jacobian evaluations, norm comparisons and domain tests are returning primitives; no bound on their internal cost is specified. In chord mode also supply a terminating exact linear-system backend: on each square Jacobian it reports singularity if the matrix is singular, and otherwise returns a retained factor object, and each solve on that object terminates with the exact unique solution for its right-hand side. Factorization and solve work are charged individually. The output is a last valid iterate $z\in U$, a status, and the actual residual norm $\|G(z)\|_2$.

In **updated-Newton mode**, invoke [[alg-finite-budget-newton-for-vector-residuals]] with $G,z_0,\varepsilon,N$. It recomputes the Jacobian at every correction and returns its stated residual/budget/failure status. Re-evaluate $G$ at the returned iterate to provide the output residual norm. Count each Jacobian assembly, factorization attempt, and linear solve actually performed.

In **chord mode**, for $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, first evaluate $G(z_k)$ and put $r_k=\|G(z_k)\|_2$. If $r_k\le\varepsilon$, return $(z_k,\texttt{root},r_k)$; this status means only that the residual tolerance was met. If $k=N$, return $(z_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},r_k)$. Otherwise, at $k=0,q,2q,\ldots$, refresh by forming $J_k=DG(z_k)$, attempting to factor it, and retaining the factorization until the next scheduled refresh. The factorization backend must either report singularity or return a factor object whose solve operation gives the exact unique solution of $J_k s=-G(z_k)$. If it reports singularity, return $(z_k,\texttt{singular-jacobian},r_k)$. At each correction obtain $s_k$ by calling the solve operation on that retained factor object with right-hand side $-G(z_k)$; do not refactor or invoke a fresh matrix-only solve. The exact-solve backend contract makes this the mathematical correction in [[alg-newton-correction-for-vector-residuals]]. If the correction $s_k$ has $z_k+s_k\notin U$, return $(z_k,\texttt{invalid-trial},r_k)$; otherwise set $z_{k+1}=z_k+s_k$ and continue. A refresh period $q=1$ updates the Jacobian every correction; $q>1$ is a chord iteration.

Both modes make no claim that a finite budget reaches an exact root or that a small residual is a forward-error bound. Record the number of Jacobian assemblies, factorization attempts, and linear solves actually performed; a dense LU correction uses one forward and one backward triangular solve. Sparse cost depends on the actual stage matrix and factorization backend and is not bounded here.

**Work record.** Count every Jacobian assembly and factorization attempt at a refresh, every linear solve, and, for dense LU, each correction's forward and backward triangular solve. Reuse a chord factorization only for its declared refresh period. Sparse cost depends on the actual stage matrix and backend; this procedure assigns no sparse complexity bound. No general Newton convergence or forward-accuracy claim is part of the algorithm.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: For each initial state $i$, choose a shortest path in [A1] to a state with positive escape probability. A shortest path has no repeated state, since deleting the segment between two repetitions leaves a shorter path with the same endpoint; hence it uses at most $n-1$ transitions. The probability of following that path and then escaping is $p_i=(\prod_{r<k}T_{i_r i_{r+1}})d_{i_k}>0$, where the empty product is $1$. The finitely many choices are made by induction over the finite state set.

Let $L=n$ and $\varepsilon=\min_i p_i$. A finite minimum of positive reals is positive, and every row loses at least $p_i\ge\varepsilon$ mass by step $L$, so $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$.

Since $T\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$, induction gives $T^r\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$ for $0\le r<L$. For $k=aL+r$, nonnegativity and step 2.1 give $T^k\mathbf 1=(T^L)^aT^r\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)^a\mathbf 1$. Thus $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$ and $T^k\to0$.

For any $v\in\mathbb C^n$, step 2.1 gives $\|T^Lv\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v\|_\infty$, by bounding each row sum of absolute values with the corresponding row sum of $T^L$. If $Tv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, then $|\lambda|^L\|v\|_\infty=\|T^Lv\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v\|_\infty$, so $|\lambda|\le(1-\varepsilon)^{1/L}<1$. Thus $\rho(T)<1$.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

derivations.claim: For every $z$, finite summation and [F1] give $\sum_i(Pz)_i=\sum_j(\sum_iP_{ij})z_j=\sum_jz_j$. If $z$ is a column probability vector, each coordinate of $Pz$ is a sum of nonnegative terms, so $Pz\ge0$ and its coordinate sum is one.
For each row $i$, $|(Pz)_i|=|\sum_jP_{ij}z_j|\le\sum_jP_{ij}|z_j|$ because $P_{ij}\ge0$. Summing over $i$ and regrouping finite sums gives $\|Pz\|_1\le\sum_j|z_j|\sum_iP_{ij}=\|z\|_1$.

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

derivations.claim: For $0\le r<L$, substochasticity gives $T^r\mathbf 1\le\mathbf 1$. Since $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$, induction gives $(T^L)^q\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)^q\mathbf 1$ for every $q\ge0$. Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Let $E$ be a nonempty finite set and let $p$ be a transition matrix on $E$
([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]). Then $p$ has an
invariant probability distribution
([[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]]), that is,
some probability vector $\pi$ on $E$ satisfies $\pi p=\pi$. No irreducibility,
aperiodicity or recurrence hypothesis is needed, and the argument uses no
choice principle and no Markov-chain path law.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

derivations.claim: By [F3], choose an invariant probability row vector $\pi$. At least one coordinate $\pi_j$ is positive because its finite nonnegative coordinates sum to one.

Fix any $i\in C$. By irreducibility there is a finite positive-probability path from $j$ to $i$, so for some $r\ge0$ the matrix power satisfies $(K^r)_{ji}>0$. Invariance implies $\pi K^r=\pi$, hence $\pi_i=\sum_k\pi_k(K^r)_{ki}\ge\pi_j(K^r)_{ji}>0$. Thus every coordinate of $\pi$ is positive.

For any real invariant row vector $w$, define $f_i=w_i/\pi_i$. The matrix $R$ with entries $R_{ik}=\pi_kK_{ki}/\pi_i$ is well-defined by step 2.1, is nonnegative, and has row sums $\sum_kR_{ik}=\sum_k\pi_kK_{ki}/\pi_i=1$ by invariance of $\pi$. Also $f_i=\sum_kR_{ik}f_k$, by invariance of $w$. The directed graph of $R$ reverses that of $K$, so it is irreducible.

Since $C$ is finite, choose an index $i$ at which $f_i$ attains its maximum $M$. The identity $M=f_i=\sum_kR_{ik}f_k$ is a convex combination of numbers at most $M$, so every $k$ with $R_{ik}>0$ has $f_k=M$. Repeating along directed paths of the irreducible matrix $R$ gives $f_k=M$ for every $k\in C$. Therefore $w=M\pi$.

Taking $w$ to be any invariant probability shows it equals $\pi$, because its coordinate sum is one; taking arbitrary real invariant $w$ gives the asserted one-dimensional fixed space. For $n=1$ the same argument has a single coordinate and is immediate. The proof uses finite paths, finite maxima, and finite sums only.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

If $P$ is a finite column-stochastic matrix, then $P$ maps column probability vectors to column probability vectors, preserves coordinate sums on all real vectors, and satisfies $\|Pz\|_1\le\|z\|_1$ for every $z\in\mathbb R^n$.

derivations.claim: Let $z\in H$ with $\|z\|_1=1$. Write $z=z^+-z^-$ coordinatewise, where $z_i^+=\max(z_i,0)$ and $z_i^- =\max(-z_i,0)$. Since $\sum_i z_i=0$, the positive and negative masses agree, and their sum is one; hence $\sum_i z_i^+=\sum_i z_i^-=1/2$. Therefore $u=2z^+$ and $v=2z^-$ are probability vectors and $Pz=(Pu-Pv)/2$.

We have $Pu=\sum_j u_jp_j$ and $Pv=\sum_kv_kp_k$. Thus $Pz=\frac12\sum_{j,k}u_jv_k(p_j-p_k)$. The coefficients $u_jv_k$ are nonnegative and sum to one, so the triangle inequality gives $\|Pz\|_1\le\frac12\max_{j,k}\|p_j-p_k\|_1$. Taking the supremum over such $z$ proves the upper bound.

If $n\ge2$ and the maximum is positive, a maximizing pair has $j\ne k$; if the maximum is zero, any distinct pair maximizes it. Choose such a distinct pair and set $z=(e_j-e_k)/2$. Then $z\in H$, $\|z\|_1=1$, and $Pz=(p_j-p_k)/2$, so the supremum is at least $\frac12\max_{j,k}\|p_j-p_k\|_1$. If $n=1$, both sides are zero by definition. This proves the first equality.

For two nonnegative probability columns $a,b$, $|a_i-b_i|=a_i+b_i-2\min(a_i,b_i)$. Summing gives $\frac12\|a-b\|_1=1-\sum_i\min(a_i,b_i)$. Apply this to every pair of columns; taking the maximum of the left side is one minus the minimum overlap on the right.

If $n\ge2$, [F2] bounds every norm in the defining supremum by one, so $0\le\delta(P)\le1$; if $n=1$, $\delta(P)=0$ by definition. For nonzero $z\in H$, apply the definition of $\delta(P)$ to $z/\|z\|_1$ and use homogeneity; for $z=0$ the inequality is immediate. Thus $\|Pz\|_1\le\delta(P)\|z\|_1$ on all of $H$.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

**Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.

**Algorithm input.** An exact finite real matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with indexed state set $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $n\ge1$, represented in an exact arithmetic model that terminates on the required comparisons with zero. If an entry is negative or any column sum differs from one, return `invalid-input`. Rational entries provide an effective instance of this exact-comparison interface. A rounded input without certified sign and column-sum decisions is outside this procedure's input contract.

**Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.

**Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

derivations.claim: Before processing vertex $k$, the Boolean relation records exactly the positive paths whose intermediate vertices lie among $1,\ldots,k-1$: this is true initially because the relation contains precisely zero-step paths and one-edge paths. A path with intermediate vertices among $1,\ldots,k$ either avoids $k$, or can have repeated visits to $k$ removed and be split at its single remaining visit into two paths whose intermediate vertices are among $1,\ldots,k-1$. Conversely, concatenating those two paths gives a path through $k$. Thus the update $R_{ij}\gets R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$ gives exactly the reachability relation after processing $k$. The three loops range over the finite set $S$ and all required comparisons terminate by hypothesis, so the algorithm terminates.

After $k=n$, $R_{ij}$ holds exactly when $j$ is reachable from $i$. Mutual reachability is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive by zero-step paths, reversal of the two reachability assertions, and path concatenation, respectively; hence the algorithm's grouping is exactly the strongly connected component partition. Its finite scan marks a component closed exactly when there is no edge from one of its vertices to a vertex outside it, which is precisely the definition of a closed component.

The directed graph obtained by contracting each strongly connected component is finite and has no directed cycle, since a cycle would make its components mutually reachable and therefore a single component. Starting from any component and following outgoing edges must therefore reach a sink after finitely many steps; sinks are exactly the closed components from step 2.1. Lift this component path to a state path by joining each consecutive pair of intercomponent-edge endpoints with a path inside the current strongly connected component. All edges on the resulting finite state path have positive transition probabilities. A path from a nonclosed component cannot enter a closed component and later leave it, so before its first entry into a closed class it stays in $U$. Therefore every state in $U$ has a positive path through $U$ to a row with positive escape probability into a closed class.

The block $T=K_{U,U}$ is nonnegative and row-substochastic because each row of $K$ sums to one. For every row reached at the end of the path in step 3.1, the positive transition into a closed class is omitted from $T$, so its escape probability $1-\sum_{j\in U}T_{ij}$ is positive. Thus every state of $U$ satisfies the path hypothesis of [F3], which gives the claimed finite-step escape bound and geometric decay. If $U=\varnothing$, there is no transient remainder and the same output description holds without a block $T$.

Let $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $n\ge1$. A matrix $P=(P_{ij})_{i,j\in S}$ is **column-stochastic** when $P_{ij}\ge0$ and $\sum_{i\in S}P_{ij}=1$ for every source index $j$. A **column probability vector** is $x\in\mathbb R^n$ with $x_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i x_i=1$. A **stationary probability vector** for $P$ is a column probability vector $\pi$ satisfying $P\pi=\pi$. For $z\in\mathbb R^n$, write $\|z\|_1=\sum_i|z_i|$ and $H=\{z:\sum_i z_i=0\}$.

The published transition-matrix convention [[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]] is row-stochastic: its row index is the source and its column index the destination. If $K$ is such a matrix, then $P=K^{\mathsf T}$ is column-stochastic; a row law $u$ updated by $uK$ corresponds to the column law $u^{\mathsf T}$ updated by $P u^{\mathsf T}$. All displays on this page that use $Px$ or $Qx$ use this column convention.

Let $E$ be countable with sigma-algebra $2^E$, and let $K$ be a probability kernel on it. For $x,y\in E$, set

$$p(x,y):=K(x,\{y\}),\qquad p^{(n)}(x,y):=K^n(x,\{y\})\quad(n\in\mathbb N_0),$$

where $K^0$ is the identity kernel, so $p^{(0)}(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x=y\}}$. By [[def-iterated-transition-kernels]], each $K^n$ is a probability kernel. Since measures on countable discrete spaces are their singleton-weighted sums ([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), every row satisfies

$$\sum_{y\in E}p^{(n)}(x,y)=K^n(x,E)=1.$$

No conditional-expectation version or choice function is used in this matrix definition.

**Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. This defines the communicating classes and closed classes for real matrices, whether or not their entries can be computed exactly.

**Algorithm input.** An exact finite real matrix $P\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ with indexed state set $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $n\ge1$, represented in an exact arithmetic model that terminates on the required comparisons with zero. If an entry is negative or any column sum differs from one, return `invalid-input`. Rational entries provide an effective instance of this exact-comparison interface. A rounded input without certified sign and column-sum decisions is outside this procedure's input contract.

**Output.** A partition of $S$ into the strongly connected components of the directed graph of positive transitions, the list of closed communicating classes, and the remaining transient states.

**Procedure.** Form the usual row-transition matrix $K=P^{\mathsf T}$. Initialize a Boolean relation $R_{ij}$ to true exactly when $i=j$ or $K_{ij}>0$. For $k=1,\ldots,n$, and then for every $i,j$, replace $R_{ij}$ by $R_{ij}\lor(R_{ik}\land R_{kj})$. Place $i,j$ in the same component exactly when both $R_{ij}$ and $R_{ji}$ are true. Mark a component $C$ closed exactly when $K_{ij}=0$ for every $i\in C$ and $j\notin C$. Return the closed components, the nonclosed components, and their state labels in increasing order. The procedure uses finitely many exact comparisons and Boolean updates; no sparse storage format or cost bound is asserted. It is a graph computation under the exact-comparison interface, not a claim that positivity of arbitrary unrepresented real numbers can be decided from rounded approximations.

Let $T\in[0,\infty)^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, have row sums at most one. Define the one-step escape probability $d_i=1-\sum_jT_{ij}$. Suppose that for each state $i$ there is a path $i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k$ with $T_{i_r i_{r+1}}>0$ for $0\le r<k$ and $d_{i_k}>0$. Then there are $L\le n$ and $\varepsilon>0$ such that $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$. Writing $k=aL+r$ with $0\le r<L$ gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\le(1-\varepsilon)^a$, so $T^k\to0$. In particular, every complex eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $T$ satisfies $|\lambda|<1$, and its spectral radius $\rho(T):=\max\{|\lambda|:\det(\lambda I-T)=0\}$ is less than one.

Let $K$ be a finite row-stochastic transition matrix on a finite state set, let $U$ be a nonempty subset, and put $T=K_{U,U}$. Suppose $T$ satisfies the escape hypothesis of [[lem-finite-transient-block-geometric-escape]] with constants $L\le |U|$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $i\in U$, give a finite first-exit path $(i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, with $i_0,\ldots,i_k\in U$ and $j\in U^c$, the weight $\prod_{r<k}K_{i_r i_{r+1}}\,K_{i_kj}$. The proof shows these countably many path weights sum to one, so they define a probability distribution on finite first-exit paths. Let $G\subseteq U^c$, set $b_i=\sum_{j\in G}K_{ij}$, and let $h_i$ be the probability that the path exits into $G$; let $t_i$ be the mean number of transitions to exit. Then $h=\sum_{k\ge0}T^kb$ and $t=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k\mathbf1$. The matrix $N=(I-T)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}T^k$ exists, has nonnegative entries, and

$$\|N\|_\infty\le L/\varepsilon,\qquad \|h-\widehat h\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|b-(I-T)\widehat h\|_\infty,$$

where $h_i$ is the probability that the first exit from $U$ lands in $G$ and $h=Nb$. The expected number $t_i$ of steps until the first exit from $U$ is finite and satisfies $t=N\mathbf 1$; for any $\widehat t$,

$$\|t-\widehat t\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|\mathbf 1-(I-T)\widehat t\|_\infty.$$

Thus these hitting and mean-exit systems are certified only for a proved transient block; a row-substochastic matrix without the escape hypothesis receives no such conclusion here. The matrix norm is $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$ and the vector norm is $\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|$.

Let $K$ be a finite row-stochastic transition matrix on a nonempty set $C$. Assume **irreducibility**: for every $i,j\in C$ there is a finite directed path from $i$ to $j$ whose transition probabilities are positive. Then there is a unique invariant probability row vector $\pi$, all its coordinates are positive, and every real row vector $w$ satisfying $wK=w$ is a scalar multiple of $\pi$. Equivalently, for the column matrix $P=K^{\mathsf T}$, the real fixed space of $P$ is one-dimensional.

Let $K$ be a probability kernel on a measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]), and let $\pi$ be a
probability measure on $(E,\mathcal E)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). The
probability measure $\pi$ is **invariant** for $K$, and $\pi$ is a
**stationary distribution** of $K$, when

$$(\pi K)(A):=\int_E K(x,A)\,\pi(dx)=\pi(A)\qquad\text{for every }A\in\mathcal E .$$

The set function $\pi K$ is again a probability measure: for fixed $A$ the map
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is measurable and lies in $[0,1]$, so the integral exists in
$[0,1]$; for pairwise disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal E$ the identity
$K(x,\bigcup_nA_n)=\sum_nK(x,A_n)$ of the measure $K(x,\cdot)$ and the
monotone convergence theorem for nonnegative functions
([[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]) give
$\sigma$-additivity of $\pi K$; and $K(x,E)=1$ for every $x$ gives
$(\pi K)(E)=1$. Thus $(\pi K)(A)=\pi(A)$ is an identity between two probability
measures evaluated at $A$.

A $K$-chain whose initial law is $\pi$ is called **stationary** when
$\pi K=\pi$. Stationarity of the process is a statement about all of its
finite-dimensional laws and is proved, not assumed, from $\pi K=\pi$; see
[[thm-invariant-initial-law-makes-the-chain-stationary]].

On a countable state space $E$ with sigma-algebra $2^E$ and transition matrix
$p(x,y)=K(x,\{y\})$ ([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]),
a measure on $E$ is its weighted sum of Dirac masses at singletons
([[thm-measures-on-countable-discrete-spaces-are-weighted-dirac-sums]]), so
invariance is equivalent to the matrix identity

$$\pi(y)=\sum_{x\in E}\pi(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad\text{for every }y\in E .$$

The definition fixes no irreducibility, aperiodicity or uniqueness hypothesis,
and it selects no conditional-expectation versions; the display defines a
single measure $\pi K$ and asserts an identity for it. A transient, periodic or
reducible chain may have several invariant probability measures or none.

Every bounded sequence of reals has a convergent subsequence: if $(x_k)$ is a
sequence of reals and there is $M \in \mathbb{R}$ with $|x_k| \le M$ for every
$k \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-sequence]]), then there is a strictly increasing
$n : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a real $L$ with $x_{n_j} \to L$.

Equivalently: the subsequential limit set of a bounded sequence is nonempty
([[def-subsequential-limit]]).

The theorem is the exact repair of the false claim that a bounded sequence
converges. A bounded
sequence need not converge, and the alternating sequence is the standing witness;
what boundedness does force is that *some* subsequence converges. The converse of
the theorem is false, and badly so: a sequence with a convergent subsequence need
not be bounded.

derivations.claim: The finite graph's strongly connected components form a partition, and its component graph has no directed cycle: a cycle would make its components mutually reachable and hence one component. Following outgoing edges from any component must therefore terminate at a sink, since the component graph is finite and acyclic. A sink is exactly a closed component by [F2]. From any state outside the closed classes, follow a component path to a sink. Each component edge is realized by a positive transition, and strong connectivity supplies finite positive paths from the current state to the source of each such transition and from its endpoint to the next transition's source. Concatenating these paths gives a positive-transition path into a closed class. Before its first entry, this path stays in U because a closed class has no outgoing edge. If U is nonempty, [F3] applies to T. Writing k=aL+r as in [F3] gives $\|T^k\|_\infty\to0$, so the Neumann series $N=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k$ converges and is $(I-T)^{-1}$.

For each closed class $C_j$, the restriction $K_{C_j,C_j}$ is a finite irreducible row-stochastic matrix. By [F5] it has a unique invariant probability $\pi_j$. Extending $\pi_j$ by zero outside $C_j$ preserves invariance because no transition leaves the class. Thus every convex combination in the statement is invariant.

Let $v$ be any invariant probability row vector and write its coordinates as $(v_C,v_U)$. Since closed classes have no transitions to U, the stationary equation on the transient coordinates is $v_U=v_UT$. If U is nonempty, [F3] gives $T^L\mathbf 1\le(1-\varepsilon)\mathbf 1$ for some $\varepsilon>0$, and therefore $\|v_U\|_1=\|v_UT^L\|_1\le\sum_{i\in U}(v_U)_i\sum_{k\in U}(T^L)_{ik}\le(1-\varepsilon)\|v_U\|_1$. Hence $v_U=0$. Since no closed class has transitions to another closed class, the stationary equation now restricts separately to each block $C_j$. Thus each $v_{C_j}$ is invariant on its class, so [F5] makes it $\alpha_j\pi_j$ with $\alpha_j\ge0$; their masses sum to one. This proves the asserted full set of invariant probabilities.

For each transient state i, the probability weight of first entering class $C_j$ after k transient transitions is $(e_i^{\mathsf T}T^kb_j)$. These disjoint first-entry weights sum, by [F4], to $((I-T)^{-1}b_j)_i$. Initial mass already in $C_j$ remains there, so the total class weight from u is $\alpha_j=u(C_j)+u_U(I-T)^{-1}b_j$. Moreover $\sum_jb_j=(I-T)\mathbf 1$, since every transition from a transient state either remains in U or enters exactly one of the closed classes; thus $\sum_j\alpha_j=u(C_1\cup\cdots\cup C_s)+u_U\mathbf 1=1$. If U is empty, the same formula reduces directly to $u(C_j)$.

Define $\bar u_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}uK^k$. Every coordinate lies in [0,1]. From any subsequence, apply [F7] to its first coordinate, restrict to that subsequence, and repeat for the finitely many remaining coordinates; the final subsequence converges coordinatewise. Also $\bar u_NK-\bar u_N=(uK^N-u)/N$, whose ℓ1 norm is at most $2/N$. Hence every subsequential limit is an invariant probability.

The mass $a_n=uK^n(C_j)$ is nondecreasing because $C_j$ is closed; its increment at each step is the first-entry weight from step 1.4. The partial sums of these weights tend to $u_U(I-T)^{-1}b_j$ by [F3]–[F4], and the unabsorbed transient mass tends to zero, so $a_n\to\alpha_j$. For any η>0, choose N₀ so |uKⁿ(Cⱼ)−αⱼ|<η for n≥N₀; the average error is at most the finite sum of the first N₀ errors divided by N, plus η, and hence tends to at most η. Since η is arbitrary, the Cesàro class mass tends to αⱼ. Thus every subsequential limit $\bar u$ has $\bar u(C_j)=\alpha_j$ for each j. By step 1.3 this invariant probability must be $\sum_j\alpha_j\pi_j$.

Every convergent subsequence of $(\bar u_N)$ has the same limit from step 2.1. If the full sequence did not converge to that limit, there would be ε>0 and a subsequence staying at least ε away. Its finitely many bounded coordinates admit a convergent further subsequence by repeated finite applications of [F7]; step 2.1 forces that further limit to be the stated mixture, a contradiction. Thus the full Cesàro sequence converges to the initial-law-dependent mixture stated.

$$q=1-\min_{j,k}\sum_i\min(M_{ij},M_{ik}).$$

If $q\ge1$, return `certificate-unavailable` with the corrected candidate and computed quantities; do not report an accuracy bound. If $q<1$, return `certified` with the candidate $x$, correction ledger $c$, residual $r$, coefficient $q$, and bound

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. $$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator and let $\nu\ge\max_{j<n}r_j$. If $\nu>0$, then

$$P:=I+Q/\nu$$

has nonnegative entries and every column sums to one. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

Let $K$ be a finite row-stochastic transition matrix on a finite state set, let $U$ be a nonempty subset, and put $T=K_{U,U}$. Suppose $T$ satisfies the escape hypothesis of [[lem-finite-transient-block-geometric-escape]] with constants $L\le |U|$ and $\varepsilon>0$. For each $i\in U$, give a finite first-exit path $(i=i_0,i_1,\ldots,i_k,j)$, with $i_0,\ldots,i_k\in U$ and $j\in U^c$, the weight $\prod_{r<k}K_{i_r i_{r+1}}\,K_{i_kj}$. The proof shows these countably many path weights sum to one, so they define a probability distribution on finite first-exit paths. Let $G\subseteq U^c$, set $b_i=\sum_{j\in G}K_{ij}$, and let $h_i$ be the probability that the path exits into $G$; let $t_i$ be the mean number of transitions to exit. Then $h=\sum_{k\ge0}T^kb$ and $t=\sum_{k\ge0}T^k\mathbf1$. The matrix $N=(I-T)^{-1}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}T^k$ exists, has nonnegative entries, and

$$\|N\|_\infty\le L/\varepsilon,\qquad \|h-\widehat h\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|b-(I-T)\widehat h\|_\infty,$$

where $h_i$ is the probability that the first exit from $U$ lands in $G$ and $h=Nb$. The expected number $t_i$ of steps until the first exit from $U$ is finite and satisfies $t=N\mathbf 1$; for any $\widehat t$,

$$\|t-\widehat t\|_\infty\le(L/\varepsilon)\|\mathbf 1-(I-T)\widehat t\|_\infty.$$

Thus these hitting and mean-exit systems are certified only for a proved transient block; a row-substochastic matrix without the escape hypothesis receives no such conclusion here. The matrix norm is $\|A\|_\infty=\max_i\sum_j|A_{ij}|$ and the vector norm is $\|v\|_\infty=\max_i|v_i|$.

Let $P$ be a finite real column-stochastic matrix, let $K=P^{\mathsf T}$ be its row transition matrix, and let $C_1,\ldots,C_s$ be the closed classes of the positive-transition graph defined in [[alg-finite-markov-closed-class-decomposition]]. Let $U$ be the remaining transient states. Each $C_j$ has a unique invariant probability row vector $\pi_j$, extended by zero off $C_j$. Every invariant probability row vector for $K$ is exactly

$$\sum_{j=1}^s\alpha_j\pi_j,\qquad \alpha_j\ge0,\quad\sum_j\alpha_j=1.$$

For an initial row probability $u$, set $T=K_{U,U}$ and $b_j(i)=\sum_{k\in C_j}K_{ik}$ for $i\in U$. If $U\ne\varnothing$, then

$$\delta(P)=\frac12\max_{j,k}\|p_j-p_k\|_1=1-\min_{j,k}\sum_i\min(P_{ij},P_{ik}).$$

Thus $\delta(P)$ is a computable induced contraction factor on the zero-sum subspace $H$; for every $z\in H$, $\|Pz\|_1\le\delta(P)\|z\|_1$.

Let $P$ be a finite column-stochastic matrix and let $m\ge1$. Put $q=\delta(P^m)$, where $\delta$ is the zero-sum coefficient from [[lem-dobrushin-zero-sum-l1-coefficient]]. If $q<1$, then P has a unique stationary probability vector $\pi$. Every column probability vector $x$ satisfies

$$\|x-\pi\|_1\le\frac{\|P^m x-x\|_1}{1-q}\le\frac{m\|Px-x\|_1}{1-q}.$$

The condition $q<1$ is a certified uniqueness and error condition; when a computed upper bound for $q$ is at least one, this theorem supplies no accuracy certificate.

**Graph convention.** For any finite real column-stochastic matrix $P$ on $S=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, the positive-transition graph has a directed edge $j\to i$ exactly when $P_{ij}>0$. Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

**Inputs.** An integer $n\ge1$, an exact rational matrix $P\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}$, an exact rational raw candidate $y\in\mathbb Q^n$, and an integer $m\ge1$. The represented rational entries are the exact data for this certificate; certification proceeds only when P is column-stochastic, as checked in the first instruction.

**Outputs.** Return `invalid-input` if P has a negative entry or a column not summing exactly to one. Set $y_i^+=\max(y_i,0)$ and $s=\sum_i y_i^+$. If $s=0$, return `candidate-unavailable`. Otherwise set $x=y^+/s$ and $c=\|y-x\|_1$. Compute $M=P^m$ by $M_0=I$ and $M_{k+1}=PM_k$ for $0\le k<m$. Compute $r=Px-x$ and

$$q=1-\min_{j,k}\sum_i\min(M_{ij},M_{ik}).$$

If $q\ge1$, return `certificate-unavailable` with the corrected candidate and computed quantities; do not report an accuracy bound. If $q<1$, return `certified` with the candidate $x$, correction ledger $c$, residual $r$, coefficient $q$, and bound

$$B=c+\frac{m\|r\|_1}{1-q}.$$

All operations above use exact rational arithmetic and finitely many loops. If $q\ge1$, the procedure reports no accuracy bound; if $q<1$, it returns the stated exact bound. The procedure takes $y$ as input and makes no claim about how a stationary solver produced it.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator, let $\nu>0$ satisfy $\nu\ge\max_j r_j$, and put $P=I+Q/\nu$. Let $m\ge1$ and $q=\delta(P^m)<1$. Then the finite master equation $p'=Qp$ has a unique stationary probability $\pi$, characterized among column probability vectors by $Q\pi=0$. For any raw vector $y\in\mathbb R^n$ and column probability vector $x$, set $c=\|y-x\|_1$. Then

$$\|y-\pi\|_1\le c+\frac{m\|Qx\|_1}{\nu(1-q)}.$$

The identity $Qx/\nu=Px-x$ makes the generator residual directly usable by the discrete certificate. In the exact algorithm branch, $y^+=0$ returns `candidate-unavailable`, and $q\ge1$ returns `certificate-unavailable`; neither status supplies an algorithmic accuracy certificate.

In particular, when P and y are rational and the exact branch of [[alg-corrected-stationary-residual-certificate]] returns `certified` with candidate x and correction c, those outputs satisfy the conditions above.

Let $p$ be a transition matrix on a countable state space $E$
([[def-transition-matrix-and-n-step-transition-probabilities]]), and let
$\mu:E\to[0,+\infty)$ be a state measure with $\mu(x)<+\infty$ for every
$x\in E$ that satisfies detailed balance for $p$
([[def-reversible-measure-and-detailed-balance]]). Write

$$(\mu p)(y):=\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)\,p(x,y)\qquad(y\in E),$$

the measure-matrix product, a sum of nonnegative terms in $[0,+\infty]$. Then

$$\mu p=\mu,\qquad\text{that is}\qquad(\mu p)(y)=\mu(y)\ \text{ for every }y\in E .$$

In particular the conclusion holds for a reversible state measure of infinite
total mass $\sum_{x\in E}\mu(x)=+\infty$; and if the mass is one, $\mu$ is an
invariant (equivalently stationary) probability distribution for $p$ in the
sense of [[def-invariant-and-stationary-distribution-for-a-markov-kernel]].

The coordinates of $\pi$ are nonnegative and sum to one. In the row kernel K, $\pi_0K_{01}=(1/7)(2/3)=2/21=\pi_1K_{10}$ and $\pi_1K_{12}=(2/7)(2/3)=4/21=\pi_2K_{21}$; the reverse equalities hold, all non-neighbor flows are zero in both directions, and diagonal balance is automatic. citations.quote:
Let $A$ be an $n\times n$ matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $b$ be a
nonzero vector of matching size, and let $m\ge1$. Assume the Arnoldi process
for $(A,b)$ runs through step $m$ without breakdown. Let

$$Q_m=[v_1\,\dots\,v_m], \qquad Q_{m+1}=[v_1\,\dots\,v_{m+1}],$$

and let $\bar H_m=(h_{ij})_{1\le i\le m+1,\,1\le j\le m}$, where the Arnoldi
coefficients occupy the positions $i\le j+1$ and $h_{ij}:=0$ for $i>j+1$.
Then:

1. $v_1,\dots,v_m$ are orthonormal;
2. $\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\dots,v_m\}=K_m(A,b)$;
3. $\bar H_m$ has the rectangular upper-Hessenberg zero pattern
   $h_{ij}=0$ for $i>j+1$;
4. $AQ_m=Q_{m+1}\bar H_m$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and let $A_0\in M_n(\mathbb F)$.

1. The **unshifted QR iteration** factors
   $$A_k=Q_kR_k$$
   with $Q_k$ unitary and $R_k$ upper triangular, then sets
   $$A_{k+1}:=R_kQ_k.$$
2. Given shifts $\mu_k\in\mathbb F$, the **shifted QR iteration** factors
   $$A_k-\mu_k I=Q_kR_k$$
   and sets
   $$A_{k+1}:=R_kQ_k+\mu_k I.$$
3. Given a declared tolerance $\tau_k\ge0$, **numerical deflation** at index
   $j$ occurs when $|(A_k)_{j+1,j}|\le\tau_k$: that entry is then replaced by
   $0$, splitting the matrix into the two diagonal blocks separated at index
   $j$. **Exact deflation** is the special case $\tau_k=0$.
4. For a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix, the **Wilkinson shift** is the
   eigenvalue of the trailing $2\times2$ principal block that is nearer to the
   bottom-right entry; away from a tie, this eigenvalue is unique.

If $H$ is upper Hessenberg and a shifted QR step factors
$H-\mu I=QR$ using the standard adjacent-row Givens eliminations, then

$$ H_+:=RQ+\mu I $$

is again upper Hessenberg.

A square matrix $H=(h_{ij})$ is **upper Hessenberg** when
$h_{ij}=0$ for every $i>j+1$, so entries below the first subdiagonal vanish.

A real symmetric matrix $T=(t_{ij})$ is **tridiagonal** when
$t_{ij}=0$ for every $|i-j|>1$. Thus a real symmetric tridiagonal matrix is
exactly a symmetric upper Hessenberg matrix.

Let $n\ge 2$ and let $0\le i<j\le n-1$.

A **real Givens rotation** in the $(i,j)$-plane is the identity matrix except on
rows and columns $i,j$, where it has the $2\times 2$ block

$$\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-s&c\end{pmatrix}\qquad(c,s\in\mathbb R,\ c^2+s^2=1).$$A **complex Givens transformation** in the $(i,j)$-plane is the identity except on rows and columns $i,j$, where it has block$$\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\-\overline s&c\end{pmatrix},$$

with $c\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}$, $s\in\mathbb C$, and $c^2+|s|^2=1$. The modulus
$|s|$ is the one from [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]].

Such transformations act only on the two chosen coordinates and are designed to
zero one targeted entry while preserving the Euclidean norm from
[[def-inner-product-norm]].

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

derivations.claim: For $0\le j\le m-1$, $A^jv_1=V_mH_m^je_1$: the claim holds at $j=0$, and if it holds at $j<m-1$, [F1] gives $A^{j+1}v_1=V_mH_m^{j+1}e_1+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*H_m^je_1$. By [F4], $H_m^je_1$ is supported in rows $1$ through $j+1$, so $e_m^*H_m^je_1=0$ when $j<m-1$; induction proves the identity through degree $m-1$.

Since $\deg q=p<m$, step 1.1 gives $q(A)v_1=V_mq(H_m)e_1$. Put $P_j=Q_1\cdots Q_j$ and $P_0=I$; the cumulative similarities give $H_{j-1}=P_{j-1}^*H_mP_{j-1}$. Thus $H_m-\mu_jI=P_{j-1}(H_{j-1}-\mu_jI)P_{j-1}^*=P_{j-1}Q_jR_jP_{j-1}^*=P_jR_jP_{j-1}^*$. Because scalar factors commute, order the product as $q(H_m)=(H_m-\mu_pI)\cdots(H_m-\mu_1I)$; substituting these factorizations cancels every adjacent $P_{j-1}^*P_{j-1}$ and gives $q(H_m)=P_p(R_p\cdots R_1)=QR$. The product $R_p\cdots R_1$ is upper triangular, and $Re_1=\rho e_1$, so $q(A)v_1=\rho V_mQe_1$.

For $0\le j<r$, $p+j\le m-1$, so applying step 1.1 to each monomial of $z^jq(z)$ gives $A^jq(A)v_1=V_mH_m^jq(H_m)e_1=\rho V_mQ(H^+)^je_1$. By [F3], $H^+$ is upper Hessenberg, so $(H^+)^je_1$ is supported in its first $j+1$ coordinates and the resulting vector lies in $\operatorname{range}(V_mQ(:,1:r))$. Thus $K_r(A,q(A)v_1)$ is contained in the retained range; both have dimension $r$, the former by hypothesis and the latter because $V_mQ$ has orthonormal columns, so they are equal.

In each shifted QR step the top-down left eliminations use row pairs $(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$; by [F5] the unitary factor is the ordered product of their adjoints. In $Q_i e_j$, rotations with index greater than $j$ act first and fix $e_j$, rotation $j$ adds at most row $j+1$, and rotations with smaller indices add only rows less than $j$; by [F4], each $Q_i$ is upper Hessenberg. If $C$ has lower bandwidth $a$ and $D$ lower bandwidth $b$, a nonzero term in $(CD)_{ij}=\sum_k C_{ik}D_{kj}$ requires $k\ge i-a$ and $k\le j+b$, so $CD$ has lower bandwidth at most $a+b$. Hence $Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p$ has lower bandwidth $p$ and $e_m^*Qe_j=0$ for $j<m-p=r$. Multiplying the Arnoldi factorization in [F1] by $Q$ yields $AV_mQ=V_mQH^++\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*Q$; since $H^+$ is upper Hessenberg, restricting to columns 1 through $r$ gives $AV_mQ(:,1:r)=V_mQ(:,1:r)H_r^++(h^+V_mQe_{r+1}+\beta_m(e_m^*Qe_r)v_{m+1})e_r^*$, the stated identity with residual vector $g$.

The vector $V_mQe_{r+1}$ is orthogonal to the first $r$ columns of $V_mQ$, and [F1] makes $v_{m+1}$ orthogonal to the range of $V_m$; hence $g$ is orthogonal to the retained columns. If $g\ne0$, normalization gives the next Arnoldi residual direction with coefficient $\|g\|_2$; if $g=0$, step 3.2 says $A$ maps the retained range into itself.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $v\ne0$, and choose integers
$1\le r<m\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a restart budget
$N_{\max}\ge1$, and a restart mode `thick` or `implicit`. All operations
below use the exact arithmetic model and projected-solver input specified next. The number $k$ of locked pairs is the number
of linearly independent locked vectors; it starts at zero. If a restart is
needed, a target rule may be supplied for thick mode and is required for an
implicit-mode restart after one or more pairs are locked. When invoked, it
must return $r-k$ current Ritz vectors independent modulo the span of all
locked vectors, or report `unavailable`; no rule, an unavailable selection,
or a wrong-size or dependent selection gives status `rank-loss`. For an implicit-mode
restart with no locked pairs, a shift rule supplies exactly $p=m-r$ complex
shifts for the current cycle or reports `unavailable`; an unavailable list or
a list of any other length gives status `shift-count-unavailable`. The shifts
may be chosen from unwanted Ritz values, but the procedure allows any
supplied list and asserts no convergence for an arbitrary schedule.

**Projected-solver input and exact operations.** Supply a projected eigensolver $S$. derivations.claim: For thick or implicit restarted Arnoldi, one cycle has at most $m$ Arnoldi steps. The thick restart processes finite matrices and blocks using finite exact rank-revealing orthogonalization loops, and its block-Arnoldi queue processes at most $m$ basis columns once each; an unavailable target selection, a missing target rule, or a wrong-size or dependent target block returns `rank-loss`. An implicit restart with no locked pairs uses exactly $p=m-r$ shifts and finite QR steps; an unavailable or wrong-length shift list returns `shift-count-unavailable`. The implicit-mode thick fallback with locked pairs uses the same finite target and orthogonalization steps. The Arnoldi projected-solver contract makes its call finite-return; the finite shape, residual and coefficient checks either produce a valid current Ritz list or return one of its two listed projected-solve failure statuses. Under [A1] an exact returned eigensolve passes those checks. Assumption [A1] makes the other invoked rules and projected eigensolves finite-return. Thus each cycle either returns a listed status or reaches its single restart-counter update.

For block LOBPCG, every pass through steps 1--4 is finite: its trial block has finitely many columns, its $B$-orthogonalization processes at most those columns, and the projected eigensolve and finite-dimensional operations return in finite work by [A1]. A pass either returns a status or completes one update and increments $k$.

The counter begins at $0$ and increases by one before each further cycle. After at most $N_{\max}$ such increments, the next completed cycle reaches the test $c=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted` unless an earlier acceptance or breakdown status has already returned. The number of cycles is therefore at most $N_{\max}+1$, so the Arnoldi execution terminates.

Starting from $k=0$, no more than $N_{\max}$ updates can occur. After those updates the next pass tests $k=N_{\max}$ and returns `budget-exhausted`, unless convergence or rank loss already returned. Hence the block LOBPCG execution terminates after finitely many operations.

Let $B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
be Hermitian positive definite, with Cholesky factor $B=LL^*$ and $L$ lower
triangular with positive diagonal. This factor exists and is unique by
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]].
Define the linear-first **B-inner product** by
$$\langle x,y\rangle_B:=y^*Bx,$$
the **B-norm** by
$$\|x\|_B:=\|L^*x\|_2=\sqrt{x^*Bx},$$
and the **B-dual residual norm** by
$$\|r\|_{B^{-1}}:=\|L^{-1}r\|_2 =\sqrt{r^*B^{-1}r}.$$
The B-orthogonality condition is $x^*By=0$; since $B=B^*$ it is equivalent
to $\langle x,y\rangle_B=0$.

Let $A=A^*$ and let $B=B^*$ be positive definite in
$\mathbb F^{n\times n}$, where $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.
If $B=LL^*$ is its Cholesky factorisation, then
$$C=L^{-1}AL^{-*}$$
is self-adjoint and has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues
$\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n$. The vectors
$$x_i=L^{-*}y_i\quad (i=1,\ldots,n)$$
form a basis satisfying $Ax_i=\lambda_iBx_i$ and
$x_i^*Bx_j=\delta_{ij}$. The generalized eigenvalues of $(A,B)$ are exactly
$[\lambda_i:1]$; none is infinite.

derivations.claim: For $Q_S$, the compression $H_S=Q_S^*AQ_S$ is Hermitian. Diagonalize it with an orthonormal eigenbasis $z_1,\ldots,z_s$ and ordered eigenvalues $\theta_1(S)\le\cdots\le\theta_s(S)$; the vectors $Q_Sz_i$ are B-orthonormal and every Rayleigh quotient on $S$ is their weighted average. Any j-dimensional $W\subseteq S$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(Q_Sz_j,\ldots,Q_Sz_s)$ nontrivially by dimension count, so its maximum quotient is at least $\theta_j(S)$; equality is attained on $\operatorname{span}(Q_Sz_1,\ldots,Q_Sz_j)$. This proves the min-max formula, and a unitary change between B-orthonormal bases conjugates the compression, proving basis invariance.

Let $u_1,\ldots,u_n$ be the ambient B-orthonormal generalized eigenbasis from [F2], ordered by $\lambda_i$. Any j-dimensional $W\subseteq S$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(u_j,\ldots,u_n)$ nontrivially, again by dimension count. The quotient of a nonzero vector in that span is a weighted average of $\lambda_j,\ldots,\lambda_n$ and is at least $\lambda_j$; the min-max formula from step 1.1 gives $\theta_j(S)\ge\lambda_j$.

If $S\subseteq T$, every j-dimensional subspace considered for $\theta_j(S)$ is also available for $\theta_j(T)$. The minimum over the larger family therefore cannot be greater, so $\theta_j(T)\le\theta_j(S)$.

Let $A=A^*\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, let $B=B^*>0$, and let
$T=T^*>0$ be a fixed preconditioning operator. Here $B>0$ and $T>0$ mean
$x^*Bx>0$ and $x^*Tx>0$ for every nonzero $x$. The $B$-inner product and
norm are those of [[def-b-inner-product-and-dual-norm-for-definite-pencil]].
Choose a block width $1\le q\le n$, a residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, a finite
iteration budget $N_{\max}\ge0$, and an input matrix $X_0\in\mathbb C^{n\times q}$.
The output is a block of Ritz pairs and one of
`converged`, `budget-exhausted`, `rank-loss`, or `invalid-initial-block`.

1. If $X_0$ does not have full column rank or does not satisfy
   $X_0^*BX_0=I_q$, return `invalid-initial-block`. Diagonalize the Hermitian
   compression $X_0^*AX_0=Z_0\Theta_0Z_0^*$ with $Z_0$ unitary and the $q$
   Ritz values in increasing order, then replace $X_0$ by $X_0Z_0$. Thus the
   columns used in the first residual block are the actual B-orthonormal Ritz
   vectors paired with the diagonal entries of $\Theta_0$. Set the previous
   search block $D_0$ empty and initialize the iteration counter $k=0$.

2. At iteration $k$, form the original residual block
   $R_k=AX_k-BX_k\Theta_k$. If every column has Euclidean norm at most
   $\tau$, return `converged`. If $k=N_{\max}$, return
   `budget-exhausted` with $(\Theta_k,X_k)$.

3. Compute the preconditioned residual block $W_k=TR_k$ and set
   $Y_k=[X_k,W_k,D_k]$, omitting the empty block at $k=0$. Compute an exact
   rank-revealing $B$-QR with column pivoting as follows. Starting with no
   columns in $Q_k$, for each remaining column $y_j$ of $Y_k$ compute its
   residual $c_j=y_j-Q_k(Q_k^*By_j)$ and choose a column with largest
   $B$-norm $\|c_j\|_B$ (break ties by original column order). If the largest
   residual norm is zero, stop; otherwise append the normalized residual to
   $Q_k$ and remove that pivot column. Let $s_k$ be the number of columns
   appended and let $\Pi_k$ record the pivot order followed by the unused
   columns. If $s_k<q$, return `rank-loss` with the current Ritz pairs; no
   projected solve is attempted on that branch. Otherwise set
   $$S_k=Q_k^*BY_k\Pi_k(:,1:s_k).$$

   Dependent trial columns are discarded and their count is recorded as a
   rank-compression diagnostic.

   $$X_{k+1}=X_kC_X+W_kC_W+D_kC_D,\qquad D_{k+1}=W_kC_W+D_kC_D,$$

   diagonal Ritz-value matrix and increment $k$.

   budget or rank-loss branch is returned. The exact SPD conditions on $B$ and
   $T$ define the permitted metric and preconditioner; no particular
   incomplete-factorization procedure is assumed.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $n\ge1$, choose a shift
$\sigma\in\mathbb C$, and put $M=A-\sigma I$. This procedure returns candidate
values and their residual data; it asserts no convergence or forward-error
bound. Its branch statuses are `available`, `arnoldi-breakdown`,
`linear-solve-unavailable`, `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`,
`infinite-harmonic-value`, `projected-pencil-unresolved`,
`qz-budget-exhausted`, and `qz-certificate-inconclusive`.

**Shift-invert branch.** This branch requires $M$ to be invertible, equivalently
that $\sigma$ is not an eigenvalue of $A$ by
[[prop-eigenvalue-iff-shift-is-not-invertible]]. Its inputs also include a
nonzero starting vector $v$, an integer Arnoldi dimension $1\le m\le n$, a
residual tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine. Normalize
$v_1=v/\|v\|_2$. For $j=1,\ldots,m$, request either the exact solution
$y_j=M^{-1}v_j$ or a computed vector $y_j$ together with its actual equation
residual $s_j=My_j-v_j$. If a requested solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the residuals already recorded. Set $w=y_j$.
For $i=1,\ldots,j$, compute $h_{ij}=\langle w,v_i\rangle$ and replace
$w\gets w-h_{ij}v_i$. Repeat this pass once, adding each second-pass
coefficient to the corresponding $h_{ij}$. Set $h_{j+1,j}=\|w\|_2$. If this
norm is zero, set the current dimension to $k=j$ and stop with status
`arnoldi-breakdown`; otherwise set $v_{j+1}=w/h_{j+1,j}$. After $m$ columns,
set $k=m$ and stop with status `available`.
When every solve is exact, this is Arnoldi applied to $M^{-1}$. When any solve
is inexact, the projected matrix is only the one produced from the computed
vectors; the procedure makes no exact-Arnoldi or convergence claim for that
branch.

Compute the Ritz pairs $(\theta,z)$ of the current $k\times k$ matrix $H$ as
in [[def-ritz-values-and-ritz-vectors-from-arnoldi]], normalize $z$ to unit
norm, and lift $u=V_kz$. For each $\theta\ne0$, report the transformed candidate
$\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$, the lifted vector $u$, and the directly computed
original residual $r_A=Au-\lambda u$. Mark this candidate accepted exactly
when $\|r_A\|_2\le\tau$. If $\theta=0$, assign no finite inverse map and mark
that candidate `zero-transformed-Ritz-value`. To record the solve-error
transfer for a candidate with $\theta\ne0$, request one additional solve
$My=u$; if it is available, store $s_0=My-u$ and $r_T=y-\theta u$ alongside
the directly computed residual $r_A$.
If this additional solve is unavailable, return
`linear-solve-unavailable` with the candidate and accumulated ledger.

**Harmonic Ritz branch.** This branch takes a full-column-rank trial basis
$U\in\mathbb C^{n\times k}$, $k\ge1$; it does not require $M$ to be
invertible. Form $W=MU$ and
$$G=W^*W=U^*M^*MU,\qquad C=W^*U=U^*M^*U.$$
Compute an exact column-pivoted QR of $W$ as in
[[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]] and let
$r_W$ be its exact rank. If $r_W<k$, choose $z\ne0$ with $Wz=0$. Then
$z^*G=(Wz)^*W=0$ and $z^*C=(Wz)^*U=0$. Thus the nonzero row
$z^*$ annihilates $G-\eta C$ for every $\eta$; if this matrix were invertible,
right multiplication by its inverse would force $z^*=0$, a contradiction.
Hence $G-\eta C$ is singular for every $\eta$; return
`projected-pencil-unresolved`. If $W$ has full column rank, then
$z^*Gz=\|Wz\|_2^2>0$ for every $z\ne0$. Thus $G$ is positive definite and
the pencil $G-\eta C$ is regular in the convention of
[[def-regular-generalized-eigenvalue-pencil]], since
$\det(G-0C)=\det G\ne0$.

Supply a finite QZ sweep budget $N\ge0$ and tolerance $\tau_{QZ}\ge0$, and run
[[alg-finite-budget-qz-iteration-with-deflation-and-residual]] on $(G,C)$.

must include their formation errors in the perturbation ledger or return
`qz-certificate-inconclusive`. On `qz-computed`, require its exact-factor and
local-update certificates; if either is unavailable, return
`qz-certificate-inconclusive`. With these certificates,

`infinite-harmonic-value`. These are values of the computed perturbed
pencil, with the QZ residual and perturbation ledger retained; no exact-root,
eigenvector, or forward-error claim is made. After processing all diagonal

the old matrix plus its recorded perturbation.

entries, so their deflation perturbations remain exact regardless of the test.
A one-by-one diagonal pair at $k$ is isolated when $H_{k,k-1}=0$ and
$H_{k+1,k}=0$, omitting a boundary entry when $k=a$ or $k=b$. If it has
$T_{k,k}=0$ and $H_{k,k}\ne0$, report an infinite candidate for the computed pencil and deflate it

remove the first row/column from the active block.

$T_{b,b}\ne0$; if $T_{b,b}=0$, use $[0:1]$. Write
$\widehat H=H_{a:b,a:b}$ and $\widehat T=T_{a:b,a:b}$, with relative indices

$$x=(\beta\widehat H-\alpha\widehat T)e_0.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

If $Au=\lambda u$, then $Mu=(\lambda-\sigma)u$. Invertibility of $M$ and $u
e0$ imply $\lambda
e\sigma$, so applying $M^{-1}$ gives $M^{-1}u=(\lambda-\sigma)^{-1}u$. Conversely, if $M^{-1}u=	heta u$ with $u
e0$, multiplying by $M$ gives $Mu=	heta^{-1}u$; hence $Au=(\sigma+	heta^{-1})u$. Thus the eigenvalue map is exact and the inverse Ritz value cannot be zero.

From [F2], $Mr_T=My-\theta Mu=u+s_0-\theta Mu$. Rearranging yields $Mu-\theta^{-1}u=\theta^{-1}(s_0-Mr_T)$. Since $M=A-\sigma I$ and $\lambda=\sigma+1/\theta$, the left side is $(A-\lambda I)u$, proving the residual identity.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and suppose an exact $m$-step Arnoldi
factorization without breakdown is
$$AV_m=V_mH_m+\beta_m v_{m+1}e_m^*,\qquad V_m^*V_m=I_m,$$
where $H_m$ is upper Hessenberg and $\beta_m>0$. Let $1\le r<m$,
$p=m-r$, and let $H_{j-1}-\mu_jI=Q_jR_j$ be exact shifted QR factorizations
using the ordered top-down adjacent-row Givens eliminations on pairs
$(1,2),(2,3),\ldots,(m-1,m)$, with $R_j$ upper triangular. Put
$$Q=Q_1\cdots Q_p,\qquad H^+=Q^*H_mQ,\qquad q(z)=\prod_{j=1}^p(z-\mu_j).$$
Assume $q(A)v_1\ne0$, the exact filtered Krylov space
$K_r(A,q(A)v_1)$ has dimension $r$, and $\rho\ne0$ in the factorization
$q(H_m)=QR$ with $R$ upper triangular. Then
$$\operatorname{range}(V_mQ(:,1:r))=K_r(A,q(A)v_1).$$
Writing $H_r^+=H^+(1:r,1:r)$, $h^+=H^+_{r+1,r}$, and
$$g=h^+V_mQe_{r+1}+\beta_m(e_m^*Qe_r)v_{m+1},$$
the truncated restart has the exact residual identity
$$AV_mQ(:,1:r)=V_mQ(:,1:r)H_r^++g e_r^*.$$
If $g\ne0$, then $v_{r+1}^+=g/\|g\|_2$ is orthogonal to the retained
columns and the new Arnoldi residual coefficient is $\beta_r^+=\|g\|_2$;
if $g=0$, the retained subspace is exactly invariant.

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

derivations.claim: Every projected $H_2=V_2^*AV_2$ in this example is Hermitian because $A^*=A$, so the supplied two-dimensional solver returns valid complete projected data in finite exact work. By [F1], $q(A)v=(-19e_1-9e_2+e_3)/(10\sqrt3)$. The squared component weights are proportional to $361,81,1$, so the Rayleigh quotient of the restarted vector is $(1\cdot361+2\cdot81+3\cdot1)/(361+81+1)=526/443<2$, whereas the initial quotient is $(1+2+3)/3=2$. The wanted component-to-$e_1$ component ratio falls from 1 to 1/19.

Repeating the same exact restart multiplies the $e_3$ component by $q(3)=1/10$ and the $e_1$ component by $q(1)=-19/10$ at every cycle. Hence after $t$ cycles their magnitude ratio is $(1/19)^t$, which tends to zero. This shift choice suppresses the wanted eigendirection and gives no general convergence claim.

For each finite $t$, the restart vector is proportional to $q(A)^tv$, with all coordinates nonzero because none of $q(1),q(2),q(3)$ vanishes. If a Ritz residual were zero, its lifted vector would satisfy $Au=\theta u$; the diagonal equations $(\lambda_i-\theta)u_i=0$ and distinct $\lambda_i$ force $u$ to be proportional to some $e_i$. No $e_i$ lies in $K_2(A,q(A)^tv)$: representing one would require $c+d\lambda_j=0$ for the other two distinct eigenvalues, hence $c=d=0$. Also $q(A)^tv,Aq(A)^tv,A^2q(A)^tv$ are independent because their coordinate determinant is the product of the three nonzero coordinates and the Vandermonde determinant for $1,2,3$. Thus no pair is accepted at tolerance zero and the space is not invariant before each scheduled restart.

In a separate boundary run with shift $\mu=3$, the filter has $q(3)=0$ and $q(A)v=(-2e_1-e_2)/\sqrt3$, so the wanted $e_3$ component is removed exactly in one filtering step. The filtered vector is still nonzero, so this is not filtered breakdown; it is a shift-selection failure.
