citations.quote:
Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N.$$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. Let $d,m\ge1$ be finite, $T>0$, and let $W$ and $\xi$ satisfy
the filtered Brownian hypotheses in
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] with $U=\mathbb R^d$.
Consider the autonomous SDE
$$dX_t=b(X_t)\,dt+\sigma(X_t)\,dW_t,\qquad X_0=\xi,$$
where $b\in C^1(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb R^d)$, $\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to
\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ is globally Lipschitz, and for constants $L,C<\infty$
and an integer $q\ge1$,
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le L|x-y|^2, \qquad \|Db(x)\|\le C(1+|x|^q).$$
Suppose $\mathbb E|\xi|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$. Then the
maximal local strong solution is global on $[0,T]$, is unique up to
indistinguishability, and for every finite $p\ge1$,
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^p<\infty.$$
The bound may depend on $p,T$, the coefficient constants, and the initial
moments. No global Lipschitz condition on the drift is assumed.

Assume AC. Fix a finite horizon $T>0$, finite dimensions $d,m\ge1$, and an
open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$. Use a complete usual filtered probability
space and an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments
after time $s$ are independent of $\mathcal F_s$, as in
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] and
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. Let $b:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^d$
and $\sigma:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be Borel maps. Require
that they are bounded on every compact subset of $[0,T]\times U$ and locally
Lipschitz in the state uniformly in time: for every compact $K\subset U$ there
is $L_K<\infty$ such that, for every $t\in[0,T]$ and $x,y\in K$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L_K|x-y|.$$
Let $\xi$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, take values in $U$ almost surely, be
independent of the future Brownian increments, and satisfy $\mathbb E|\xi|^2<\infty$.

For $n\ge1$, set
$$K_n=\{x\in U: |x|\le n,\ \operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)\ge n^{-1}\}.$$
When $U=\mathbb R^d$, interpret $\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)=+\infty$.
If $U^c\ne\varnothing$, the distance function is $1$-Lipschitz, so each
$K_n$ is closed; it is bounded, hence compact by Heine--Borel. For
$U=\mathbb R^d$, each $K_n$ is a closed ball and is compact as well. As $n$
increases, the radius bound increases and the distance threshold decreases, so
the sets are nested. Every $x\in U$ belongs to $\operatorname{int}K_n$ for all
sufficiently large $n$: choose $n>|x|$ and, when $U^c\ne\varnothing$,
$n^{-1}<\operatorname{dist}(x,U^c)$. Thus their interiors exhaust $U$.
[[lem-distance-to-set-is-lipschitz]] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]

A **local strong solution up to exit** is the compatible family of stopped
adapted continuous processes $X^{(n)}$ and stopping times $\tau_n$
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] such that
$$\tau_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:X^{(n)}_t\notin\operatorname{int}K_n\}\wedge T, \qquad X^{(n)}_{t\wedge\tau_n}=\xi+\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}b(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,ds+ \int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}\sigma(s,X^{(n)}_s)\,dW_s,$$
with the equation holding indistinguishably and with $X^{(n)}$ constant after
$\tau_n$. Empty early $K_n$ simply give $\tau_n=0$. Compatibility means that
for $m\ge n$, $X^{(m)}$ stopped at $\tau_n$ equals $X^{(n)}$ up to
indistinguishability. The maximal lifetime is $\zeta=\lim_n\tau_n$; for
$t<\zeta$, the common value of $X^{(n)}_t$ for sufficiently large $n$ defines
the maximal local solution $X_t$.

This definition records a local integral equation; it does not assert that a
solution exists or that $\zeta=T$. Those are separate theorem obligations.
The local coefficient conditions allow superlinear growth; global Lipschitz
hypotheses will be imposed only on the coefficient truncations used in the
existence proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The drift $b(x)=-x^3$ satisfies $(x-y)(b(x)-b(y))=-(x-y)^2(x^2+xy+y^2)\le0$, since $x^2+xy+y^2=(x+y/2)^2+3y^2/4\ge0$. Also $|b'(x)|=3x^2\le3(1+|x|^2)$, and $\sigma(x)=1$ is globally Lipschitz. Thus [F3] applies with deterministic $X_0=0$, so $\mathbb E|X_T|^p<\infty$ for every finite $p\ge1$.

The algorithm [F1] gives the displayed recursion. For $h\le1/4$, set $$E_N=\{h^{-1}\le\Delta W_0\le2h^{-1}\}\cap \bigcap_{n=1}^{N-1}\{|\Delta W_n|\le1\}.$$ The increments are independent by [F2]. The normal density, bounded below on $[h^{-1},2h^{-1}]$ by its value at $2h^{-1}$, gives $$\mathbb P(h^{-1}\le\Delta W_0\le2h^{-1}) \ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}}.$$ Also $\mathbb P(|\Delta W_n|>1)\le\mathbb E|\Delta W_n|^2=h$, since $1_{\{|z|>1\}}\le |z|^2$. For $h\le1/4$, $(1-h)^{N-1}\ge e^{-2h(N-1)}\ge e^{-2T}$. Hence $$\mathbb P(E_N)\ge (2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-2T}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}}.$$

On $E_N$, $Y_1=\Delta W_0\ge h^{-1}$. If $|y|\ge h^{-1}$ and $|\delta|\le1$, then $$|y-hy^3+\delta|\ge h|y|^3-|y|-1 =h|y|^3\left(1-\frac1{h|y|^2}-\frac1{h|y|^3}\right) \ge\frac h2|y|^3,$$ because the two fractions are at most $h$ and $h^2$, whose sum is at most $5/16<1/2$. The lower bound is at least $h^{-1}$ when $h\le1/2$ and $|y|\ge h^{-1}$. Induction therefore gives $|Y_n|\ge h^{-1}$ for all $1\le n\le N$ on $E_N$. With $z_n=\sqrt{h/2}|Y_n|$, the same inequality gives $z_{n+1}\ge z_n^3$, while $z_1\ge(2h)^{-1/2}>1$. Thus $$|Y_N|\ge\sqrt{2/h}\,(2h)^{-3^{N-1}/2}\quad\text{on }E_N.$$

Combining steps 1.2 and 2.1 yields $$\mathbb E|Y_N|^p\ge(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-2T}h^{-3/2}e^{-2h^{-3}} \left(\sqrt{2/h}\,(2h)^{-3^{N-1}/2}\right)^p.$$ Here $h=T/N$. The positive logarithmic term $\frac p2 3^{N-1}\log((2h)^{-1})$ grows faster than the negative term $2h^{-3}=2N^3/T^3$, so this lower bound tends to $+\infty$. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=(0,\infty)$. The input consists of $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfying
the Feller condition $2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, a step $h>0$, a current
transformed value $z_n\ge0$, and a finite Brownian increment $\Delta W_n$.
Set
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8},\qquad A=1+\frac{\kappa h}{2},\qquad c=z_n+\frac{\sigma}{2}\Delta W_n.$$
For valid parameters, $a>0$ and $A>0$. Compute
$$z_{n+1}=\frac{c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}}{2A},\qquad x_{n+1}=z_{n+1}^2.$$
This is the positive-root solution of
$$A z_{n+1}^2-cz_{n+1}-ah=0,$$
which is the drift-implicit Euler equation for the Lamperti variable
$Z=\sqrt X$ in the CIR model
$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$.

Return `invalid-input` for parameters outside the stated domain or a
non-finite input. Otherwise return `success` with $(z_{n+1},x_{n+1})$. In
exact real arithmetic the discriminant is strictly positive and the displayed
root is finite and positive for every $z_n\ge0$ and $\Delta W_n\in\mathbb R$;
the algorithm has no rejected root branch. A floating-point implementation
that cannot verify a finite positive root returns `solve-failure` and does
not advance the state. This is a specific implicit square-root update, not
the ordinary Euler–Maruyama update for $X$.

Let $\kappa,\theta,\sigma>0$ satisfy the Feller condition
$2\kappa\theta\ge\sigma^2$, and put
$$a=\frac{4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2}{8}.$$
For a positive local strong solution of the CIR SDE
$$dX_t=\kappa(\theta-X_t)dt+\sigma\sqrt{X_t}\,dW_t$$
on $U=(0,\infty)$, the Lamperti variable $Z_t=\sqrt{X_t}$ satisfies
$$dZ_t=\left(\frac a{Z_t}-\frac\kappa2 Z_t\right)dt+ \frac\sigma2dW_t$$
up to every compact exit time. Moreover, for every $h>0$, $z\ge0$, and
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R$, the drift-implicit step
$$z_+=z+h\left(\frac a{z_+}-\frac\kappa2z_+\right) +\frac\sigma2\Delta W$$
has exactly one positive root. It is the value defined by
[[alg-cir-lamperti-positive-implicit-scheme]]. The boundary input $z=0$ is
included for the numerical root statement; the CIR solution theorem below
uses $X_0>0$.

derivations.claim: From the parameter assumptions, $4\kappa\theta-\sigma^2\ge\sigma^2>0$, so $a>0$; also $A=1+\kappa h/2>0$. With $z_n=0$ and $\Delta W_n=-r$, $c=-\sigma r/2\le0$.

Since $4Aah>0$, $$\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}>|c|=\sigma r/2.$$ Therefore the numerator $c+\sqrt{c^2+4Aah}$ and denominator $2A$ are both strictly positive, so the algorithm's next Lamperti state is positive. Its square is also strictly positive. The uniqueness and equation interpretation follow from [F2], including the case $r=0$. AC is exactly [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice as required by the stochastic-integral interfaces
below. Fix a finite horizon $T\ge0$ and finite integers $d,m\ge1$. Work on
a complete filtered probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T},P)$ whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$ (the usual conditions).

Let $W=(W_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion
[[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]] adapted to this filtration, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ for $0\le s<t\le T$. Let
$X_0:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ be $\mathcal F_0$-measurable, satisfy
$E|X_0|^2<\infty$, and be independent of the future Brownian increments.
Explicitly, $X_0$ is independent of the sigma-algebra
$\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.

Continuity of a process means continuity on one measurable event of
probability one. We use an everywhere-continuous adapted representative: if
the chosen process is continuous only on such an event $A$, replace it off $A$
by its initial value. Since $A^c$ is a null set and the filtration is complete,
$A^c\in\mathcal F_0$; the replacement preserves adaptedness and changes the
SDE identity only on a null event, hence preserves it up to
indistinguishability.

The drift and diffusion coefficients are jointly Borel maps
$$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d,\qquad \sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}.$$
For nonnegative finite constants $L,K$, assume for every $t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$ that
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|).$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and
$\|A\|_F^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{k=1}^m|A^{ik}|^2$ is the Frobenius norm.

For an adapted continuous candidate $X:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$,
the vector Itô equation
$$X_t=X_0+\int_0^t b(s,X_s)\,ds+\left(\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}(s,X_s)\,dW_s^k\right)_{i=1}^d,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
uses a pathwise Lebesgue integral for the drift and, in each coordinate, the
localized Itô integral from
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], clause 2. Require
$\int_0^T|b(s,X_s)|ds<\infty$ and
$\int_0^T\|\sigma(s,X_s)\|_F^2ds<\infty$ almost surely; these are the local
coefficient-integrability conditions in that definition. When a coordinate
integrand has finite expected energy, its integral is the square-integrable
Itô integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]];
the Picard estimates below establish that stronger condition for every input
in $\mathcal H_T$. Equality of processes means
equality for every $t$ on one measurable event of probability one, that is,
indistinguishability
[[def-law-modification-and-indistinguishability-of-processes]]. A **strong
solution on $[0,T]$** is an adapted continuous process satisfying this
integral equation indistinguishably. No moment bound is included in the
definition; the existence theorem proves its $L^2$ path-sup bound.
The usual-filtration, continuity, and finite-coordinate conventions agree
with the multidimensional class of continuous Brownian Itô processes
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. This definition makes no ellipticity,
transition-density, forward-equation, or time-reversal assertion.

Brownian motion here means the finite-horizon version of the cited definition:
$W_0=0$ almost surely, with continuous paths and the stated increments on
$[0,T]$. All cited stochastic-calculus interfaces are used on this interval.
Their constructions require no extension of $W$ beyond $T$: elementary
integrals use only increments between partition points in $[0,T]$, and their
$L^2$ limits and continuous versions are constructed on that same interval.
For a predictable scalar integrand $H$ with finite pathwise energy, localize
at $\rho_n=\inf\{t\in[0,T]:\int_0^t H_s^2ds\ge n\}\wedge T$.
Here $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$.
The stopped integrands have expected energy at most $n$; their continuous
integrals agree up to the smaller stop by the finite-energy stopping identity.
On the full event of finite energy, $\rho_n=T$ for all sufficiently large
$n$, so these integrals paste uniquely on the whole closed interval $[0,T]$,
exactly as in the localized construction of
[[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]]. At $T=0$ every integral is zero.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $m,d\ge1$ be finite
integers, let $B=(B^1,\dots,B^m)$ be a standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion,
and let $X$ be an $\mathbb R^d$-valued continuous Brownian Ito process
$$X^i_t=X^i_0+\int_0^tb^i_s\,ds+\sum_{k=1}^m\int_0^t\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s, \qquad i=1,\dots,d,$$
in the sense of [[def-continuous-brownian-ito-process]], including its usual-filtration and almost-sure coefficient-integrability conventions. Let
$f\in C^{1,2}([0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^d)$, meaning that $f,\partial_tf$,
$\partial_if$ and $\partial_i\partial_jf$ ($1\le i,j\le d$) exist and are
continuous. Then, up to indistinguishability, for every $t\ge0$
$$f(t,X_t)=f(0,X_0)+\int_0^t\Bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\Bigr)(s,X_s)\,ds+\sum_{i,k}\int_0^t\partial_if(s,X_s)\sigma^{ik}_s\,dB^k_s,$$
For the displayed integrands, intersect the measurable full events of continuity and the decomposition of $X$, and of coefficient integrability at all integer horizons. Its null complement belongs to $\mathcal F_0$ under the usual conditions. Set $X,X_0,b,\sigma$ to zero there. These representatives preserve all coefficient classes and the decomposition up to indistinguishability, with everywhere continuous $X$ and everywhere locally finite coefficient path integrals. All displayed integrands use these representatives.

The stochastic integrals are localized Ito integrals of the predictable
locally square-integrable integrands $\partial_if(\cdot,X)\sigma^{ik}$, and
$(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}_s=\sum_k\sigma^{ik}_s\sigma^{jk}_s$. In
differential form,
$df(t,X_t)=\bigl(\partial_tf+\sum_ib^i\partial_if+\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}(\sigma\sigma^{\mathsf T})^{ij}\partial_i\partial_jf\bigr)(t,X_t)\,dt+\sum_{i,k}\partial_if(t,X_t)\sigma^{ik}_t\,dB^k_t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. An
$\mathbb R^d$-valued process $B=(B_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a **standard
$d$-dimensional Brownian motion** if:

1. $B_0=0$ almost surely;
2. for every finite list $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n$, the vector increments
   $$B_{t_j}-B_{t_{j-1}},\qquad 1\le j\le n,$$
   are mutually independent and have laws
   $N_d(0,(t_j-t_{j-1})I_d)$; and
3. there is one measurable event $A$ with $P(A)=1$ such that
   $t\mapsto B_t(\omega)$ is continuous from $[0,\infty)$ to
   $\mathbb R^d$ for every $\omega\in A$.

Equivalently, its $d$ coordinate processes $B^\alpha=(B_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}$
are independent standard one-dimensional Brownian motions. Here independence
of the processes means the following precise assertion. Put
$I=[0,\infty)$ and equip $\mathbb R^I$ with its cylinder sigma-algebra. The
maps
$$ \Phi_\alpha:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb R^I, \qquad \Phi_\alpha(\omega)(t)=B_t^\alpha(\omega), \qquad 1\le\alpha\le d, $$
are independent random elements.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. Fix finite integers $d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, and $N\ge1$ such that
$h=T/N\le1$. Work on a filtered probability space whose filtration is
right-continuous and contains every $P$-null subset of $\mathcal F$ in
$\mathcal F_0$. Let $W$ be an adapted standard
$m$-dimensional Brownian motion whose increments after time $s$ are
independent of $\mathcal F_s$. Let $X_0$ be finite, $\mathcal F_0$-measurable,
and independent of $\sigma(W_t-W_0:0\le t\le T)$.
Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$g:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be $C^1$. Assume finite constants
$\mu,c,D\ge0$ and an integer $q\ge1$ satisfy, for all $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$\langle x-y,f(x)-f(y)\rangle\le\mu|x-y|^2,\qquad \|g(x)-g(y)\|_F^2\le c|x-y|^2,$$
$$|f(x)-f(y)|^2\le D(1+|x|^q+|y|^q)|x-y|^2.$$
Here $|\cdot|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ is the Frobenius
norm.

Set $t_k=kh$ and construct the grid approximation recursively by
$$Y_0=X_0,\qquad Y_{k+1}=Y_k+f(Y_k)h+g(Y_k)(W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}),\quad 0\le k<N.$$
The output also includes the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_k\quad(t_k\le t<t_{k+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_k+f(Y_k)(t-t_k)+g(Y_k)(W_t-W_{t_k})\quad(t_k\le t\le t_{k+1}).$$
The recursion makes the two interpolation formulas agree at every shared
endpoint. The finite recursion is defined pathwise: $C^1$ coefficients are
finite-valued, each $Y_k$ is finite almost surely by induction, and Brownian
paths are continuous. This algorithm defines no moment or convergence claim.

Assume AC and the Brownian conventions of
[[def-locally-lipschitz-ito-sde-and-maximal-solution]] on $[0,T]$ with
$U=\mathbb R^d$. An admissible mathematical input has finite dimensions
$d,m\ge1$, $T>0$, $N\ge1$ with $h=T/N\le1$, an autonomous continuous drift
$b:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$, a finite-valued Borel diffusion
$\sigma:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$, and a finite
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial state $\xi$. It also has a constant
$\mu\ge0$ such that
$$\langle x-y,b(x)-b(y)\rangle\le-\mu|x-y|^2\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^d).$$
This global condition is a precondition on the mathematical input, not a
runtime test over all $x,y$. For $h>0$, set $H_h(x)=x-hb(x)$ and let
$R_h=H_h^{-1}$, which is defined uniquely on all of $\mathbb R^d$ by
[[thm-backward-euler-dissipative-resolvent-contraction]].

First check that $d,m$ are positive integers, $T$ is finite and positive,
$N$ is a positive integer, $0<h=T/N\le1$, and $\xi$ is finite. If any of
these checks fails, return `invalid-input`. An exact execution then sets
$Y_0=\xi$ and, for $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, computes
$$u_n=Y_n+\sigma(Y_n)(W_{t_{n+1}}-W_{t_n}),\qquad Y_{n+1}=R_h(u_n).$$
It returns the grid values, the left-endpoint step process
$$\bar Y_t=Y_n\quad(t_n\le t<t_{n+1}),\qquad \bar Y_T=Y_N,$$
and the continuous interpolation
$$Y_t=Y_n+(t-t_n)b(Y_{n+1})+\sigma(Y_n)(W_t-W_{t_n}), \qquad t_n\le t\le t_{n+1}.$$
This is a pathwise continuous extension of the grid values. At each shared
endpoint the interpolation agrees with the grid update.

A finite implementation may instead receive a root-solver interface $S$ and
an integer work cap $M\ge0$. Each call $S(H_h,u_n,M)$ must terminate after at
most $M$ declared solver iterations and return either
`certified-root(z, proof)` or `no-certificate(last-iterate, residual)` (with
`last-iterate = null` if the cap permits no iterate). The
supplied exact verifier must terminate and accepts a certificate precisely when it proves that
$z\in\mathbb R^d$ is finite and $H_h(z)=u_n$. At the first call returning
`no-certificate`, or at the first certificate rejected by the verifier, stop
and return `solve-failure` with zero-based failed index $n$, the valid grid prefix through
$Y_n$, the step process on $[0,t_n]$, the interpolation on $[0,t_n]$, and the
solver diagnostic. For `no-certificate`, retain its last iterate and residual;
for a rejected certificate with candidate $z$, report $z$ and residual
$H_h(z)-u_n$. If the diagnostic has no finite candidate, its iterate and
residual are null. Do not assign $Y_{n+1}$ or continue. A
verified root equals $R_h(u_n)$ by uniqueness. If every call is verified,
return `success` and the exact grid, step process, and interpolation above.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Define $X_t=\exp(-7t/2+\sqrt3W_t)$. Itô's formula [F2] gives $dX_t=(-7/2+3/2)X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t=-2X_tdt+\sqrt3X_t\,dW_t$ and $X_0=1$. The coefficients are globally Lipschitz, so [F1] identifies this with the unique strong solution. For $t>0$, completing the square in the $N(0,t)$ density gives $\mathbb E e^{uW_t}=e^{u^2t/2}$; at $t=0$ both sides are $1$. Hence $\mathbb E|X_t|^2=e^{-7t}\mathbb E e^{2\sqrt3W_t}=e^{-7t}e^{6t}=e^{-t}$.

Let $Y_n$ be explicit Euler with $h=1/2$. Since $b(x)=-2x$ and $\sigma(x)=\sqrt3x$, [F4] gives $Y_{n+1}=\sqrt3Y_n\Delta W_n$. Conditional on $\mathcal F_{t_n}$, independence and variance $h$ imply $\mathbb E(|Y_{n+1}|^2\mid\mathcal F_{t_n}) =3h|Y_n|^2=\tfrac32|Y_n|^2.$ Without the noise term, the deterministic multiplier is $1-2h=0$, so the factor greater than one here is caused by the stochastic increment.

For drift-implicit Euler, the resolvent equation is $Y_{n+1}+2hY_{n+1}=Y_n+\sqrt3Y_n\Delta W_n$. At $h=1/2$ this gives $Y_{n+1}=\tfrac12(1+\sqrt3\Delta W_n)Y_n$. Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and certificate data $(\mathcal C,c,Q,V)$. Here $c\in\mathcal C$ is a supplied certificate, $Q$ is a declared predicate on completed rows, and $V(W,c)$ is a supplied deterministic verifier that terminates with a Boolean for every completed row $W$ and satisfies $V(W,c)=\mathrm{true}\Rightarrow Q(W)$. Without certificate data, take $V$ to return false. Every map call is required to terminate with a state or declared failure. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output contains every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint when one exists, and a status. If initialization never completes, return an empty completed-row table and no endpoint.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. When initialization and all $K$ requested sweeps finish, call $V$ on the final row and $c$ (or use false when no certificate was supplied). Return status converged if this returns true, certifying the declared predicate $Q$; otherwise return status budget-exhausted. Completion of the finite budget alone is not a convergence certificate.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

derivations.claim: At sweep $k=0$, the only claimed node is $n=0$, and $U_0^0=x_0=x_0$ by initialization and the definition of the fine trajectory [F1].

Suppose the claim holds at sweep $k$. At sweep $k+1$, $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$ by [F2]. Induct on $n$ from $0$ to $\min\{k,N-1\}$; if $U_n^{k+1}=x_n$, then $n\le k$ also gives $U_n^k=x_n$, so [F2] yields $U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(x_n)+F_n(x_n)-G_n(x_n)=F_n(x_n)=x_{n+1}$ by [F1]. Thus the claim holds through node $\min\{k+1,N\}$.
Induction on k proves the first assertion. If the requested rows 0,...,K all complete and K>=N, applying it at k=K gives U_n^K=x_n for every 0<=n<=N; by [F2], row K is in the returned table.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

At node $0$, $E_0^k=0$ for every $k$ by [F2]. At sweep $k=0$, [A1] gives $E_n^0\le M\le MA^n$. These are the initial cases for induction on the node, simultaneously over all completed sweeps.

Assume the bound holds at node $n$. For the level-zero row at node $n+1$, [A1] gives $E_{n+1}^0\le M\le MA^{n+1}$. For each $k\ge0$, [step 1.1] gives $E_{n+1}^{k+1}\le MA^n b^{k+1}\left(a\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)\le MA^{n+1}b^{k+1}\left(\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk\right)$. The last inequality uses $a\le A$ and $1\le A$. Partitioning the $(k+1)$-element subsets of an $(n+1)$-element set according to whether they contain its final element gives $\binom n{k+1}+\binom nk=\binom{n+1}{k+1}$, including the zero convention. Thus the bound holds at node $n+1$, and induction proves the first estimate.

In the fixed-horizon branch, $A\le1+C_aH\le\exp(C_aH)$ by [A2], [F4], and the definition of $\exp$ in [F6]. Repeated use of [F5] gives $A^N\le\exp(C_aNH)=\exp(C_aT)$. Each $k$-element subset of an $N$-element set has a unique increasing $k$-tuple, so $\binom Nk\le N^k$. Substituting these bounds and $b\le C_bH^{q+1}$ into the first estimate gives $\|U_N^k-x_N\|\le M N^k\exp(C_aT)(C_bH^{q+1})^k=M(C_bT)^k\exp(C_aT)H^{qk}$. For fixed $T,k$ and uniform $M$, this is $O(H^{qk})$.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $\Phi_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le i\le N$, and let $u_0\in\mathbb R^d$ be fixed. The linear part of a fine propagator in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]] is represented by $\Phi_i$. For forcing vectors $g_i\in\mathbb R^d$, write the fine recurrence as $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$. On the unknown vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, define $A_t$ by $(A_tv)_1=v_1$ and $(A_tv)_i=v_i-\Phi_i v_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le N$. With $b_1=\Phi_1u_0+g_1$ and $b_i=g_i$ for $i\ge2$, the recurrence is exactly $A_tv=b$.

For a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$, the coarse indices are $0,m,2m,\ldots,N$. Among unknowns, let $C=\{m,2m,\ldots,N\}$ and $F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus C$. Reordering the unknown vector as $(v_F,v_C)$ gives
$$A_t=\begin{pmatrix}A_{FF}&A_{FC}\\ A_{CF}&A_{CC}\end{pmatrix}.$$
A practical coarse propagator $\Psi_j$ on each interval is the linear subcase of the coarse maps $G_n$ in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]]; the exact coarse operator is determined by eliminating F-points and is not generally the same as this practical choice. This definition asserts no stability or convergence property.

derivations.claim: For any right-hand side, solve the fine equations in increasing index: the first unknown is determined by its identity diagonal block, and each later unknown is uniquely $u_i=r_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. This proves $A_t$ is invertible. Holding all C-values fixed, the F-equations in each interval between consecutive C-points have the same forward-substitution form with identity diagonal blocks, so they uniquely determine the F-values; hence $A_{FF}$ is invertible.

In the reordered block system, the F rows give $u_F=A_{FF}^{-1}(b_F-A_{FC}u_C)$. Substituting this expression in the C rows gives $(A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC})u_C=b_C-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}b_F$. Conversely, any solution $u_C$ of this coarse system, together with the displayed formula for $u_F$, satisfies both the F and C rows. Thus elimination preserves exactly the solution set.

Repeated substitution in $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$, for $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm$, gives $u_{jm}=(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}+\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s}$. For $s=m$ the product is empty and equals $I$. This is exactly the coarse recurrence in the Statement; the coefficient product reduces to $\Phi^m$ when every $\Phi_i=\Phi$.

Let $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$ be the sequential fine trajectory and let $U_n^k$ be the exact-arithmetic table from [[alg-parareal-correction-sweeps]]. Let $D\subseteq X$ contain every $x_n$ and every iterate used in the requested sweeps. Suppose constants $a,b,M\ge0$ satisfy, for every $0\le n<N$ and $u,v\in D$,
$$\|G_n(u)-G_n(v)\|\le a\|u-v\|,\qquad \|(F_n-G_n)(u)-(F_n-G_n)(v)\|\le b\|u-v\|,$$
and $\|U_n^0-x_n\|\le M$ for all $0\le n\le N$. Use $\binom nk$ for the number of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element set, set it to $0$ for $k>n$, and put $A=\max\{1,a\}$. Then for every node $0\le n\le N$ and completed sweep $k\ge0$,
$$\|U_n^k-x_n\|\le M\binom nk A^n b^k,$$
with $b^0=1$. The hypotheses include all comparison points; invariance of $D$ under $F_n,G_n$ alone does not ensure that corrected iterates stay in $D$.

For a fixed horizon $T=NH$, suppose $a\le1+C_aH$, $b\le C_bH^{q+1}$ for constants $C_a,C_b\ge0$ and integer $q\ge1$, and one $M$ works uniformly as $N$ varies. Then, for each fixed $k\le N$,
$$\|U_N^k-x_N\|\le M(C_bT)^k\exp(C_aT)H^{qk}.$$
Thus the exact-solve error is $O(H^{qk})$ at each fixed iteration $k$ under these uniform assumptions. Neither estimate includes finite-solver error; that effect requires a separate update-defect analysis.

derivations.claim: Set $e_n^k=\|V_n^k-x_n\|$. Subtracting $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$ from the computed recurrence, splitting off the update defect, and applying the two Lipschitz inequalities gives $e_{n+1}^{k+1}\le a e_n^{k+1}+b e_n^k+\eta\le A e_n^{k+1}+b e_n^k+\eta$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Use the notation and Lipschitz hypotheses of [[thm-parareal-binomial-error-bound]], with $A=\max\{1,a\}$. Let computed iterates $V_n^k$ satisfy $V_0^k=x_0$, $\|V_n^0-x_n\|\le M$, and, for each requested correction,
$$\left\|V_{n+1}^{k+1}-\left[G_n(V_n^{k+1})+(F_n-G_n)(V_n^k)\right]\right\|\le\eta$$
for a constant $\eta\ge0$. Define $P_n^k=M\binom nk A^n b^k$ and a nonnegative forcing array by $R_0^k=0$, $R_n^0=0$, and
$$R_{n+1}^{k+1}=A R_n^{k+1}+bR_n^k+\eta.$$
Then $\|V_n^k-x_n\|\le P_n^k+R_n^k$ for every completed node and sweep.

The base envelope $M$ includes coarse-initialization error relative to the fine trajectory. The per-update defect $\eta$ must bound the actual combined effect of fine/coarse evaluation errors and correction-solve error; a residual tolerance alone supplies no forward-error bound.

Input: a linear fine-grid system $A_tu=b$ with $N\ge1$ fine intervals as in [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]], a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$ and its C/F partition as in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], practical coarse propagators $\Psi_j\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le j\le N_c:=N/m$, an initial fine-grid iterate $u_{\rm in}$, pre- and post-relaxation choices from $\{F,FCF\}$, a real-valued norm on the fine-grid residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], a nonnegative integer cycle budget $J_{\rm cyc}$, and a residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The symbol $J_{\rm cyc}$ is the number of permitted cycles; the coarse-interval count is $N_c$ (the letter $J$ in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]] denotes that lemma's coarse-interval count). The output is the last iterate, its residual norm, the number of completed cycles, and status `converged` or `budget-exhausted`.

In F/C ordering define ideal interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$ by
$$P=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}\\ I_C\end{bmatrix}, \qquad R=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}&I_C\end{bmatrix}.$$

The exact coarse operator is the Schur complement $RA_tP=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}$ from [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]]. The practical correction matrix $A_c$ has identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_j$ for $2\le j\le N_c$; its first row corresponds to the fixed zero initial correction $z_0=0$. For any right-hand side $\rho$, forward substitution uniquely solves $A_cz=\rho$ by setting $z_0=0$ and, in increasing order for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, setting $z_j=\rho_j+\Psi_jz_{j-1}$. Thus $A_c$ is invertible even when an individual $\Psi_j$ is singular.

Define the relaxations on $A_tu=b$ as follows. An F-relaxation holds every C-value fixed and, for each coarse interval $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, updates its F-indices $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm-1$ in increasing order: set $u_1=b_1$ if $i=1$, and otherwise set $u_i=b_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. Different coarse intervals have independent F-updates and may be processed in parallel. A C-relaxation holds every F-value fixed and, for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$ in increasing order, sets $u_{jm}=b_{jm}+\Phi_{jm}u_{jm-1}$; these C-updates are independent because $m\ge2$ and each predecessor is an F-index. An FCF-relaxation applies F-relaxation, then C-relaxation, then F-relaxation. Each relaxation is a finite linear update; write $S_{\rm pre}$ and $S_{\rm post}$ for the error maps of the selected pre- and post-relaxations.

For one cycle from a current iterate $u$, apply the selected pre-relaxation; form $r=b-A_tu$ and $\rho=Rr$; solve $A_cz=\rho$ by the forward substitution above; correct $u\leftarrow u+Pz$; then apply the selected post-relaxation. The exact error-propagation matrix of this fixed cycle is
$$E=S_{\rm post}(I-PA_c^{-1}RA_t)S_{\rm pre}.$$

Initialize $u^{(0)}=u_{\rm in}$ and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(0)}\|$. If this is at most $\varepsilon$, return $u^{(0)}$, zero completed cycles, and status `converged`. Otherwise, for $j_{\rm cyc}=1,\ldots,J_{\rm cyc}$, perform one cycle, call the resulting iterate $u^{(j_{\rm cyc})}$, and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(j_{\rm cyc})}\|$. If this norm is at most $\varepsilon$, return that iterate, $j_{\rm cyc}$ completed cycles, and status `converged`; if not, continue. If all $J_{\rm cyc}$ cycles finish without this condition (including when $J_{\rm cyc}=0$), return the last iterate, its residual norm, and status `budget-exhausted`. The matrix $E$ describes exact arithmetic and exact coarse solves; inexact solves contribute an update defect that needs its own bound.

Use [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]] with $N=Jm$, $m\ge2$, and its F/C partition. Both $A_t$ and $A_{FF}$ are invertible. Eliminating the F unknowns from $A_tv=b$ gives the coarse system with Schur complement
$$S=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}.$$
On coarse interval $j$, its recurrence is
$$u_{jm}-(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}=\bar g_j,$$
where
$$\bar g_j=\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s},$$
with an empty product defined to be the identity. If $\Phi_i=\Phi$ for every fine step, the exact coarse propagator is $\Phi^m$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

The following are the explicit Runge–Kutta tableaus in the convention of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]].

Forward Euler has $s=1$, $A=(0)$, $b=(1)$, and $c=(0)$.

Explicit midpoint has $s=2$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(0,1)$, and $c=(0,1/2)$.

The classical four-stage Runge–Kutta method has $s=4$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0&0\\[2pt]1/2&0&0&0\\[2pt]0&1/2&0&0\\[2pt]0&0&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $b=(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)$, and $c=(0,1/2,1/2,1)$.

Each displayed $c_i$ is the row sum required in the definition of an explicit tableau. These tableaus specify the stage equations; their order and scalar stability functions are proved separately.

Let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ define a first-order initial-value problem on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$. Given a time $t_n$, step $h_n>0$, and state $y_n$ with $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, an admissible endpoint $y_{n+1}$ must satisfy $(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1})\in D$. The backward Euler endpoint is any such $y_{n+1}$ satisfying

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and certificate data $(\mathcal C,c,Q,V)$. Here $c\in\mathcal C$ is a supplied certificate, $Q$ is a declared predicate on completed rows, and $V(W,c)$ is a supplied deterministic verifier that terminates with a Boolean for every completed row $W$ and satisfies $V(W,c)=\mathrm{true}\Rightarrow Q(W)$. Without certificate data, take $V$ to return false. Every map call is required to terminate with a state or declared failure. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output contains every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint when one exists, and a status. If initialization never completes, return an empty completed-row table and no endpoint.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. When initialization and all $K$ requested sweeps finish, call $V$ on the final row and $c$ (or use false when no certificate was supplied). Return status converged if this returns true, certifying the declared predicate $Q$; otherwise return status budget-exhausted. Completion of the finite budget alone is not a convergence certificate.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $\Phi_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le i\le N$, and let $u_0\in\mathbb R^d$ be fixed. The linear part of a fine propagator in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]] is represented by $\Phi_i$. For forcing vectors $g_i\in\mathbb R^d$, write the fine recurrence as $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$. On the unknown vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, define $A_t$ by $(A_tv)_1=v_1$ and $(A_tv)_i=v_i-\Phi_i v_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le N$. With $b_1=\Phi_1u_0+g_1$ and $b_i=g_i$ for $i\ge2$, the recurrence is exactly $A_tv=b$.

For a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$, the coarse indices are $0,m,2m,\ldots,N$. Among unknowns, let $C=\{m,2m,\ldots,N\}$ and $F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus C$. Reordering the unknown vector as $(v_F,v_C)$ gives
$$A_t=\begin{pmatrix}A_{FF}&A_{FC}\\ A_{CF}&A_{CC}\end{pmatrix}.$$
A practical coarse propagator $\Psi_j$ on each interval is the linear subcase of the coarse maps $G_n$ in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]]; the exact coarse operator is determined by eliminating F-points and is not generally the same as this practical choice. This definition asserts no stability or convergence property.

Use [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]] with $N=Jm$, $m\ge2$, and its F/C partition. Both $A_t$ and $A_{FF}$ are invertible. Eliminating the F unknowns from $A_tv=b$ gives the coarse system with Schur complement
$$S=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}.$$
On coarse interval $j$, its recurrence is
$$u_{jm}-(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}=\bar g_j,$$
where
$$\bar g_j=\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s},$$
with an empty product defined to be the identity. If $\Phi_i=\Phi$ for every fine step, the exact coarse propagator is $\Phi^m$.

Input: a linear fine-grid system $A_tu=b$ with $N\ge1$ fine intervals as in [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]], a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$ and its C/F partition as in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], practical coarse propagators $\Psi_j\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le j\le N_c:=N/m$, an initial fine-grid iterate $u_{\rm in}$, pre- and post-relaxation choices from $\{F,FCF\}$, a real-valued norm on the fine-grid residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], a nonnegative integer cycle budget $J_{\rm cyc}$, and a residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The symbol $J_{\rm cyc}$ is the number of permitted cycles; the coarse-interval count is $N_c$ (the letter $J$ in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]] denotes that lemma's coarse-interval count). The output is the last iterate, its residual norm, the number of completed cycles, and status `converged` or `budget-exhausted`.

In F/C ordering define ideal interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$ by
$$P=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}\\ I_C\end{bmatrix}, \qquad R=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}&I_C\end{bmatrix}.$$

The exact coarse operator is the Schur complement $RA_tP=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}$ from [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]]. The practical correction matrix $A_c$ has identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_j$ for $2\le j\le N_c$; its first row corresponds to the fixed zero initial correction $z_0=0$. For any right-hand side $\rho$, forward substitution uniquely solves $A_cz=\rho$ by setting $z_0=0$ and, in increasing order for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, setting $z_j=\rho_j+\Psi_jz_{j-1}$. Thus $A_c$ is invertible even when an individual $\Psi_j$ is singular.

Define the relaxations on $A_tu=b$ as follows. An F-relaxation holds every C-value fixed and, for each coarse interval $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, updates its F-indices $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm-1$ in increasing order: set $u_1=b_1$ if $i=1$, and otherwise set $u_i=b_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. Different coarse intervals have independent F-updates and may be processed in parallel. A C-relaxation holds every F-value fixed and, for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$ in increasing order, sets $u_{jm}=b_{jm}+\Phi_{jm}u_{jm-1}$; these C-updates are independent because $m\ge2$ and each predecessor is an F-index. An FCF-relaxation applies F-relaxation, then C-relaxation, then F-relaxation. Each relaxation is a finite linear update; write $S_{\rm pre}$ and $S_{\rm post}$ for the error maps of the selected pre- and post-relaxations.

For one cycle from a current iterate $u$, apply the selected pre-relaxation; form $r=b-A_tu$ and $\rho=Rr$; solve $A_cz=\rho$ by the forward substitution above; correct $u\leftarrow u+Pz$; then apply the selected post-relaxation. The exact error-propagation matrix of this fixed cycle is
$$E=S_{\rm post}(I-PA_c^{-1}RA_t)S_{\rm pre}.$$

Initialize $u^{(0)}=u_{\rm in}$ and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(0)}\|$. If this is at most $\varepsilon$, return $u^{(0)}$, zero completed cycles, and status `converged`. Otherwise, for $j_{\rm cyc}=1,\ldots,J_{\rm cyc}$, perform one cycle, call the resulting iterate $u^{(j_{\rm cyc})}$, and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(j_{\rm cyc})}\|$. If this norm is at most $\varepsilon$, return that iterate, $j_{\rm cyc}$ completed cycles, and status `converged`; if not, continue. If all $J_{\rm cyc}$ cycles finish without this condition (including when $J_{\rm cyc}=0$), return the last iterate, its residual norm, and status `budget-exhausted`. The matrix $E$ describes exact arithmetic and exact coarse solves; inexact solves contribute an update defect that needs its own bound.

Let $A_tu_*=b$ be the fine-grid system from [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]]. By [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], $A_t$ is invertible. Let $E$ be the exact error matrix for one fixed two-level cycle in [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]]. Choose a real-valued norm $\|\cdot\|$ on $(\mathbb R^d)^N$ and define its induced operator norm by $\|T\|=\sup_{v\ne0}\|Tv\|/\|v\|$. Assume $\|A_t\|$ and $\|A_t^{-1}\|$ are finite for this norm. If a direct calculation or other proof establishes $\|E\|\le q<1$, then after $r\ge0$ cycles the error satisfies $\|e^{(r)}\|\le q^r\|e^{(0)}\|$, with the convention $q^0=1$. The residual $s^{(r)}=b-A_tu^{(r)}=A_te^{(r)}$ obeys $\|s^{(r)}\|\le\|A_t\|q^r\|e^{(0)}\|$, and for every error/residual pair,
$$\|s\|\le\|A_t\|\|e\|,\qquad \|e\|\le\|A_t^{-1}\|\|s\|.$$

The contraction hypothesis is a property to prove for the declared operators, norm, and cycle. The MGRIT name alone supplies no such bound, and this theorem makes no multilevel convergence claim.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

derivations.claim: By [F1], each fine Euler step for $\dot y=-y$ multiplies by $\alpha=1-h=3/4$. By [F2], a backward-Euler macro step solves $z=x-\frac12z$, so its multiplier is $\psi=2/3$.

In fine order the error operator is $A_t=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\-\alpha&1&0&0\\0&-\alpha&1&0\\0&0&-\alpha&1\end{pmatrix}$. In F/C order $F=(1,3)$, $C=(2,4)$, its blocks are $A_{FF}=I$, $A_{FC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-\alpha&0\end{pmatrix}$, $A_{CF}=\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha&0\\0&-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, and $A_{CC}=I$. Hence [F4] gives $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\alpha^2&1\end{pmatrix}$.

F-relaxation maps an error $(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)$ to $(0,e_2,\alpha e_2,e_4)$, so the F-row residuals vanish and the ideal restriction in [F5] reduces to the C residual $(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$. Solving the practical coarse system $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\psi&1\end{pmatrix}z=(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$ gives $z_1=e_2$, $z_2=e_4+(\psi-\alpha^2)e_2$. Subtracting the ideal interpolation [F5] leaves $(0,0,0,(\alpha^2-\psi)e_2)$; post-F-relaxation leaves this vector unchanged.

Therefore $E$ has its only nonzero entry in row $4$, column $2$, equal to $\alpha^2-\psi=\frac9{16}-\frac23=-\frac5{48}$. For the norm in [A1], $\|Ee\|_\infty=\frac5{48}|e_2|\le\frac5{48}\|e\|_\infty$, with equality when $e=(0,1,0,0)$. Thus $\|E\|_\infty=5/48<1$.

For every $e\in\mathbb R^4$, $\|e\|_\infty=\max_i|e_i|$ is nonnegative and vanishes only when every coordinate is zero; $\|\lambda e\|_\infty=|\lambda|\|e\|_\infty$; and $\|e+f\|_\infty\le\|e\|_\infty+\|f\|_\infty$. Thus the norm in [A1] satisfies [F7]. For any matrix $B$, $\|Bv\|_\infty\le(\max_i\sum_j|B_{ij}|)\|v\|_\infty$ by applying the finite triangle inequality to each row. The row sums of $A_t$ are at most $1+\alpha=7/4$. If $A_tu=w$, forward substitution gives $u_1=w_1$ and $u_i=w_i+\alpha u_{i-1}$, hence by induction $u_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\alpha^{i-j}w_j$. Therefore $A_t^{-1}$ has entries $\alpha^{i-j}$ for $i\ge j$ and zero otherwise, with row sums at most $1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\alpha^3=175/64$. Thus $\|A_t\|_\infty\le7/4$ and $\|A_t^{-1}\|_\infty\le175/64$. All hypotheses of [F6] hold with $q=5/48$, so the error after $r$ cycles is at most $(5/48)^r$ times its initial value.

citations.quote:
Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, integer sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and certificate data $(\mathcal C,c,Q,V)$. Here $c\in\mathcal C$ is a supplied certificate, $Q$ is a declared predicate on completed rows, and $V(W,c)$ is a supplied deterministic verifier that terminates with a Boolean for every completed row $W$ and satisfies $V(W,c)=\mathrm{true}\Rightarrow Q(W)$. Without certificate data, take $V$ to return false. Every map call is required to terminate with a state or declared failure. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output contains every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint when one exists, and a status. If initialization never completes, return an empty completed-row table and no endpoint.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. When initialization and all $K$ requested sweeps finish, call $V$ on the final row and $c$ (or use false when no certificate was supplied). Return status converged if this returns true, certifying the declared predicate $Q$; otherwise return status budget-exhausted. Completion of the finite budget alone is not a convergence certificate.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

derivations.claim: Initialization makes $N$ coarse calls. Each of the $K$ sweeps in [F1] makes $N$ fine calls and $N$ new coarse calls, so the totals are $KN$ and $(K+1)N$. Multiplying by the stipulated costs and adding $K$ synchronization charges gives $W$.

Each fine phase has $N$ independent equal-cost calls. Filling each batch except possibly the last gives $\lceil N/P\rceil$ batches, taking $\lceil N/P\rceil c_F$ without idle time. Initialization takes $Nc_G$, and each sweep has this fine phase followed by $N$ serial coarse calls and one synchronization charge. Adding these sequential phases gives $S$, including $K=0$ and zero call costs.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires N>=1; no empty fine phase. K=0 has no correction sweep and step 1.1 counts exactly N initialization calls.
Statement and steps 1.1, 2.1 allow c_F=c_G=tau_sync=0; both charges vanish. K=0 gives W=S=Nc_G, including c_G=0.
Statement and step 2.1 cover N=1, P=1 and P>N: one fine batch when N=1, N batches when P=1, one batch when P>N.

Statement explicitly requires full batches except possibly the last and no idle time. N=P=2 then has one fine batch; two singleton batches are excluded. Without this schedule qualification the asserted fine-phase span need not hold.

Statement concerns initialization and all K successfully completed sweeps. Failure/expiry before completion is outside the formula; verifier cost and undeclared overhead remain excluded, and initialization Nc_G remains included.

boundaries.reason: Proof 1.1 enumerates the already specified N initialization slots and K times N fine/new-coarse slots. Proof 2.1 groups the fixed ordered fine slots into ceil(N/P) full batches except the last. It neither selects a propagator output from a family nor chooses an optimizer or representative; K=0 simply leaves the stipulated initialization. Successful supplied calls are being counted, with no nonempty-set selection obligation.

Successful initialization and K completed Parareal sweeps are premises, not one side of an equivalence. Proof 1.1 counts N initial coarse calls and N fine plus N new coarse calls per sweep; 2.1 derives the span only with full P-call batches except the last and no idle time. These give the two displayed W and S identities in the stated direction; the Statement contains no biconditional to split.

The work/span identities do not certify successful Parareal completion or the prescribed schedule. With c_F=c_G=tau_sync=0 both displayed charges are zero independently of the call totals, so a charge cannot recover completed sweeps. The last Statement sentence also excludes a measured speedup guarantee; no converse from W or S to execution, scheduling, or speedup is claimed.

lem-parareal-sweep-work-and-span.axiom_note: Finite arithmetic and counting only; no AC.

risk_review.notes: Independent current proof review after the different creator: N cached coarse initialization calls plus N fine and N new coarse calls for each successful sweep give KN and (K+1)N. Corrected the schedule qualification: N=P=2 admits two singleton batches under the old at-most-P wording; full batches except the last and no idle time give exactly ceil(N/P). K=0 leaves W=S=Nc_G; P>N gives one batch; zero costs remain valid. Arithmetic/storage/verifier overhead is excluded and synchronization is an explicitly additive charge in this model, not a universal physical runtime claim. All claims are proved by the current two steps without AC.

prior_review.notes: Counted N initial coarse calls and N new fine/coarse calls per successful sweep; the exact batched schedule gives ceil(N/P), including P>N, K=0 and zero costs. Model excludes verifier and arithmetic overhead explicitly; finite counting uses no AC.

At each level $\ell<L$, form the practical coarse matrix $A_{\ell+1}$ with identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_{\ell,j}$ as in [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]]. Each noncoarsest level has a positive integer recursive visit count $\nu_\ell$. Also supply an initial fine-level iterate, a chosen norm on the fine-level residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], outer cycle budget $J_{\rm out}\ge0$, and residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The hierarchy must provide a nonsingular coarse system at every level and an exact solve on level $L$. V-cycles use $\nu_\ell=1$ and W-cycles use $\nu_\ell=2$. This algorithm gives no existence or convergence claim for a hierarchy that fails these input conditions.

For a recursive call at level $\ell$, perform the following operations on an initial guess $u_\ell$:
1. If $\ell=L$, solve $A_Lu_L=b_L$ exactly by forward substitution and return.
2. Apply the selected pre-relaxation to $A_\ell u_\ell=b_\ell$; compute $r_\ell=b_\ell-A_\ell u_\ell$ and restrict it to $r_{\ell+1}=R_\ell r_\ell$.
3. Set the coarse correction $z_{\ell+1}=0$. Repeat $\nu_\ell$ times: form $\rho_{\ell+1}=r_{\ell+1}-A_{\ell+1}z_{\ell+1}$; recursively apply the level $\ell+1$ cycle to $A_{\ell+1}\delta_{\ell+1}=\rho_{\ell+1}$ from zero initial correction; then set $z_{\ell+1}\leftarrow z_{\ell+1}+\delta_{\ell+1}$.
4. Correct $u_\ell\leftarrow u_\ell+P_\ell z_{\ell+1}$ and apply the selected post-relaxation.

Return the updated fine-level vector when the call completes. At level $0$, check the residual before the first outer cycle and after every completed cycle; return status converged only when the residual tolerance is met. After $J_{\rm out}$ cycles without a verified residual certificate, return the last iterate with status budget-exhausted. Inexact level solves contribute explicit update defects; no such defect is hidden in the exact-arithmetic cycle.

No two-grid contraction is transferred to this recursive cycle; convergence requires a bound for its actual full recursive error operator.

For the literal operations of [[alg-mgrit-two-level-cycle]], put $N_f=N$ and $N_c=N/m$. One F-relaxation uses $N_f-N_c-1$ fine-propagator calls; one C-relaxation uses $N_c$; and one FCF-relaxation uses $2(N_f-N_c-1)+N_c$. The specified coarse forward substitution uses $N_c$ practical coarse-propagator applications, including the evaluation at $z_0=0$. These counts concern completed operations without eliminating calls at zero inputs.

In an additive accounting model with nonnegative call costs $c_\Phi,c_\Psi$, the modeled work is $n_\Phi c_\Phi+n_\Psi c_\Psi+\kappa$, where $n_\Phi,n_\Psi$ count all executed calls and $\kappa$ accounts for all remaining work. Residuals, restriction, interpolation and stopping checks must contribute their actual calls and overhead; cached values incur no new call. A parallel schedule must respect the serial order within each F-interval and in the coarse solve, and its communication and synchronization. No measured speedup is asserted.
