Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. By contrast, $h^\alpha$ is the finite product in $\mathbb R$ of [[def-finite-sum]], with the natural exponents interpreted by [[def-integer-power]]. For the zero multi-index $0$, set $D^0f:=f$. For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Since $U\subset\mathbb R_{>0}^m$, each coordinate $y_j$ stays bounded away from zero on $\overline U$. On $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ the reciprocal $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ has derivatives $-s^{-2}$ and $2s^{-3}$, obtained from the difference quotients $-1/(s(s+t))$ and $(2s+t)/(s^2(s+t)^2)$; composing with the coordinate projection gives continuous first and second partials for $y\mapsto y_j^{-1}$. Applying the product rule [F7] twice shows every entry $A_{ij}(y)=p_{ij}(y)y_j^{-1}$ ($i
e j$), and hence every diagonal sum, is $C^2$ on $U$; [F6] applied to these entries and their first partials supplies continuous total derivatives through order two. The row equations give $A(y)y=F(y)$: the off-diagonal terms contribute $\sum_{j
e i}p_{ij}$, and the diagonal term is $-\sum_{j
e i}d_{ij}$. For column $j$, $\sum_i A_{ij}=0$ because $A_{jj}=-\sum_{i
e j}A_{ij}$.

The off-diagonal entries of $A$ are nonnegative and its diagonal entries are nonpositive. Thus $I-hA(y)$ has positive diagonal, nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and strict column diagonal-dominance margin $1$; [F3] makes it invertible. On $[0,h_0]\times\overline U$, the entries of $I-hA(y)$ and its determinant are $C^2$; the determinant is nonzero by [F3]. Its cofactors and determinant are finite sums of products of entries, and the scalar reciprocal of the determinant is $C^2$ by the same reciprocal calculation as in step 1.1. The adjugate formula therefore makes the inverse a $C^2$ matrix-valued function there; compactness gives uniform bounds for the inverse and its first derivatives.

The matrix identity $(I-hA)^{-1}=I+hA+h^2A^2(I-hA)^{-1}$ yields $\Phi_h(y)=y+hF(y)+h^2G(h,y)$ with $G(h,y):=A(y)^2(I-hA(y))^{-1}y$. Step 2.1 and compactness bound $G$ uniformly. Along the exact solution, [F5]–[F7] give $y''(t)=DF(y(t))F(y(t))$, which is uniformly bounded on the compact tube. Taylor's formula [F11] gives $y(t+h)=y(t)+hF(y(t))+O(h^2)$ uniformly. Subtracting the expansions proves the local-defect estimate in [F4].

The function $G$ in step 3.1 is continuously differentiable in $y$ with uniformly bounded derivative on $\overline U$ by [F5]–[F7] and step 2.1. Differentiating that identity gives $D_y\Phi_h(y)=I+hDF(y)+h^2D_yG(h,y)$. Compactness bounds $\|DF(y)\|_2$ by $L_0$ and $\|D_yG(h,y)\|_2$ by $G_0$. The matrix-norm triangle inequality from [F8] and $\|I\|_2=1$ from [F9] yield $\|D_y\Phi_h(y)\|_2\le1+hL_0+h^2G_0\le1+(L_0+h_0G_0)h$ for $0<h\le h_0$.

Apply [F10] to $\Phi_h$ on the convex open set $U$ using the uniform derivative bound from step 4.1. This gives $\|\Phi_h(u)-\Phi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$ for every $u,v\in U$, exactly the one-step stability assertion of [F4].

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]]. A **source-factored transfer representation** on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ containing a compact set $K\subseteq[0,\infty)^m$ consists of functions $a_{ij}:U\to\mathbb R$, $i\ne j$, such that each $a_{ij}$ is $C^2$ on the open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ in the multivariable sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], is nonnegative on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$, and, for every $y\in U\cap[0,\infty)^m$,

$$p_{ij}(y)=y_j a_{ij}(y),\qquad d_{ij}(y)=y_i a_{ji}(y),\qquad a_{ii}:=0.$$

Here $a_{ij}$ is the transfer rate from donor $j$ to recipient $i$ per unit of donor quantity. Nonnegativity is required on admissible nonnegative states; the $C^2$ extension to the open neighborhood is used for local analysis and need not be nonnegative at inadmissible states with negative coordinates. The factorization is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of nonnegative rates and the identity $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$. On strictly positive states the ratio $p_{ij}(y)/y_j$ equals $a_{ij}(y)$; at a zero donor coordinate the factorized coefficient remains defined and avoids the indeterminate expression $0/0$.

Let $K$ be a compact nonnegative state set with a source-factored transfer representation [[def-source-factored-production-destruction-rates]]. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and a step size $h$, if $y^n\notin K$ or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any factor. Otherwise form $B(y^n)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$B_{ij}(y^n)=a_{ij}(y^n)\ (i\ne j),\qquad B_{jj}(y^n)=-\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}(y^n).$$

Return the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently, component $i$ satisfies

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(a_{ij}(y^n)y_j^{n+1}-a_{ji}(y^n)y_i^{n+1}\right).$$

This procedure uses no denominator $y_j^n$ and is defined when some donor coordinates vanish. It is the factorized extension of the first-order Patankar Euler formula to the zero-state boundary. In exact arithmetic its linear system is uniquely solvable by [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]].

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$. A **multi-index** is $\alpha=(\alpha_0,\ldots,\alpha_{m-1})\in\mathbb N^m$. Put

$$|\alpha|:=\sum_{i<m}\alpha_i,\qquad \alpha!:=\prod_{i<m}\alpha_i!,\qquad h^\alpha:=\prod_{i<m}h_i^{\alpha_i}\quad(h\in\mathbb R^m).$$

Here $|\alpha|$ and $\alpha!$ use the natural-number sum and product of [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], and $n!$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]]. $$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then

   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

about one $x$ at a time.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and $h$, if $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, any coordinate of $y^n$ is nonpositive, or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating rates or solving a system. First compute the stage $z$ by invoking [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with denominators $\sigma_i=y_i^n$:

$$z_i=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_j}{y_j^n}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_i}{y_i^n}\right).$$

If the stage solve does not return a unique vector, return stage-failure. If its output $z\notin\Omega_+$, return rate-domain-failure before evaluating rates at $z$. Otherwise form $B(y^n,z)$ with, for $i\ne j$,

$$B_{ij}(y^n,z):=\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z)}{2z_j},\qquad B_{jj}(y^n,z):=-\sum_{i\ne j}B_{ij}(y^n,z),$$

and solve

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n,z)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently,

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+\frac h2\sum_{j\ne i}\left((p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z))\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{z_j}-(d_{ij}(y^n)+d_{ij}(z))\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{z_i}\right).$$

If the final solve is not uniquely solvable, return update-failure; otherwise return its unique solution $y^{n+1}$. The stage solve is uniquely solvable and its output is positive under the finite conservative PDS and positive-input hypotheses; when the rate-domain check passes, [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]] also guarantees a unique final solve. No zero-stage or denominator-regularized second-order variant is defined here.

derivations.claim: For the stage, $M^{(1)}:=I-hA(y^n)$ has off-diagonal entries $-hp_{ij}(y^n)/y_j^n\le0$ and diagonal entries $1+h\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}(y^n)/y_j^n>0$ in column $j$. The sum of the absolute off-diagonal entries in that column is $h\sum_{i\ne j}p_{ij}(y^n)/y_j^n$, so its strict column-dominance margin is $1$. By [F3], $z=(M^{(1)})^{-1}y^n>0$. Also $\sum_i M^{(1)}_{ij}=1$ for every column, hence $\sum_i z_i=\sum_i y_i^n$.

Since $z>0$, every denominator in $B(y^n,z)$ is positive. Its off-diagonal entries are nonnegative, its diagonal entries are nonpositive, and its columns sum to zero by [F2]. Thus $M^{(2)}:=I-hB(y^n,z)$ has positive diagonal, nonpositive off-diagonal entries, and column diagonal-dominance margin $1$. Applying [F3] to $M^{(2)}$ gives a unique $y^{n+1}=(M^{(2)})^{-1}y^n>0$.

For nonzero $\alpha$, write

$$D^\alpha f:=\partial_0^{\alpha_0}\cdots\partial_{m-1}^{\alpha_{m-1}}f$$

for this displayed, canonical order whenever it exists. Coordinate partial derivatives have the meaning fixed in [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

For $k\in\mathbb N$, $f$ is of class $C^k$ on $U$ when, for every word $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ of coordinate indices with $0\le r\le k$, the iterated derivative $\partial_{i_r}\cdots\partial_{i_1}f$ exists and is continuous on $U$; the word of length $0$ denotes $f$. Thus this definition does **not** presuppose that differently ordered derivatives are equal. Equality of their values is a later theorem under these regularity hypotheses.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. Suppose every partial derivative $\partial_jf$ exists on a neighbourhood of $a\in U$ and is continuous at $a$. Then $f$ is totally differentiable at $a$, and $Df(a)$ is the linear map with matrix $Jf(a)$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U \subseteq X$ be open in a real Banach space $X$, and let $Y$, $Z$, $W$ be
real Banach spaces. Then:

1. **Sum rule.** If $f_1, f_2 : U \to Y$ are Fréchet differentiable at $x \in U$
   and $a, b \in \mathbb R$, then $af_1+bf_2$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$
   with $D(af_1+bf_2)(x) = a\,Df_1(x) + b\,Df_2(x)$.
2. **Bounded-bilinear product rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ and $g : U \to Z$ are
   Fréchet differentiable at $x$, and $B : Y \times Z \to W$ is bounded
   bilinear, then $U \ni u \mapsto B(f(u),g(u))$ is Fréchet differentiable at
   $x$ and

$$D\bigl(B(f,g)\bigr)(x)h = B\bigl(Df(x)h,\ g(x)\bigr) + B\bigl(f(x),\ Dg(x)h\bigr) \qquad (h \in X).$$

3. **Chain rule.** If $f : U \to Y$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$, if
   $W_0 \subseteq Y$ is an open set with $f[U] \subseteq W_0$, and if
   $g : W_0 \to Z$ is Fréchet differentiable at $f(x)$, then
   $g \circ f$ is Fréchet differentiable at $x$ and
   $$D(g \circ f)(x) = Dg\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\,Df(x).$$

No continuity of any derivative map is assumed; these are pointwise statements
about one $x$ at a time.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and convex, $a,a+h\in U$, and $f\in C^{k+1}(U)$. Write $\iota:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ for the canonical-natural map of [[def-multivariable-taylor-polynomial]]. Then some $\theta\in(0,1)$ satisfies

$$f(a+h)=T_kf(a;h)+\sum_{|\alpha|=k+1}\frac{D^\alpha f(a+\theta h)}{\iota(\alpha!)}h^\alpha.$$

Under the hypotheses of [[thm-taylor-schlomilch-roche-remainder]], there are points $\xi_L,\xi_C$ between $a$ and $x$ such that
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_L)}{\iota((n+1)!)}(x-a)^{n+1}$$
and
$$R_{n,a}f(x)=\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi_C)}{\iota(n!)}(x-\xi_C)^n(x-a).$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$ be open, and consider a first-order IVP and solution in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **one-step method** is a family of maps $\Psi_h(t,v)$, defined for admitted times $t$, positive step sizes $h$, and states $v$, whose value is the method's approximation at time $t+h$ from the single input state $v$ at time $t$. It does not use earlier numerical states.

If $y$ is an exact solution on an interval containing $[t,t+h]$, the **local defect** is

$$\delta_h(t;y):=\Psi_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h).$$

Let $K\subseteq D$ be a fixed compact time-state set. The method has **uniform local order $p$ on $K$ along $y$** if there are constants $C\ge0$ and $h_0>0$, independent of the admitted starting time $t$ and step $0<h\le h_0$, such that

$$\|\delta_h(t;y)\|_2\le C h^{p+1}$$

whenever the exact solution graph on $[t,t+h]$ and the associated method time-state inputs, stages, and outputs under consideration lie in $K$. Here $p$ is a positive integer and $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]].

The method has **one-step Lipschitz stability on $K$** with constant $L\ge0$ if

$$\|\Psi_h(t,u)-\Psi_h(t,v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$

for every admitted step size $h$, admitted time $t$, and input states $u,v$ with $(t,u),(t,v)\in K$. This is a bound on the change in one step; it is separate from absolute or linear stability regions and does not itself assert a global error estimate.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be convex and open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at every point. If $M\ge0$ satisfies $\|Df(z)v\|_2\le M\|v\|_2$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in\mathbb R^m$, then

$$\|f(y)-f(x)\|_2\le M\|y-x\|_2\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

derivations.claim: Define $A(y)$ as in [F2]. On $U$, the coordinate reciprocals $y_j^{-1}$ have continuous partials $\partial_k(y_j^{-1})=-\delta_{jk}y_j^{-2}$ and $\partial_\ell\partial_k(y_j^{-1})=2\delta_{jk}\delta_{\ell j}y_j^{-3}$, as follows from the scalar reciprocal difference quotients on $\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$; the product rule [F7] then makes every entry of $A$ $C^2$ from the rate data [F6]. By the continuous-partials theorem [F6], these entries have continuous total derivatives through order two. Direct multiplication gives $A(y)y=F(y)$. The matrix $I-hA(y)$ is invertible for $h>0$ by [F4] and equals $I$ at $h=0$; its determinant and cofactors are $C^2$ finite sums of products, and its determinant is nonzero, so the adjugate formula and the scalar reciprocal calculation make its inverse $C^2$ on the compact set of admitted $(h,y)$. It is uniformly bounded there for small $h$. Since $y>0$, [F4] gives $z=(I-hA(y))^{-1}y>0$. The identity $(I-hA)^{-1}=I+hA+h^2A^2(I-hA)^{-1}$ now gives $z=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$ uniformly; in particular $z-y=O(h)$, so after decreasing $h_0$ we have $z\in V\subset\Omega$ uniformly for $y\in U$. Thus all stage denominators and the final rate evaluations are valid.

Write $B=B(y,z)$ for the final coefficient matrix in [F3]. Its entries are $C^2$ on the compact region of pairs produced inside $V$ by step 1.1: the rates are $C^2$, the stage map is $C^2$, and each reciprocal $z_j^{-1}$ has the same coordinate derivative formulas as in step 1.1. Its columns sum to zero, and direct multiplication using $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$ gives $B(y,z)z=\tfrac12(F(y)+F(z))$. For small $h$, step 1.1 keeps every $z_j$ bounded away from zero, so $B$ and its first derivatives are uniformly bounded. Also $B(y,y)=A(y)$; the mean-value theorem on the compact tube and $z-y=O(h)$ give $B(y,z)=A(y)+O(h)$. The final matrix $I-hB$ is invertible by [F4] and its inverse is uniformly bounded by the adjugate formula. Expanding its inverse yields $\Psi_h(y)=y+hB(y,z)y+O(h^2)=y+hF(y)+O(h^2)$. Comparing with step 1.1 gives $\Psi_h(y)-z=O(h^2)$.

The stage and final maps are $C^1$ in $y$ near the compact positive tube: their rates are $C^2$, their denominators stay bounded away from zero, and their matrix inverses are $C^2$ by the adjugate formula and the reciprocal calculation in steps 1.1–2.1. For any direction $v$, differentiating $z=y+hA(y)z$ gives $(I-hA)D_yz[v]=v+h(DA(y)[v])z$; boundedness from step 1.1 therefore gives $D_yz[v]=v+O(h)$ uniformly for $\|v\|_2\le1$.

Using $\Psi_h-y=hB\Psi_h$, substitute $z$ and use step 2.1 to obtain $\Psi_h-y=hBz+hB(\Psi_h-z)=\tfrac h2(F(y)+F(z))+O(h^3)$. Taylor expansion of $F$ at $y$, together with $z-y=hF(y)+O(h^2)$ from step 1.1, gives $F(z)=F(y)+hDF(y)F(y)+O(h^2)$. Thus $\Psi_h(y)=y+hF(y)+\tfrac{h^2}{2}DF(y)F(y)+O(h^3)$. By [F5]–[F7], the exact solution has the same expansion: $y''=DF(y)F(y)$ and its third derivative is bounded, so the one-variable Taylor remainder applied coordinatewise is $O(h^3)$. Their difference is the asserted uniform exact-start defect in [F9].
Differentiating $\Psi_h=y+hB(y,z)\Psi_h$ in direction $v$ gives $D_y\Psi_h[v]=(I-hB(y,z))^{-1}(v+h(D_1B(y,z)[v]+D_2B(y,z)[D_yz[v]])\Psi_h)$, with the inverse defined by step 2.1.

Steps 1.1–2.2 give $z=y+O(h)$, $\Psi_h=y+O(h)$, $B(y,z)=A(y)+O(h)$, and $(I-hB)^{-1}=I+hB+O(h^2)$ uniformly. Substitution yields $D_y\Psi_h[v]=v+h(A(y)v+(D_1B(y,y)[v]+D_2B(y,y)[v])y)+o(h)$. Differentiating $B(y,y)y=F(y)$ with the chain and product rules identifies the coefficient as $DF(y)v$; compactness makes the remainder uniform, so $D_y\Psi_h(y)=I+hDF(y)+hE(h,y)$ with $\sup_{y\in U}\|E(h,y)\|_2\to0$.

Compactness bounds $\|DF(y)\|_2$ uniformly, and step 4.1 makes the $E$ contribution at most $h$ for sufficiently small $h$. The norm properties in [F10] then give $\|D_y\Psi_h(y)\|_2\le1+Lh$ after decreasing $h_0$ and increasing $L$. Applying [F11] on convex $U$ proves $\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$.

The positive compact closure has positive distance from V complement, so uniform z-y=O(h) puts stages in V and bounds z_j away from zero for small h; no rate-domain branch is skipped. Smooth inverse matrices follow from nonzero determinants. The identities B(y,y)=A(y), B(y,z)z=(F(y)+F(z))/2 and Psi-z=O(h2) give Psi=y+hF+(h2/2)DF F+O(h3). citations.quote:
Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $F$ be the vector field of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] on a bounded open convex set $U\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ with $\overline U\subset\mathbb R_{>0}^m$. Suppose there is an open set $V$ with $\overline U\subset V\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ on which the transfer rates are multivariable $C^2$ and their derivatives through order two are bounded. For $y\in U$, let $\Phi_h(y)$ be [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with the standard denominators $\sigma_i=y_i$. Then there are constants $C,L,h_0>0$ such that, for $0<h\le h_0$:

1. for every exact solution $y(t)$ whose segment and the method states under consideration remain in a compact subset of $U$, the exact-start local defect satisfies $\|\Phi_h(y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le Ch^2$; and
2. for all $u,v\in U$, $\|\Phi_h(u)-\Phi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$.

The defect is the method output minus the exact next state and the second inequality is one-step Lipschitz stability in the convention of [[def-one-step-ode-method-local-defect-order-and-stability]]. This result is restricted to a compact positive tube; it does not define the standard ratio formula at zero compartments.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,

Fix an integer $m\ge1$ and a domain $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$; its admissible nonnegative states are $\Omega_+:=\Omega\cap[0,\infty)^m$. For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and $h$, if $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, any coordinate of $y^n$ is nonpositive, or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating rates or solving a system. First compute the stage $z$ by invoking [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with denominators $\sigma_i=y_i^n$:

$$z_i=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_j}{y_j^n}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_i}{y_i^n}\right).$$

If the stage solve does not return a unique vector, return stage-failure. If its output $z\notin\Omega_+$, return rate-domain-failure before evaluating rates at $z$. Otherwise form $B(y^n,z)$ with, for $i\ne j$,

$$B_{ij}(y^n,z):=\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z)}{2z_j},\qquad B_{jj}(y^n,z):=-\sum_{i\ne j}B_{ij}(y^n,z),$$

and solve

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n,z)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently,

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+\frac h2\sum_{j\ne i}\left((p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z))\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{z_j}-(d_{ij}(y^n)+d_{ij}(z))\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{z_i}\right).$$

If the final solve is not uniquely solvable, return update-failure; otherwise return its unique solution $y^{n+1}$. The stage solve is uniquely solvable and its output is positive under the finite conservative PDS and positive-input hypotheses; when the rate-domain check passes, [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]] also guarantees a unique final solve. No zero-stage or denominator-regularized second-order variant is defined here.

Let $M=(m_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ for a finite $m\ge1$. Suppose $m_{jj}>0$, $m_{ij}\le0$ for $i\ne j$, and

$$m_{jj}>\sum_{i\ne j}|m_{ij}|\qquad(j=1,\ldots,m).$$

Then $M$ is invertible and every entry of $M^{-1}$ is nonnegative. If $b\in\mathbb R^m$ has nonnegative coordinates, then $M^{-1}b\ge0$; if every coordinate of $b$ is positive, then every coordinate of $M^{-1}b$ is positive.

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

By [F1]–[F2], each such matrix has column sum one and strict column-dominance margin one, so [F3] gives $M^{-1}\ge0$.
Put $r:=M\widehat y-b$. By [F5] and the triangle inequality, $\|r\|_2\le\|\widehat w\|_2+\|r-\widehat w\|_2\le\|\widehat w\|_2+W\le\eta_w+W=\rho$.
Multiplying $\mathbf1^TM=\mathbf1^T$ on the right by $M^{-1}$ gives $\mathbf1^TM^{-1}=\mathbf1^T$.

The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and $h$, if $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, any coordinate of $y^n$ is nonpositive, or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating rates or solving a system. First compute the stage $z$ by invoking [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] with denominators $\sigma_i=y_i^n$:

$$z_i=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_j}{y_j^n}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{z_i}{y_i^n}\right).$$

If the stage solve does not return a unique vector, return stage-failure. If its output $z\notin\Omega_+$, return rate-domain-failure before evaluating rates at $z$. Otherwise form $B(y^n,z)$ with, for $i\ne j$,

$$B_{ij}(y^n,z):=\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z)}{2z_j},\qquad B_{jj}(y^n,z):=-\sum_{i\ne j}B_{ij}(y^n,z),$$

and solve

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n,z)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently,

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+\frac h2\sum_{j\ne i}\left((p_{ij}(y^n)+p_{ij}(z))\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{z_j}-(d_{ij}(y^n)+d_{ij}(z))\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{z_i}\right).$$

If the final solve is not uniquely solvable, return update-failure; otherwise return its unique solution $y^{n+1}$. The stage solve is uniquely solvable and its output is positive under the finite conservative PDS and positive-input hypotheses; when the rate-domain check passes, [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]] also guarantees a unique final solve. No zero-stage or denominator-regularized second-order variant is defined here.

For every finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with domain $\Omega$, every strictly positive input $y^n\in\Omega_+$, and every step size $h>0$, compute the Patankar Euler stage $z$. If $z\in\Omega_+$, the stage and output of [[alg-mprk22-1]] are uniquely defined, strictly positive, and conserve total mass:

$$z>0,\qquad y^{n+1}>0,\qquad \sum_i z_i=\sum_i y_i^n=\sum_i y_i^{n+1}.$$

If $z\notin\Omega_+$, the algorithm returns rate-domain-failure before its second rate evaluation and makes no output claim. These preservation properties do not use the smoothness or compact-tube assumptions needed for the separate second-order error theorem.

Let $F$ be the vector field of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] on a bounded open convex set $U\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ with $\overline U\subset\mathbb R_{>0}^m$. Assume there is an open set $V$ with $\overline U\subset V\subset\Omega\cap\mathbb R_{>0}^m$ on which the transfer rates are multivariable $C^2$, with derivatives through order two bounded there. Let $\Psi_h(y)$ be [[alg-mprk22-1]]. For sufficiently small $h>0$, there are constants $C,L,h_0>0$ such that:

1. for every exact solution segment in a compact subset of $U$, the exact-start defect satisfies $\|\Psi_h(y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le Ch^3$; and
2. for all $u,v\in U$, $\|\Psi_h(u)-\Psi_h(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$.

The local order-two estimate requires the positive lower bound on the stage denominators and the stated smoothness. Positivity and conservation for every $h>0$ are separate preservation properties and are not used to claim the local error order.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

For a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with domain $\Omega$, an admissible input $y^n\in\Omega_+$, step $h>0$, and any positive denominators $\sigma_i>0$, the step of [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] is uniquely defined, satisfies $y^{n+1}\ge0$, and conserves total mass:

$$\sum_{i=1}^m y_i^{n+1}=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i^n.$$

If $y^n>0$ coordinatewise, then $y^{n+1}>0$ coordinatewise. These conclusions do not assert order for arbitrary denominators; the first-order choice and its accuracy hypotheses are treated separately.

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]]. A **source-factored transfer representation** on an open set $U\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ containing a compact set $K\subseteq[0,\infty)^m$ consists of functions $a_{ij}:U\to\mathbb R$, $i\ne j$, such that each $a_{ij}$ is $C^2$ on the open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ in the multivariable sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], is nonnegative on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$, and, for every $y\in U\cap[0,\infty)^m$,

$$p_{ij}(y)=y_j a_{ij}(y),\qquad d_{ij}(y)=y_i a_{ji}(y),\qquad a_{ii}:=0.$$

Here $a_{ij}$ is the transfer rate from donor $j$ to recipient $i$ per unit of donor quantity. Nonnegativity is required on admissible nonnegative states; the $C^2$ extension to the open neighborhood is used for local analysis and need not be nonnegative at inadmissible states with negative coordinates. The factorization is an additional hypothesis, not a consequence of nonnegative rates and the identity $p_{ij}=d_{ji}$. On strictly positive states the ratio $p_{ij}(y)/y_j$ equals $a_{ij}(y)$; at a zero donor coordinate the factorized coefficient remains defined and avoids the indeterminate expression $0/0$.

Let $K$ be a compact nonnegative state set with a source-factored transfer representation [[def-source-factored-production-destruction-rates]]. Given $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$ and a step size $h$, if $y^n\notin K$ or $h\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any factor. Otherwise form $B(y^n)\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$B_{ij}(y^n)=a_{ij}(y^n)\ (i\ne j),\qquad B_{jj}(y^n)=-\sum_{i\ne j}a_{ij}(y^n).$$

Return the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$\bigl(I-hB(y^n)\bigr)y^{n+1}=y^n.$$

Equivalently, component $i$ satisfies

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(a_{ij}(y^n)y_j^{n+1}-a_{ji}(y^n)y_i^{n+1}\right).$$

This procedure uses no denominator $y_j^n$ and is defined when some donor coordinates vanish. It is the factorized extension of the first-order Patankar Euler formula to the zero-state boundary. In exact arithmetic its linear system is uniquely solvable by [[lem-strict-column-dominance-implies-nonnegative-inverse]].

Let a finite conservative PDS have a source-factored representation on an open neighborhood $U\subseteq\Omega$ of a compact set $K\subseteq[0,\infty)^m$, with factors that are multivariable $C^2$ on $U$ and nonnegative on $U\cap[0,\infty)^m$, as in [[def-source-factored-production-destruction-rates]]. For every $y^n\in K$ and $h>0$, [[alg-zero-compatible-modified-patankar-euler]] has a unique output $y^{n+1}\ge0$ and conserves $\sum_i y_i$. For the accuracy clause, fix a compact set $K_*\subset U$ containing $K$ and all exact solution segments under consideration, and define the $C^2$ extension $\widetilde F_i(y):=\sum_{j\ne i}(y_j a_{ij}(y)-y_i a_{ji}(y))$ on $U$. If those exact segments remain in $K_*\cap[0,\infty)^m$, then the exact-start local defect is uniformly $O(h^2)$ as $h\downarrow0$, including when some coordinates of $y^n$ are zero. The claim is local; no global error bound at the boundary is asserted.

For every ordered pair $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ let $p_{ij},d_{ij}:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ be production and destruction transfer rates that are nonnegative on $\Omega_+$. A **finite conservative production destruction system** (finite conservative PDS) is the autonomous ODE

$$y_i'=F_i(y):=\sum_{j=1}^m\bigl(p_{ij}(y)-d_{ij}(y)\bigr),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,$$

with internal-transfer identities

$$p_{ij}(y)=d_{ji}(y),\qquad p_{ii}(y)=d_{ii}(y)=0.$$

The index $j$ is the donor/source of $p_{ij}$ and the index $i$ is its recipient/destination; $d_{ji}$ is the same transfer viewed as destruction from $j$. The total mass is $M(y):=\sum_{i=1}^m y_i$. The ODE is considered at states in $\Omega_+$. The definition describes a closed system: external sources and sinks must be specified separately and are not included in the conservation claims on this page. No existence, positivity, or regularity assertion about solutions is part of this definition.

Let $m\ge1$, let $(p_{ij},d_{ij})$ be the rates of a finite conservative PDS [[def-finite-conservative-production-destruction-system]] with state domain $\Omega$, and take an input state $y^n\in\mathbb R^m$, a step size $h$, and declared denominators $\sigma_i$. If $y^n\notin\Omega_+$, $h\le0$, or any $\sigma_i\le0$, return an inadmissible-input status before evaluating any rate. Otherwise the **modified Patankar Euler step** returns the unique solution $y^{n+1}$ of

$$y_i^{n+1}=y_i^n+h\sum_{j\ne i}\left(p_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_j^{n+1}}{\sigma_j}-d_{ij}(y^n)\frac{y_i^{n+1}}{\sigma_i}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m.$$

Equivalently, form $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ by

$$M_{ii}=1+h\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{d_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_i},\qquad M_{ij}=-h\frac{p_{ij}(y^n)}{\sigma_j}\quad(i\ne j),$$

and solve $My^{n+1}=y^n$. The rates in the solve are evaluated only at the admissible state $y^n\in\Omega_+$. For every input passing the branch, return the unique exact solution of the stated linear system. The standard first-order choice is $\sigma_i=y_i^n$, which is admissible only when every $y_i^n>0$. A separately defined rate-factor form extends a first-order step to zero donor coordinates under an additional source-factorization hypothesis.

Let $M\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$ be the exact real matrix represented by the stored coefficients of a successfully completed [[alg-modified-patankar-euler]] step with admissible positive denominators, or of a completed stage/final solve of [[alg-mprk22-1]], for a finite conservative PDS. Let $b\ge0$ be its stored right-hand side, interpreted exactly as a real vector. For either scheme, the PDS transfer identity gives $\mathbf 1^TM=\mathbf 1^T$ and strict column diagonal dominance, so $M^{-1}\ge0$. Let $\widehat y\in\mathbb R^m$ be a stored candidate. Assume all entries of $M$, $\widehat y$, and $b$ are stored in a common operationwise format $\mathbb F$ with unit roundoff $u$, and compute $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(M\widehat y)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-b)$ in the model of [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]], with $0<u<1$, $(m-1)u<1$, every nonzero exact intermediate normal, zero operations exact, and successful sequential dot products and subtraction. Let $W$ be the certified allowance from [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]], with its norm inputs exact or certified upper bounds. Let $\eta_w$ be the exact value of $\|\widehat w\|_2$ or a certified upper bound for it, and set $\rho:=\eta_w+W$.

$$\|M\widehat y-b\|_2\le\rho,\qquad \left|\mathbf1^T\widehat y-\mathbf1^Tb\right|\le\sqrt m\,\rho.$$

If $y^*:=M^{-1}b$ is the exact solution of the stored linear system, then

$$\|\widehat y-y^*\|_1\le\sqrt m\,\rho.$$

Consequently, the componentwise margin condition $\widehat y_i\ge\sqrt m\,\rho$ for every $i$ certifies $y^*\ge0$. A residual bound alone does not certify that the computed candidate $\widehat y$ is nonnegative. This certificate is relative to the stated stored matrix and right-hand side; any coefficient-assembly or right-hand-side data error relative to the intended real system must be separately bounded and added to the residual allowance.

Under the smoothness and compact-tube hypotheses of [[prop-explicit-rk-order-conditions-through-four]], the forward Euler, explicit midpoint, and classical four-stage tableaus of [[def-euler-midpoint-rk4-tableaus]] have uniform local orders at least one, two, and four, respectively.

For the scalar test equation $y'=\lambda y$, set $z=h\lambda$. The corresponding stability functions, defined by $y^+=R(z)y$, are
$$R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z,\qquad R_{\mathrm M}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2},\qquad R_{\mathrm{RK4}}(z)=1+z+\frac{z^2}{2}+\frac{z^3}{6}+\frac{z^4}{24}.$$
The absolute stability region of a listed method is $\{z\in\mathbb C:|R(z)|\le1\}$. On the negative real axis, the Euler and midpoint regions are exactly $[-2,0]$. No maximal real interval is asserted here for RK4.

For forward Euler applied to $y'=\lambda y$, let $z=h\lambda$. Its stability function is $R_{\mathrm E}(z)=1+z$, and its absolute-stability region is exactly the closed disk

$$\{z\in\mathbb C:|z+1|\le1\}.$$

On the negative real axis, for $y'=-\rho y$ with $\rho>0$, the method is absolutely stable exactly when $0<h\rho\le2$.

Fix a finite horizon $T>0$. Let mortality and fertility be bounded Lipschitz functions $\mu,\beta:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, and let $n_0\in L^1(0,\infty)$ be nonnegative. The **linear age-structured renewal transport problem** is

$$n_t(t,a)+n_a(t,a)=-\mu(a)n(t,a),\qquad a>0,\quad 0<t\le T,$$

with initial density $n(0,a)=n_0(a)$ and inflow condition

$$n(t,0)=B(t),\qquad B(t):=\int_0^\infty \beta(a)n(t,a)\,da.$$

Here $a$ is age, $B$ is the birth rate, and the characteristic age path solves the first-order initial value problem $a'(s)=1$ in the sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]], hence $a(s)=a(0)+s$. Define survival from age $a$ over duration $s\ge0$ by

$$S(a,s):=\exp\!\left(-\int_a^{a+s}\mu(r)\,dr\right).$$

A **weak solution** on $[0,T]$ is a nonnegative $n\in C([0,T];L^1(0,\infty))$ with continuous $B:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and, for every $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ with $\phi(T,a)=0$,

$$-\int_0^T\!\int_0^\infty n(t,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu(a)\phi)\,da\,dt=\int_0^\infty n_0(a)\phi(0,a)\,da+\int_0^T B(t)\phi(t,0)\,dt.$$

A **mild solution** is a weak solution that also satisfies, for almost every $a\ge0$,

$$n(t,a)=\begin{cases}n_0(a-t)S(a-t,t),&a\ge t,\\B(t-a)S(0,a),&0\le a<t,\end{cases}$$

The formula follows the age characteristics $a'(s)=1$ and their mortality survival. No delay equation or finite-age cutoff is identified with this model by definition.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

derivations.claim: The old-cohort branch in the Statement follows the characteristic $a(s)=x+s$ and survival $S(x,t)$ from [F1]; the newborn branch starts from the boundary value $B(t-a)$ at time $t-a$ and follows survival $S(0,a)$. These are the characteristic branches in the definition of a mild solution. We use them to construct a candidate after solving the Volterra equation; no pointwise differentiability of a weak solution is assumed.

The functions $K$ and $G$ are continuous. Indeed, $K$ is a product of Lipschitz functions; for $s,t\in[0,T]$, the integrand multiplier in $G$ changes by at most $(\operatorname{Lip}(\beta)+\|\beta\|_\infty\|\mu\|_\infty)|t-s|$, since $|e^{-u}-e^{-v}|\le|u-v|$ for $u,v\ge0$. Multiplication by $n_0\in L^1$ and integration gives continuity of $G$.
Substitute the two branches into $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)\,da$ and split at $a=t$. In the old-cohort part set $x=a-t$; the result is exactly $G(t)+\int_0^t\beta(a)e^{-M(a)}B(t-a)\,da$.

On any interval of length $\tau$ with $\tau\|K\|_\infty<1$, the right side of the Volterra equation is a contraction in the sup norm on continuous birth-rate functions: the difference of two outputs is bounded by $\tau\|K\|_\infty$ times the input difference. If $\|K\|_\infty=0$, the equation is simply $B=G$. Starting at time zero and then treating the already determined history as a fixed forcing term, finitely many such intervals cover $[0,T]$; each interval therefore has one continuous solution and the solutions agree at their shared endpoints.

Let $\phi\in C_c^1([0,T]\times[0,\infty))$ satisfy $\phi(T,a)=0$. On an initial cohort with coordinate $x=a-t\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}[n_0(x)S(x,t)\phi(t,x+t)]=n(t,x+t)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(t,x+t)$ for almost every $t$. Integrating from $0$ to $T$ makes the terminal term zero and leaves $-n_0(x)\phi(0,x)$; integration over $x\ge0$ gives the initial-data contribution to the weak identity.

For a newborn cohort with birth time $s=t-a\ge0$, the chain rule gives $\frac{d}{da}[B(s)S(0,a)\phi(s+a,a)]=n(s+a,a)(\phi_t+\phi_a-\mu\phi)(s+a,a)$. Integrating from $a=0$ to $T-s$ gives $-B(s)\phi(s,0)$ because $\phi(T,T-s)=0$; integrating over $s\in[0,T]$ gives the renewal-boundary contribution.

When $n_0\ge0$, $G,K\ge0$. Picard iteration from the zero function on the first interval preserves nonnegativity and converges to its unique fixed point; the same argument applies on each continuation interval because its known-history forcing is nonnegative. Thus $B\ge0$, and the characteristic formula gives $n\ge0$.

The formula has finite $L^1$ norm because its old-cohort contribution is at most $\|n_0\|_1$ and its newborn contribution is at most $\int_0^t B(s)\,ds$. On the old branch, continuity in time follows from translation continuity of $n_0$ in $L^1$ and dominated convergence for the survival multiplier. On the newborn branch, continuity follows from continuity and boundedness of $B$ and $S$, with the interval of newly entering cohorts having length tending to zero. Thus $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$.

The old-cohort region $a\ge t$ and newborn region $a<t$ partition the time-age domain up to a measure-zero diagonal. Adding their integrals from steps 2.3 and 2.4, then multiplying by $-1$, gives exactly the weak identity in [F1] with initial term $\int n_0(x)\phi(0,x)dx$ and boundary term $\int_0^T B(s)\phi(s,0)ds$. Step 2.1 gives $B(t)=\int_0^\infty\beta(a)n(t,a)da$, and step 4.1 gives $n\in C([0,T];L^1)$ and nonnegativity. Thus the characteristic formula is a weak, hence mild, solution.

Any mild solution has a birth rate satisfying the Volterra equation in step 2.1. Uniqueness from step 2.2 forces that same birth rate, and the characteristic formula in step 1.1 then forces the same density.
