citations.quote:
Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $\int_a^b f \ge 0$.
2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then
   $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$
3. **Two-sided bound.** If $m \le f(x) \le M$ for every $x \in [a,b]$, with
   $m, M$ real, then
   $$m\,(b-a) \;\le\; \int_a^b f \;\le\; M\,(b-a) .$$

**Equality in claim 1 does not force $f$ to vanish.** A nonnegative integrable
function with integral $0$ may be positive at infinitely many points; that is
[[fs-nonnegative-integrable-with-zero-integral-vanishes]] on the previous page's
companion. Under the additional hypothesis of continuity the conclusion does
hold, and that is [[thm-nonnegative-continuous-with-zero-integral-vanishes]]
below.

**Claim 2 is stated for $a < b$ and is not orientation-invariant.** With the
convention of [[def-oriented-integral]], $f \le g$ gives
$\int_u^v f \le \int_u^v g$ when $u \le v$ and the reverse inequality when
$u \ge v$, since both sides change sign together.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Put $e:=x-x_*$ and $g(t):=r(x_*+te)$ for $0\le t\le1$. Convexity gives $x_*+te\in K\subseteq U$; openness supplies the local parameter neighborhoods needed for the derivative at each point, one-sided at the endpoints. The chain rule [F3] gives $g'(t)=J(x_*+te)e$. The Jacobian Lipschitz bound makes this derivative continuous, so its components are integrable by [F4] and [F5].

By [F6], $r(x)-r(x_*)=\int_0^1J(x_*+te)e\,dt$. For each coordinate, [F12] gives the antiderivative $t\mapsto t(J(x)e)_i$, so the constant vector function with value $J(x)e$ has integral $J(x)e$. Linearity [F4] therefore gives $r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)e=\int_0^1[J(x_*+te)-J(x)]e\,dt$.

For $0\le t\le1$, the integrand in step 2.1 has norm at most $L(1-t)\|e\|_2^2$ by [F9], [F10], and the Lipschitz hypothesis. The norm inequality [F7] and integral monotonicity [F11] bound the norm of the integral by $L\|e\|_2^2\int_0^1(1-t)\,dt=(L/2)\|e\|_2^2$ using [F12]. This proves the Statement for every $m,n\ge1$.

boundaries.reason: The Statement fixes m,n>=1 and contains actual points x_*,x in K, so K is nonempty. Proof step 1.1 integrates along their defined closed segment, not an empty path.

boundaries.evidence: Step 3.1 remains valid for L=0 or e=0 and yields zero remainder.
Steps 1.1–3.1 use arbitrary positive m,n and componentwise FTC, including m=n=1.
Step 3.1 includes L=0 and x=x_* without division by either quantity.
Steps 1.1–2.1 use the full closed segment t∈[0,1] and the endpoint FTC identity.
Steps 1.1–3.1 define one path and use componentwise integrals and finite-dimensional inequalities; no arbitrary family is selected.

boundaries.reason: The rectangular residual linearization bound asserts its displayed implication, construction or example, not a characterization equivalent to its input hypotheses; no forward iff direction is omitted.
The rectangular residual linearization bound does not claim that its resulting error bound, minimizer or status implies all its hypotheses, so there is no reverse iff to establish.

Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required
that $B=\nabla^2f(x)$ in this definition; exact Hessians and symmetric model
approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted
reduction is nonpositive, so an algorithm must use a separately justified
fallback or return a failure status in that case.

Let $B$ be the real symmetric positive-definite model matrix of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]], with $n\ge1$, $g\in\mathbb R^n$,
and radius $\Delta>0$. There is a unique $p_N\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfying
$Bp_N=-g$. The [[alg-dogleg-trust-region-step]] procedure is well-defined on
this input and returns a feasible vector. If its boundary-intersection branch
is taken, the displayed scalar formula is the unique root $t\in(0,1)$ of
$\|p_C+t(p_N-p_C)\|_2^2=\Delta^2$. On a nonstationary input the
procedure performs one linear solve and, only on its boundary branch, one
scalar-root computation; it has no iteration loop.

   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: For every nonzero $v$, $v^T(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD)v=\|Jv\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dv\|_2^2>0$ because $D$ is nonsingular. The matrix is symmetric positive definite, so [F2] gives a unique $p_\lambda$. With $z=Dp$, the system is equivalent, after left multiplication by $D^{-T}$, to $(\widetilde J^T\widetilde J+\lambda I)z=-\widetilde J^Tr$. Expanding $q_\lambda$ and completing the square around its unique critical point shows $q_\lambda(z)-q_\lambda(z_\lambda)=\tfrac12(z-z_\lambda)^T(\widetilde J^T\widetilde J+\lambda I)(z-z_\lambda)\ge0$, with equality only at $z=z_\lambda$.

If $\|z\|_2\le\|z_\lambda\|_2$, minimality from step 1.1 gives $m(z_\lambda)+\tfrac\lambda2\|z_\lambda\|_2^2\le m(z)+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2\le m(z)+\tfrac\lambda2\|z_\lambda\|_2^2$. Subtracting the common penalty proves $m(z_\lambda)\le m(z)$ for every feasible $z$, so $z_\lambda$ globally minimizes $m$ on the stated ball. Expanding $m$ shows its linear coefficient is $\widetilde J^Tr$ and its symmetric quadratic coefficient is $\widetilde J^T\widetilde J$, so it is the trust-region model of [F1].

The damped system gives $-g^Tp_\lambda=\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2$. Expanding $m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=-g^Tp_\lambda-\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2$ yields the displayed formula. Since $g\ne0$, invertibility of the damped matrix gives $p_\lambda\ne0$, and nonsingularity of $D$ makes the displayed reduction strictly positive. Thus the ratio denominator is valid.

Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required
that $B=\nabla^2f(x)$ in this definition; exact Hessians and symmetric model
approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted
reduction is nonpositive, so an algorithm must use a separately justified
fallback or return a failure status in that case.

citations.quote:
Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb R)$ with $m\ge n\ge 1$ and full column rank.
Let

$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R$$

be a reduced QR factorisation, with
$$\widehat Q^{\mathsf T}\widehat Q=I_n$$
and
$\widehat R$ upper triangular. Then:

1. The least-squares minimiser of $\|Ax-b\|_2$ is the unique solution of
   $$\widehat R x=\widehat Q^{\mathsf T}b.$$
2. The spectral condition number of $\widehat R$ equals that of $A$, whereas
   the normal-equation matrix satisfies
   $$\kappa_2(A^{\mathsf T}A)=\kappa_2(A)^2.$$
   Thus the QR route solves with a factor of condition $\kappa_2(A)$ rather
   than the squared factor $\kappa_2(A)^2$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ have singular value decomposition
$A=U\Sigma V^*$, and let $\tau\ge0$ be a declared threshold. The
**truncated singular-value pseudoinverse at threshold $\tau$** is

$$ A_\tau^+ := V\Sigma_\tau^+U^*, $$

where $\Sigma_\tau^+\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb F)$ is the transposed-shape
diagonal matrix whose $i$th diagonal entry is $\sigma_i^{-1}$ when
$\sigma_i>\tau$ and is $0$ when $\sigma_i\le\tau$; every off-diagonal entry is
$0$.

The threshold is part of the definition, exactly as in
[[def-numerical-rank-relative-to-a-norm-scale-and-tolerance]]: changing
$\tau$ changes which singular directions are retained.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Input a real active column $x\in\mathbb R^r\subseteq\mathbb F^r$ and trailing block $B\in\mathbb F^{r\times q}$ with entries in the floating-point system, $r\ge1$, $q\ge0$. If every component of $x$ is zero, return the identity action and a copy of $B$, with the active output column set to exact zeros, so that $C_+=[0e_1\;B]$; return $(v=0,\widehat\tau=0,\widehat\alpha=0,C_+)$ marked `identity`. Otherwise compute $s=\max_{1\le i\le r}|x_i|>0$, and then, in increasing $i$, compute $z_i=\operatorname{fl}(x_i/s)$. Initialize $t=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i z_i)$ followed by $t=\operatorname{fl}(t+a_i)$. Compute $h=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt t)$ and then $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(s h)$. Set $\sigma=1$ if $x_1=0$ and $\sigma=\operatorname{sign}(x_1)$ otherwise, and set $\widehat\alpha=-\sigma\widehat r$ using the exact sign change. Compute $v_1=\operatorname{fl}(x_1-\widehat\alpha)$, then copy $v_i=x_i$ exactly for $i=2,\ldots,r$.

Initialize $w=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_i=\operatorname{fl}(v_i v_i)$ followed by $w=\operatorname{fl}(w+a_i)$. Then compute $\widehat\tau=\operatorname{fl}(2/w)$. For each column $j=1,\ldots,q$ in increasing order, initialize $d_j=0$ and, in increasing $i$, compute $a_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(v_i B_{ij})$ followed by $d_j=\operatorname{fl}(d_j+a_{ij})$. After all $d_j$ have been computed, in increasing $i$ compute $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$. Then, in increasing $j$ and within each column in increasing $i$, compute $U_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(p_i d_j)$ and $\widehat B_{ij}=\operatorname{fl}(B_{ij}-U_{ij})$ in that order. The complete active output is $C_+=[\widehat\alpha e_1\;\widehat B]$, with exact zeros written below its first diagonal entry. If any elementary operation fails, return the first range failure with its stage and indices in the order above. Also return failure if $t$, $\widehat r$, or $w$ is not positive normal, or any intermediate is nonfinite. Otherwise return $(v,\widehat\tau,\widehat\alpha,C_+)$ marked `reflector`. For a separate block $Y\in\mathbb F^{r\times q'}$, $q'\ge0$, apply the stored reflector by computing its sequential column dots in increasing column order, then the vector $p_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat\tau v_i)$ in increasing $i$, and then each rounded product and subtraction by increasing column and row; omit the target-column overwrite. Store reflector factors with their identity/reflector marker to represent the exact orthogonal product; a rounded explicit dense product is a separate output with its own arithmetic error. For a nonzero stored $v$, the associated exact reflector is $H(v)=I-2vv^T/(v^Tv)$, using [[def-householder-reflector]] and the QR convention of [[def-full-reduced-and-column-pivoted-computational-qr-factorisations]]. Since $v$ is real, this matrix acts on $\mathbb F^r$ as an orthogonal reflector over $\mathbb R$ and a unitary reflector over $\mathbb C$. This definition does not assert a local backward-error bound.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. For fixed $m,n$, both perturbation coefficients are $O(u)$. If additionally $\beta_Q\le19\gamma_{n+3}/(1+\gamma_{n+3})$ and $\beta_b\le20\gamma_{n+3}$, both relative data perturbation bounds are at most $20\gamma_{n+3}$. These two coefficient comparisons are additional checks; they do not follow from $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$ alone. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let $F$ be a field, let $n\ge 1$, and let $b\in F^n$.

If $L=(\ell_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is lower triangular with every diagonal entry
$\ell_{ii}\ne 0$, the **forward substitution solve** of $Lx=b$ is the recursive
construction

$$x_i:=\frac{1}{\ell_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j<i}\ell_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(0\le i<n).$$If $U=(u_{ij})\in M_n(F)$ is upper triangular with every diagonal entry $u_{ii}\ne 0$, the **backward substitution solve** of $Ux=b$ is the recursive construction$$x_i:=\frac{1}{u_{ii}}\left(b_i-\sum_{j>i}u_{ij}x_j\right)\qquad(n-1\ge i\ge 0).$$

The triangular vocabulary is from
[[def-triangular-and-diagonal-matrices-over-a-commutative-ring]]. The matrix
product convention from [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] is the one
used when later items rewrite these recursions as matrix equations.

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

routine_steps.claim: In QR mode the loop has exactly $n$ calls. Each call either returns its specified block or a failure by [F5]; after a successful loop the diagonal and solve branches have finite checks and a finite recursion by [F7]. The SVD report is an input, and its branch has finitely many comparisons and at most $mn+n^2$ scheduled dot-product updates. Every computed operation returns a rounded value or a failure by [F8], so every input returns one of the listed statuses in finite work.

In the exact full-rank QR branch, [F1] and [F2] show that the returned solution of $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ uniquely minimizes $\|r+Jp\|_2$. In the exact SVD branch with all $\sigma_i>\tau\ge0$, orthogonality gives $J^TJ=V\Sigma_n^2V^T$ and $J^T(-r)=-V\Sigma_nU_1^Tr$, so the displayed $p$ solves the normal system; full column rank makes it unique, and [F3] gives the least-squares minimizer. If a threshold or rank test fails, the algorithm returns a status rather than asserting that minimizer.

The exact-step status is reachable only from the supplied exact reduced factorization in the exact route; a rounded Householder report reaches only the computed-status branches. There, a nonzero computed diagonal without a verified full-rank certificate is rank-unverified, and the backward-stability conclusion [F6] is attached only under its stated execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses. In the computed SVD route, an interval contained at or below $\tau$ yields rank-below-threshold, while an interval straddling $\tau$ yields rank-unverified; the report supports no accuracy claim in either case. Thus no computed branch silently strengthens the exact full-rank result of step 2.1.

Input a stored residual $r\in\mathbb R^m$, a stored Jacobian $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$ (using the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a factorization mode QR or SVD, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), and a declared singular-value threshold $\tau\ge0$. If $m<n$, immediately return unsupported-shape without requesting a factorization report; all remaining branches assume $m\ge n$. A computed QR report may also carry a verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ asserting $\|Jv\|_2\ge s\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. The target exact step, when it is returned, is the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|r+Jp\|_2^2$ and hence solves $J^TJp=-J^Tr$; this target is asserted only on a full-column-rank branch. Do not form $J^TJ$ in either solve path.

The threshold $\tau$ is used only by the SVD route. For QR mode the exact and computed routes are disjoint. Exact mode requires a supplied exact reduced factorization $J=QR$ with $Q^TQ=I_n$; only this exact factorization may reach the exact-step branch. Computed mode either consumes the report produced from this input pair $(J,-r)$ or forms it by setting $C=[J\mid-r]$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,n$, applying [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] to rows $k,\ldots,m$ of column $k$ and all trailing columns of $C$, including its last right-hand-side column. Embed each returned active block in those rows, leaving earlier rows and columns unchanged, and propagate the first factorization failure. After a successful computed loop, the report consists of the computed upper-triangular block $\widehat R$, the first $n$ entries $\widehat y$ of the transformed last column, and the ordered stored reflector records (including identity markers). The exact orthogonal representatives of those records define the $Q$ used by the conditional backward-stability result; the rounded outputs themselves are not an exact factorization of $J$ and cannot be supplied to the exact branch. In exact mode, a zero diagonal in $R$ returns rank-deficient; otherwise solve $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ by backward substitution and return exact-step($p$). In computed mode, a zero diagonal returns rank-deficient-candidate. Otherwise initialize storage for $\widehat p_0,\ldots,\widehat p_{n-1}$ with all components unassigned, then for $i=n-1,n-2,\ldots,0$ compute $s_i$ by setting $s_i=0$ and, for $j=i+1,i+2,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, updating $s_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat R_{ij}\widehat p_j))$; then compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat y_i-s_i)$ and $\widehat p_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/\widehat R_{ii})$. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. A nonzero computed diagonal without an independently verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ for the input matrix $J$ returns rank-unverified with the computed candidate but no full-rank claim. With that certificate, return computed-candidate($\widehat p$). A nonzero computed diagonal alone is not a full-rank certificate. The computed-QR backward-stability conclusion of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]] is attached only when all of that theorem's successful-execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses are supplied; otherwise no backward-stability conclusion is returned.

For SVD mode, the input includes an exact factorization $J=U\Sigma V^T$, or a computed report with finite stored factors $\widehat U_1\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $\widehat\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ whose entries are nonnegative, and $\widehat V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, together with certified intervals $[\ell_i,u_i]$ satisfying $0\le\ell_i\le\sigma_i(J)\le u_i$ for each singular value $i=1,\ldots,n$. In the exact case, if any $\sigma_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold and no Gauss-Newton step. If every $\sigma_i>\tau$, return
$$p=-V\,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_n^{-1})\,U_1^Tr,$$
where $U_1$ consists of the corresponding $n$ left singular vectors. For a computed report, if any $u_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold; otherwise, if any interval satisfies $\ell_i\le\tau<u_i$, return rank-unverified; if every lower endpoint exceeds $\tau$ but some stored $\widehat\sigma_i=0$, return factorization-failure. In the remaining branch, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order initialize $z_i=0$ and, for $j=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set $z_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(z_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat U_{ji}r_j))$. After these dots, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ set $w_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i/\widehat\sigma_i)$. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$ initialize $t_j=0$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $t_j\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(t_j+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat V_{ji}w_i))$; set $\widehat p_j=-t_j$ by exact sign change. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. Otherwise return the finite candidate
$$\widehat p=-\widehat V\,\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^{-1})\,\widehat U_1^Tr$$
with status computed-candidate and make no accuracy claim beyond the supplied report. The displayed formula names the result of the preceding schedule; it is not a second computation. The certified intervals determine only the threshold branch; no computed-SVD accuracy bound is asserted. A computed SVD routine is not defined here; the SVD branch consumes its report.

If the selected factorization reports failure, return factorization-failure; every status other than exact-step is explicitly not a certified exact full-rank Gauss-Newton step.

Let $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $r\in\mathbb R^m$, $m,n\ge1$, let
$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$
Set $z_\lambda:=Dp_\lambda$, $\widetilde J:=JD^{-1}$, and
$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$
over the trust-region ball $\|z\|_2\le\Delta_\lambda$ of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required
that $B=\nabla^2f(x)$ in this definition; exact Hessians and symmetric model
approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted
reduction is nonpositive, so an algorithm must use a separately justified
fallback or return a failure status in that case.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

At each precision, let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be an instance of [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]] specialized to a finite binary format of integer precision $p\ge2$ and integer normal-exponent bounds $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$. Its normal values are $\pm m2^{j-p+1}$ for integers $2^{p-1}\le m<2^p$ and $j_{\min}\le j\le j_{\max}$, with $N_{\min}=2^{j_{\min}}$ and $N_{\max}=(2^p-1)2^{j_{\max}-p+1}$. The rounding rule is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even by the parity of the normalized significand. Each precision in a mixed-precision procedure has its own format, range, and valid unit-roundoff bound. On every real exact result that is zero or normal, $\operatorname{fl}$ uses this rule; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range $x$, $\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt{x})$ is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression $ab+c$; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

routine_steps.claim: In exact mode, the augmented matrix satisfies $A_\lambda^TA_\lambda=J^TJ+\lambda D^TD$ and $A_\lambda^Ts_\lambda=J^Tr$. For every $v\ne0$, $\|A_\lambda v\|_2^2=\|Jv\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dv\|_2^2>0$, so it has full column rank. The supplied exact QR factorization and [F1] give the unique minimizer of the augmented least-squares problem, which solves the displayed damped system. In computed mode, only a computed-candidate accompanied by the specified certificate is eligible; rank-unverified and all other non-candidate statuses return linear-solve-failure. The computed report is not used to assert the exact matrix identities or an exact minimizer. Construction and solving occur within each attempt at its current damping, and an earlier damping value's augmented factorization or report is not substituted.

Let $\Psi(y)=\|y\|_2^2/2$. For every $y,z$, $\Psi(y+z)-\Psi(y)-\langle y,z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2/2=o(\|z\|_2)$, so $D\Psi(y)[z]=\langle y,z\rangle$. Since $r$ is $C^1$ and $J=Dr$, the chain rule [F3] gives $D\phi(x)[h]=\langle r(x),J(x)h\rangle=(J(x)^Tr(x))^Th$; thus $J^Tr$ is the exact objective gradient. In exact arithmetic, if $J^Tr=0$, $x$ is stationary, and the algorithm returns before the solve or any ratio. In a computed run the same return is made only with the stated exact-zero certificate; a rounded zero without it returns gradient-unverified. For an exact nonstationary step, [F2] gives $p\ne0$ and positive predicted reduction. The computed path does not use [F2] to infer either property: its zero candidate returns zero-step-unverified, and its nonzero candidate reaches the ratio only after the explicit positive-prediction check.

Every attempt consists of finitely many gradient/status checks, a finite augmented construction and solve at the current damping, finitely many model and trial evaluations, and one of the listed branches. Any reported failure returns immediately. The attempt index increases by one after every rejection and is bounded by $N$, so execution returns a status after at most $N$ trials. Every attempted damping multiplication or division either produces the stated next damping or returns damping-range-failure, and a trial is accepted only after its next damping is available. In exact arithmetic the high-ratio boundary update is still $\max\{\lambda_{\min},\lambda/\gamma\}$; the unchanged-parameter branch is retained.

citations.quote:
Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let
$r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^2$ (each component
has continuous partial derivatives through order two, as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Define
$$\phi(x):=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,$$
and let $J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be the Jacobian with $i$th row
$\nabla r_i(x)^T$. Then $\phi$ is of class $C^2$ and
$$\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^T r(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x).$$

The second term in the Hessian is the residual-curvature term. It vanishes
when $r(x)=0$, but need not vanish at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$
and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$. If $a<b$, assume that $f$ is integrable
([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Then:

1. if $a < b$, the real-valued function $t \mapsto \lVert f(t)\rVert_2$ is
   integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]);
2. $$\Bigl\lVert \int_a^b f \Bigr\rVert_2 \;\le\; \int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2 .$$

**The hypothesis $a \le b$ is not decoration.** With the orientation convention
of [[def-oriented-integral]] and
[[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], interchanging the limits changes
the sign of the right-hand side but not of the left, so for $b < a$ the correct
statement is $\bigl\lVert\int_a^b f\bigr\rVert_2 \le \bigl|\int_a^b \lVert f\rVert_2\bigr|$;
the displayed inequality as written is false in that case. This is the same trap
the scalar inequality of
[[cor-integrability-of-absolute-values-products-and-lattice-operations]] carries.

**Clause 1 is a genuine obligation and is discharged before the estimate.** That
each $f_i$ is integrable does not by itself say that
$\sqrt{\sum_{i<m} f_i^{2}}$ is; the square root has to be brought in through
[[thm-composition-with-a-continuous-function]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: For each $x\in B$, the SVD [F4] writes $J(x)=U_1\Sigma V^T$ with every diagonal entry of $\Sigma$ at least $\sigma$. Thus $A(x)=V\Sigma^2V^T$ is invertible and $A(x)^{-1}=V\Sigma^{-2}V^T$. By [F4]–[F5], $\|A(x)^{-1}\|_2\le\sigma^{-2}$.

Fix $x\in B$, put $e=x-x_*$, and set $x_t=x_*+te$. The path $t\mapsto\nabla\phi(x_t)$ is continuously differentiable; [F1] and [F6] give derivative $(A(x_t)+S(x_t))e$. This derivative is continuous and hence componentwise integrable, so [F2] and [A1] yield $J(x)^Tr(x)=\int_0^1(A(x_t)+S(x_t))e\,dt$.

For $0\le t\le1$, write $A(x)-A(x_t)=J(x)^T(J(x)-J(x_t))+(J(x)^T-J(x_t)^T)J(x_t)$. An SVD of $J(x)-J(x_t)$ also gives an SVD of its transpose with the same singular values, so [F4] gives $\|J(x)^T-J(x_t)^T\|_2=\|J(x)-J(x_t)\|_2$ and $\|J(x)^T\|_2=\|J(x)\|_2$. The Lipschitz and boundedness hypotheses, with [F3], now give $\|A(x)-A(x_t)\|_2\le2ML(1-t)\|e\|_2$.

The exact step satisfies $x+p(x)-x_*=A(x)^{-1}(A(x)e-J(x)^Tr(x))$. Step 1.2 makes the parenthesized term $\int_0^1(A(x)-A(x_t)-S(x_t))e\,dt$. By step 1.3, $\|S(x_t)\|_2\le\kappa$, and [F7] bounds the integral norm by $(ML\|e\|_2+\kappa)\|e\|_2$. Step 1.1 therefore gives $\|x+p(x)-x_*\|_2\le\sigma^{-2}(ML\|e\|_2+\kappa)\|e\|_2\le q\|e\|_2$, since $\|e\|_2\le R$.
Because $q<1$, step 2.1 keeps every iterate in $B$ and gives $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le q^k\|x_0-x_*\|_2$, which tends to zero.

boundaries.reason: The Statement has x_* in a closed ball of radiusR>0, so its domain and comparison segment are nonempty. The positive singular-value bound excludes an empty or rank-deficient solve domain.

boundaries.evidence: The bound in step 2.1 includes κ=0 and zero residual curvature; it gives a contraction factor q<1.
The SVD and induced-norm proof in steps 1.1–3.1 applies for n=1 and any m≥1.
Step 1.1 uses σ>0 to exclude singular Jacobians, while q may be zero and still satisfies q<1.
The theorem assumes a closed ball B; steps 2.1–3.1 preserve membership including its boundary.
Step 2.1 fixes an arbitrary x∈B and uses a single path and finite-dimensional SVD; it makes no choice from an infinite family.

The conditional exact Gauss-Newton local contraction does not claim that its resulting error bound, minimizer or status implies all its hypotheses, so there is no reverse iff to establish.

Transpose norm equality and two product differences give 2ML(1-t)||e||, whose integral is ML||e||. Residual-curvature bound contributes kappa; q<1 makes the ball invariant and q^k proves convergence. x=x*, L=0 and q=0 cause no divisions by zero. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ with
$m,n\ge1$, and let $J(x)=Dr(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Let $K\subseteq U$
be convex and let $x_*,x\in K$. Suppose $L\ge0$ and
$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_2\le L\|y-z\|_2$ for all $y,z\in K$, where the matrix norm is
the Euclidean induced operator norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Then
$$\|r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\tfrac L2\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$
The dimensions $m$ and $n$ need not be equal.

Input a stored residual $r\in\mathbb R^m$, a stored Jacobian $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$ (using the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a factorization mode QR or SVD, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), and a declared singular-value threshold $\tau\ge0$. If $m<n$, immediately return unsupported-shape without requesting a factorization report; all remaining branches assume $m\ge n$. A computed QR report may also carry a verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ asserting $\|Jv\|_2\ge s\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. The target exact step, when it is returned, is the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|r+Jp\|_2^2$ and hence solves $J^TJp=-J^Tr$; this target is asserted only on a full-column-rank branch. Do not form $J^TJ$ in either solve path.

The threshold $\tau$ is used only by the SVD route. For QR mode the exact and computed routes are disjoint. Exact mode requires a supplied exact reduced factorization $J=QR$ with $Q^TQ=I_n$; only this exact factorization may reach the exact-step branch. Computed mode either consumes the report produced from this input pair $(J,-r)$ or forms it by setting $C=[J\mid-r]$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,n$, applying [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] to rows $k,\ldots,m$ of column $k$ and all trailing columns of $C$, including its last right-hand-side column. Embed each returned active block in those rows, leaving earlier rows and columns unchanged, and propagate the first factorization failure. After a successful computed loop, the report consists of the computed upper-triangular block $\widehat R$, the first $n$ entries $\widehat y$ of the transformed last column, and the ordered stored reflector records (including identity markers). The exact orthogonal representatives of those records define the $Q$ used by the conditional backward-stability result; the rounded outputs themselves are not an exact factorization of $J$ and cannot be supplied to the exact branch. In exact mode, a zero diagonal in $R$ returns rank-deficient; otherwise solve $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ by backward substitution and return exact-step($p$). In computed mode, a zero diagonal returns rank-deficient-candidate. Otherwise initialize storage for $\widehat p_0,\ldots,\widehat p_{n-1}$ with all components unassigned, then for $i=n-1,n-2,\ldots,0$ compute $s_i$ by setting $s_i=0$ and, for $j=i+1,i+2,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, updating $s_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat R_{ij}\widehat p_j))$; then compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat y_i-s_i)$ and $\widehat p_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/\widehat R_{ii})$. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. A nonzero computed diagonal without an independently verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ for the input matrix $J$ returns rank-unverified with the computed candidate but no full-rank claim. With that certificate, return computed-candidate($\widehat p$). A nonzero computed diagonal alone is not a full-rank certificate. The computed-QR backward-stability conclusion of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]] is attached only when all of that theorem's successful-execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses are supplied; otherwise no backward-stability conclusion is returned.

For SVD mode, the input includes an exact factorization $J=U\Sigma V^T$, or a computed report with finite stored factors $\widehat U_1\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $\widehat\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ whose entries are nonnegative, and $\widehat V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, together with certified intervals $[\ell_i,u_i]$ satisfying $0\le\ell_i\le\sigma_i(J)\le u_i$ for each singular value $i=1,\ldots,n$. In the exact case, if any $\sigma_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold and no Gauss-Newton step. If every $\sigma_i>\tau$, return
$$p=-V\,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_n^{-1})\,U_1^Tr,$$
where $U_1$ consists of the corresponding $n$ left singular vectors. For a computed report, if any $u_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold; otherwise, if any interval satisfies $\ell_i\le\tau<u_i$, return rank-unverified; if every lower endpoint exceeds $\tau$ but some stored $\widehat\sigma_i=0$, return factorization-failure. In the remaining branch, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order initialize $z_i=0$ and, for $j=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set $z_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(z_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat U_{ji}r_j))$. After these dots, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ set $w_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i/\widehat\sigma_i)$. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$ initialize $t_j=0$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $t_j\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(t_j+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat V_{ji}w_i))$; set $\widehat p_j=-t_j$ by exact sign change. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. Otherwise return the finite candidate
$$\widehat p=-\widehat V\,\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^{-1})\,\widehat U_1^Tr$$
with status computed-candidate and make no accuracy claim beyond the supplied report. The displayed formula names the result of the preceding schedule; it is not a second computation. The certified intervals determine only the threshold branch; no computed-SVD accuracy bound is asserted. A computed SVD routine is not defined here; the SVD branch consumes its report.

If the selected factorization reports failure, return factorization-failure; every status other than exact-step is explicitly not a certified exact full-rank Gauss-Newton step.
