derivations.claim: Fix $x\in B$, put $e=x-x_*$, and write $E=r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)e$. By [F1] and [A1], $r(x)=J(x)e+E$ with $\|E\|_2\le(L/2)\|e\|_2^2$.

Let $p$ be the exact Gauss-Newton step and set $h:=p+e$. For every $v\in\mathbb R^n$, minimality of $p$ gives $\frac12\|r(x)+J(x)(p+tv)\|_2^2\ge\frac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2$ for all real $t$. Expanding in $t$ shows the linear coefficient $v^TJ(x)^T(r(x)+J(x)p)$ must be zero (otherwise a sufficiently small $t$ of the opposite sign decreases the quadratic). Since this holds for every $v$, $J(x)^T(J(x)h+E)=0$ by step 1.1.

Set $q:=-h$. Step 2.1 gives $J(x)^T(E-J(x)q)=0$, so $E-J(x)q$ is orthogonal to $J(x)q$; hence $\|E\|_2^2=\|J(x)q\|_2^2+\|E-J(x)q\|_2^2\ge\|J(x)q\|_2^2$. By [A2], $\|J(x)q\|_2\ge\sigma\|q\|_2$. Therefore $\|x+p-x_*\|_2=\|h\|_2=\|q\|_2\le\|E\|_2/\sigma\le C\|e\|_2^2$.

If $C=0$ and $x_0\in B$, step 3.1 gives $x_1=x_*$. If $C>0$ and $\|x_0-x_*\|_2\le1/(2C)$, the stated hypothesis also puts $x_0\in B$, and step 3.1 gives $\|x_1-x_*\|_2\le\frac12\|x_0-x_*\|_2$, so $x_1\in B$; induction repeats the same bound for every $k$, and $\|x_k-x_*\|_2\le2^{-k}\|x_0-x_*\|_2\to0$.

citations.quote:
This algorithm performs one finite-budget LM trial update. Inputs are $x\in U$, a $C^1$ residual function $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ on open $U$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $J=Dr$, the exact values $r(x)$ and $J(x)$, a fixed nonsingular $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), a floor $\lambda_{\min}>0$, current damping $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, factors $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, a trust radius $\Delta>0$, and an attempt cap $N\ge1$. In computed mode the input values are finite stored numbers treated as the exact data for this update; only arithmetic performed below is rounded. A computed run may include a certificate that the exact scalar product $J(x)^Tr(x)$ is zero. Put $\phi(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2/2$ and $m_0(p)=\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2/2$. In exact mode the step is the unique minimizer of
$$\tfrac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|Dp\|_2^2,$$
which is equivalent to solving
$$(J(x)^TJ(x)+\lambda D^TD)p=-J(x)^Tr(x).$$
In computed mode the returned vector is only a candidate for this same subproblem; no exact minimizer claim is made.


In computed mode use [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Evaluate every dot product by initializing $s=0$ and, for indices in increasing order, computing $u=\operatorname{fl}(a_i b_i)$ followed by $s=\operatorname{fl}(s+u)$. Matrix-vector products and squared norms use this schedule row by row and coordinate by coordinate. Each other scalar arithmetic operation uses $\operatorname{fl}$, with copies and sign changes exact; the first failed operation returns the status assigned to its stage. Function evaluation returns either a finite stored residual vector or failure.

For attempts $j=1,\ldots,N$, do the following with the current damping. After a damping change, construct a new augmented matrix and obtain a report for that actual matrix; do not reuse an earlier damping value's factorization or report.

1. In exact arithmetic, if $J(x)^Tr(x)=0$, return stationary before calling the linear solver. In a computed run, evaluate $J(x)^Tr(x)$ by the stated dot schedule and return stationary before the solve only with the supplied certificate that this exact gradient is zero; if evaluating the product fails, return gradient-evaluation-failure; if the computed product is a rounded zero without that certificate, return gradient-unverified and do not form a ratio. Otherwise perform the augmented construction and linear solve afresh inside this attempt at its current damping: Form $A_\lambda=[J(x);\sqrt\lambda D]$ and $s_\lambda=[r(x);0]$, then call [[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] in QR mode on $(A_\lambda,s_\lambda)$. Exact mode uses the exact positive square root and requires a supplied exact reduced factorization of $A_\lambda$ for each call; absence of that factorization returns linear-solve-failure. This matrix has full column rank because $D$ is nonsingular and $\lambda>0$. In computed mode, copy the stored $J(x)$ and $r(x)$ into the top blocks, compute $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)$, then fill the bottom block entries $\operatorname{fl}(tD_{ij})$ in increasing row and column order and fill the appended residual entries with exact zeros. Any first arithmetic or range failure in this construction returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. The call receives a computed QR report for this actual stored $A_\lambda$. A computed-candidate is usable only when that report includes the low-level procedure's independently verified full-rank certificate $s_\lambda>0$ for the actual stored matrix, namely $\|A_\lambda v\|_2\ge s_\lambda\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Pass this bound as the computed report's certificate field; it is not inferred from a nonzero computed diagonal or from positive definiteness of the ideal exact system alone. A rank-unverified report and every other status besides exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode are unusable and return linear-solve-failure with the report. A computed-candidate remains a candidate and carries no convergence guarantee. If the solver status is not exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode, return linear-solve-failure with its report; in particular, rank-unverified is a failure, not a usable trial.
2. If exact mode returns $p=0$ after the nonzero-gradient check, return linear-solve-failure with the inconsistent exact solve report. If computed mode returns $p=0$, return zero-step-unverified and do not compute a ratio. For every remaining candidate $p$ (the zero candidates have already returned a status), compute $\operatorname{pred}=m_0(0)-m_0(p)$. If this computation fails, return model-evaluation-failure; if $\operatorname{pred}\le0$, return nonpositive-predicted-decrease. In either case do not compute a ratio.
3. If computing $x+p$ or $Dp$ fails in the selected arithmetic, return trial-evaluation-failure. If $x+p\notin U$ or $\|Dp\|_2>\Delta$, reject the trial and compute the damping update $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$ and continue.
4. Otherwise evaluate $r(x+p)$ and compute $\operatorname{ared}=\phi(x)-\phi(x+p)$ and $\rho=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}$. A failed trial evaluation or nonfinite computed result returns trial-evaluation-failure. If $\rho<\eta_1$, reject and compute $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that damping update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$. If this was attempt $N$, return rejection-budget-exhausted; otherwise continue.
5. If $\rho\ge\eta_1$, first determine the next damping. If also $\rho\ge\eta_2$ and $\|Dp\|_2=\Delta$, compute $q=\lambda/\gamma$ in exact mode and $q=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda/\gamma)$ in computed mode. If this division fails, has a nonfinite or nonpositive result, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report, without accepting that trial. Otherwise set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\max\{\lambda_{\min},q\}$. In every other accepted case set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\lambda$. Only after the next damping is available, accept and return $x+p$, $p$, $\rho$, and $\lambda_{\rm next}$.

If all $N$ attempts are rejected, return rejection-budget-exhausted. The equality in the boundary test is exact for exact arithmetic and is the equality test on stored values in a computed run. No claim is made that every finite budget succeeds.

Let $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $r\in\mathbb R^m$, $m,n\ge1$, let
$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$
Set $z_\lambda:=Dp_\lambda$, $\widetilde J:=JD^{-1}$, and
$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$
over the trust-region ball $\|z\|_2\le\Delta_\lambda$ of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ with
$m,n\ge1$, and let $J(x)=Dr(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$. Let $K\subseteq U$
be convex and let $x_*,x\in K$. Suppose $L\ge0$ and
$\|J(y)-J(z)\|_2\le L\|y-z\|_2$ for all $y,z\in K$, where the matrix norm is
the Euclidean induced operator norm of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. Then
$$\|r(x)-r(x_*)-J(x)(x-x_*)\|_2\le\tfrac L2\|x-x_*\|_2^2.$$
The dimensions $m$ and $n$ need not be equal.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in S$ with $g=J(x)^Tr(x)\ne0$, and let $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$. By [F1] the exact trial solves $Q_\lambda p=-g$ for $Q_\lambda=J^TJ+\lambda D^TD$. For $v\ne0$, $v^TQ_\lambda v=\|Jv\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dv\|_2^2>0$, so the solution is nonzero. By [F2], $\operatorname{pred}=\frac12\|Jp\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp\|_2^2$. The transpose norm equality [F6] and submultiplicativity [F4] give $\|g\|_2=\|Q_\lambda p\|_2\le(M^2+\lambda d_+^2)\|p\|_2\le\lambda C_D\|p\|_2$. Also $\lambda d^2\|p\|_2^2\le p^TQ_\lambda p=-p^Tg\le\|p\|_2\|g\|_2$ by [F5], so $\|p\|_2\le\|g\|_2/(\lambda d^2)\le MR_0/(\lambda d^2)$ using [F4], [F6], and [A1].

If $\lambda\ge\Lambda$, step 1.1 gives $\|p\|_2\le P\le1$ and therefore $\|Dp\|_2\le d_+P\le\Delta/2$. The segment from $x$ to $x+p$ lies in $S_1$, since every point on it is within $\|p\|_2\le1$ of $x\in S$. Apply [F3] on that segment and write $E=r(x+p)-r(x)-Jp$; then $\|E\|_2\le(L/2)\|p\|_2^2$. Expanding the two squared norms and using [F5] yields $|\phi(x+p)-m_0(p)|=|(r(x)+Jp)^TE+\frac12\|E\|_2^2|\le C_E\|p\|_2^2$.

By step 1.1, step 2.1, and [F2], $\operatorname{pred}\ge\lambda\|Dp\|_2^2\ge\lambda d^2\|p\|_2^2$. From $g=-Q_\lambda p$ and [F4], $\|p\|_2\ge\|g\|_2/(\lambda C_D)$, so $\operatorname{pred}\ge d^2\|g\|_2^2/(\lambda C_D^2)$. The preceding bounds therefore give
$$|\rho-1|=\frac{|\phi(x+p)-m_0(p)|}{\operatorname{pred}}\le\frac{C_EC_D^2}{\lambda d^6}\le1-\eta_2,$$
and hence $\rho\ge\eta_2$.

Since $\Lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, after at most $\lceil\log(\Lambda/\lambda_{\min})/\log\gamma\rceil$ consecutive rejections the damping reaches at least $\Lambda$. At that trial step 2.1 makes it radius-feasible and step 3.1 gives $\rho\ge\eta_2>\eta_1$, so it is accepted. An earlier feasible trial with $\rho\ge\eta_1$ is already accepted by [F1]. The extra one in $N$ counts the final trial at or above $\Lambda$, proving the finite attempt bound.

boundaries.reason: The Statement fixes x_0 in U and its compact sublevelS containing x_0, then quantifies over nonstationaryx inS. If no suchx exists the conditional trial claim is vacuous rather than requiring an empty solve.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement handles L=0 through C_E=0 and keeps Λ at least λ_min, whose denominator terms are positive by the stated hypotheses.
The bounds and matrix inequalities in steps 1.1–4.1 apply unchanged in one parameter and one residual dimension.
Statement and step 1.1 permit zero residual-curvature/Lipschitz constants and use d,d_+,λ_min>0 to keep every denominator nonzero.
Step 2.1 controls the entire closed segment from x to x+p inside S_1, and the radius-feasibility inequality is non-strict.
Step 4.1 defines and applies an explicit finite geometric damping count; no arbitrary infinite selection is used.

boundaries.reason: The large-damping sufficient acceptance result asserts its displayed implication, construction or example, not a characterization equivalent to its input hypotheses; no forward iff direction is omitted.
The large-damping sufficient acceptance result does not claim that its resulting error bound, minimizer or status implies all its hypotheses, so there is no reverse iff to establish.

risk_review.notes: Checked all four steps and ten direct supplier interfaces. With g=J^Tr!=0, positivity gives nonzero p and pred>=lambda*d^2*||p||^2. The system gives ||g||/(lambda*C_D)<=||p||<=||g||/(lambda*d^2) and ||g||<=MR0. lambda>=Lambda ensures ||p||<=P<=1, so its segment lies in S1 even though S1 need not be convex, and ||Dp||<=Delta/2. Residual remainder yields C_E||p||^2 objective error; combining the upper step bound and lower prediction gives C_E*C_D^2/(lambda*d^6). Ceiling plus one counts the first acceptable trial, including Lambda=lambda_min. C1 suffices throughout; the reader correctly removed the C2-only gradient citation and supplied exact QR hypothesis. Exact solves/evaluations and N attempts remain essential.

citations.quote:
This algorithm performs one finite-budget LM trial update. Inputs are $x\in U$, a $C^1$ residual function $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ on open $U$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $J=Dr$, the exact values $r(x)$ and $J(x)$, a fixed nonsingular $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), a floor $\lambda_{\min}>0$, current damping $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, factors $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, a trust radius $\Delta>0$, and an attempt cap $N\ge1$. In computed mode the input values are finite stored numbers treated as the exact data for this update; only arithmetic performed below is rounded. A computed run may include a certificate that the exact scalar product $J(x)^Tr(x)$ is zero. Put $\phi(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2/2$ and $m_0(p)=\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2/2$. In exact mode the step is the unique minimizer of
$$\tfrac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|Dp\|_2^2,$$
which is equivalent to solving
$$(J(x)^TJ(x)+\lambda D^TD)p=-J(x)^Tr(x).$$
In computed mode the returned vector is only a candidate for this same subproblem; no exact minimizer claim is made.


In computed mode use [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Evaluate every dot product by initializing $s=0$ and, for indices in increasing order, computing $u=\operatorname{fl}(a_i b_i)$ followed by $s=\operatorname{fl}(s+u)$. Matrix-vector products and squared norms use this schedule row by row and coordinate by coordinate. Each other scalar arithmetic operation uses $\operatorname{fl}$, with copies and sign changes exact; the first failed operation returns the status assigned to its stage. Function evaluation returns either a finite stored residual vector or failure.

For attempts $j=1,\ldots,N$, do the following with the current damping. After a damping change, construct a new augmented matrix and obtain a report for that actual matrix; do not reuse an earlier damping value's factorization or report.

1. In exact arithmetic, if $J(x)^Tr(x)=0$, return stationary before calling the linear solver. In a computed run, evaluate $J(x)^Tr(x)$ by the stated dot schedule and return stationary before the solve only with the supplied certificate that this exact gradient is zero; if evaluating the product fails, return gradient-evaluation-failure; if the computed product is a rounded zero without that certificate, return gradient-unverified and do not form a ratio. Otherwise perform the augmented construction and linear solve afresh inside this attempt at its current damping: Form $A_\lambda=[J(x);\sqrt\lambda D]$ and $s_\lambda=[r(x);0]$, then call [[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] in QR mode on $(A_\lambda,s_\lambda)$. Exact mode uses the exact positive square root and requires a supplied exact reduced factorization of $A_\lambda$ for each call; absence of that factorization returns linear-solve-failure. This matrix has full column rank because $D$ is nonsingular and $\lambda>0$. In computed mode, copy the stored $J(x)$ and $r(x)$ into the top blocks, compute $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)$, then fill the bottom block entries $\operatorname{fl}(tD_{ij})$ in increasing row and column order and fill the appended residual entries with exact zeros. Any first arithmetic or range failure in this construction returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. The call receives a computed QR report for this actual stored $A_\lambda$. A computed-candidate is usable only when that report includes the low-level procedure's independently verified full-rank certificate $s_\lambda>0$ for the actual stored matrix, namely $\|A_\lambda v\|_2\ge s_\lambda\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Pass this bound as the computed report's certificate field; it is not inferred from a nonzero computed diagonal or from positive definiteness of the ideal exact system alone. A rank-unverified report and every other status besides exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode are unusable and return linear-solve-failure with the report. A computed-candidate remains a candidate and carries no convergence guarantee. If the solver status is not exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode, return linear-solve-failure with its report; in particular, rank-unverified is a failure, not a usable trial.
2. If exact mode returns $p=0$ after the nonzero-gradient check, return linear-solve-failure with the inconsistent exact solve report. If computed mode returns $p=0$, return zero-step-unverified and do not compute a ratio. For every remaining candidate $p$ (the zero candidates have already returned a status), compute $\operatorname{pred}=m_0(0)-m_0(p)$. If this computation fails, return model-evaluation-failure; if $\operatorname{pred}\le0$, return nonpositive-predicted-decrease. In either case do not compute a ratio.
3. If computing $x+p$ or $Dp$ fails in the selected arithmetic, return trial-evaluation-failure. If $x+p\notin U$ or $\|Dp\|_2>\Delta$, reject the trial and compute the damping update $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$ and continue.
4. Otherwise evaluate $r(x+p)$ and compute $\operatorname{ared}=\phi(x)-\phi(x+p)$ and $\rho=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}$. A failed trial evaluation or nonfinite computed result returns trial-evaluation-failure. If $\rho<\eta_1$, reject and compute $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that damping update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$. If this was attempt $N$, return rejection-budget-exhausted; otherwise continue.
5. If $\rho\ge\eta_1$, first determine the next damping. If also $\rho\ge\eta_2$ and $\|Dp\|_2=\Delta$, compute $q=\lambda/\gamma$ in exact mode and $q=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda/\gamma)$ in computed mode. If this division fails, has a nonfinite or nonpositive result, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report, without accepting that trial. Otherwise set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\max\{\lambda_{\min},q\}$. In every other accepted case set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\lambda$. Only after the next damping is available, accept and return $x+p$, $p$, $\rho$, and $\lambda_{\rm next}$.

If all $N$ attempts are rejected, return rejection-budget-exhausted. The equality in the boundary test is exact for exact arithmetic and is the equality test on stored values in a computed run. No claim is made that every finite budget succeeds.

Let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^1$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let
$J=Dr$, and let $\phi=\|r\|_2^2/2$. Fix $x_0\in U$ and suppose its sublevel set
$S=\{x\in U:\phi(x)\le\phi(x_0)\}$ is compact. Put
$S_1=\{y\in\mathbb R^n:\operatorname{dist}(y,S)\le1\}$ and assume $S_1\subseteq U$.
On $S_1$, suppose $\|r(x)\|_2\le R_0$, $\|J(x)\|_2\le M$, and $J$ is
$L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean induced matrix norm.
Fix nonsingular $D$, numbers $d,d_+>0$ with
$\|Dv\|_2\ge d\|v\|_2$ and
$\max\{\|D\|_2,\|D^T\|_2\}\le d_+$, and parameters
$\lambda_{\min}>0$, $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, and $\Delta>0$.
Define
$$C_D:=d_+^2+M^2/\lambda_{\min},\quad C_E:=\tfrac L2(R_0+M)+\tfrac{L^2}{8},\quad P:=\min\{1,\Delta/(2d_+)\},$$
$$\Lambda:=\max\left\{\lambda_{\min},\frac{MR_0}{d^2P},\frac{C_EC_D^2}{(1-\eta_2)d^6}\right\},\quad N:=1+\left\lceil\frac{\log(\Lambda/\lambda_{\min})}{\log\gamma}\right\rceil.$$
At any $x\in S$ with $g:=J(x)^Tr(x)\ne0$, an exact LM trial with damping
$\lambda\ge\Lambda$, using a supplied exact reduced QR factorization of
its augmented matrix, has $0<\operatorname{pred}$, $\|Dp_\lambda\|_2\le\Delta/2$,
and $\rho\ge\eta_2$. Therefore, if the algorithm starts an iteration with
$\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$ and has at least $N$ trials, it either accepts an
earlier trial with $\rho\ge\eta_1$ or accepts by the $N$th trial. This conclusion
assumes exact subproblem solves and exact objective evaluations.

Let $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $r\in\mathbb R^m$, $m,n\ge1$, let
$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$
Set $z_\lambda:=Dp_\lambda$, $\widetilde J:=JD^{-1}$, and
$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$
over the trust-region ball $\|z\|_2\le\Delta_\lambda$ of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If every partial derivative $\partial_jf_i(a)$ of $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ exists, the **Jacobian matrix** is $Jf(a)=(\partial_jf_i(a))_{i<n,j<m}$. For scalar-valued $f$, its **gradient** is

$$\nabla f(a):=(\partial_0f(a),\ldots,\partial_{m-1}f(a))\in\mathbb R^m,$$

with coordinates understood in the standard basis ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]). The partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]].

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. The map $f$ is
**continuously differentiable**, or of class $C^1$, when it is totally
differentiable at every point of $U$ and the entries of its derivative matrix
are continuous functions on $U$.

For an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and $a\in U$, a **local inverse of $f$ at
$a$** is a function $g:W\to V$ for open neighbourhoods $a\in V\subseteq U$
and $f(a)\in W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ such that $f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective and
$g=(f|_V)^{-1}$. If both $f|_V$ and $g$ are $C^1$, this restriction is a
**local diffeomorphism** at $a$.

If $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ is totally differentiable at $a\in U$, then some $C,\delta>0$ satisfy $\|f(a+h)-f(a)\|_2\le C\|h\|_2$ whenever $\|h\|_2<\delta$ and $a+h\in U$. In particular $f$ is continuous at $a$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

derivations.claim: Let $\Psi(y)=\|y\|_2^2/2$. The identity $\Psi(y+z)-\Psi(y)-\langle y,z\rangle=\|z\|_2^2/2=o(\|z\|_2)$ gives $D\Psi(y)[z]=\langle y,z\rangle$. Since $r$ is $C^1$ and $J=Dr$, the chain rule yields $D\phi(x)[h]=\langle r(x),J(x)h\rangle=(J(x)^Tr(x))^Th$, so $\nabla\phi=J^Tr$. At a nonstationary $x_k\in S$, [F2] shows that the iteration either accepts an earlier trial or accepts once $\lambda\ge\Lambda$, within $N$ attempts. Thus no rejection-budget status occurs. The accepted actual reduction is $\rho\,\operatorname{pred}\ge\eta_1\operatorname{pred}>0$ by [F1], so $\phi(x_{k+1})<\phi(x_k)\le\phi(x_0)$ and $x_{k+1}\in S$. Induction keeps all iterates in $S$.

The damping remains at least $\lambda_{\min}$ by [F1]. If $\lambda_k\ge\Lambda$, [F2] accepts the trial with $\|Dp_k\|_2\le\Delta/2$, so it is not a boundary step and the damping is unchanged. Input a stored residual $r\in\mathbb R^m$, a stored Jacobian $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$ (using the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a factorization mode QR or SVD, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), and a declared singular-value threshold $\tau\ge0$. If $m<n$, immediately return unsupported-shape without requesting a factorization report; all remaining branches assume $m\ge n$. A computed QR report may also carry a verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ asserting $\|Jv\|_2\ge s\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. The target exact step, when it is returned, is the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|r+Jp\|_2^2$ and hence solves $J^TJp=-J^Tr$; this target is asserted only on a full-column-rank branch. Do not form $J^TJ$ in either solve path.

The threshold $\tau$ is used only by the SVD route. For QR mode the exact and computed routes are disjoint. Exact mode requires a supplied exact reduced factorization $J=QR$ with $Q^TQ=I_n$; only this exact factorization may reach the exact-step branch. Computed mode either consumes the report produced from this input pair $(J,-r)$ or forms it by setting $C=[J\mid-r]$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,n$, applying [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] to rows $k,\ldots,m$ of column $k$ and all trailing columns of $C$, including its last right-hand-side column. Embed each returned active block in those rows, leaving earlier rows and columns unchanged, and propagate the first factorization failure. After a successful computed loop, the report consists of the computed upper-triangular block $\widehat R$, the first $n$ entries $\widehat y$ of the transformed last column, and the ordered stored reflector records (including identity markers). The exact orthogonal representatives of those records define the $Q$ used by the conditional backward-stability result; the rounded outputs themselves are not an exact factorization of $J$ and cannot be supplied to the exact branch. In exact mode, a zero diagonal in $R$ returns rank-deficient; otherwise solve $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ by backward substitution and return exact-step($p$). In computed mode, a zero diagonal returns rank-deficient-candidate. Otherwise initialize storage for $\widehat p_0,\ldots,\widehat p_{n-1}$ with all components unassigned, then for $i=n-1,n-2,\ldots,0$ compute $s_i$ by setting $s_i=0$ and, for $j=i+1,i+2,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, updating $s_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat R_{ij}\widehat p_j))$; then compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat y_i-s_i)$ and $\widehat p_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/\widehat R_{ii})$. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. A nonzero computed diagonal without an independently verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ for the input matrix $J$ returns rank-unverified with the computed candidate but no full-rank claim. With that certificate, return computed-candidate($\widehat p$). A nonzero computed diagonal alone is not a full-rank certificate. The computed-QR backward-stability conclusion of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]] is attached only when all of that theorem's successful-execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses are supplied; otherwise no backward-stability conclusion is returned.

For SVD mode, the input includes an exact factorization $J=U\Sigma V^T$, or a computed report with finite stored factors $\widehat U_1\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $\widehat\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ whose entries are nonnegative, and $\widehat V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, together with certified intervals $[\ell_i,u_i]$ satisfying $0\le\ell_i\le\sigma_i(J)\le u_i$ for each singular value $i=1,\ldots,n$. In the exact case, if any $\sigma_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold and no Gauss-Newton step. If every $\sigma_i>\tau$, return
$$p=-V\,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_n^{-1})\,U_1^Tr,$$
where $U_1$ consists of the corresponding $n$ left singular vectors. For a computed report, if any $u_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold; otherwise, if any interval satisfies $\ell_i\le\tau<u_i$, return rank-unverified; if every lower endpoint exceeds $\tau$ but some stored $\widehat\sigma_i=0$, return factorization-failure. In the remaining branch, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order initialize $z_i=0$ and, for $j=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set $z_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(z_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat U_{ji}r_j))$. After these dots, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ set $w_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i/\widehat\sigma_i)$. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$ initialize $t_j=0$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $t_j\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(t_j+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat V_{ji}w_i))$; set $\widehat p_j=-t_j$ by exact sign change. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. Otherwise return the finite candidate
$$\widehat p=-\widehat V\,\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^{-1})\,\widehat U_1^Tr$$
with status computed-candidate and make no accuracy claim beyond the supplied report. The displayed formula names the result of the preceding schedule; it is not a second computation. The certified intervals determine only the threshold branch; no computed-SVD accuracy bound is asserted. A computed SVD routine is not defined here; the SVD branch consumes its report.

If the selected factorization reports failure, return factorization-failure; every status other than exact-step is explicitly not a certified exact full-rank Gauss-Newton step.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,

derivations.claim: At $x_*=(2,1)$, the residual components are $r_1=2-2=0$ and $r_2=2e^{-1}-2e^{-1}=0$. By [F2], the Jacobian is $J(a,k)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\e^{-k}&-ae^{-k}\end{bmatrix}$, hence $J(x_*)=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\e^{-1}&-2e^{-1}\end{bmatrix}$.

Put $c=e^{-1}>0$ and $s=\sqrt{1+c^2}$. Supply the exact reduced QR factorization $Q=\begin{bmatrix}1/s&c/s\\c/s&-1/s\end{bmatrix}$ and $R=\begin{bmatrix}s&-2c^2/s\\0&2c/s\end{bmatrix}$, for which $Q^TQ=I$ and $QR=J(x_*)$; its diagonal entries are positive. This algorithm performs one finite-budget LM trial update. Inputs are $x\in U$, a $C^1$ residual function $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ on open $U$ with $m,n\ge1$ and $J=Dr$, the exact values $r(x)$ and $J(x)$, a fixed nonsingular $D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), a floor $\lambda_{\min}>0$, current damping $\lambda\ge\lambda_{\min}$, factors $\gamma>1$, $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, a trust radius $\Delta>0$, and an attempt cap $N\ge1$. In computed mode the input values are finite stored numbers treated as the exact data for this update; only arithmetic performed below is rounded. A computed run may include a certificate that the exact scalar product $J(x)^Tr(x)$ is zero. Put $\phi(x)=\|r(x)\|_2^2/2$ and $m_0(p)=\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2/2$. In exact mode the step is the unique minimizer of
$$\tfrac12\|r(x)+J(x)p\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|Dp\|_2^2,$$
which is equivalent to solving
$$(J(x)^TJ(x)+\lambda D^TD)p=-J(x)^Tr(x).$$
In computed mode the returned vector is only a candidate for this same subproblem; no exact minimizer claim is made.


In computed mode use [[def-operationwise-real-complex-floating-point-model-with-sqrt-and-fma]]. Evaluate every dot product by initializing $s=0$ and, for indices in increasing order, computing $u=\operatorname{fl}(a_i b_i)$ followed by $s=\operatorname{fl}(s+u)$. Matrix-vector products and squared norms use this schedule row by row and coordinate by coordinate. Each other scalar arithmetic operation uses $\operatorname{fl}$, with copies and sign changes exact; the first failed operation returns the status assigned to its stage. Function evaluation returns either a finite stored residual vector or failure.

For attempts $j=1,\ldots,N$, do the following with the current damping. After a damping change, construct a new augmented matrix and obtain a report for that actual matrix; do not reuse an earlier damping value's factorization or report.

1. In exact arithmetic, if $J(x)^Tr(x)=0$, return stationary before calling the linear solver. In a computed run, evaluate $J(x)^Tr(x)$ by the stated dot schedule and return stationary before the solve only with the supplied certificate that this exact gradient is zero; if evaluating the product fails, return gradient-evaluation-failure; if the computed product is a rounded zero without that certificate, return gradient-unverified and do not form a ratio. Otherwise perform the augmented construction and linear solve afresh inside this attempt at its current damping: Form $A_\lambda=[J(x);\sqrt\lambda D]$ and $s_\lambda=[r(x);0]$, then call [[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] in QR mode on $(A_\lambda,s_\lambda)$. Exact mode uses the exact positive square root and requires a supplied exact reduced factorization of $A_\lambda$ for each call; absence of that factorization returns linear-solve-failure. This matrix has full column rank because $D$ is nonsingular and $\lambda>0$. In computed mode, copy the stored $J(x)$ and $r(x)$ into the top blocks, compute $t=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)$, then fill the bottom block entries $\operatorname{fl}(tD_{ij})$ in increasing row and column order and fill the appended residual entries with exact zeros. A computed-candidate is usable only when that report includes the low-level procedure's independently verified full-rank certificate $s_\lambda>0$ for the actual stored matrix, namely $\|A_\lambda v\|_2\ge s_\lambda\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. Pass this bound as the computed report's certificate field; it is not inferred from a nonzero computed diagonal or from positive definiteness of the ideal exact system alone. A rank-unverified report and every other status besides exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode are unusable and return linear-solve-failure with the report. A computed-candidate remains a candidate and carries no convergence guarantee. If the solver status is not exact-step in exact mode or computed-candidate in computed mode, return linear-solve-failure with its report; in particular, rank-unverified is a failure, not a usable trial.
2. If exact mode returns $p=0$ after the nonzero-gradient check, return linear-solve-failure with the inconsistent exact solve report. If computed mode returns $p=0$, return zero-step-unverified and do not compute a ratio. For every remaining candidate $p$ (the zero candidates have already returned a status), compute $\operatorname{pred}=m_0(0)-m_0(p)$. If this computation fails, return model-evaluation-failure; if $\operatorname{pred}\le0$, return nonpositive-predicted-decrease. In either case do not compute a ratio.
3. If computing $x+p$ or $Dp$ fails in the selected arithmetic, return trial-evaluation-failure. If $x+p\notin U$ or $\|Dp\|_2>\Delta$, reject the trial and compute the damping update $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$ and continue.
4. Otherwise evaluate $r(x+p)$ and compute $\operatorname{ared}=\phi(x)-\phi(x+p)$ and $\rho=\operatorname{ared}/\operatorname{pred}$. A failed trial evaluation or nonfinite computed result returns trial-evaluation-failure. If $\rho<\eta_1$, reject and compute $\lambda^+=\gamma\lambda$ in the selected arithmetic. If that damping update fails, is nonfinite, or is outside the representable range, return damping-range-failure with the current $x,\lambda$ and the trial report. Otherwise set $\lambda\leftarrow\lambda^+$. If this was attempt $N$, return rejection-budget-exhausted; otherwise continue.
5. If $\rho\ge\eta_1$, first determine the next damping. If also $\rho\ge\eta_2$ and $\|Dp\|_2=\Delta$, compute $q=\lambda/\gamma$ in exact mode and $q=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda/\gamma)$ in computed mode. Otherwise set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\max\{\lambda_{\min},q\}$. In every other accepted case set $\lambda_{\rm next}=\lambda$. Only after the next damping is available, accept and return $x+p$, $p$, $\rho$, and $\lambda_{\rm next}$.

If all $N$ attempts are rejected, return rejection-budget-exhausted. The equality in the boundary test is exact for exact arithmetic and is the equality test on stored values in a computed run. No claim is made that every finite budget succeeds.

Let $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $r\in\mathbb R^m$, $m,n\ge1$, let
$D\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be nonsingular, let $\lambda>0$, and put
$g:=J^Tr$. Assume $g\ne0$. There is a unique $p_\lambda$ satisfying
$$\bigl(J^TJ+\lambda D^TD\bigr)p_\lambda=-g.$$
Set $z_\lambda:=Dp_\lambda$, $\widetilde J:=JD^{-1}$, and
$\Delta_\lambda:=\|z_\lambda\|_2>0$. Then $z_\lambda$ uniquely minimizes
$$q_\lambda(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2+\tfrac\lambda2\|z\|_2^2$$
over $\mathbb R^n$, and globally minimizes the unregularized model
$$m(z):=\tfrac12\|r+\widetilde Jz\|_2^2$$
over the trust-region ball $\|z\|_2\le\Delta_\lambda$ of
[[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]]. Its predicted reduction is
positive and, in the original step coordinates,
$$m(0)-m(Dp_\lambda)=\tfrac12\|Jp_\lambda\|_2^2+\lambda\|Dp_\lambda\|_2^2>0.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

derivations.claim: At $(0,0)$, $r=(-1,-2)^T$, $J=\begin{bmatrix}1&1\\2&2\end{bmatrix}$, and $J^TJ=\begin{bmatrix}5&5\\5&5\end{bmatrix}$. The two columns of $J$ coincide, so its rank is $1<2$. Supply the exact reduced QR $Q=\frac1{\sqrt5}\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\2&1\end{bmatrix}$ and $R=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt5&\sqrt5\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$, which satisfies $Q^TQ=I$ and $QR=J$. The exact QR branch therefore returns rank-deficient. The objective is $\frac52(a+b-1)^2$, whose minimizers are the full line $a+b=1$; hence the parameters are not separately identifiable. The linearized problem at $(0,0)$ is minimized whenever $p_1+p_2=1$, so it has no unique Gauss-Newton step.

For $D=I$ and $\lambda=1$, the augmented matrix and residual are $A_1=[J;I]$ and $s_1=[r;0]$. Supply the exact reduced QR $Q=\begin{bmatrix}1/\sqrt6&1/\sqrt{66}\\2/\sqrt6&2/\sqrt{66}\\1/\sqrt6&-5/\sqrt{66}\\0&6/\sqrt{66}\end{bmatrix}$ and $R=\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt6&5/\sqrt6\\0&\sqrt{66}/6\end{bmatrix}$, which satisfies $Q^TQ=I$ and $A_1=QR$. The damped system is $\begin{bmatrix}6&5\\5&6\end{bmatrix}p=(5,5)^T$, whose unique solution is $p=(5/11,5/11)^T$. Let $n,m\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let
$r=(r_1,\ldots,r_m)^T:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be of class $C^2$ (each component
has continuous partial derivatives through order two, as in
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]). Define
$$\phi(x):=\tfrac12\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)^2=\tfrac12\|r(x)\|_2^2,$$
and let $J(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ be the Jacobian with $i$th row
$\nabla r_i(x)^T$. Then $\phi$ is of class $C^2$ and
$$\nabla\phi(x)=J(x)^T r(x),\qquad \nabla^2\phi(x)=J(x)^TJ(x)+\sum_{i=1}^m r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x).$$

The second term in the Hessian is the residual-curvature term. It vanishes
when $r(x)=0$, but need not vanish at a nonzero-residual stationary point.

Input a stored residual $r\in\mathbb R^m$, a stored Jacobian $J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$ with $m,n\ge1$ (using the convention of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]), a factorization mode QR or SVD, an arithmetic mode (exact or computed), and a declared singular-value threshold $\tau\ge0$. If $m<n$, immediately return unsupported-shape without requesting a factorization report; all remaining branches assume $m\ge n$. A computed QR report may also carry a verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ asserting $\|Jv\|_2\ge s\|v\|_2$ for every $v\in\mathbb R^n$. The target exact step, when it is returned, is the unique minimizer of $\frac12\|r+Jp\|_2^2$ and hence solves $J^TJp=-J^Tr$; this target is asserted only on a full-column-rank branch. Do not form $J^TJ$ in either solve path.

The threshold $\tau$ is used only by the SVD route. For QR mode the exact and computed routes are disjoint. Exact mode requires a supplied exact reduced factorization $J=QR$ with $Q^TQ=I_n$; only this exact factorization may reach the exact-step branch. Computed mode either consumes the report produced from this input pair $(J,-r)$ or forms it by setting $C=[J\mid-r]$ and, for $k=1,\ldots,n$, applying [[alg-scaled-householder-reflector-formation-and-application]] to rows $k,\ldots,m$ of column $k$ and all trailing columns of $C$, including its last right-hand-side column. Embed each returned active block in those rows, leaving earlier rows and columns unchanged, and propagate the first factorization failure. After a successful computed loop, the report consists of the computed upper-triangular block $\widehat R$, the first $n$ entries $\widehat y$ of the transformed last column, and the ordered stored reflector records (including identity markers). The exact orthogonal representatives of those records define the $Q$ used by the conditional backward-stability result; the rounded outputs themselves are not an exact factorization of $J$ and cannot be supplied to the exact branch. In exact mode, a zero diagonal in $R$ returns rank-deficient; otherwise solve $Rp=Q^T(-r)$ by backward substitution and return exact-step($p$). In computed mode, a zero diagonal returns rank-deficient-candidate. Otherwise initialize storage for $\widehat p_0,\ldots,\widehat p_{n-1}$ with all components unassigned, then for $i=n-1,n-2,\ldots,0$ compute $s_i$ by setting $s_i=0$ and, for $j=i+1,i+2,\ldots,n-1$ in increasing order, updating $s_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(s_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat R_{ij}\widehat p_j))$; then compute $t_i=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat y_i-s_i)$ and $\widehat p_i=\operatorname{fl}(t_i/\widehat R_{ii})$. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. A nonzero computed diagonal without an independently verified full-rank certificate $s>0$ for the input matrix $J$ returns rank-unverified with the computed candidate but no full-rank claim. With that certificate, return computed-candidate($\widehat p$). A nonzero computed diagonal alone is not a full-rank certificate. The computed-QR backward-stability conclusion of [[thm-computed-full-rank-least-squares-backward-stability]] is attached only when all of that theorem's successful-execution, arithmetic, and nonsingularity hypotheses are supplied; otherwise no backward-stability conclusion is returned.

For SVD mode, the input includes an exact factorization $J=U\Sigma V^T$, or a computed report with finite stored factors $\widehat U_1\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $\widehat\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n)\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ whose entries are nonnegative, and $\widehat V\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, together with certified intervals $[\ell_i,u_i]$ satisfying $0\le\ell_i\le\sigma_i(J)\le u_i$ for each singular value $i=1,\ldots,n$. In the exact case, if any $\sigma_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold and no Gauss-Newton step. If every $\sigma_i>\tau$, return
$$p=-V\,\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\sigma_n^{-1})\,U_1^Tr,$$
where $U_1$ consists of the corresponding $n$ left singular vectors. For a computed report, if any $u_i\le\tau$, return rank-below-threshold; otherwise, if any interval satisfies $\ell_i\le\tau<u_i$, return rank-unverified; if every lower endpoint exceeds $\tau$ but some stored $\widehat\sigma_i=0$, return factorization-failure. In the remaining branch, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order initialize $z_i=0$ and, for $j=1,\ldots,m$ in increasing order, set $z_i\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(z_i+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat U_{ji}r_j))$. After these dots, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ set $w_i=\operatorname{fl}(z_i/\widehat\sigma_i)$. For each $j=1,\ldots,n$ initialize $t_j=0$ and, for $i=1,\ldots,n$ in increasing order, set $t_j\leftarrow\operatorname{fl}(t_j+\operatorname{fl}(\widehat V_{ji}w_i))$; set $\widehat p_j=-t_j$ by exact sign change. Any first arithmetic or range failure returns linear-solve-failure with its stage and indices. Otherwise return the finite candidate
$$\widehat p=-\widehat V\,\operatorname{diag}(\widehat\sigma_1^{-1},\ldots,\widehat\sigma_n^{-1})\,\widehat U_1^Tr$$
with status computed-candidate and make no accuracy claim beyond the supplied report. The displayed formula names the result of the preceding schedule; it is not a second computation. The certified intervals determine only the threshold branch; no computed-SVD accuracy bound is asserted. A computed SVD routine is not defined here; the SVD branch consumes its report.

If the selected factorization reports failure, return factorization-failure; every status other than exact-step is explicitly not a certified exact full-rank Gauss-Newton step.

Let $r:U\to\mathbb R^m$ be $C^2$ on an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let
$\phi=\|r\|_2^2/2$, $J=Dr$, $A=J^TJ$, and
$S(x)=\sum_i r_i(x)\nabla^2r_i(x)$. Let $x_*\in U$ satisfy
$J(x_*)^Tr(x_*)=0$, and let the closed ball
$B=\{x:\|x-x_*\|_2\le R\}$ lie in $U$, with $R>0$. Suppose on $B$:

- $J(x)$ has full column rank and smallest singular value at least $\sigma>0$;
- $\|J(x)\|_2\le M$;
- $J$ is $L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean induced matrix norm;
- $\|S(x)\|_2\le\kappa$.

Define $q=(\kappa+MLR)/\sigma^2$ and assume $q<1$. For the exact full-rank
Gauss-Newton step $p(x)=-A(x)^{-1}J(x)^Tr(x)$, supply an exact reduced QR
factorization of $J(x)$ to the exact branch of
[[alg-gauss-newton-qr-svd-step-with-rank-safeguard]] at each $x\in B$; the
full-column-rank hypothesis guarantees such a factorization. Every $x\in B$ satisfies
$$\|x+p(x)-x_*\|_2\le q\|x-x_*\|_2.$$
Consequently the exact iterates from any $x_0\in B$ stay in $B$ and converge
to $x_*$ at a linear rate no larger than $q$. The curvature hypothesis
controls the residual term $S$; no quadratic rate is claimed when it is
nonzero.

derivations.claim: Here $J(x)=(1,x)^T$, so $J(x)^TJ(x)=1+x^2>0$ for every $x$. Also $J(x)^Tr(x)=x+\frac12x+\frac12x^3=\frac32x+\frac12x^3$, which vanishes at $x_*=0$ while $r(0)=(0,1/2)^T$ has norm $1/2$.

For each $x$, the exact reduced QR supplied to the algorithm is $Q(x)=\frac1{\sqrt{1+x^2}}\begin{bmatrix}1\\x\end{bmatrix}$ and $R(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2}$, so $Q(x)^TQ(x)=1$ and $J(x)=Q(x)R(x)$. The scalar normal equation is $(1+x^2)p=-\frac32x-\frac12x^3$, so $p=-x(3+x^2)/(2(1+x^2))$; the supplied QR branch returns this unique least-squares step. Adding $x$ gives $x_+=x(x^2-1)/(2(1+x^2))$. For $0<|x|<1$, $|x_+|/|x|=(1-x^2)/(2(1+x^2))<1/2$, so every such iterate stays in the interval and converges to zero.

On $B=[-1/10,1/10]$, both $\|J(x)\|_2$ and $\|J(x)^T\|_2$ are at most $11/10$, both are $1$-Lipschitz, and $\|J(x)v\|_2\ge|v|$; also $S(x)=1/2+x^2/2\le101/200$. Thus the local contraction theorem [F3] applies with $R=1/10$, $M=11/10$, $L=1$, $\sigma=1$, $\kappa=101/200$, and $q=123/200<1$.

As $x\to0$ through nonzero values, $|x_+|/|x|\to1/2$, whereas $|x_+|/|x|^2=(1-x^2)/(2|x|(1+x^2))\to+\infty$. No finite quadratic error constant can therefore hold near the stationary point. This exact example shows that the linear rate in [F3] cannot generally be strengthened when the residual is nonzero.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].

routine_steps.claim: Differentiability at $x$ gives the affine first-order models $h(x)+Dh(x)p$ and $g(x)+Dg(x)p$; the positive-definite quadratic model is finite for every $p\in\mathbb R^n$. Thus the displayed feasible set is a well-defined polyhedron, possibly empty.

For an active affine inequality, the multiplier convention in the Lagrangian contributes $Dg_i(x)^T\lambda_i$ to stationarity, while complementarity is $\lambda_i(g_i(x)+Dg_i(x)p)=0$. Hence the stated KKT tuple uses the same sign convention as [F1].

Statement inherits zero equality/inequality dimensions from the program definition; proof step 1.1 remains valid for empty maps.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$
be $C^2$. Let $p,m\in\mathbb N$ with zero allowed; when the target
dimension is positive, let $h:U\to\mathbb R^p$ and
$g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):U\to\mathbb R^m$ be componentwise $C^2$, and when it
is zero use the unique empty map. The $C^2$ convention for positive
dimensions is [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]].
The smooth inequality program is to minimize $f(x)$ subject to
$h(x)=0$ and $g_i(x)\le0$ for every $i$. Its feasible set is
$C=\{x\in U:h(x)=0,\ g_i(x)\le0\ (1\le i\le m)\}$. A feasible point $x_*$ is
a local minimizer if some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_*$ satisfies
$f(x_*)\le f(y)$ for every $y\in C\cap V$.

At a feasible $x$, the active set is
$I(x)=\{i:g_i(x)=0\}$. The Bouligand tangent cone and linearized cone are,
respectively,
$$
T_C(x)=\{d:\exists\,t_k>0,\ t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ x+t_kd_k\in C\},
$$
and
$$
\mathcal L_C(x)=\{d:Dh(x)d=0,\ Dg_i(x)d\le0\text{ for every }i\in I(x)\}.
$$
Gradients are column vectors and $Dg_i(x)d=\nabla g_i(x)^Td$.

The linear independence constraint qualification (LICQ) holds at $x$ when the rows of $Dh(x)$ together with
$\{\nabla g_i(x)^T:i\in I(x)\}$ are linearly independent. MFCQ holds at $x$
when $Dh(x)$ has full row rank (its rows are linearly independent) and there is $w\in\ker Dh(x)$ with
$Dg_i(x)w<0$ for every active $i$; the latter condition is vacuous if
$I(x)=\varnothing$. Here full row rank for a matrix with zero rows is
understood vacuously.

The Mangasarian–Fromovitz constraint qualification (MFCQ) is the condition
just stated. The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) system is the stationarity,
feasibility, dual-feasibility, and complementarity system below.

For $\nu\in\mathbb R^p$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R^m$, the Lagrangian and KKT
system are
$$
L(x,\nu,\lambda)=f(x)+\nu^Th(x)+\lambda^Tg(x),
$$
$$
h(x)=0,\quad g(x)\le0,\quad \lambda\ge0,\quad \lambda_i g_i(x)=0\ (1\le i\le m),\quad \nabla_xL(x,\nu,\lambda)=0.
$$
The critical cone for a KKT tuple is
$\mathcal K(x,\nu,\lambda)=\mathcal L_C(x)\cap
\{d:\nabla f(x)^Td=0\}$. These definitions use the differentiability and
gradient conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], and [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]].
