citations.quote:
Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\widehat K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a nonempty bounded open
reference cell, let $q\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. A **reference finite element** is a
triple $(\widehat K,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ where $\widehat P$ is an
$N$-dimensional subspace of $[C(\overline{\widehat K};\mathbb K)]^q$ for
$N\in\mathbb N_0$ and
$\widehat\Sigma=(\widehat\sigma_1,\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N)$ is a list of
linear functionals on $\widehat P$ for which
$$J_{\widehat\Sigma}:\widehat P\to\mathbb K^N,\qquad J_{\widehat\Sigma}(p):=(\widehat\sigma_1(p),\ldots,\widehat\sigma_N(p)),$$
is bijective. The functionals are the **degrees of freedom** and the triple
is **unisolvent**. Its **shape functions** are the unique dual basis
$\widehat\phi_1,\ldots,\widehat\phi_N\in\widehat P$ satisfying
$\widehat\sigma_i(\widehat\phi_j)=\delta_{ij}$.

If $X$ is a normed vector space of functions on $\widehat K$ containing
$\widehat P$ and each $\widehat\sigma_i$ has a well-defined bounded linear
extension to $X$, the associated **reference interpolation operator** is
$$\widehat I:X\to\widehat P,\qquad \widehat I v:=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat\sigma_i(v)\widehat\phi_i.$$
The definition of a reference finite element does not assert that any
particular list of functionals is unisolvent or bounded on a given Sobolev
space; those are separate proof obligations. For $N=0$, $\widehat P=\{0\}$,
$\mathbb K^0=\{0\}$, the empty list gives the unique bijection between these
zero spaces, and the shape-function list is empty. The corresponding
interpolation formula is the empty sum, hence the zero map into $\{0\}$.

Let $\mathcal T$ be a matching affine simplicial mesh of $\Omega$ as defined
in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. Fix $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and an integer $q\ge1$. On each
cell let $\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q)$ denote the
restrictions to $K$ of $\mathbb K^q$-valued polynomials of total degree at
most $k$. The **broken polynomial space** is the finite product
$$V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:=\prod_{K\in\mathcal T}\mathbb P_k(K;\mathbb K^q),$$
viewed as functions defined almost everywhere cell by cell. For an interior
facet $F=K\cap K'$, the **jump** is the difference of the two polynomial
traces, with either fixed ordering of $K,K'$; its vanishing is independent of
that ordering. The **conforming polynomial space** is
$$V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}:=\{v\in V_h^{\mathrm{br}}:v|_{F,K}=v|_{F,K'}\text{ on every interior facet }F\}.$$
The **zero-boundary subspace** consists of those $v\in V_h^{\mathrm{conf}}$
whose polynomial trace is zero on every boundary facet. These are algebraic
definitions. The Sobolev inclusions and the zero-boundary closure conclusion
are proved separately in the corresponding local theorems on matching
piecewise polynomials and zero-boundary values. If $\mathcal T=\varnothing$,
then $\Omega=\varnothing$ by the mesh definition; the empty product is the
zero vector space consisting of the unique empty function, and the trace
conditions are vacuous.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $k\ge0$, $1\le p<\infty$, and let
$(\widehat S_d,\widehat P,\widehat\Sigma)$ be a reference finite element
whose polynomial space contains $\mathbb P_k$. Assume its degrees of
freedom are bounded on $W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)$ for an integer
$\ell\ge1$, let $r,m\in\mathbb N_0$, and let $\widehat I$ be its
interpolant. Thus
$\widehat Iq=q$ for $q\in\mathbb P_k$. On a shape-regular affine mesh
as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], for each cell $K$ with its
orientation-preserving reference map $F_K$ define
$$I_Kv=(\widehat I(v\circ F_K))\circ F_K^{-1}.$$
For every such cell, if $\ell\le r\le k+1$ and $0\le m\le r$, then for
$v\in W^{r,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)}\le C h_K^{r-m}|v|_{W^{r,p}(K)}.$$
If $\ell>k+1$ and $0\le m\le k+1$, then for $v\in W^{\ell,p}(K)$,
$$|v-I_Kv|_{W^{m,p}(K)} \le C\sum_{n=k+1}^{\ell}h_K^{n-m}|v|_{W^{n,p}(K)}.$$
The constants are uniform over the mesh family and depend on the stated
reference element, exponents and shape-regularity bound. For Lagrange
elements in the existing mesh dimension range $d\ge2$, assume additionally
the Axiom of Choice for the automatic nodal-boundedness application. Then
[[thm-lagrange-point-evaluation-threshold-on-reference-simplex]] supplies
the boundedness hypothesis when $\ell>d/p$; unisolvence of a particular
node set remains a separate hypothesis.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.
Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.

Let $m \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Write $c^*(E)$ and $c_*(E)$ for the Jordan outer and
inner content of a bounded $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$
([[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_m^*(E) \le c^*(E)$ for **every** bounded $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$,
   Jordan measurable or not;
2. if $E$ is bounded and Jordan measurable, with Jordan content
   $\operatorname{cont}(E) = c_*(E) = c^*(E)$, then $E$ is Lebesgue measurable
   and
   $$\lambda_m(E) \;=\; \operatorname{cont}(E).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $E$ be measurable with $\mu(E)=0$.
Then
$$\int_E f\,d\mu=0.$$

derivations.claim: By [A2], the reference nodal degrees of freedom are bounded on $W^{2,2}$; together with unisolvence [F2], this gives the local Lagrange interpolants required by [F4]. Unisolvence also identifies each restriction $I_hu|_K$ with the local interpolant $I_Ku$. Apply [F4] with $p=2$, $\ell=r=2$, $m=1$, and $\ell>d/p$ on every cell $K$.

On a shared facet, both neighboring P1 traces are affine and have the same values at every facet vertex, so the traces agree. Every boundary facet has zero values at all its vertices, so its affine trace is zero. Thus the assembled function has the conformity and boundary traces in [F3]; its membership in $V$ is the explicit hypothesis [A1].

Let $\Sigma$ be the union of the mesh facets. Each facet lies in an affine hyperplane; choosing a coordinate with nonzero normal coefficient writes that hyperplane as the graph of an affine function over the other coordinates. A closed nondegenerate rectangle containing the facet's projection gives a bounded graph containing the facet, so [F6] makes each facet, and hence $\Sigma$, a Lebesgue null set. By [F7], for every nonnegative measurable $q$ the integral over $\Omega$ is the sum of its integrals over the disjoint cell interiors $K^\circ$, since $\Omega\setminus\Sigma=\bigsqcup_K K^\circ$ and $\int_\Sigma q=0$. Applying this to the squared first derivatives of $u-I_hu$ and the squared second derivatives of $u$ gives the global seminorm decompositions used next.

Square the cell estimate in [F4] and sum over the cells using step 1.3. Their interiors are disjoint and $h_K\le h$, so $|u-I_hu|_{H^1(\Omega)}^2\le C_I^2h^2|u|_{H^2(\Omega)}^2$, hence $|u-I_hu|_{H^1(\Omega)}\le C_Ih|u|_{H^2(\Omega)}$.

Apply [F5] with $v_h=I_hu$ and use $\|u-I_hu\|_V\le C_V|u-I_hu|_{H^1}$ from the stated norm bound and step 2.1. This gives the displayed error estimate without absorbing the form, geometry, quadrature, or load defects.

Input real endpoints $a,b$, an integer $n$, and a function $f$. If $a\ge b$
or $n<1$, return invalid-grid without evaluating $f$. For the remaining inputs,
require a real-valued function $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ evaluable at every point
of $[a,b]$. Put $h=(b-a)/n$ and $m_j=a+(j+\tfrac12)h$ for $0\le j<n$. The
composite midpoint rule returns

$$Q_M(f;a,b,n):=h\sum_{j<n} f(m_j).$$

The sum is the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. The admissibility conditions
$a<b$ and $n\ge1$ ensure $h>0$ and all $m_j\in(a+jh,a+(j+1)h)$. The rule is an
exact-real formula; floating-point evaluation and summation error are separate
from its quadrature error.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded coercive form with boundedness constant $M$ and coercivity constant $\alpha>0$, and $F:V\to\mathbb K$ a bounded functional linear in the real case and conjugate-linear in the complex test argument. Let $V_h\subseteq V$ be finite-dimensional, and let $a_h:V_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ and $F_h:V_h\to\mathbb K$ be bounded, with $F_h$ having the same test-linearity as $F$, and $a_h$ coercive with constant $\alpha_h>0$ in the inherited norm. There are unique exact and discrete solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\left((1+M/\alpha_h)\|u-v_h\|_V+\frac{\delta_{a,h}(v_h)+\delta_{F,h}}{\alpha_h}\right),$$

where the defects are those of [[def-variational-crime-error-framework]]. For a family of meshes this is a uniform estimate whenever $\inf_h\alpha_h>0$ and the displayed approximation and defect terms are uniformly controlled. The term $\delta_{F,h}$ retains source approximation and data oscillation.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mu)$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $f=g$ almost everywhere;
2. for every measurable $A$,
   $$\int_A f\,d\mu=\int_A g\,d\mu.$$

For integrable real or complex $h$, the notation in condition 2 means
$\int_A h\,d\mu:=\int h\chi_A\,d\mu$; the product is integrable because
$|h\chi_A|\le|h|$.

$\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$ be the completed product of two sigma-finite
measure spaces.

1. If $f : X 	imes Y 	o [0,\infty]$ is $\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}$-measurable, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that $f_x$ is $\overline{\mathcal B}$-measurable for $x
otin A$ and $f^y$ is $\overline{\mathcal A}$-measurable for $y
otin B$. Define $I_f(x)=\int_Y f_x\,d\overline
u$ for $x
otin A$ and $I_f(x)=0$ on $A$; define $J_f(y)=\int_X f^y\,d\overline\mu$ for $y
otin B$ and $J_f(y)=0$ on $B$. Then $I_f,J_f$ are measurable and
$$\int f\,d\overline{\mu 	imes 
u}=\int_X I_f\,d\mu=\int_Y J_f\,d
u.$$
2. If $f \in L^1(\overline{\mu 	imes 
u})$, there are measurable null sets $A\subseteq X$ and $B\subseteq Y$ such that the sections are measurable and integrable outside them. Define $I_f,J_f$ by the same section integrals outside $A,B$ and by zero on $A,B$. They are measurable and integrable, and the same equality holds.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, $a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ bounded and coercive, and $F$ a bounded functional with the test-linearity required by $a$. Let $V_h$ be a finite-dimensional Hilbert space with norm $\|\cdot\|_h$, not necessarily a subspace of $V$. Suppose the algebraic sum $X_h=V+V_h$ is equipped with a norm extending these norms, and $\widetilde a_h:X_h\times V_h\to\mathbb K$ is a bounded extension of a discrete form $a_h$ with bound $M_h$. Assume $a_h$ is coercive on $V_h$ with constant $\alpha_h>0$, and let $F_h$ be bounded on $V_h$ with the matching test-linearity. The exact and discrete equations have unique solutions $u$ and $u_h$, and

$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+M_h/\alpha_h)\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\alpha_h,$$

where $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)=\sup_{w_h\ne0}|F_h(w_h)-\widetilde a_h(u,w_h)|/\|w_h\|_h$. The estimate requires the bounded extension and does not assert that every nonconforming, penalty, or discontinuous Galerkin form has one.

For a family of these problems, suppose $M_h\le\overline M<\infty$ and $\alpha_h\ge\underline\alpha>0$ uniformly. Writing $E_h=\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_h$, the uniform bound is
$$\|u-u_h\|_h\le(1+\overline M/\underline\alpha)E_h+\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)/\underline\alpha.$$
Thus uniform control of $E_h$ and $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(u)$ gives a uniform error budget; if both tend to zero, the errors tend to zero, and if both are $O(h^p)$ for a fixed $p>0$, the error is $O(h^p)$. No rate is inferred without those approximation, residual, and stability bounds.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $V$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb K$ be linear in its first argument, conjugate-linear
in its second, bounded by $M$, and coercive with constant $\alpha>0$:
$$|a(v,w)|\le M\|v\|_V\|w\|_V,\qquad \operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|_V^2.$$
Let $F:V\to\mathbb K$ be bounded and conjugate-linear, and let $V_h\subseteq V$
be finite-dimensional. Then there are unique $u\in V$ and $u_h\in V_h$ with
$$a(u,v)=F(v)\quad(v\in V).$$
$$a(u_h,v_h)=F(v_h)\quad(v_h\in V_h).$$
The solutions satisfy
$$\|u-u_h\|_V\le\frac M\alpha\inf_{v_h\in V_h}\|u-v_h\|_V.$$
The real bilinear case uses linear functionals and reads $\operatorname{Re}$ as
the identity.

Every Cauchy sequence of real numbers ([[def-real-limit]]) converges to a real
number. Together with [[thm-reals-ordered-field]], this completes the
construction: $\mathbb{R}$ is a complete totally ordered field.
The proof uses no form of the axiom of choice.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $E \subseteq [a,b]$ be finite
([[def-countable]], [[def-equinumerous]]), and let $g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$
satisfy

$$g(x) \;=\; f(x) \qquad \text{for every } x \in [a,b] \setminus E .$$

Then $g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and

$$\int_a^b g \;=\; \int_a^b f .$$

In particular the values of an integrand at the endpoints of the interval, and at
any finite set of points, are irrelevant to both questions.

Let $a < c < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Then:

1. $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]) **if and only if** its
   restrictions to $[a,c]$ and to $[c,b]$ are integrable;
2. and in that case
   $$\int_a^b f \;=\; \int_a^c f \;+\; \int_c^b f .$$
3. **Oriented form.** Let $\alpha < \beta$ be reals, let $f : [\alpha,\beta] \to
   \mathbb{R}$ be integrable, and let $u, v, w \in [\alpha,\beta]$ be arbitrary.
   Then, with the convention of [[def-oriented-integral]],
   $$\int_u^v f \;+\; \int_v^w f \;=\; \int_u^w f .$$

Claim 3 is where [[def-oriented-integral]] earns its place: it holds for every
arrangement of the three points, including the degenerate ones, and it is the
form used everywhere below.

derivations.claim: The functional $L(g):=\int_0^1g$ is linear by [F12] and bounded by [F2], since $\|1\|_2=1$ by [F10]. Thus $V=\ker L$ is a closed linear subspace of $L^2$. If $(g_n)$ is Cauchy in $V$, [F1] gives an $L^2$ limit $g$; continuity of $L$ gives $L(g)=0$, so $g\in V$. Hence $V$ is a Hilbert space.

For $\omega_h=c_L\omega_L+c_R\omega_R$, [F10, F11, F13] give $\|\omega_h\|_h^2=\int_0^1|\omega_h|^2=2(c_L^2+c_R^2)$ and $\|U_{\omega_h}\|_2^2=(c_L^2+c_R^2)/6=\|\omega_h\|_h^2/12$, by integrating the bounded piecewise-polynomial representatives. They also give $\|6x\|_2^2=\int_0^1 36x^2\,dx=12$. A Cauchy sequence in $V_h$ therefore has Cauchy coefficient sequences; [F8] gives their limits and the same norm formula gives convergence in $V_h$. Thus $V_h$ is a two-dimensional Hilbert space. Moreover, $\omega_L+\omega_R=2$ is constant, and every $g\in L^2(0,1)$ decomposes as $g=(g-\int_0^1g)+\frac12(\int_0^1g)(\omega_L+\omega_R)$; the first summand lies in $V$ and the second in $V_h$. Thus $X_h=V+V_h=L^2(0,1)$, with the common $L^2$ norm restricting to both spaces. The discrete form has coercivity constant $1$, and the extension $\widetilde a_h(g,\omega_h)=\int g\omega_h$ is bounded by [F2]. Holder [F2] and the displayed finite $L^2$ norms show $F_h(\omega_h)=\int_0^1 6xU_{\omega_h}(x)\,dx$ is bounded. Hence the stability and bounded-extension hypotheses of [F6] hold.

The polynomial $g_u=1-3x^2$ has Lebesgue integral zero by [F9, F11], so $g_u\in V$, and its primitive is $U_{g_u}=x-x^3$. By [F2], $|U_h(x)|\le\|h\|_2$, hence $\|U_h\|_2\le\|h\|_2$ using [F10]. The function $(x,t)\mapsto6x h(t)\mathbf1_{0\le t\le x\le1}$ is absolutely integrable, with absolute integral at most $6\|h\|_1\le6\|h\|_2$. Fubini [F4] gives $F(h)=\int_0^1h(t)3(1-t^2)\,dt$. Linearity [F12] and $\int h=0$ yield $F(h)=\int_0^1h(t)(1-3t^2)\,dt=a(g_u,h)$. The form is the $L^2$ inner product, hence bounded and coercive, so [F5] confirms the unique exact solution is $g_u$.

The associated broken function for $\omega_L$ is $\phi_L$. By [F9, F11, F13], $F_h(\omega_L)=\int_0^{1/2}12x^2\,dx=1/2$, whereas $\widetilde a_h(g_u,\omega_L)=\int_0^{1/2}2(1-3x^2)\,dx=2[x-x^3]_0^{1/2}=3/4$. The residual is $-1/4$ and $\|\omega_L\|_h=\sqrt2$, so $\delta_h^{\mathrm{nc}}(g_u)\ge1/(4\sqrt2)>0$.

The slope field $\omega_L$ has integral $1$, so $\omega_L\notin V$ and $V_h\nsubseteq V$. Thus the conforming hypothesis in [F7] fails; independently, step 2.2 shows that the exact solution does not satisfy the discrete equation on $V_h$. This is the consistency term retained by [F6].

Let $a<b$ be real numbers, let $m\ge1$ be an integer, and let
$r\in\{2m-1,2m\}$. A **Gaussian quadrature moment datum of order $r$** is a
finite positive measure $\mu$ on the relative Borel sigma-algebra
$\mathcal B([a,b])$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-measure-space]],
[[def-measure]], [[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) such that
$\mu([a,b])>0$, and whose **relative support**
$$ S_\mu:=\{x\in[a,b]:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open }U\subseteq[a,b]\text{ with }x\in U\} $$
contains at least $m+1$ distinct points. For every integer $0\le k\le r$,
require $x\mapsto |x|^k$ to be integrable with respect to $\mu$
([[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]) and put
$M_k:=\int_{[a,b]}x^k\,d\mu(x)$. Powers use the natural-exponent
recursion of [[def-integer-power]], with $x^0=1$ for every real $x$, including
$x=0$; thus $M_0$ is the integral of the constant function $1$.

The branch $r=2m-1$ supplies all moments used to construct the monic
degree-$m$ orthogonal polynomial and prove rule exactness. The stronger branch
$r=2m$ also defines its squared norm and is used for the remainder formula.
Because $[a,b]$ is bounded and $\mu$ is finite, these absolute-moment
integrability conditions follow from finiteness; they are stated to make the
two moment interfaces explicit.

Let $(a,b,m,r,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], with $m\ge1$ and $r\ge2m-1$. For each
$j=0,\ldots,m$ there is a unique monic real polynomial $p_j$ of degree $j$
such that
$$ \int_{[a,b]}p_j(x)q(x)\,d\mu(x)=0 $$
for every real polynomial $q$ of degree less than $j$. For $j=0$, this means
$p_0=1$ and the orthogonality condition is vacuous. The $j=m$ polynomial uses
moments only through degree $2m-1$; its squared norm is asserted only when the
moment datum has order $2m$.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_m$ be its monic degree-$m$ orthogonal
polynomial and write its ordered roots as
$a<x_1<\cdots<x_m<b$, as established in
[[thm-gauss-orthogonal-polynomial-has-simple-interior-zeros]]. For
$i=1,\ldots,m$, define the Lagrange cardinal polynomial
$$ \ell_i(X):=\prod_{\substack{1\le j\le m\\j\ne i}}\frac{X-x_j}{x_i-x_j} $$
using the convention of [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]]. Define
the **Gaussian quadrature weights** and the **m-node Gaussian rule** by
$$ w_i:=\int_{[a,b]}\ell_i(x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad Q_m(f):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i f(x_i) $$
for any real-valued function $f$ defined at the nodes. This definition
asserts no accuracy; well-definedness of the nodes, cardinal polynomials,
weights, and finite sum is proved in
[[lem-gauss-quadrature-rule-data-well-defined]].

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,

derivations.claim: By [F8], each low-frequency cosine difference in $L_j$ expands into the corresponding cosine/sine modes in $\mathcal T_N$. For even $N=2K$, its Nyquist term expands into $\cos(Kx)\cos(Kx_j)+\sin(Kx)\sin(Kx_j)$; [F7] makes the second coefficient zero because $Kx_j=\pi j$. At a grid difference $x_i-x_j=2\pi(i-j)/N$, Euler's identity [F6] rewrites the cosine sum defining $L_j(x_i)$ as the normalized sum of all characters in a complete residue system modulo $N$: for odd $N=2K+1$ the residues are $-K,\ldots,K$, and for even $N=2K$ they are $-K+1,\ldots,K$. Character orthogonality [F3] gives $L_j(x_i)=1$ when $i=j$ and $0$ otherwise. Thus $I_NU$ takes the prescribed nodal values and lies in $\mathcal T_N$.

Let $q\in\mathcal T_N$. Euler's formula expands each low-frequency cosine/sine pair into the characters $e^{ikx_j}$ and $e^{-ikx_j}$. If $N=2K+1$, the resulting residues are $-K,\ldots,K$; if $N=2K$, they are $-K+1,\ldots,K-1$ together with the Nyquist residue $K$, because $\cos(Kx_j)=e^{iKx_j}$. In either case this is one coefficient for each residue modulo $N$, and the change from the real basis coefficients to these character coefficients is invertible (for each low mode it is the usual two-by-two Euler change, and the Nyquist coefficient is unchanged). Thus if $q$ vanishes at the nodes, its finite Fourier transform is zero and inversion [F4] makes every character coefficient, hence every real basis coefficient, zero. This proves uniqueness.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and put $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The ordering is decreasing: $x_0=1$ and $x_N=-1$. These are the Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes; [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] gives $T_N(x_j)=(-1)^j$. They are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]].

For interpolation using [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]], use the increasing reindexing $z_k=x_{N-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,N$. For descending-grid data $U_j$, the corresponding increasing data are $Y_k=U_{N-k}$.

For nodal data $U_0,\ldots,U_N$, define $I_N^LU$ to be the cardinal interpolant of $(Y_k)_{k=0}^N$ at $(z_k)_{k=0}^N$. For a function $f$ defined on the interval, write $I_N^Lf$ for the interpolant of its nodal values. The increasing-node interpolation theorem [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]] makes this polynomial unique.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For every $n\in\mathbb N$ and real $\theta$,
$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $n\in\mathbb N$, $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Then $I_n y$ from [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]] is the unique real polynomial of degree at most $n$ satisfying $p(x_i)=y_i$ for every $i=0,\ldots,n$.

For $n\ge1$, $T_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, while $U_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-integer-power]].

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

By [F4], $T_r$ has degree $r\le N$. Interpolation uniqueness [F3] therefore gives $I_N^LT_n=T_r$.

Input an integer $N\ge2$, real functions $a,b,f$ given at the Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$, and endpoint data $g_-,g_+\in\mathbb R$. The continuous BVP being discretized is
$$
-u''(x)+a(x)u'(x)+b(x)u(x)=f(x),\quad -1<x<1,\qquad u(-1)=g_-,\quad u(1)=g_+.
$$
The finite algorithm uses only the values at the nodes and does not assume a continuous BVP solvability theorem. Construct the Chebyshev differentiation matrix $D_N$ by [[alg-chebyshev-gauss-lobatto-differentiation-matrix]] and set $D_N^{(2)}=D_ND_N$. For each interior row $i=1,\ldots,N-1$ and each column $j=0,\ldots,N$, put
$$
C_{ij}=-(D_N^{(2)})_{ij}+a(x_i)(D_N)_{ij}+b(x_i)\delta_{ij}.
$$
Let $A=(C_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le N-1}$ and $r_i=f(x_i)-C_{i0}g_+-C_{iN}g_-$. If $A$ is singular, return status singular-interior-matrix and the matrix $A$. If $A$ is invertible, solve $AU_I=r$, set $U_0=g_+$ and $U_N=g_-$, and return success with $U=(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$. This exact-arithmetic finite solve asserts no unconditional nonsingularity, stability, convergence, or PDE error bound.

Steps 1.1–2.2 prove the success claim and the stated singular-matrix limit.

If $m\ne n$, [F3], cosine parity [F5], and $\sin(k\pi)=0$ from [F5] make the integral of each nonzero-frequency cosine vanish by [F4]. If $m=n\ge1$, [F3] gives $\frac12(1+\cos(2m\theta))$, whose integral is $\pi/2$. If $m=n=0$, the integrand is $1$ and its integral is $\pi$. Linearity [F10] passes from the product-to-sum identity to these integrals.

The recurrence [F6] shows inductively that $T_n$ has degree $n$ and nonzero leading coefficient: this holds for $T_0,T_1$, and the leading term of $2XT_n$ cannot cancel with the lower-degree $T_{n-1}$. Eliminating the leading term of any polynomial successively proves that $T_0,T_1,\ldots$ span all polynomials; their distinct degrees also give linear independence. Step 1.1 gives positive squared norms and pairwise orthogonality.

The bound $M=\|h\|_\infty<\infty$ follows from [F8]. The pointwise bounds $-M\varepsilon\le h(\cos\theta)(h-q)(\cos\theta)\le M\varepsilon$ and [F9] give $0\le\langle h,h\rangle_C=\langle h,h-q\rangle_C\le\pi M\varepsilon$, where the equality uses bilinearity [F10]. For any continuous $h$, if $\langle h,h\rangle_C=0$ but $h(\cos\theta_0)\ne0$ at some $\theta_0\in[0,\pi]$, continuity gives a one-sided interval at an endpoint, or a two-sided interval in the interior, on which $h(\cos\theta)^2$ is bounded below by a positive number. For either Chebyshev node family, every $n\geq0$, and every
$f\in C[-1,1]$,
$$\|f-I_n^\sigma f\|_\infty \leq (1+\Lambda_n^\sigma)E_n(f).$$
Here $E_n$ is the best degree-$n$ uniform error and $\Lambda_n^\sigma$
is the operator norm defined in
[[def-best-uniform-polynomial-approximation-error-and-chebyshev-interpolants]].

For continuous real functions $f,g$ on $[-1,1]$, define
$$
\langle f,g\rangle_C:=\int_0^\pi f(\cos\theta)g(\cos\theta)\,d\theta,\qquad \|f\|_C^2:=\langle f,f\rangle_C.
$$
This is the arcsine-weighted pairing on the compact Chebyshev interval: in the variable $x=\cos\theta$ its weight is $\omega_C(x)=(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ for $-1<x<1$. The angular integral is the endpoint convention, so no endpoint value of the singular density is required.

They are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]].

For interpolation using [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]], use the increasing reindexing $z_k=x_{N-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,N$. For descending-grid data $U_j$, the corresponding increasing data are $Y_k=U_{N-k}$.

For nodal data $U_0,\ldots,U_N$, define $I_N^LU$ to be the cardinal interpolant of $(Y_k)_{k=0}^N$ at $(z_k)_{k=0}^N$. For a function $f$ defined on the interval, write $I_N^Lf$ for the interpolant of its nodal values. The increasing-node interpolation theorem [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]] makes this polynomial unique.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ be the set of formal real polynomials of
[[def-real-polynomial-degree-leading-coefficient-and-monic]]. Associate to every
$P\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$ an eventually zero coefficient sequence $(p_k)$:
use its displayed finite coefficient list and extend it by zeros when $P\ne0$,
and put $p_k=0$ for every $k$ when $P=0$. Do the same for $Q$, with coefficients
$(q_k)$. Define $P+Q$ coefficientwise and define $PQ$ by the convolution
coefficients
$$ (P+Q)_k=p_k+q_k,\qquad (PQ)_k=\sum_{j=0}^{k}p_jq_{k-j}. $$
using the real finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]]. In either construction, discard
trailing zero coefficients; if every coefficient is zero, the result is the zero
polynomial. Scalar multiplication and subtraction are the corresponding
coefficientwise operations. Thus these formulas define operations on the formal
coefficient-list objects, independently of evaluation.

Write $1=(1)$ and $X=(0,1)$, and define
$$ \Phi(P,Q):=(Q,2XQ-P)\qquad(P,Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}). $$
Apply [[thm-recursion]] to the set
$\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}\times\mathcal P_{\mathbb R}$, first with initial value
$(1,X)$ and then with initial value $(1,2X)$, always using the function $\Phi$.
This gives unique pair sequences $H^T,H^U$. Define $T_n$ and $U_n$ to be the
first coordinates of $H^T_n$ and $H^U_n$, respectively. Since the first
coordinate of $\Phi(P,Q)$ is $Q$, the second coordinate of $H^T_n$ is
$T_{n+1}$ and the second coordinate of $H^U_n$ is $U_{n+1}$. Consequently
$$ T_0=1,\quad T_1=X,\quad T_{n+2}=2XT_{n+1}-T_n, $$
$$ U_0=1,\quad U_1=2X,\quad U_{n+2}=2XU_{n+1}-U_n $$
for every $n\in\mathbb N$. These unique sequences are the **Chebyshev
polynomials of the first and second kinds**.

For $n\ge1$, $T_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^{n-1}$, while $U_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $2^n$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-induction-principle]], [[def-integer-power]].

$$T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos(n\theta),\qquad U_n(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((n+1)\theta).$$ In particular, for $n\ge1$ and $0\le j\le n$, $T_n(\cos(j\pi/n))=(-1)^j$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-chebyshev-polynomials-first-and-second-kind]], [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-induction-principle]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(-x)=-\sin x,\qquad\cos(-x)=\cos x,\qquad\sin^2x+\cos^2x=1.$$
Consequently $|\sin x|\le1$ and $|\cos x|\le1$.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ with $n\ge0$, let $x_0<\cdots<x_n$ be distinct real nodes, and let $y_0,\ldots,y_n\in\mathbb R$. Define the node polynomial and barycentric weights by
$$\omega_n(X)=\prod_{k=0}^{n}(X-x_k),\qquad w_j=\left(\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}(x_j-x_k)\right)^{-1}\quad(0\le j\le n).$$
An empty product is $1$, so $w_0=1$ when $n=0$.

In these formulas, $X$ is a real argument, and for real $a$ and nonzero real $b$, $a/b$ denotes $ab^{-1}$ in the field $\mathbb R$ ([[def-field]]).

For each $j$, the cardinal function is
$$\ell_j(X)=\prod_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\k\ne j}}\frac{X-x_k}{x_j-x_k}.$$
The interpolation function for the data $y=(y_0,\ldots,y_n)$ is
$$I_n y(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}y_j\ell_j(X).$$

The integrability hypotheses and [F1] make every term in the finite sum integrable, and [F4] distributes its integral. Orthogonality of the $p_j$ then gives, for each $i\le N$, $\int (u-\Pi_Nu)p_i\,d\mu =\int u p_i\,d\mu-\sum_{j=0}^{N}\frac{\int u p_j\,d\mu}{h_j}\int p_jp_i\,d\mu =0,$ because all terms with $j\ne i$ vanish and the $j=i$ term equals $\int u p_i\,d\mu$. Thus $\Pi_Nu\in V_N(\mu)$ has the required residual orthogonality.

If $v\in V_N(\mu)$ has the same residual property, then $w=v-\Pi_Nu$ lies in $V_N(\mu)$ and is orthogonal to every basis vector, hence to itself. Positive definiteness in [F2] gives $\int w^2\,d\mu=0$, so $w=0$ in $L^2(\mu)$ and $v=\Pi_Nu$. This proves uniqueness.

Let $(a,b,m,2m-1,\mu)$ be moment data as in
[[def-gauss-moment-data]], and let $Q_m$ and $w_i$ be the rule and weights of
[[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. For every real polynomial $f$ of degree at most
$2m-1$,
$$ \int_{[a,b]} f(x)\,d\mu(x)=Q_m(f)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_if(x_i). $$
Moreover, $w_i>0$ for every $i$ and $\sum_iw_i=\mu([a,b])$.

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive Borel measure on a compact interval $[a,b]$ with infinite relative support. For each integer $N\ge0$, the moment data $(a,b,m=N+1,r=2N+1,\mu)$ satisfy the hypotheses of [[def-gauss-moment-data]]. Let $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ be the monic orthogonal polynomials supplied by [[thm-monic-gauss-orthogonal-polynomials-exist-uniquely]], and write
$$
h_n=\int_{[a,b]}p_n(x)^2\,d\mu(x)>0.
$$
The finite-dimensional weighted Galerkin space is
$$
V_N(\mu)=\operatorname{span}\{p_0,\ldots,p_N\}\subset L^2(\mu).
$$
Here $L^2(\mu)$ means measurable functions with finite integral of the squared absolute value, modulo equality $\mu$-almost everywhere.

For a coefficient sequence $(c_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n<\infty$, define its weighted spectral Sobolev norm by
$$\left\|\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n\right\|_{H^s_\mu}^2 =\sum_{n\ge0}(1+n^2)^s|c_n|^2h_n,\qquad s\ge0.$$
The real powers are those of [[def-real-power]]; since every base $1+n^2$ is positive, [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] makes every weight positive.
The associated orthogonal Galerkin projection is $\Pi_N(\sum_{n\ge0}c_np_n)=\sum_{n=0}^Nc_np_n$. This coefficient-defined scale is specific to the weight $\mu$ and the selected orthogonal-polynomial family; no equivalence with a derivative-based Sobolev norm is asserted here.

Input a degree $N\ge0$, the monic orthogonal basis $p_0,\ldots,p_N$ and the $(N+1)$-node Gaussian rule for the same positive measure $\mu$ from [[def-gauss-quadrature-rule]]. With Gaussian nodes $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_{N+1}$ and weights $w_1,\ldots,w_{N+1}$, output the matrix
$$
M_{ij}^{G}:=\sum_{r=1}^{N+1}w_r p_i(\xi_r)p_j(\xi_r),\qquad 0\le i,j\le N.
$$
The inputs are admissible only when the moment data have order at least $2N+1$ and the rule nodes, weights, and basis all use the same measure. The algorithm performs the displayed finite exact-arithmetic sums; no floating-point conditioning claim is made.

For each integer $n\ge0$, define the Legendre polynomial
$$
P_n(x):=\frac{1}{2^n n!}\frac{d^n}{dx^n}(x^2-1)^n,
$$
with $n!$ as in [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]] and repeated derivatives as in [[def-higher-derivatives-and-smoothness]]. Define the unweighted pairing of real polynomials by
$$
\langle p,q\rangle_L:=\int_{-1}^1p(x)q(x)\,dx,\qquad \|p\|_L^2:=\langle p,p\rangle_L.
$$
The integral is the ordinary integral of a continuous function; polynomial products are continuous and hence integrable by [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]] and [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]. The normalization and all polynomial identities needed for the orthogonal Galerkin scale are proved in [[lem-legendre-weighted-derivative-orthogonality-and-norm]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

derivations.claim: Write $(x^2-1)^n=(x-1)^n(x+1)^n$. For every $j<n$, its $j$th derivative vanishes at both endpoints: by the product rule, every term differentiates each factor at most $j<n$ times and retains a positive power of the factor that vanishes at that endpoint. Thus $n$ integrations by parts in [F2] give, for every polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, $\int_{-1}^1P_nq=\frac{(-1)^n}{2^nn!}\int_{-1}^1(x^2-1)^nq^{(n)}=0,$ because $q^{(n)}=0$ by [F3]. Hence $P_n$ is orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial.

The leading term of $(x^2-1)^n$ is $x^{2n}$; differentiating it $n$ times gives $(2n)!/n!$ times $x^n$ by [F3]. All other terms have lower degree after differentiation. Therefore $P_n$ has degree $n$ and leading coefficient $\kappa_n=(2n)!/(2^n(n!)^2)>0$. The distinct degrees imply the family $P_0,\ldots,P_N$ is linearly independent and spans every polynomial of degree at most $N$, by successive elimination of leading terms.

Since $P_n-\kappa_nx^n$ has degree less than $n$, step 1.1 gives $\int_{-1}^1P_n^2=\kappa_n\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n.$ Apply [F2] $n$ times to the Rodrigues formula against $x^n$. The endpoint terms vanish as in step 1.1 and $(x^n)^{(n)}=n!$, so $\int_{-1}^1P_nx^n=\frac1{2^n}\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n\,dx.$

Put $J_n=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)^n dx$. Then $J_0=2$. For $n\ge1$, the endpoint values of $x(1-x^2)^n$ are zero, so integrating its derivative gives $0=J_n-2n(J_{n-1}-J_n),\qquad J_n=\frac{2n}{2n+1}J_{n-1}.$ Induction yields $J_n=2^{2n+1}(n!)^2/(2n+1)!$. Substituting this and $\kappa_n$ from step 2.1 into step 3.1 gives $\int P_n^2=2/(2n+1)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves the first orthogonality formula, including $n=0$.

When $n=0$, $P_0=1$ and $Q_0=-((1-x^2)P_0')'=0$, so $Q_0=0\cdot P_0$. Now take $n\ge1$ and define $Q_n=-((1-x^2)P_n')'$. Its leading term is $n(n+1)\kappa_nx^n$, so $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ has degree less than $n$. For any polynomial $q$ of degree less than $n$, two integrations by parts give $\int_{-1}^1Q_nq=\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'q'=-\int_{-1}^1P_n((1-x^2)q')'=0,$ where both boundary terms vanish because of the factor $1-x^2$, and the last polynomial paired with $P_n$ has degree less than $n$, so step 1.1 applies. Therefore $Q_n-n(n+1)P_n$ is a lower-degree polynomial orthogonal to every lower-degree polynomial. Expand it in the basis from step 2.1; the first formula and the positive norms in step 4.1 force every coefficient to be zero. Thus $Q_n=n(n+1)P_n$.

One integration by parts and step 5.1 give $\int_{-1}^1(1-x^2)P_n'P_m'=\int_{-1}^1Q_nP_m=n(n+1)\int_{-1}^1P_nP_m.$ The first formula, already proved in step 4.1 and step 1.1, yields the displayed weighted derivative identity for every $m,n\ge0$.

Let $N\ge1$ be an integer and put $x_j=\cos(j\pi/N)$ for $j=0,\ldots,N$. The ordering is decreasing: $x_0=1$ and $x_N=-1$. These are the Chebyshev–Gauss–Lobatto nodes; [[thm-chebyshev-multiple-angle-identities]] gives $T_N(x_j)=(-1)^j$. They are distinct because cosine is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]].

For interpolation using [[def-cardinal-polynomial-interpolation]], use the increasing reindexing $z_k=x_{N-k}$, $k=0,\ldots,N$. For descending-grid data $U_j$, the corresponding increasing data are $Y_k=U_{N-k}$.

For nodal data $U_0,\ldots,U_N$, define $I_N^LU$ to be the cardinal interpolant of $(Y_k)_{k=0}^N$ at $(z_k)_{k=0}^N$. For a function $f$ defined on the interval, write $I_N^Lf$ for the interpolant of its nodal values. The increasing-node interpolation theorem [[thm-cardinal-polynomial-interpolant-exists-uniquely]] makes this polynomial unique.

For all real $u,v$,
$$\sin(u-v)=\sin u\cos v-\cos u\sin v,\qquad \cos(u-v)=\cos u\cos v+\sin u\sin v.$$ The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-sine-and-cosine-addition-formulas]], [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y,$$
$$\cos(x+y)=\cos x\cos y-\sin x\sin y.$$

For $0\leq u\leq\pi/2$,
$$\sin u\geq \frac{2u}{\pi}.$$
For all real $u,v$,
$$|\sin u-\sin v|\leq |u-v|.$$

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Let $F$ be an ordered field, with field structure as in [[def-field]], and for
$n \ge 1$ let $n \cdot 1_F$ denote the canonical natural number
$\underbrace{1_F + \cdots + 1_F}_{n}$, defined recursively by $1 \cdot 1_F = 1_F$
and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F = n \cdot 1_F + 1_F$. Then for every $n \ge 1$:

- $n \cdot 1_F > 0$ and $(n+1) \cdot 1_F > n \cdot 1_F$;
- the map $n \mapsto n \cdot 1_F$ is strictly increasing, hence injective, on $\{1, 2, 3, \dots\}$;
- $(m+n) \cdot 1_F = m \cdot 1_F + n \cdot 1_F$ and $(mn) \cdot 1_F = (m \cdot 1_F)(n \cdot 1_F)$ for all $m, n \ge 1$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

Let $(x_k)$ and $(y_k)$ be sequences of reals ([[def-sequence]]) converging to
$x$ and $y$ respectively ([[def-real-limit]]), and let $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Then

$$x_k + y_k \to x + y, \qquad c\,x_k \to c\,x, \qquad x_k - y_k \to x - y, \qquad x_k y_k \to x y,$$

and if in addition $y \ne 0$ and $y_k \ne 0$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, then

$$\frac{1}{y_k} \to \frac{1}{y} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \frac{x_k}{y_k} \to \frac{x}{y}.$$

The quotient case rests on an eventual lower bound for $|y_k|$, proved below
rather than assumed: $|y_k| > |y|/2$ for all sufficiently large $k$.

derivations.claim: The subtraction and addition identities [F2] give $x_j-x_{j+1}=2\sin\left(\frac{(2j+1)\pi}{2N}\right)\sin\left(\frac\pi{2N}\right),\qquad x_0-x_1=2\sin^2\left(\frac\pi{2N}\right).$ By [F3], $\sin(\pi/(2N))\le\pi/(2N)$, hence $x_0-x_1\le\pi^2/(2N^2)$.

If $N$ is odd, choose $j=(N-1)/2$; then $(2j+1)\pi/(2N)=\pi/2$ and [F4] gives sine equal to $1$, so the gap formula in step 1.1 and [F3] give a central gap at least $2/N\ge\sqrt2/N$. If $N$ is even, choose $j=N/2-1$ and write $t=\pi/2-\pi/(2N)\ge\pi/4$. The addition and subtraction formulas [F2] give $\sin(\pi/4)=\cos(\pi/4)$ and $2\sin(\pi/4)\cos(\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/2)=1$. Thus $\sin^2(\pi/4)=1/2$; the chord bound [F3] gives $\sin(\pi/4)\ge1/2>0$, so uniqueness of the nonnegative square root [F5] gives $\sin(\pi/4)=\sqrt2/2$. Monotonicity [F4] now gives $\sin t\ge\sqrt2/2$. In either parity, [F3] also gives $\sin(\pi/(2N))\ge1/N$, so the selected central gap in step 1.1 is at least $\sqrt2/N$.

Put $a=\pi/(2N)$. Every adjacent gap has the form $2\sin((2j+1)a)\sin a$, with $a\le(2j+1)a\le\pi-a$. Reflecting about $\pi/2$ and using monotonicity [F4] gives $\sin((2j+1)a)\ge\sin a$; equality occurs at $j=0$ and $j=N-1$. Hence the smallest spacing is exactly $2\sin^2a$, and [F3] bounds it by $2/N^2\le2\sin^2a\le\pi^2/(2N^2)$. For every $\varepsilon>0$, [F6] supplies an integer $n\ge1$ with $1/n<\varepsilon$; for every integer $N\ge\max\{2,n\}$, positivity and monotonicity of the canonical naturals and reciprocal order give $0<1/N\le1/n<\varepsilon$. Thus $1/N\to0$, and the endpoint-to-central-gap ratio is at most $\pi^2/(2N)$, which tends to zero by the fixed-multiple limit law in [F6]. For $N\ge3$, the selected central angle, reflected into $[0,\pi/2]$ if necessary, is strictly larger than $a$; strict monotonicity in [F4] makes its gap larger than the endpoint gap. For $N=2$, the nodes are $1,0,-1$ and both gaps equal $1$. This proves the quadratic endpoint scale with its stated nonuniformity exception.
