citations.quote:
Every $P\in\mathcal P_r$ belongs to the admissible density domain
$\mathcal D_r$.

Let $n\ge2$, $1\le r<n$, and use the real Hermitian matrix space $\mathbb H_n$
and projector set $\mathcal P_r$ of
[[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]]. Let $U\subseteq\mathbb H_n$ be open
and let $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ be a specified map. For a Hermitian matrix $H$,
write its eigenvalues with multiplicity in ascending order as
$$\lambda_1(H)\le\cdots\le\lambda_n(H).$$
Write $\sigma(H):=\{\lambda_j(H):1\le j\le n\}$ for its finite spectrum,
with multiplicity omitted in this set notation.
For any Hermitian $H$ with $\lambda_r(H)<\lambda_{r+1}(H)$, write $\Pi_r(H)$
for the orthogonal projector onto the sum of eigenspaces belonging to its $r$
lowest eigenvalues. At a point $X\in U$ where
$$\lambda_r(F(X))<\lambda_{r+1}(F(X)),$$
define $\Phi(X):=\Pi_r(F(X))$. The strict gap separates the occupied cluster
from the unoccupied cluster; eigenvalue multiplicities within either cluster
are allowed. The construction's well-definedness as a unique member of
$\mathcal P_r$ is proved in [[lem-gapped-projector-map-well-defined]].

A set $K\subseteq U$ has a **uniform occupied/unoccupied gap** $g>0$ when the
displayed gap is at least $g$ for every $X\in K$. A self-consistent fixed point
is a point $X_*$ with $\Phi(X_*)=X_*$. Its fixed-point residual is
$\rho(X):=\|X-\Phi(X)\|_F$ whenever $\Phi(X)$ is defined. The map is not
asserted to be contractive merely because its gap is positive.

For every $X\in U$ at which the response map of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] has a strict $r$th gap,
$\Phi(X)$ is a uniquely defined member of $\mathcal P_r$. Degeneracies among
the first $r$ eigenvalues or among the remaining eigenvalues do not affect it.

If $D\in\mathcal D_r$ and the gapped map $\Phi(D)$ of
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]] is defined, then for every
$\alpha\in[0,1]$,
$$D^+=(1-\alpha)D+\alpha\Phi(D)$$
belongs to $\mathcal D_r$. The conclusion does not assert $D^+\in\mathcal P_r$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $P_0$ is a Hermitian idempotent of trace $1$, so $P_0\in\mathcal P_1$ and $P_0\in\mathcal D_1$ by [F1]. The constant response matrix has eigenvalues $0<1$, so [F2] gives $\Phi(P_0)=P_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$.
Direct calculation gives $D=(1-\alpha)P_0+\alpha\Phi(P_0)=\tfrac12 I_2$. By [F3], $D\in\mathcal D_1$; explicitly it is Hermitian, satisfies $0\preceq D\preceq I_2$, and has trace $1$.
But $D^2=\tfrac14 I_2\ne D$, so $D$ is not idempotent and hence $D\notin\mathcal P_1$. This verifies that relaxed density iterates must not be silently identified with projectors.

Let $S=S^*\succ0$ be an $n\times n$ finite-basis overlap matrix and supply its
Cholesky factor $L$ with $S=LL^*$, $L$ invertible
([[def-cholesky-factorisation-with-positive-diagonal]],
[[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]]).
If $h_0=h_0^*$ is the coefficient-basis one-body matrix, set
$h=L^{-1}h_0L^{-*}$, where $L^{-*}=(L^*)^{-1}$; this is the Cholesky
whitening whose generalized Ritz quotient is preserved by
[[prop-positive-definite-overlap-whitening-preserves-generalized-ritz-pencil]].
For coefficient vectors use $y=L^*c$; the interaction map and chosen
exchange-correlation functional below are supplied in these orthonormal
coordinates. Fix $1\le r<n$ and the
projector domain $\mathcal P_r$ of [[def-rank-r-orthogonal-projector-domain]].

Supply a Hermitian matrix $h$, a real-linear self-adjoint map
$G:\mathbb H_n\to\mathbb H_n$ for the Frobenius inner product, and a real-valued
$C^2$ functional $E_{xc}$ on an open neighborhood of $\mathcal P_r$. Define
$$E(P):=\operatorname{tr}(hP)+\tfrac12\operatorname{tr}(P G(P))+E_{xc}(P),\qquad F(P):=h+G(P)+\nabla E_{xc}(P).$$
Here $F(P)$ is the Hermitian Frobenius-gradient formula justified by
[[prop-finite-projector-energy-reality-and-gradient]].

The finite-basis Hartree–Fock model is the special case $E_{xc}=0$ with a
supplied symmetry-compatible Coulomb/exchange tensor defining $G$. A
Kohn–Sham-like model supplies its density map and chosen differentiable
exchange-correlation functional. These are finite-dimensional mathematical
models; this definition makes no assertion that the selected functional is an
exact continuum physical energy.

Let $s\ge1$, let $R_1,\ldots,R_s$ be complex matrices of one fixed shape,
and let $C\ge1$. Define
$$\mathcal C_{s,C}:=\{c\in\mathbb R^s:\sum_{i=1}^s c_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^s|c_i|\le C\}$$
and $J(c):=\|\sum_{i=1}^s c_iR_i\|_F^2$. Then $J$ attains a minimum on
$\mathcal C_{s,C}$. Among all minimizers there is a unique vector of minimum
Euclidean norm. This rule defines the exact capped DIIS coefficient vector even
when the least-squares Gram matrix is singular.

Input: the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ with $P_k\in\mathcal P_r$ and
$F(P_k)$ Hermitian; up to $m-1$ earlier pairs $(P_i,F(P_i))$, in chronological
order, with $P_i\in\mathcal P_r$ and $F(P_i)$ Hermitian; memory cap $m\ge1$;
coefficient cap $C\ge1$; a constrained least-squares solver that either returns
a globally minimizing coefficient vector selected by minimum Euclidean norm
among all minimizers, with certificates for feasibility and optimality, or
reports failure; and a Hermitian eigensolver for mixed Fock matrices. The
eigensolver returns a certified ordered spectrum and, when the $r$th gap is
strict, its occupied projector, or reports failure. The procedure is one
proposal step:

1. Form each commutator residual $R_i=[F(P_i),P_i]:=F(P_i)P_i-P_iF(P_i)$ for the earlier pairs followed by the current pair. This gives at most $m$ residuals.
2. Call the constrained solver on these residuals with $c\in\mathbb R^s$, $\sum_i c_i=1$, and $\|c\|_1\le C$. If it reports failure, including a singular Gram-system failure, return $(P_k,\texttt{singular-or-uncertified-ls})$; the caller then performs the baseline SCF update. The returned vector must be the certified global minimizer with the minimum-norm tie-break guaranteed to exist by [[lem-capped-diis-coefficient-minimizer-exists]].
3. If the returned coefficients fail either constraint or their feasibility certificate, return $(P_k,\texttt{coefficient-cap-failure})$; the caller then performs the baseline update. Otherwise form $F_{mix}=\sum_i c_iF(P_i)$ and call the eigensolver on it. If the eigensolver fails or does not certify a strict $r$th gap, return $(P_k,\texttt{candidate-gap-failure})$; the caller then performs the baseline update.
4. If the eigensolver certifies a strict gap, return $(Y,\texttt{candidate})$, where $Y$ is its occupied projector $\Pi_r(F_{mix})$.

The commutator least-squares objective defines a proposal; it is not a fixed-point
error certificate. The outer safeguarded procedure checks $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$
separately before accepting a candidate. This algorithm makes no bare DIIS
convergence claim.

derivations.claim: The matrices $P_0,P_1,X$ are mutually Frobenius-orthogonal and $\|P_0\|_F^2=\|P_1\|_F^2=1$. Put $\Delta=P_0-P_1$, so the displayed map is $G(A)=\langle A,\Delta\rangle_F X+\langle A,X\rangle_F\Delta$. Since this is a real-linear map into the Hermitian span of $X,\Delta$, symmetry of the Frobenius inner product gives $\langle G(A),B\rangle_F=\langle A,\Delta\rangle_F\langle X,B\rangle_F+\langle A,X\rangle_F\langle\Delta,B\rangle_F=\langle A,G(B)\rangle_F$ for Hermitian $A,B$. Thus the model data satisfy [F1].

Substitution gives $G(P_0)=X$ and $G(P_1)=-X$. The matrices $X$ and $-X$ have eigenvalues $-1,1$, so both iterates have gap $2$. Direct multiplication gives $[G(P_0),P_0]=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}=[G(P_1),P_1]\ne0.$

Writing the common residual as $J$, the Gram matrix is $B_{ij}=\langle J,J\rangle_F=2,\qquad B=\begin{pmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{pmatrix},$ which is singular. The equality-constrained bordered system has matrix $\begin{pmatrix}2&2&1\\2&2&1\\1&1&0\end{pmatrix}$, whose first two rows coincide, so a solver that reports singularity takes the prescribed fallback. With $C=2$, $c=(1/2,1/2)$ is feasible and minimizes the objective; the objective is constant on $c_1+c_2=1$, so [F2] selects this unique minimum-norm minimizer. If a rank-revealing solver returns it instead of reporting singularity, then $F_{mix}=\tfrac12X-\tfrac12X=0$ has no strict gap, and the proposal algorithm again falls back by its candidate-gap branch. Thus either outcome of this configured solve uses the baseline.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space and let $\Phi:K\to K$ be a
contraction with constant $0\le q<1$. In the SCF application, $K$ is a
complete invariant subset of the response-map domain from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], with $d(X,Y)=\|X-Y\|_F$.
Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $X_*$ and exact iterates
$X_{k+1}=\Phi(X_k)$ satisfy
$$d(X_k,X_*)\le q^k d(X_0,X_*).$$
For every $X\in K$,
$$d(X,X_*)\le\frac{d(X,\Phi(X))}{1-q}.$$
If computed updates $X_{k+1}\in K$ obey
$d(X_{k+1},\Phi(X_k))\le\eta_k$, then
$$e_{k+1}\le q e_k+\eta_k,\qquad e_k\le q^k e_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^{k-1-j}\eta_j,$$
where $e_k=d(X_k,X_*)$ and $X_0$ is the supplied initial point.
Use the convention $q^0=1$, including when $q=0$.

citations.quote:
Input: $n,r$, a response matrix map $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$ and its occupied
projector map $\Phi$ from [[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], an
invariant set $K\subseteq U$, an initial projector $P_0\in K\cap\mathcal P_r$,
a required gap $g_{min}>0$, residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$, update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, and a Hermitian eigensolver. On each input $F(P_k)$ the
eigensolver must return either a certified ascending eigenvalue list and, when
the gap is strict, the corresponding occupied projector $\Phi(P_k)$, or a
failure to certify the spectrum; assume $\Phi(P)\in K$ whenever $P\in K$ and
its gap is at least $g_{min}$. Use the Frobenius metric and the fixed-point interface of
[[alg-fixed-point-iteration]].

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Call the eigensolver on $F(P_k)$. If it fails to certify the ordered spectrum, return $(P_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},\varnothing,k)$. If the certified gap satisfies $\lambda_{r+1}(F(P_k))-\lambda_r(F(P_k))<g_{min}$, return $(P_k,\texttt{gap-loss},\varnothing,k)$.
2. Set $P_{k+1}^{raw}$ to the returned occupied projector $\Phi(P_k)$ and compute $\rho_k=\|P_k-P_{k+1}^{raw}\|_F$. If $\rho_k\le\varepsilon$, return $(P_k,\texttt{residual-tolerance-met},\rho_k,k)$.
3. If $k=N$, return $(P_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},\rho_k,k)$. Otherwise set $P_{k+1}=P_{k+1}^{raw}\in K$ and continue.

It reports a residual stopping status, gap loss, eigensolver failure, or budget
exhaustion separately. A finite budget
does not guarantee that the residual tolerance will be met, and the definition
asserts no convergence from damping or from a positive gap alone.

Input: $D_0\in\mathcal D_r$ from
[[def-admissible-hermitian-density-domain]], a response map $\Phi$ defined at
each required iterate and its Hermitian matrix map $F$ from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]], a Hermitian eigensolver that
for each $F(D_k)$ returns a certified ordered spectrum and occupied projector
when the gap is strict, a certified no-gap result, or a failure status, a fixed
mixing parameter $\alpha\in[0,1]$, a fixed-point residual tolerance
$\varepsilon\ge0$, and a finite update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$. For
$k=0,\ldots,N$, first call the eigensolver on $F(D_k)$. If it fails, return
$(D_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},\varnothing,k)$; if the gap is absent, return
$(D_k,\texttt{gap-loss},\varnothing,k)$. Otherwise use the returned occupied
projector as $\Phi(D_k)$ and compute
$$r_k=\|D_k-((1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k))\|_F.$$
If $r_k\le\varepsilon$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{residual-tolerance-met},r_k,k)$. If $k=N$, return
$(D_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},r_k,k)$. Otherwise update
$$D_{k+1}=(1-\alpha)D_k+\alpha\Phi(D_k)$$
and continue.

By [[lem-density-mixing-preserves-domain-but-not-projectors]], each successful
update stays in $\mathcal D_r$; it need not be idempotent. This algorithm uses
the residual and finite-budget update pattern of [[alg-fixed-point-iteration]]
for the relaxed map, with a gap check before each response evaluation. It makes
no convergence claim unless the derivative-bound and invariance
hypotheses in [[thm-density-mixing-contracts-under-jacobian-certificate]] are
verified. If $\alpha=0$, then the relaxed residual is identically zero and the
update does not move; that stop status alone says nothing about the unmixed
response residual.

Input: an open domain $U$, a Hermitian response matrix map $F:U\to\mathbb H_n$,
and its gapped occupied-projector map $\Phi$ from
[[def-self-consistent-projector-response-map]]; a nonempty complete invariant
set $K\subseteq U\cap\mathcal P_r$ with $\Phi(K)\subseteq K$ and certified
contraction factor $0\le q<1$; an initial projector $P_0\in K$; a certified
initial error bound $E_0\ge\|P_0-P_*\|_F$ for the unique fixed point $P_*$;
residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$; finite update budget $N\in\mathbb N_0$;
memory $m\ge1$; coefficient cap $C\ge1$; a Hermitian eigensolver that, for a
matrix $M$, returns a certified ordered spectrum and occupied projector when
the $r$th gap is strict, a certified no-gap result, or a failure to certify the
spectrum; an approximate response evaluator that at $X\in K$ returns
$\widetilde\Phi(X)\in K$ and $\eta(X)\ge0$ with
$\|\widetilde\Phi(X)-\Phi(X)\|_F\le\eta(X)$, or a failure status; and a
constrained least-squares solver that either returns the certified global
minimizer with the minimum-norm tie-break for the residuals and cap $C$, or
reports failure. Every called solver returns one of its specified results.

The terminal output is $(P_k,\texttt{status},b,k)$, where $P_k$ is the current
projector and $b$ is its certified error bound. The current budget $E_k$
remains valid at gap, eigensolver, or invariance-certificate failure statuses.

For $k=0,\ldots,N$:

1. If no certified response evaluation is cached for $P_k$, compute $F(P_k)$ and call the eigensolver on it. If the eigensolver certifies no strict gap, return $(P_k,\texttt{gap-loss},E_k,k)$; if it fails to certify the spectrum, return $(P_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},E_k,k)$. With a certified strict gap, call the approximate response evaluator. If it fails, return $(P_k,\texttt{eigensolve-failure},E_k,k)$. Cache $(F(P_k),\widetilde\Phi(P_k),\eta(P_k))$ at exactly $P_k$. Whether this evaluation is new or cached, check that the certified baseline output belongs to $K$; if not, return $(P_k,\texttt{invariance-certificate-failure},E_k,k)$. Retain the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ for this proposal step. Set $\bar\rho_k=\|P_k-\widetilde\Phi(P_k)\|_F+\eta(P_k)$. If $\bar\rho_k\le\varepsilon$, return $(P_k,\texttt{residual-tolerance-met},\bar\rho_k/(1-q),k)$.
2. If $k=N$, return $(P_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted},E_k,k)$.
3. Call [[alg-capped-diis-projector-proposal]] with the up-to-$m-1$ preceding stored pairs, the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$, the constrained least-squares solver, the eigensolver, $m$, and $C$. For a candidate $Y$, certify $Y\in K$, compute $F(Y)$, certify its strict gap with the eigensolver, and obtain one approximate response evaluation $\widetilde\Phi(Y)$ with error $\eta(Y)$. Accept $Y$ only if all certificates succeed and
$$\frac{\|Y-\widetilde\Phi(Y)\|_F+\eta(Y)}{1-q}\le qE_k.$$
If accepted, set $P_{k+1}=Y$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k$.
4. If step 3 does not accept a candidate for any reason, use the certified baseline evaluation already obtained and checked in step 1. In particular, this includes a least-squares failure, coefficient-cap or affine-constraint failure, failed candidate $K$-membership, failed candidate gap, failed candidate response-error certificate, or failed candidate fixed-point residual test. Set $P_{k+1}=\widetilde\Phi(P_k)$ and $E_{k+1}=qE_k+\eta(P_k)$.
5. Append the current pair $(P_k,F(P_k))$ to the preceding-iterate history, retaining at most the newest $m-1$ preceding pairs. If step 3 accepted $Y$, cache its certified evaluation $(F(Y),\widetilde\Phi(Y),\eta(Y))$ as the next iteration's current evaluation; if the baseline branch was used, evaluate its new iterate when the next loop begins. Never attach a response matrix evaluated at one density to a different density.

The DIIS commutator objective is only a proposal score. Acceptance uses the
separate fixed-point residual $\|Y-\Phi(Y)\|_F$ with its additive eigensolver
error certificate. The algorithm makes no unconditional success claim: finite
budget exhaustion and each certificate failure are explicit outcomes.

derivations.claim: At the initial entered index $0$, no update has occurred. Each baseline procedure permits at most one residual test after its spectrum and gap checks; the certified DIIS procedure permits one current residual test and, only if $0<N$, at most one candidate residual test.

Before an entered index $k\le N$, its preceding entered indices are exactly $0,\ldots,k-1$, with at most $k$ preceding updates, at most $k$ residual tests for either baseline procedure, and at most $2k$ residual tests for the certified DIIS procedure.

A baseline pass permits at most one residual test; a certified DIIS pass permits at most two, for its current point and a candidate. A continuing pass requires $k<N$ and makes at most one update before entering $k+1$. Thus the preceding counts increase by at most one update and, respectively, one or two residual tests, proving step 1.2 at the next index. Any earlier gap, eigensolver, invariance, residual or budget return creates no further pass.

The base and induction step show that entered indices form an initial segment of $0,\ldots,N$, with at most $N+1$ residual tests for either baseline procedure and at most $2N+1$ for certified DIIS, since index $N$ checks the current response and returns before a candidate attempt or update. All three make at most $N$ updates. Every entered pass has finitely many returning primitives, so each procedure terminates with a stated status, including when $N=0$. These are only outer-work and status bounds.

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(\exp(-k^2t)u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<\exp(-k^2t)\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

Throughout, $\mathbb F$ is $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and families are indexed by
an arbitrary set $I$, with no enumeration or countability assumed. Finite real lists use [[def-finite-sum]], and sums over finite subsets use [[def-finite-sum-in-a-commutative-monoid]] in the additive monoid of the scalar field. Disjoint splitting is [[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]], and scalar modulus estimates use [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]; all suprema and infima of real sets below are
taken in the complete ordered field $\mathbb R$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) or in $[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-reals]], [[lem-extended-reals-complete]]).

**Sums of nonnegative families.** Let $(c_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of
nonnegative reals and let $\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ be the set of finite subsets of
$I$, ordered by inclusion. Define

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i:=\sup\Bigl\{\sum_{i\in F}c_i \;:\; F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)\Bigr\}\in[0,+\infty] .$$

The set of finite subsums is nonempty, since $\varnothing$ contributes the empty
sum $0$, so the supremum exists in $[0,+\infty]$; it is a real number exactly
when the finite subsums are bounded above in $\mathbb R$, and $+\infty$
otherwise. For finite $I$ the finite subsum at $I$ is the largest of all finite
subsums, because all terms are nonnegative, so the definition agrees with the
finite sum; in particular $\sum_{i\in I}c_i=0$ when every $c_i$ is $0$, and
$I=\varnothing$ gives the empty sum $0$.

**Splitting identity and small tails.** Fix a finite $F\subseteq I$. Every
finite $G\subseteq I$ splits as the disjoint union $(G\cap F)\cup(G\setminus F)$,
so $\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in G\cap F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i\le\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i$;
conversely the finite $G$ with $F\subseteq G$ satisfy
$\sum_{i\in G}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in G\setminus F}c_i$. Taking suprema,
with the constant $\sum_{i\in F}c_i$ passing through the supremum,

$$\sum_{i\in I}c_i=\sum_{i\in F}c_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i . \qquad (1)$$

Consequently, if $S:=\sum_{i\in I}c_i$ is finite, then for every real
$\varepsilon>0$ there is a finite $F\subseteq I$ with
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i<\varepsilon$: the finite subsums form a nonempty
bounded-above set with supremum $S$, so by the epsilon characterisation of the
supremum ([[lem-sup-epsilon]]) some finite $F$ has
$S-\varepsilon<\sum_{i\in F}c_i$, and (1) gives
$\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}c_i=S-\sum_{i\in F}c_i<\varepsilon$. Such an $F$ is
called a **tail-control set** for $\varepsilon$.

**Sums of scalar families.** Now let $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family in $\mathbb F$
and put $s_F:=\sum_{i\in F}a_i$ for finite $F\subseteq I$. The set
$\operatorname{Fin}(I)$ with inclusion is a directed preorder: it is nonempty and
$F\cup G$ is a common upper bound of $F$ and $G$
([[def-directed-set-and-net]]). Hence $(s_F)_{F\in\operatorname{Fin}(I)}$ is a
net in $\mathbb F$, the **finite-subset net** of the family, and the family is
**summable** when this net converges
([[def-net-convergence-and-cluster-point]]). The scalar metric is the usual real metric or [[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]. These metric spaces are Hausdorff by [[thm-metric-hausdorff-separation]]. A net in $\mathbb F$ has at most one limit
([[thm-hausdorff-iff-net-limits-are-unique]]), so for a summable family the
limit is unique and we write $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\lim_F s_F$ for it. The family is
**absolutely summable** when $\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|<+\infty$ in the sense above.

**Every absolutely summable family is summable, in ZF.** Assume
$S:=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|$ is finite and put $S_F:=\sum_{i\in F}|a_i|$ for finite
$F$. For finite $F,G\subseteq I$ the triangle inequality for finite sums and the
fact that a finite subsum is at most the whole nonnegative sum give

$$|s_F-s_G|\le\sum_{i\in F\triangle G}|a_i|\le S-S_{F\cap G} . \qquad (2)$$

Now fix a real $\varepsilon>0$, let $F_0$ be a tail-control set for
$\varepsilon$, and let $F,G\supseteq F_0$ be finite. Then $F\cap G\supseteq F_0$,
so $S-S_{F\cap G}\le S-S_{F_0}<\varepsilon$ and (2) gives
$|s_F-s_G|<\varepsilon$.

First suppose $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. For each finite $F$ define
$A_F:=\inf\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ and $B_F:=\sup\{s_G : G\supseteq F\}$ over
finite $G$. Both are real numbers, because $|s_G|\le S_G\le S$, so the two sets
are nonempty and bounded, and $A_F\le B_F$. If $H\supseteq F$ then
$A_H\ge A_F$ and $B_H\le B_F$. Let $L:=\sup_FA_F$ and $U:=\inf_FB_F$.
Since $A_F\le s_{F\cup H}\le B_H$ for all finite $F,H$, we get $L\le U$.
Moreover, the preceding estimate holds for every pair $F,G\supseteq F_0$;
taking the supremum over $F$ and the infimum over $G$ gives
$B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$. Hence
$0\le U-L\le B_{F_0}-A_{F_0}\le\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon>0$, so
$L=U=:s$. If $F\supseteq F_0$, then both $s_F$ and $s$ lie in
$[A_{F_0},B_{F_0}]$, and therefore $|s_F-s|\le\varepsilon$.

If $\mathbb F=\mathbb C$, apply the real argument just proved to the families
$(\operatorname{Re}a_i)$ and $(\operatorname{Im}a_i)$. They are absolutely
summable because $|\operatorname{Re}a_i|,|\operatorname{Im}a_i|\le|a_i|$.
Their finite-subset nets converge to real numbers $r$ and $t$, respectively,
so $s_F\to r+it$ in $\mathbb C$. Thus every absolutely summable real or complex
family is summable. **No choice principle is used**: the construction uses only
two-sided suprema in $\mathbb R$.

**Linearity and absolute value.** If $(a_i)$ and $(b_i)$ are absolutely
summable and $\lambda\in\mathbb F$, then so are $(a_i+b_i)$ and
$(\lambda a_i)$, and

$$\sum_{i\in I}(a_i+b_i)=\sum_{i\in I}a_i+\sum_{i\in I}b_i,\qquad \sum_{i\in I}\lambda a_i=\lambda\sum_{i\in I}a_i,\qquad \Bigl|\sum_{i\in I}a_i\Bigr|\le\sum_{i\in I}|a_i| ,$$

because the corresponding identities hold for every finite subsum, both sides
are limits of the corresponding finite-subset nets, and addition, scalar
multiplication and the modulus are continuous. The splitting identity (1)
likewise passes to absolutely summable scalar families:
$\sum_{i\in I}a_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i+\sum_{i\in I\setminus F}a_i$ for every finite
$F$, because finite subsums over sets containing $F$ converge to the left-hand
side and equal the finite sum over $F$ plus the finite subsum of the tail, whose
net converges to the tail sum.

**The finite-dimensional Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.** Let $(u_k)_{0\le k<m}$ and $(v_k)_{0\le k<m}$ be scalar lists, for $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $t\in\mathbb R$. Every term of
$\sum_{k<m}(|u_k|-t|v_k|)^2$ is nonnegative, so for all real $t$

$$0\le\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2-2t\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|+t^2\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2 .$$

If $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2>0$, substituting
$t=\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)/\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$ gives
$\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\bigr)^2\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)$;
if $\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2=0$ then every $v_k=0$ and both sides are $0$. In either case
$\sum_{k<m}|u_k||v_k|\le\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}\bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\bigr)^{1/2}$
after taking square roots, and applying the modulus inequality for finite sums
to $u_k\overline{v_k}$ also gives

$$\Bigl|\sum_{k<m}u_k\overline{v_k}\Bigr|\le\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|u_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\Bigl(\sum_{k<m}|v_k|^2\Bigr)^{1/2} . \qquad (3)$$

**The space $\ell^2(I)$.** For a family $a=(a_i)_{i\in I}$ in $\mathbb F$ define
$Q(a):=\sum_{i\in I}|a_i|^2$. If $Q(a)$ is finite, set $\|a\|_2:=\sqrt{Q(a)}$, using the nonnegative real square root of [[thm-of-square-roots]]; if $Q(a)=+\infty$, set $\|a\|_2:=+\infty$. This is a case definition, not exponentiation of an extended real. Let

$$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F):=\{\,a=(a_i)_{i\in I} : \|a\|_2<+\infty\,\}.$$

The set $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is a vector space over $\mathbb F$: it contains the
zero family, is closed under scalar multiplication because
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$, and is closed under addition because (3)
applied to finite subsums gives $\|a+b\|_2\le\|a\|_2+\|b\|_2<+\infty$. The same
inequality is the triangle inequality for $\|\cdot\|_2$, which is moreover
nonnegative, vanishes only for the zero family (an arbitrary sum of nonnegative
terms with supremum $0$ has every term $0$) and satisfies
$\|\lambda a\|_2=|\lambda|\,\|a\|_2$; thus $\|\cdot\|_2$ is a norm on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$. Finally the **pairing**
$\langle a,b\rangle:=\sum_{i\in I}a_i\overline{b_i}$ is well defined on
$\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)\times\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$, because
$|a_i\overline{b_i}|=|a_i||b_i|$ has finite nonnegative sum by (3); it is linear
in the first variable, conjugate symmetric, positive definite, and satisfies
$\langle a,a\rangle=\|a\|_2^2$, all by the corresponding finite identities and
the linearity of the sum. Consequently $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is an inner-product
space, and $e_i\in\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ denotes the family that is $1$ at $i$ and
$0$ elsewhere. **Nothing here asserts that $\ell^2(I,\mathbb F)$ is complete**;
that follows later, from an orthonormal basis of a Hilbert space.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim: Coordinatewise, [F2] gives $\exp(-k^2(t+s))=\exp(-k^2t)\exp(-k^2s)$ and $E_0u=u$, so $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$. If $t\ge0$, [F3] gives $0<\exp(-k^2t)\le1$; hence $\sum_k|(E_tu)_k|^2\le\sum_k|u_k|^2$, proving that $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself and is a contraction.

At $x=0$ the bound $0\le1-\exp(-x)\le x$ is equality; for $x>0$, [F4] applied to $s\mapsto\exp(-s)$ on $[0,x]$ gives $1-\exp(-x)=x\exp(-\xi)$ for some $\xi\in(0,x)$, and [F3] bounds $\exp(-\xi)$ by $1$. Thus the bound holds for all $x\ge0$. For $u\in D(A)$, the $k$th coordinate of $(E_tu-u)/t$ tends to $-k^2u_k$ by the chain rule and exponential derivative in [F4]. Its difference from that limit has absolute value at most $2k^2|u_k|$, by the same bound. The squared tail of these differences is therefore at most $4\sum_{k>K}k^4|u_k|^2$, which tends to zero; on every finite head the coordinate limits give norm convergence. Hence the right limit exists in $\mathcal H$ and equals $Au$.

Fix $u\in\mathcal H$ and $\varepsilon>0$. By convergence of its square sum, choose $K$ so that $\sum_{k>K}|u_k|^2<\varepsilon^2/4$. The squared norm of the tail of $E_tu-u$ is at most this tail because $|\exp(-k^2t)-1|\le1$ by [F3]; for the finitely many indices $k\le K$, continuity of the exponential at zero from [F4] makes their squared sum less than $\varepsilon^2/4$ for all sufficiently small $t>0$. Thus $\|E_tu-u\|_2<\varepsilon$, proving strong continuity at zero.

Conversely, suppose $(E_tu-u)/t$ converges in $\mathcal H$ to $v$. For each $k$, coordinate evaluation is continuous since $|w_k|\le\|w\|_2$; therefore its limit is $v_k=-k^2u_k$, using [F4]. Since $v\in\mathcal H$, $\sum_k k^4|u_k|^2=\sum_k|v_k|^2<\infty$, so $u\in D(A)$. Together with step 1.2 this identifies the generator domain and its value.

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]).

$(X,d)$ is **complete** if every Cauchy sequence in $(X,d)$
([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]) converges to a point of $X$
([[def-metric-convergence]]).

A subset $A \subseteq X$ is called **complete** when the metric subspace
$(A, d_A)$ is complete ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); as always, the
metric is part of the data, and $d_A$ is the restriction of $d$ to $A \times A$.

**The limit is unique when it exists**, since limits in a metric space are unique
([[lem-metric-limits-unique]]), so a complete space assigns to each of its Cauchy
sequences one point and not a set of points.

**Completeness is a property of the pair $(X,d)$, not of $X$ and not of the
topology of $d$.** Both quantifiers in the definition are about the metric: the
Cauchy condition is stated with distances, and so is convergence. Two metrics on
the same set can have the same open sets while exactly one of them is complete,
which is the content of [[fs-completeness-is-a-topological-property]] and its
witness. Read the word *complete* as an abbreviation for *complete with respect
to this metric*, always.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) constructed in this
library ([[def-real-numbers]]) and carrying its order ([[def-real-order]]).

Let $X$ be a set. A **metric** on $X$ is a function
$d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $x, y, z \in X$:

- **(M1) Separation.** $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
- **(M2) Symmetry.** $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$.
- **(M3) Triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le d(x,y) + d(y,z)$.

A **metric space** is a pair $(X,d)$ consisting of a set $X$ and a metric $d$ on
it. The elements of $X$ are its **points** and $d(x,y)$ is the **distance** from
$x$ to $y$. When only one metric is in play we write $X$ for $(X,d)$; when
several are, the metric is always named.

**The values of a metric are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$d(x,y)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and every
inequality above is an inequality there. No infinite value is permitted;
[[rem-metric-axiom-conventions]] records why extended metrics are not treated in
this library.

**Nonnegativity is deliberately absent from the axiom list.** Many texts add a
fourth axiom $d(x,y) \ge 0$. It is redundant: (M1), (M2) and (M3) already force
it, as [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]] proves. Nothing below assumes it before that
lemma is available.

**Pseudometric.** A **pseudometric** on $X$ is a function
$p : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying (M2), (M3) and the weakening

- **(M1') Reflexivity.** $p(x,x) = 0$ for every $x \in X$

of (M1). A pseudometric may therefore assign distance $0$ to two distinct
points. Every metric is a pseudometric, and a pseudometric is a metric exactly
when $p(x,y) = 0$ forces $x = y$.

**Ultrametric.** An **ultrametric** on $X$ is a metric $d$ that in addition
satisfies

- **(M3') Strong triangle inequality.** $d(x,z) \le \max\{d(x,y), d(y,z)\}$

for all $x, y, z \in X$, where the maximum is that of a two-element subset of
$\mathbb{R}$, which exists and is one of the two elements
([[def-max-min]], [[lem-finite-set-has-max]]). An **ultrametric space** is a pair
$(X,d)$ with $d$ an ultrametric.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function. Recall that a metric takes nonnegative real values
([[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]).

- $f$ is **Lipschitz** with **constant** $L$, where $L \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $L \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; L \, d_X(x,x') \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X .$$
  $f$ is *Lipschitz* if it is Lipschitz with some such constant.
- Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $0 < \alpha \le 1$ ([[def-rat-order]]). $f$ is
  **$\alpha$-Hölder** with **constant** $C$, where $C \in \mathbb{R}$ and
  $C \ge 0$, if
  $$d_Y\big(f(x), f(x')\big) \;\le\; C \, d_X(x,x')^{\alpha} \qquad \text{for all } x, x' \in X ,$$
  the power being the rational power of a nonnegative base
  ([[def-rational-power]]). $f$ is *$\alpha$-Hölder* if it is so with some such
  constant, and *Hölder* if it is $\alpha$-Hölder for some rational
  $\alpha \in (0,1]$.
- $f$ is a **contraction** with constant $q$ if it is Lipschitz with constant $q$
  and $0 \le q < 1$. The number $q$ is then called a **contraction constant** for
  $f$.

**The power $d_X(x,x')^{\alpha}$ is defined at every pair, including $x = x'$.**
The base $d_X(x,x')$ is a nonnegative real, and [[def-rational-power]] defines
$a^{\alpha}$ for every $a > 0$ and, by its supplementary clause, sets
$0^{\alpha} = 0$ for every rational $\alpha > 0$. Since $\alpha > 0$ is required
here, the displayed inequality at $x = x'$ reads $0 \le C \cdot 0$, which holds;
so no separate clause and no restriction to $x \ne x'$ is needed. Note that this
does not by itself explain the strict inequality $\alpha>0$: if one extended the
formula to $\alpha=0$ using the convention $0^0=1$ of [[def-integer-power]], the
equal-point inequality would still be the automatic $0\le C$. Globally, however,
that extension would reduce to the bounded-diameter condition
$d_Y(f(x),f(x'))\le C$, outside the standard Hölder range adopted here.

**Why the exponent is rational on this page and why it is at most $1$.** At this
point in the reading order only rational powers are available
([[def-rational-power]]), so $\alpha$ ranges over the rationals. The upper
bound $\alpha \le 1$ is the standard convention, and it is where the notion is
useful: the classical theory reserves the name for $\alpha \in (0,1]$, and
nothing in this library uses an exponent outside that range. No claim is made
here about what an exponent $\alpha > 1$ would do.

**Constants are not unique and are not part of the data.** If $f$ is Lipschitz
with constant $L$ it is Lipschitz with every constant $L' \ge L$, and likewise
for Hölder constants; the adjectives above are existential statements. A
*contraction*, by contrast, requires a constant strictly below $1$, and that is a
real restriction: exhibiting the constant is part of exhibiting a contraction, and
a map that shrinks every distance without admitting one uniform constant is not a
contraction here.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty complete metric space ([[def-complete-metric-space]])
and let $f : X \to X$ be a contraction with constant $q$, so
$d(f(u),f(v)) \le q\,d(u,v)$ for all $u,v \in X$ and $0 \le q < 1$
([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]). Then:

1. There is exactly one $x^{*} \in X$ with $f(x^{*}) = x^{*}$.
2. For every $x_0 \in X$ the sequence of **iterates**, defined by recursion
   ([[thm-recursion]]) by $x_{n+1} := f(x_n)$, converges to $x^{*}$ in $(X,d)$
   ([[def-metric-convergence]]). In particular the limit does not depend on
   $x_0$.
3. For all $m, n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge n$,
   $$d(x_m, x_n) \;\le\; \frac{q^{\,n}\, d(x_1,x_0)}{1-q},$$
   with the integer power of [[def-integer-power]].

Claim 3 is the quantitative form of the argument that proves claims 1 and 2, and
it is recorded in the statement because the error estimates
([[cor-banach-error-estimates]]) are read off from it.

derivations.claim: The ball is nonempty because it contains $c$. If $(z_n)$ is Cauchy in the ball, it is Cauchy in $\mathbb R^d$, so [F2] gives a limit $z\in\mathbb R^d$. By [F4], $\|z-c\|_2\le\|z-z_n\|_2+\|z_n-c\|_2\le\|z-z_n\|_2+R$; letting $n\to\infty$ gives $\|z-c\|_2\le R$, so $z$ remains in the ball. Thus the ball is a nonempty complete metric space by [F3].

Define $T(z):=c+h b(z)$. For every $z$ in the ball, $\|T(z)-c\|_2=h\|b(z)\|_2\le hM\le R$, so $T$ maps the ball into itself; for $z,w$ in the ball, $\|T(z)-T(w)\|_2\le hL\|z-w\|_2$, and $hL<1$ makes $T$ a contraction as in [F5].
Applying [F6] to the complete ball and the contraction from step 1.2 gives a unique fixed point $Y$, which is exactly the unique solution of $Y=c+hb(Y)$ in the ball.

For any $\widetilde Y$ in the ball, [F4] and step 2.1 give $\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-T(\widetilde Y)\|_2+\|T(\widetilde Y)-T(Y)\|_2\le\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2+hL\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2$. Since $1-hL>0$, rearranging proves the residual bound.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
Let $k\ge2$. If $f\in C^k(U)$ for an open $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, then every iterated derivative of $f$ of order $k$ is unchanged by any permutation of its coordinate differentiations.

derivations.claim: For a $C^3$ field $c$ and a smooth scalar coordinate function $q(y)=y_j$, define $L_cq:=Dq\,c$. By [F2], differentiating $q(\Phi_c^t(y))$ successively in $t$ gives $L_cq$, $L_c^2q$, and $L_c^3q$, evaluated along the flow. Three uses of [F3] give the expansion through degree two with integral remainder $\frac12\int_0^h(h-s)^2(L_c^3q)(\Phi_c^s(y))\,ds$; [A1] bounds this remainder uniformly by $C h^3$ and continuity at $s=0$ gives cubic coefficient $\frac16L_c^3q(y)$ with pointwise remainder $o(h^3)$. The same reasoning applies successively to the finite flow compositions.

For a map $M$, define its pullback by $M^*q:=q\circ M$, and for a vector field $c$ put $L_cq:=Dq\,c$. Set $X=L_a$ and $Y=L_b$. The pullback of a composition reverses composition order, so [F1] and step 1.1 give, through degree two, $L_h^*q=q+h(X+Y)q+h^2\left(\frac12X^2+XY+\frac12Y^2\right)q+O(h^3).$ The exact total-flow pullback is $q+h(X+Y)q+\frac12h^2(X+Y)^2q+O(h^3)$. Subtracting leaves $\frac12h^2(XY-YX)q+O(h^3)$.

For any $C^2$ scalar $q$, the chain rule gives $[L_a,L_b]q=D^2q(a,b)+Dq\,Db\,a-D^2q(b,a)-Dq\,Da\,b=Dq\,(Db\,a-Da\,b),$ where [F4] cancels the Hessian terms. Thus $[X,Y]q=L_{[a,b]}q$. Applying this to each coordinate function in step 2.1 gives the stated Lie map expansion.

Pullback reversal and [F1] give $S_h^*=\Phi_a^{h/2*}\Phi_b^{h*}\Phi_a^{h/2*}$. Expanding its three factors by step 1.1 gives the cubic part $\frac16X^3+\frac16Y^3+\frac18X^2Y+\frac14XYX+\frac18YX^2+\frac14XY^2+\frac14Y^2X.$ Multiplying the three degree-three Taylor polynomials gives these coefficients: the $X^3$ term is $1/48+1/48+1/16+1/16=1/6$, and the $Y^3$ term is $1/6$. The mixed coefficients are $X^2Y:(1/8)(1)=1/8$, $XYX:(1/2)(1)(1/2)=1/4$, $YX^2:(1)(1/8)=1/8$, $XY^2:(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$, and $Y^2X:(1/2)(1/2)=1/4$; $YXY$ is absent because neither outer factor contains $Y$. The exact total-flow cubic part is $\frac16(X+Y)^3$, whose eight words each have coefficient $1/6$. Degrees zero through two agree, so subtraction gives $-\frac1{24}(X^2Y-2XYX+YX^2)-\frac1{12}(2YXY-Y^2X-XY^2)+o(h^3).$

Step 3.1 also applies with the second field equal to $[a,b]$, which is $C^2$ under the $C^3$ hypotheses. Hence $[X,[X,Y]]=L_{[a,[a,b]]}$ and $[Y,[X,Y]]=L_{[b,[a,b]]}$. Applying step 3.2 to each coordinate yields the stated Strang coefficient and pointwise $o(h^3)$ remainder. The uniform $O(h^3)$ defect follows already from the uniform degree-two remainder in step 1.1 and the equality of all coefficients through degree two.

Let $\mathcal H=\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, with square-summability as in [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Define the diagonal operator $A$ by
$$D(A)=\left\{u\in\mathcal H:\sum_{k\ge1} k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad (Au)_k=-k^2u_k.$$
Let $g\in\mathcal H$ be the fixed sequence $g_k=1/k$ for odd $k$ and $g_k=0$ for even $k$; membership follows from [[thm-p-series-real-exponents]] with exponent $2$. The split evolution is $u'=Au+g$. For $t\ge0$, define the exact diagonal subflow $E_tu=(\exp(-k^2t)u_k)_{k\ge1}$ and the exact translation subflow $B_tu=u+tg$. By [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]] and [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $0<\exp(-k^2t)\le1$, so each $E_t$ maps $\mathcal H$ to itself; each $B_t$ does so because $g\in\mathcal H$. The associated Strang modal step is
$$S_h=E_{h/2}\circ B_h\circ E_{h/2},\qquad h>0,$$
where the rightmost map is applied first. Each coordinate of $E_t$ solves $u_k'=-k^2u_k$, and each coordinate of $B_t$ solves $u_k'=g_k$. This is a precisely defined sequence-space model; it records one Dirichlet sine-mode boundary mismatch and makes no general convergence assertion for unbounded PDE operators.

Let $\mathcal H$, $A$, and $E_t$ be as in [[def-dirichlet-sine-mode-heat-splitting-model]]. The maps $E_t$ for $t\ge0$ satisfy $E_0=I$ and $E_{t+s}=E_tE_s$, are contractions in $\ell^2$, and are strongly continuous at $t=0$. Define the generator domain to consist of those $u\in\mathcal H$ for which the right limit
$$\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{E_tu-u}{t}$$
exists in $\mathcal H$. This domain is exactly $D(A)=\{u:\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|u_k|^2<\infty\}$, and the limit equals $Au=(-k^2u_k)_{k\ge1}$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin(x+\pi/2)=\cos x,\quad\cos(x+\pi/2)=-\sin x,\quad\sin(x+\pi)=-\sin x,\quad\cos(x+\pi)=-\cos x.$$
In particular,
$$\sin(\pi/2)=1,\quad\cos(\pi/2)=0,\quad\sin\pi=0,\quad\cos\pi=-1.$$

Let $\gamma$ be the unique smallest positive zero of cosine supplied by [[thm-cosine-has-a-smallest-positive-zero]]. Define
$$\pi:=2\gamma.$$

Thus $\pi>0$ and $\pi/2=\gamma$.

The squared coefficients sum to $\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^{-2}\le\sum_{k\ge1}k^{-2}<\infty$ by [F2], so $g\in\mathcal H$.
The generator-domain sum is $\sum_{k\ge1}k^4|g_k|^2=\sum_{j\ge0}(2j+1)^2$, whose partial sums are at least the number of terms and hence unbounded. Therefore $g\notin D(A)$ by [F1].

By [F6], the constant forcing $f=\pi/4$ is nonzero. By [F5], every sine mode $\sin(kx)$ vanishes at both $x=0$ and $x=\pi$. Hence the forcing is incompatible with the homogeneous Dirichlet endpoint values. This modal observation supplies no general PDE error theorem.

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

Let $d\ge1$, $c\in\mathbb R^d$, $R>0$, $h>0$, and let $b$ be defined on the closed Euclidean ball $\overline B(c,R)$. Suppose $\|b(z)\|_2\le M$ and $\|b(z)-b(w)\|_2\le L\|z-w\|_2$ there, with $hM\le R$ and $hL<1$. Then the IMEX Euler equation $Y=c+h b(Y)$ has exactly one solution in $\overline B(c,R)$. Every $\widetilde Y$ in that ball satisfies
$$\|\widetilde Y-Y\|_2\le\frac{\|\widetilde Y-c-hb(\widetilde Y)\|_2}{1-hL}.$$
In the algorithm [[alg-imex-euler-step]], $c=y+h a(y)$; this is a local branch result and gives no root outside the selected ball.

   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then

2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at

Let $m,d\ge1$, $h>0$, $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}$, and centers $c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m)\in(\mathbb R^d)^m$. On block vectors define

$$\|Y\|_{\infty,2}:=\max_{1\le i\le m}\|Y_i\|_2,\qquad \|A\|_\infty:=\max_i\sum_{j=1}^m|a_{ij}|.$$

Let $F:\mathcal B\to(\mathbb R^d)^m$, with components $F_i:\mathcal B\to\mathbb R^d$, be defined on the closed product ball $\mathcal B=\{Y:\|Y-c\|_{\infty,2}\le R\}$, where $R>0$. Suppose constants $M,L\ge0$ satisfy, for all $Y,Z\in\mathcal B$,

$$\|F(Y)\|_{\infty,2}\le M,\qquad \|F(Y)-F(Z)\|_{\infty,2}\le L\|Y-Z\|_{\infty,2},$$

and $h\|A\|_\infty M\le R$, $q:=h\|A\|_\infty L<1$. Define $\Phi(Y)=c+h(A\otimes I_d)F(Y)$ and $G(Y)=Y-\Phi(Y)$. Then $\Phi$ has a unique fixed point $Y^*\in\mathcal B$, equivalently $G(Y^*)=0$. Every approximate stage vector $\widetilde Y\in\mathcal B$ satisfies

$$\|\widetilde Y-Y^*\|_{\infty,2}\le\frac{\|G(\widetilde Y)\|_{\infty,2}}{1-q}.$$

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

$$x(t)=x_0+\int_{t_0}^{t}F(s,x(s))\,ds\qquad(t\in I).$$

The integral is oriented, so the assertion applies on either side of $t_0$.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. For the autonomous split problem $y'=a(y)+b(y)$ of [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], set
$$\gamma:=1-\frac1{\sqrt2},\qquad \delta:=-\frac1{\sqrt2}.$$
The explicit tableau and the lower-triangular implicit tableau, using the separate stage conventions of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] and [[def-implicit-runge-kutta-stage-equations]], are
$$\widetilde A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\\gamma&0&0\\\delta&1-\delta&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \widetilde b=(\delta,1-\delta,0),\quad \widetilde c=(0,\gamma,1),$$
$$A=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\0&\gamma&0\\0&1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix},\quad b=(0,1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(0,\gamma,1).$$
For a step $h>0$ from $y$, the method is defined by
$$Y_1=y,\qquad Y_2=y+\gamma h a(Y_1)+\gamma h b(Y_2),$$
$$Y_3=y+h\bigl[\delta a(Y_1)+(1-\delta)a(Y_2)\bigr]+h\bigl[(1-\gamma)b(Y_2)+\gamma b(Y_3)\bigr],\qquad y^+=Y_3.$$
Thus there are two implicit solves per step, one for each nonzero diagonal implicit stage. The unscaled stage-equation residual uses the update-residual convention of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. The tableaus and stages alone assert neither branch existence nor stability.

For $\gamma=1-1/\sqrt2$ and $\delta=-1/\sqrt2$ in [[def-ars222-additive-tableau-and-stages]], one has $\gamma>0$ and
$$\delta=1-\frac1{2\gamma},\qquad \gamma(1-\delta)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(2-\gamma)=\frac12,\qquad \gamma(1-\gamma-\delta)=\frac12-\gamma^2.$$

Form the polynomial ring $\mathbb R[x]$
([[def-polynomial-ring-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and define the **complex
numbers** by the quotient ring
$$\mathbb C:=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$$
([[def-quotient-ring]]). Write $a$ for the constant class $a+(x^2+1)$ and set
$$i:=x+(x^2+1).$$
Thus $i^2=-1$ in the quotient. The constant-class map
$\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is the specified real map; its injectivity and the
field structure are proved in [[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]], after which
$\mathbb C/\mathbb R$ is a field extension in the sense of
[[def-field-extension-generated-subfields-and-simple-extension]].

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

For the additive ODE partition [[def-additive-ode-and-partition]], take a current state $y\in U$, a step $h>0$, a closed ball $\overline B(c,R)\subset U$ centered at $c:=y+h a(y)$, bounds $M_b,L_b\ge0$ for $\|b\|_2$ and its Lipschitz constant on that ball, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$, and a solve routine that returns either a candidate $z\in\overline B(c,R)$ or a failure status. The procedure is:

1. If the solve routine is unavailable, return `solver-unavailable`.
2. If $hM_b>R$ or $hL_b\ge1$, return `branch-not-certified` without claiming a root.
3. Call the solve routine on $z=c+h b(z)$.
4. If it returns failure, return that failure status. If it returns $z\notin\overline B(c,R)$, return `out-of-branch-ball`.
5. Compute the update residual $r:=z-c-hb(z)$ in the state units of [[def-implicit-residual-and-algebraic-error-units]]. If $\|r\|_2>\tau$, return `residual-too-large` with $z$ and $r$; otherwise return `success` with $z$ and $r$.

When the routine returns an exact root, $r=0$ and $z$ is the IMEX Euler step $Y=y+h a(y)+h b(Y)$. A success status records only the requested residual check; the forward error conclusion is supplied separately by the residual theorem. This procedure uses one explicit evaluation of $a$ and one implicit solve.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: With $a(y)=-\kappa y$ and $b=0$, [F1] gives $Y=(1-h\kappa)y$, so after $N$ steps the numerical value is $(1-h\kappa)^N$. If $h\kappa>2$, then $1-h\kappa<-1$ and $|1-h\kappa|^N>1$ for every $N\ge1$. By [F2], $y(t)=\exp(-\kappa t)$ is the exact solution, and [F3] gives $|y(Nh)|=\exp(-\kappa Nh)<1$.

With $a=0$ and $b(y)=-\kappa y$, the equation in [F1] becomes $(1+h\kappa)Y=y$. Since $0<1<1+h\kappa$, [F4] gives $0<(1+h\kappa)^{-1}<1$. Thus the implicit treatment damps every such scalar step, while the explicit treatment grows whenever $h\kappa>2$.

At the boundary $h\kappa=2$, the explicit amplification is $-1$, whose magnitude is exactly one. Thus the strict instability condition is $h\kappa>2$; equality is neutral for this scalar test equation.

Let $a,b:U\to\mathbb R^d$ be $C^3$ fields on an open set, and restrict attention to points and time intervals for which the unique local solutions of $x'=a(x)$ and $x'=b(x)$ remain in $U$. Denote their exact solution maps by $\Phi_a^t$ and $\Phi_b^t$. The **Lie split map** applies $a$ and then $b$:
$$L_h:=\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^h.$$
The **Strang split map** applies half of $a$, then $b$, then half of $a$:
$$S_h:=\Phi_a^{h/2}\circ\Phi_b^h\circ\Phi_a^{h/2}.$$
Define the vector-field Lie bracket convention
$$[a,b](y):=Db(y)a(y)-Da(y)b(y).$$
This definition is finite-dimensional. It asserts neither that an unbounded operator has a common invariant domain nor that its commutators are bounded.

Let $a,b\in C^3(U,\mathbb R^d)$ on an open set and let $K_0\subset K\subset U$, where $K_0$ is compact and $K$ is compact and convex. Assume the exact $a$- and $b$-subflows, their Lie and Strang compositions, and the exact flow $\Phi_{a+b}^h$ from $K_0$ are defined and remain in $K$ for all sufficiently small $h>0$, and the fields and derivatives through order three are bounded on $K$. Uniformly for $y\in K_0$,
$$L_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=\frac{h^2}{2}[a,b](y)+O(h^3),$$
and the Strang expansion, pointwise in $y$, is
$$S_h(y)-\Phi_{a+b}^h(y)=-\frac{h^3}{24}[a,[a,b]](y)-\frac{h^3}{12}[b,[a,b]](y)+o(h^3).$$
The Strang defect is also uniformly $O(h^3)$ on $K_0$. The maps and bracket use [[def-exact-split-flows-lie-strang-and-bracket]]; the claim is finite-dimensional.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the linear fields have global exact flows. Direct multiplication gives $BA=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad AB=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad C:=BA-AB=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.$ By [F1], $[a,b](x)=Cx$.

Multiplying once more gives $CA-AC=\begin{pmatrix}0&-2\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\2&0\end{pmatrix}.$ These are the matrices of $[a,[a,b]]$ and $[b,[a,b]]$ under the same convention.
At $e_1$, $Ce_1=-e_1\ne0$, so [F2] gives Lie local defect $-\frac12h^2e_1+O(h^3)$, whose leading coefficient is nonzero. Thus its local error has exact order two.

The Strang leading matrix from step 2.1 is $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)=\begin{pmatrix}0&1/12\\-1/6&0\end{pmatrix}.$ It sends $e_1$ to $(0,-1/6)^T\ne0$, so [F2] gives a nonzero cubic leading local defect and exact local order three.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

derivations.claim: Let $H$ be any of $H_K$, $V$, or $H_K+V$. Its exact flow exists for all real time by [F7], and every solution obeys $\psi'=-iH\psi$. By [F3]–[F6], differentiating the real function $\psi^*\psi$ gives $\frac{d}{dt}(\psi^*\psi)=(\psi')^*\psi+\psi^*\psi'=i\psi^*H^*\psi-i\psi^*H\psi=0,$ where [A1] supplies $H^*=H$. Therefore [F6] makes $\|\psi(t)\|_2^2$ constant on every admitted interval, and each exact subflow and the total flow preserve norm.

Direct multiplication gives $C:=BA-AB=H_KV-VH_K=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\ne0.$ This is the linear matrix of $[a,b]$ by [F1]. Also $CA-AC=i\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad CB-BC=2i\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}.$
By [F1], a Lie or Strang step is a composition of exact component flows. Each factor preserves norm by step 1.1, so the composition preserves norm by repeated application of the same equality.

For $\psi=e_1$, the Lie coefficient $\frac12C\psi$ is nonzero. The Strang coefficient $-\frac1{24}(CA-AC)\psi-\frac1{12}(CB-BC)\psi$ is also nonzero, since its first coordinate is $-i/6$. Applying [F2] shows the exact subflows retain norm while the Lie and Strang maps have their respective nonzero local splitting defects.
